Why New Zealand needs an official Pie Trail – Glenn Dwight

New Zealand Herald August 08, 2026

Levain Bakery's bacon and egg pie was the supreme winner at this year's Bakels NZ Supreme Pie Awards.

The Bakels Supreme Pie Awards have just wrapped up.

It’s a fitting way to describe an event dedicated to food that’s literally wrapped in pastry.

And somewhere in New Zealand there’s now a baker who’s gone from being a local legend to a national one.

That honour belongs to Sean Vo and the team at Auckland’s Levain Bakery, whose bacon and egg pie was crowned this year’s supreme winner.

Give it a week and people across New Zealand will be claiming a direct link to this wizard of pastry.

“We used to play rugby together.”

“My cousin worked with his sister.”

“I’ve been eating his pies for years.”

It’s one of my favourite Kiwi traits.

We can find that one-degree of separation to just about anyone who’s had a bit of success.

And pie success? That’s worth signing up to Ancestry. com just to see if there’s a family link somewhere.

And maybe it’s that pie prestige that’s always made me think of the Pie Awards as New Zealand’s version of the Oscars.

For one night, the spotlight shines on the stars of the baking industry.

Bakers arrive trying not to look nervous, despite secretly having an acceptance speech tucked away just in case.

Friends and family gather hoping their local bakery gets a mention.

There are favourites, there are dark horses and, just like every great awards night, there are always a few surprises.

Somewhere in that room is a baker who’s spent years getting up at ridiculous o’clock every morning, obsessing over pastry, perfecting fillings and wondering if anyone notices the little things.

Then they hear their bakery called out ... and we discover this year’s Peter Jackson of pastry.

But unlike Hollywood, where the excitement fades almost as quickly as the after-party hangover, the Pie Awards are just the beginning.

The first bite at pie fame.

The winners are announced, social media fills with congratulations and pie pics, every town insists its local bakery was robbed, and before long someone says those nine dangerous words.

“Apparently the best pie in New Zealand is in ...”

That’s it.

The plans for your weekend have just changed.

Suddenly you’re heading off on a road trip because if a group of judges reckon a bakery in the middle of nowhere has produced the best pie in the country, then surely it’s worth finding out whether it’s really pastry perfection ... or whether Nana’s bacon and egg pie is still the undisputed champion.

And I love that about us.

We’ll happily take the long way home for a pie.

We’ll drive past three perfectly good bakeries because someone we trust reckons there’s a better one just up the road.

We’ll stand in a queue for 20 minutes, finally take that first bite, nod knowingly and say something completely ridiculous like, “The pastry’s excellent, but I reckon it could’ve handled another touch of pepper”.

For a few minutes we all become the pie version of wine critics.

But instead of discussing notes of blackcurrant and hints of oak, we’re analysing gravy consistency and whether the cheese has achieved the perfect level of melt.

Thankfully, nobody has to swirl a mouthful of mince around before spitting it into a silver tasting bucket.

This got me thinking.

France has wine trails.

Scotland has whisky trails.

America has Route 66.

Maybe we’ve been underselling one of New Zealand’s greatest tourism opportunities.

New Zealand should have a Pie Trail. (Working title. I’m open to suggestions.)

The funny thing is, I don’t think anyone would have to convince us.

We already do it.

Every Kiwi has that bakery they’d tell you to stop at.

Every family have a favourite pie that somehow tastes even better because you had to drive an extra half hour to get it.

All we’d really be doing is joining the dots.

But the idea can be bigger. I remember back in the 1990s every town seemed desperate to have a slogan.

Absolutely Positively Wellington.

Hamilton. More Than You Expect.

Somewhere, a creative wearing black-rimmed glasses still considers that the best day’s work of their career.

There were dozens of them.

It was all about local pride.

Maybe it’s time we reheated that local pride and wrapped it in pastry instead of words.

Every town has its own pie.

The Invercargill “Cheese Roll” Pie.

Everyone will be rolling into town for one.

The Hamilton “Fog” Pie.

Its contents would be a myst-ery, but you know there’s a splash of Waikato Draught in there.

The Auckland “Housing Market” Pie.

Packed with in-fill and the price has skyrocketed to $18 since you ordered it.

The Wellington “Bureaucrat” Pie.

Seventeen layers of pastry, very little meat, and you’ll need approval from three different departments before you can eat it.

And Central Otago would undoubtedly produce a slow-cooked lamb and pinot noir pie that costs more than you’d planned on spending but somehow still feels worth every dollar.

Before long, every road trip would become a quest worthy of Middle Earth.

Not for the One Ring ... but for the one pie to rule them all.

Motorhomes of tourists and motor home association members would crawl around the country like giant road slugs, ticking off pies instead of wineries.

Families would argue over which pie, I mean town, would be the next stop.

Which brings me to this.

Some young tech genius sitting in a co-working space somewhere, wearing a black T-shirt and building the next billion-dollar app, needs to forget dating apps for five minutes and invent Pie Maps.

It would become the Kiwi version of Google Maps.

“In 500 metres, continue straight for New Zealand’s best steak and cheese.”

And that is the end of the road for this article, so finally, congratulations to this year’s winners of the Bakels Supreme Pie Awards.

You’ve reminded us that the humble pie is more than something we grab on the way to work.

It’s part of every road trip, every smoko break and every small town worth pulling over for.

Kem Ormond’s vegetable garden: A beginner’s guide to moon planting

New Zealand Herald August 08, 2026

Gardening by the moon has been practised through the ages. Photo / 123rf

Have you ever wondered why some gardeners like to use a moon calendar to plant their crops?

I do not practise planting by the moon, because I have enough trouble keeping the everyday calendar on my phone sorted and I am pretty conventional when it comes to my planting.

I feel more connected to the warmth of the soil, the seasons, the climate in my area and the distribution of my extremely limited spare time.

The Maramataka is the traditional Māori lunar calendar, used as a guide to planting, harvesting, fishing and hunting.

It translates as “moon rotating”.

In years gone by, the consistent phases of the moon helped bring the seasons into order.

Maramataka helped Māori understand the environmental cues around them and take notice of the rhythms of nature.

Crops were planted and grown according to their season, and the new year traditionally began with the rising of the Matariki cluster of stars, recognising that the year’s cropping cycles had been completed.

With all crops harvested and stored, it meant it was now midwinter and a time to rest up and enjoy the fruits of their labours with festivals and celebrations.

Generally, a farewell to the old year was undertaken, as well as paying respects to those who had passed on.

This was followed by a welcome to the new season and those born since the last Matariki.

Gardening by the moon has been practised through the ages.

Many gardeners believe that seeds and plants grow more quickly during some parts of the month than others.

The reason is that the moon has a strong gravitational pull.

Some gardeners believe the moon’s gravitational pull, which influences ocean tides, may also affect soil moisture and plant growth.

During the new moon phase, moon gardeners believe there is a strong gravitational pull that increases the light.

Traditionally, this is regarded as a favourable time to plant green leafy crops.

During the first quarter, moonlight is stronger, although the gravitational pull becomes less.

This is the time when moon gardeners recommend planting most seedlings, especially crops with seeds inside.

As the moon moves past full moon and light begins to decrease, moon gardeners believe energy shifts towards root development.

Therefore, moon gardeners generally consider the full moon period a good time for planting root vegetables.

The last quarter brings decreased light and gravitational pull and is a time for rest.

Avoid sowing seeds but use the time to prune, transplant and harvest.

One such gardener who always plants his crops by the moon is Mark Christensen, research director of Whanganui’s Heritage Food Crops Research Trust.

He said his experience with planting by the moon has been consistently positive.

“I get strong germination, healthy early growth and good resilience in my crops,” he said.

“Although I haven’t run a formal side‑by‑side trial, mainly because I’ve always intuitively recognised the benefits of working with lunar cycles, I’ve observed enough over many seasons to trust the pattern.

“For me, moon planting isn’t about proving a mechanism in a laboratory; it’s about aligning with natural rhythms that growers across cultures have relied on for generations.

“When I follow the lunar calendar, my work feels more in sync with the environment, and the plants respond well. That practical, repeated success is what keeps me using it.”

So, if you are having trouble with a certain crop in your garden, maybe try planting by the moon and see if it makes a difference.

Gardening is all about trial and error and having an open mind.

Kem Ormond is a features writer for The Country. She’s also a keen gardener.

Let a sleeping dog lie: Family asks Purewa Cemetery to return concrete Labrador to father’s grave

New Zealand Herald August 08, 2026

Professional golfer Richard Lee objected to Purewa Cemetery removing a sentimental Labrador ornament, special painted stone and succulent collection from his father Bruce's grave. Photo / Dean Purcell

A family is reeling after treasured mementos were removed from their father’s memorial at Purewa Cemetery in Auckland, as part of a move by its managers to make the grounds more environmentally friendly.

Professional golfer Richard Lee said he normally visited his father Bruce’s grave twice a year and always recognised it by the small concrete Labrador his family had laid beside the memorial many years ago.

But Lee told the Herald that when he was there last week, he noticed the dog, as well as a succulent collection and a special stone painted by his granddaughter, had vanished from the grave in the Meadowbank cemetery’s Y Block.

“It was quite distressing. My 87-year-old mum has been quite sick and hasn’t been to the cemetery for a while. Dad died about 31 years ago. Whenever I see the Labrador, I know I’m in the right place.

“When it comes to family, these things are very personal. They’ve been there for a long time and never bothered anyone. Mum left the sleeping Labrador with Dad to keep him company. It’s a sentimental thing.

“Mum was very upset. She was crying,” Lee said.

A sign at Purewa explained the situation, advising families that plastic flowers and unapproved items would be removed from Y Block on May 1, 2025.

The sign encouraged families to instead use natural flowers, and vases approved by the cemetery’s administration office.

Lee’s sister, who asked to be identified only as Juliet, was also offended. “Why does everything have to look the same? Why must every resting place be stripped?

“Imagine burying a child and then being told you can’t leave a little memento or tribute; natural flowers die.”

Juliet contacted Purewa Cemetery’s general manager Alistair Crombie on July 22 to question why families were no longer allowed to leave personal mementoes on the graves of their loved ones.

“Not everyone can get to the cemetery to leave fresh flowers regularly,” Juliet wrote in her email to Crombie.

“I think this policy is uncaring and mean-spirited. The rows that have been cleared looked sad, unloved, boring and lifeless now.”

Juliet wrote that she could understand restrictions on items such as plastic windmills, but questioned how a “relatively flat concrete dog”, a painted stone and small succulent garden could pose any risk of being damaged by, or becoming caught in, lawnmowing equipment, which was the explanation she said she had been given.

“My mother was very upset ... she especially bought that little dog to be with my father as he had always had Labradors. It had been there causing no issue for over 30 years. She lived in Napier for 11 years and was comforted to know that dad had a little companion with him,” she wrote.

Juliet received a response on Tuesday after the Herald sent questions to the cemetery.

Crombie apologised for the delayed response and for the distress caused to Juliet’s mother, Bev.

Crombie wrote that the initiative was aimed at addressing plastic flowers and other items such as windmills that are non-compliant under cemetery bylaws.

“This is proving very difficult though and we are finding some visitors really like it and some others are not keen on it, so yes there is a bit of tension about this project. We haven’t progressed this initiative very far yet, as you will have observed, due to these concerns.

“There is also a safety component involved for our maintenance staff and cemetery visitors where broken vases can be mowed over or walked on, and wire from the plastic flowers punctures mower tyres, which happens quite often.

“The berms are also not designed to hold a lot of items, so there’s also an issue with things encroaching on to neighbouring plots, that’s also quite common.”

Crombie wrote that he thought there was merit to Juliet’s suggestion of a review of the “green up” project, and he would look into it further and communicate with her about that. He also offered to meet.

“I would also like to offer you a custom-built concrete planter box designed for the Y Block berms at no charge,” he wrote. “The stone that was removed could be placed in the planter along with your plants.”

Bruce Lee died on his 61st birthday. His family said he was a quiet man who owned a small orchard in Hawke’s Bay and loved gardening, the outdoors – and his Labradors.

Crombie acknowledged in an email to the Herald that the “green up” policy had become polarising and would take years to implement.

“We acknowledge the customer’s complaint as valid and deeply regret the sadness they have experienced. As this was a new trial initiative for Purewa, we will review how we continue it.”

Richard Lee said being offered a free vase at this point “feels off”.

Juliet and her mother plan to take Crombie up on his offer to meet them.

And in the latest twist in the plot, Purewa Cemetery has emailed the family to confirm their beloved Labrador can return to its spot on their father’s grave.

A small victory for a small dog that was never really the problem.

Carolyne Meng-Yee is an Auckland-based investigative journalist who won Best Documentary at the Voyager Media Awards. She worked for the Herald on Sunday from 2007-2011 and rejoined the Herald in 2016 after working as an award-winning current affairs producer at TVNZ’s 60 Minutes, 20/20 and Sunday.

‘They hid it away’: The DNA test that revealed an Australian cricketer’s family secret

Sydney Morning Herald August 09, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

In January 1958, a young West Australian fast bowler by the name of Ron Gaunt was flown into South Africa as an injury replacement for the Australian Test team.

Within a few days, the 23-year-old Gaunt made his debut in Durban, claiming figures of 2-87 in a drawn match under the captaincy of Ian Craig.

Gaunt’s story was a good one, of a strapping quick bowler with a shock of red hair, who may well have played many more games for Australia had he not been stuck behind the likes of Alan Davidson and Graham McKenzie.

“He was quick and used to swing the ball about quite nicely. Especially on the Perth wicket where he used to get a bit of pace and bounce, he was a nasty proposition for a batsman to face. He was certainly a top-rate fast bowler,” Craig told Cricinfo in 2012.

After moving to Victoria, Gaunt also made his mark in the east, notably as the longtime bowling coach for the Footscray Cricket Club. It was there he set Merv Hughes on the path to a storied career by telling the young all-rounder from Werribee that he was, in fact, a bowler.

But the true significance of Gaunt’s debut has been shrouded in a family secret for decades, only recently confirmed by DNA testing: Ron Gaunt may well have been Australia’s first Test cricketer of Indigenous heritage.

His debut came a month earlier than the sole women’s Test played by Aunty Faith Thomas at Melbourne’s Junction Oval in February 1958, and decades before Jason Gillespie took the field for Australia in Sydney in 1996.

Since then, Ash Gardner, Scott Boland and Brendan Doggett have joined the list of Indigenous Test cricketers. Boland will proudly take the field for Australia in a Test against Bangladesh in Darwin, amidst one of the nation’s largest Indigenous communities, this week.

Gaunt’s story also raises a wider question of Australian cricket, and life. How many more gifted athletes of Indigenous heritage have been part of the nation’s story in secret, because of the past strictures of the White Australia policy?

The municipality of York, about 100 kilometres east of Perth, is WA’s oldest inland town, established in 1831 after being home to the Ballardong Noongar people for thousands of years.

Because of its rich wheat farming, York was home to plenty of prosperous families, who shared the land with the Indigenous community.

In 1872, John Walkinshaw Cowan, whose brother would marry the revered social reformer and politician Edith Cowan, had a child with an unnamed Aboriginal woman. That child, Matilda Cowan, was Ron Gaunt’s grandmother.

Matilda was, by all accounts, a formidable figure. Local newspaper reports tell of how, aged 16, she took the local publican to court in York over unpaid wages and won the case. She was a landowner, and after having one child with another man, Matilda married Walter Gaunt, a local bricklayer.

Walter and Matilda raised her eldest son, Arthur, together, but also had other children, including another named Walter. After Walter junior grew up, he married Ruby Morse, and among six children Ron Gaunt was born in York in 1934.

“All this was kept a secret,” says Ron’s nephew, Dudley Gaunt. “There were laws and restrictions, and it just would’ve made their lives difficult. So they hid it away.”

The secrecy started around the time of the First World War, when two family members served, including Arthur Gaunt. When he came back from Europe, Arthur listed his mother’s heritage as Maori, the better to receive a gratitude bond of £100 for returned servicemen.

As the years went by, rumours circulated that the swarthy complexion of some children was down to Spanish ancestry, or even that someone in the family had married a Pacific Island princess. Anything but Indigenous heritage.

The Age chief cricket writer

Much had changed in WA, and Australia, between the late 19th century and the 1930s. Intermarriage between whites and Aboriginal people was first discouraged, then virtually outlawed.

In the west, a strict policy was introduced in 1927 to ban the Indigenous community from setting foot into the “Native Prohibited Area” that broadly covered the Perth central business district and select suburbs either side of the Swan River. And in Queensland, an Aboriginal fast bowler named Eddie Gilbert was swift enough to knock the bat out of Don Bradman’s hands, but not to play for Australia.

When the Gaunt family moved from York to Perth, as Walter’s building business grew, he purchased land and built a house in a suburb called Rivervale, on the eastern bank of the Swan River. Tellingly, Rivervale was the nearest suburb on the outside of the prohibited area, which was only rescinded in 1954 – well after Ron had started playing club cricket.

Gaunt was among the most promising young fast bowlers in the country, with enough of a competitive streak to indulge in a bit of “Bodyline” bowling for WA in 1956. In a game against Queensland, umpire Colley ordered WA captain Ken Meuleman to change the field, and warned Gaunt about his bowling.

It is ironic that two of Gaunt’s three Tests were played against Apartheid South African teams – just another reminder of the complexities facing a young man of mixed race in Australia in the 1950s and ’60s.

“WA was a very harsh place for Aboriginal people,” says Ron’s niece, Jenny Ewell. “I think they wanted to avoid that, and absolutely because of Ron’s cricket.

“Ron absolutely loved playing cricket, he lived and breathed the game, and I think it would have just destroyed him had he not been able to play it. So that’s probably where it came from.”

A 17-year-old Hughes walked into training at Footscray in November 1978.

“I was a middle-order batsman who bowled maybe second or third change and then got down to Footscray and had a talk to the president, the coach, Ken Eastwood was in on the conversation as seconds captain, and Ron Gaunt was there,” Hughes says.

“I reckon I bowled three balls and Ron came down and said you don’t bat any more, you’re a bowler. He stood at the top of my mark for two or three years, just talking bowling, theories, sorting batsmen out, a whole gamut of different things.

“What he did for me was extraordinary. Without him, I would’ve gone down to Footscray and battled away as a middle-order batsman and part-time bowler. If I had said to Ron, ‘You’re kidding yourself, I’m a batsman’, I’d probably still be plugging away in Footscray thirds now...”

Gaunt, by this time nicknamed “Pappy”, would also mentor Tony Dodemaide, and was instrumental in helping the club win its inaugural first-grade premiership in 1980.

Hughes remembers Gaunt’s skill as a technical coach, plus his ability to still send down beautiful outswing in the nets. But what sticks with him is the older man’s personal touch – sports psychology before it had the name.

“You could talk to him about anything,” Hughes says. “He could pick up on if you were having a bad day or whatever, and that’s the philosophy I take with kids now. You talk to them, and it’s not just about cricket, but about school, are exams coming up? If guys aren’t concentrating on their bowling, you try to get to the bottom of it, and he used to do that beautifully.

”He knew you had the talent and if you weren’t producing at training he’d try to get to the bottom of it. He’d say, ‘Listen, you’re at training, you can leave that behind, and concentrate on your training’.”

Some earthier incentives came when Hughes and Footscray were fighting for their lives in the 1980 first-grade grand final.

“In the first XI grand final I played in my second year at Footscray, there was 10 and 11 batting, and he just said, ‘Right boys, if you can get to double figures here I’ll buy you a slab’,” Hughes remembers. “How hard do you reckon we worked to get those runs?

“If you did well, he was always there for you. It wasn’t him beating his chest, it was just him patting you on the back and saying, ’Well done’.”

Dodemaide, a couple of years younger than Hughes, can recall watching Gaunt bowl, perhaps planting a seed that led an initially front-on bowler to change his action to allow for the away swingers that netted Dodemaide 10 Test caps.

“He had the tracksuit on and was clearly well past playing age, but he went in to bowl a few balls and demonstrate what he was talking about, and he had this beautiful side-on jump and action, and it was just so smooth,” says Dodemaide, now an Australian selector. “I thought, ‘Wow, could I ever bowl like this bloke?’

“Having a couple of Test players around the club was just gold for a young kid like me. He only played a handful of Tests, but that was enough as far as we were concerned – to spend any time around someone who’d played at that level of cricket.”

None of Hughes, Dodemaide or even his fellow Footscray Test cricketer Ken Eastwoood had any idea about Gaunt’s heritage.

“I never knew that, but that’s a real feather in his cap,” Hughes says. “Times have changed for the better. I thought I spent a fair bit of time with him, but it was never mentioned. Back then he might’ve been hiding that heritage.”

There is one former teammate, Lindsay James, who has told Dodemaide that Gaunt did indeed know of his Indigenous heritage, and that the pair discussed it quietly, once, long after both had finished playing and coaching.

“I couldn’t imagine him being a fearsome fast bowler,” Dodemaide says. “He had such a gentle demeanour about him, and very generous with his time and experience.”

After retirement, Gaunt moved to the NSW Central Coast to share more time with his children, Karon and Andrew. Gaunt and their mother had divorced when Andrew was two years old.

“Once a year we used to get to see my father around Christmas time for a month, [and] then he’d have to go back to Victoria to work,” Andrew says. “But when I was around 21-22, I went and stayed with him for a few years, and that was good. He was pretty much just like a mate, he spoke like a mate and that’s how we were.

“I came back to Sydney after a couple of years, and we kept in closer contact, and, eventually, he retired up the Central Coast and I went up and stayed there for a while. But work was back here in Sydney. So I was always going up there weekly, pretty much for years.”

Sport in general, and cricket in particular, was never far away from the conversation.

“You had no choice on the TV, it was cricket when it started until it finished, then he’d go, ‘OK it’s yours now’,” Andrew recalls. “He never boasted, he never bragged, that wasn’t him. Other people who knew him would say, ‘That’s Ronnie Gaunt, he used to play for Australia’. But he’d never say that. He wouldn’t talk too much about it – what happens on tour stays on tour almost.”

If Gaunt was taciturn about his cricket achievements, his heritage was buried deeper still, remaining unknown to the family when Ron died in 2012. Eight years later, during COVID-19, Andrew’s half-sister Kellie started digging into family history. Ancestry searches were followed by DNA tests, revealing a hidden Indigenous bloodline.

“One day, out of the blue she gave me a call and said, ‘Andrew, guess what, you’ll never believe it’, and I just said, ‘Nah, get out of here’. And my other sister Karon couldn’t believe it at all.

“Then Kellie got in contact with Jenny, and she took it up and ran with it. It was a such a well-kept secret, and maybe that was a reason why. He may not have played for Australia or got the chances he did if they knew he had Indigenous background.

“I was speaking to my sisters about Jason Gillespie saying, ‘Geez, he’s supposed to be the first person of Indigenous blood to play for Australia’. I started laughing about that and going, ‘Oh man, sorry about that’.”

Ask Andrew what he might have said to his father had he known, and he pauses.

“I’d probably have said, ‘What the hell were you thinking?’” he laughs. “I’m actually quite proud or glad, it just cements that footprint in our family as a full-on Aussie. But I don’t think they looked at it like that.”

While Ron got his mother Ruby’s red hair, Andrew and Jenny are both darker in complexion. Andrew can remember, as a teenager, that Ron got them together at Martin Place in Sydney.

“I met Jenny one time when I was about 16,” he says. “Dad was in Melbourne at the time, but he came up to see us. He wanted me to go and meet my cousin, he goes, ‘Come and meet your cousin’, and Karon said, ‘What about me?’ and he says, ‘Nah, just Andrew’. I thought that was a bit odd.

“That’s the first and last time I met Jenny [who moved to the United States, where she still lives]. But I think Dad was sizing me up with her because we were both darker in complexion. That’s just my take, but my sisters Karon and Kellie thought that made sense.”

After Jenny took up the family research, she passed much of the information onto Dudley Gaunt, who still lives in WA. He has had inconclusive discussions with WA Cricket about Ron’s Indigenous heritage, and has also made attempts to contact the Ballardong Noongar community. Cricket Australia is looking into the Gaunt family story.

“We want to ensure cricket’s heritage fully reflects all those from different backgrounds who have contributed to the game,” a CA spokesman said.

“The stories provided by those exploring family ancestry is an important way to ensure the diverse backgrounds of past players is recognised.”

Dudley says the main issue in his meeting with WA Cricket was not Gaunt’s Aboriginality, “It was whether he accepted his Aboriginality, whether he told people. Did he tell people at South Perth cricket club?

“If he wouldn’t have been able to play cricket, why would he tell anyone at South Perth that he was Aboriginal? It was a different time, they parked it away, hid it and got on with their lives.”

In 2005, the former chief justice of NSW, James Spiegelman, spoke about hidden Aboriginal histories in that year’s Charles Perkins Oration.

Sports Writer

“Let me state one undeniable fact: many, probably millions of Australians have an Aboriginal ancestor,” he said. “This should be recognised as an important bond. However, most do not know this fact about their family.

“There was a strong sense of racism involved in the suppression in thousands upon thousands of Australian families of the Aboriginal origins of one or more of their forebears. For most of our history this has been regarded as a matter to be suppressed.

“It appears to me that the process of reconciliation would be advanced by a wider recognition across the broad Australian community that the number of Australians who have Aboriginal ancestors probably amounts to millions.

“The reconciliation process cannot succeed if it is based, contrary to historical fact, solely on maintaining a rigid and categorical distinction between black and white. It will succeed if a significant proportion of those Australians of whom it is true take pride in acknowledging their roots in both communities.”

For Jenny, the secret is itself a significant part of the story.

“I was very proud to find that out myself, to think we’ve got heritage that goes back 60,000 years in Australia,” she says. “But in going back to speak to the family, I found out that the family did know, and didn’t say anything.

“I was shocked, thinking, ‘Gosh they kept it a good secret all those years’. But a lot of it might have been that they wanted to work and get on with their lives. This is my opinion – because Ron was playing cricket and very successful, they wanted that to keep going and that it wasn’t made more difficult for him.”

Andrew recalls one other comment from his father that has taken on new meaning.

“My dad used to tell me, ‘You have a whole other family in the west’,” he says. “It was a big secret, and back then I could understand it. Whereas now I’m like, ‘Wow, that’s cool’.”

‘We couldn’t get over that’: The AFLW norm baffling this Irish import

Sydney Morning Herald August 09, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Erone Fitzpatrick is a star – All-Australian, Carlton leader and selected in the Irish representative AFLW side – but there’s one thing about Australian rules football that leaves her baffled.

Club loyalty – or rather, the lack of it.

Hailing from County Laois in Ireland, Fitzpatrick helped lead them to their first Gaelic football title in over 20 years in 2022, before being poached by Carlton for the 2023 season.

She played with the same teammates from age four to 23; switching clubs or counties is “unheard of at home”.

“Talking to a lot of the Aussies here, they can’t get over how loyal you are to your club and your county throughout your whole career,” Fitzpatrick said.

“I would play with the one club for my whole football career, and I would play with the one county for my whole football career, and they couldn’t get over that.

“That’s why we find it really strange, the whole trade period and people leaving clubs and going to different clubs and stuff like that.”

Fitzpatrick hopes she can stick with her AFLW side in a similar way.

“I would love that,” she said. “You never know what can happen in the future, but I think it would be very weird for me to go anywhere else. I think if you asked a lot of the Irish players, they would say the exact same thing.”

Since the AFLW’s inaugural season in 2017, the presence of Gaelic football cross-coders has skyrocketed, with 44 active Irish players in the league and two inactive.

Their effect has been profound. The Irish players play a lightning-fast and attacking style. North Melbourne, who have won two consecutive AFLW premierships, currently have five Irish players on their list, while the Brisbane Lions, Adelaide, Geelong and Carlton all have a strong contingent of Irish players.

The impact in Ireland has been seismic as well. On one hand, the game’s popularity has surged, with Irish broadcasters showing AFLW games, dedicated 3am watch parties and growing fan bases on social media.

But the amount of Irish-born players lured to Australia has also left a growing hole in Gaelic football pathways, especially in smaller regions,

“I’m from a very small county, not saying that I would have been a big fish, but I probably would have been at home,” Fitzpatrick explains.

“For my county to lose like someone like me is hard ... because in a small county, talent is very limited compared to the bigger counties that have a huge pool of talent.

“Counties like Mayo have six girls playing in the AFLW – that’s a huge chunk of unbelievable talent from one county.”

There’s enough Irish talent in AFLW to make a representative game in the mould of State of Origin possible. Fitzpatrick represented Ireland in that match in Sydney, in front of a sellout crowd.

Speaking in the lead-up, Fitzpatrick was thrilled to be part of it.

“My parents are flying out for the game, which is so important to me, and I’ll also have my aunties, family friends, my grannies’ next door neighbour,” she joked.

“I want to make them proud, and I want to make all the young girls proud and know they can chase their dreams and be anything they want in life.”

Now, the focus is on the upcoming AFLW season, which begins on Sunday at Marvel Stadium when Fitzpatrick’s Blues take on the Saints before the clubs’ men’s teams do the same.

The Blues’ women’s side made it to a preliminary final last season, where they fell short against the Lions.

It was a meteoric turnaround – Carlton finished 14th in 2024 before introducing a crop of young, extroverted talent in 2025.

Fitzpatrick was a pivotal part of the resurgence last year, averaging 17.5 disposals and kicking 13 goals.

On field and on social media, fans noticed something different about the Blues – they were having fun.

Before every game, the team performed a dance and sang Australia’s unofficial national anthem – Untouched by the Veronicas – to ease pre-game nerves.

They booked in official line dancing classes and were taught choreography by youngsters Poppy Scholz and Meg Robertson.

“We want to keep chasing that joy,” Fitzpatrick said.

“We don’t want to chase last year, but we want to keep building on it. Keep building those foundation blocks … and still bringing the joy and finding the joy in it all because, ultimately, you play your best football when you’re having fun, and we have a really fun group.”

On a scale of 1-10, Fitzgerald’s rates her dancing skills as a solid four, “below average, but I can shake my hips and stuff, but that’s about it,” she adds.

Would The Veronicas still be their anthem, or will they start afresh and choose another song?

“We’re actually not 100 per cent sure,” Fitzpatrick says.

The dancing, however has stepped up a notch.

“Poppy [Scholz] taught us a dance last Thursday and we performed on Friday, and we were a bit rusty,” she laughs.

“Last year it was mainly line dancing, but the level this year was a bit hard, so we’ve told Poppy to bring it down a bit.”

After Game of Thrones, Sophie Turner had to rediscover her identity. In many ways, she still is

Sydney Morning Herald August 09, 2026

The 30-year-old, who’s set to play Lara Croft in Tomb Raider, has already lived a full life, including being a global star, married and divorced by 28.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

It is mid-May and unseasonably cold in London on the day Sophie Turner and I speak. While it may be grey and somewhat depressing outside, it’s not depressing enough to make the actor yearn for her former life in Los Angeles and Miami. “No, I don’t miss living in America,” she says with a chuckle. “I do miss the sun, but that’s it.”

So what exactly was she happy to be reunited with when she moved back to her rainy (and much maligned) home country in 2023?

“Sarcasm, baked beans on toast, Jaffa Cakes and British chocolate,” she says. “Although the thing that I missed the most was pub culture, especially in spring, when the pubs are rammed and people are spilling out onto the streets and it is all so joyful.

“I love that gathering of people. New York has it, of course, but when I lived in LA, you’d have to drive everywhere. I missed just wandering down the street and seeing a bunch of people chatting at the pub. To me, that’s England.”

Turner has packed a lot into her 30 years. In 2011, aged 15, she was thrust into the spotlight via the plum role of Sansa Stark in the mega-hit Game of Thrones. Then, in 2016, she received a message on Instagram from Joe Jonas of the Jonas Brothers, asking her for a drink.

Unsure whether she’d been catfished, Turner arrived at a north London pub with her older brother in tow. He wasn’t needed and the two young stars began a whirlwind romance that saw her move to the US, marry and become a mother of two, all before turning 27. But the fairytale ending was not to be. The pair separated in 2023 and Turner moved back to London with her daughters.

The actor has previously said that her career “stalled” in the years after having children, but she has certainly found her stride again. Since returning to the UK, she has starred in shows like Joan and Steal, and is now playing Lara Croft in Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s small-screen adaptation of Tomb Raider, which will likely come out later this year.

“Right now, my focus is Tomb Raider,” she says. “It has been for quite a while and will be for a while to come. I feel good doing it. I was birthed by Game of Thrones – TV is my bread and butter, and I love developing a character over years. If I hadn’t had Game of Thrones, this would be overwhelming. But it’s a joy.”

Lara Croft has also given Turner the opportunity to experiment with being a brunette for the first time in years. “I’ve been dyeing my hair since I was 13, when I had to go red for Game of Thrones, so I don’t really identify with any hair colour these days, although it’s interesting to see how the world reacts.

“Blonde gets the most positive reaction,” she elaborates. “Red gets less of a reaction, but when there is a reaction it’s pretty over the top. And with brunette you’re a bit camouflaged, which I’m really enjoying. I get recognised less, which is great.”

Turner may be enjoying the anonymity because she hasn’t always had an easy time at the hands of the press and the public. In the wake of her complicated divorce from Jonas, a prevailing online narrative painted him as a diligent, loving father and her as a party-obsessed starlet who couldn’t put her children first.

In an interview with British Vogue in 2024, she said: “It felt like I was watching a movie of my life that I hadn’t written, produced or starred in. It was shocking. I’m still in shock.”

Turner, who’s also talked about how isolated she felt in America, has found acting to be an excellent way of working through the more traumatic events of her 20s. “It is like a catharsis,” she says. “I need to do it creatively to process what’s been going on in my life, and to expel something from me.

“I did a movie a few years ago called Trust, about a girl who had to go into hiding because she was being manipulated by this man she’d had a baby with and needed to protect her child. She had personal things to process – and it felt like an opportunity for me to do that, too.”

It has at times been difficult for Turner to separate herself from the roles she has played, and she explains that spending half her adolescence on the set of Game of Thrones was a discombobulating experience. “I didn’t know who was Sansa and who was Sophie. And I was too young to read the books, so I kind of just developed her over time. I had a big identity crisis when I let her go; I didn’t really know who I was or what I was doing. It was a strange, hard time.”

Equally, Turner’s current life in west London is quite far removed from the tomb-raiding archaeologist she is playing. “[Lara Croft] is so different from me and my personality. Without giving too much away, there is an element of her that can be fairly toxic, but there is also an element of her that is so focused and determined, whereas I have ADHD and can’t complete a task without forgetting about it and doing something else. I am a total worrier and neurotic, which she obviously isn’t, but we’re both obsessed with history.”

As the mother of two young daughters – Willa, 5, and Delphine, 3 – Turner also doesn’t have the time or space to approach her roles with a Daniel Day-Lewis level of reverence and preparation. “Kristen Stewart once said that only men are method actors. Women have to come home and cook their kids’ dinner – and I can’t be a murdering psychopath while I’m making spaghetti, can I?”

Turner is mostly very funny and quite forthright, and I can understand why she might have found California isolating at times. She has that particularly British ability to make a joke out of almost anything. More than once, she hoots with laughter and tells me something I can’t publish, and as we chat I can see why she has such a large group of female friends – and why being close to them again has brought her so much happiness.

“All my best friends are my age and we went to school together and we’re having a year of 30th birthdays – we’re just so happy to be out of the mess of our 20s,” she says. “Each of us has had a mini breakdown but we all feel really positive now. I was very ready to leave that decade of my life behind.”

For her own 30th, Turner threw a big party and says that along with great people and great music, drinks are all you need to make it a success. “You could be in a ballroom or in the park; if you have the tunes and drinks and mates, you’re good.”

She’ll also have a steady supply of dresses for all these 30th birthdays thanks to her role as a Louis Vuitton ambassador (she has been a muse to Nicolas Ghesquière, the company’s artistic director, for nearly eight years). But for all Turner’s dazzling red-carpet outfits, her day-to-day fashion choices are more reflective of a west London mother than a Hollywood star.

“Comfort is always key,” she says. “Some days I like to look like the most tomboyish version of myself – right now I’m wearing cargo pants and an oversized T-shirt – and other times I’m quite dolled up. Mostly, I like simplicity.”

Aside from birthday bashes, Turner has started her new decade with the intention of looking after her mental and physical health, which shouldn’t be too difficult as she goes to therapy regularly and says she is “addicted to the gym”. And while she will be filming for some of the northern hemisphere summer, most of it will be spent with her daughters, which she describes as “wonderful”.

As we say goodbye, Turner tells me to check the weather forecast because she’s pretty sure there’s a heatwave on the way. Turns out she’s right. I just hope she spends some of it in a quintessentially English pub garden.

The Telegraph, London

The people that walk into Paul’s life trust nobody. This is how he helps them

Sydney Morning Herald August 09, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

While it is now dwarfed by the mega-developments that have come to define Parramatta Square, the 1885-built Leigh Memorial Church is the only building in Sydney’s second CBD where dozens – sometimes hundreds – of people line up at 7.30am each day to get in.

Inside the walls of the church and its hall, an army of volunteers has spent an hour cooking breakfast for those outside. And someone’s been here since before dawn. Paul Moussa, a 71-year-old Lebanese-Australian man with missing teeth and a grey hoodie, co-ordinates Meals Plus within Parramatta Mission, an outreach charity for people across western Sydney who are either homeless or doing it tough.

The social worker is the first port of call for hundreds in the community, which means he is often woken up by his phone ringing – to the tune of the Lebanese national anthem – in the early hours. On a warm Wednesday morning when the Herald visits in March, Moussa arrived about 3.30am. Sitting in his office surrounded by the artwork of community members, Moussa fills out NCAT paperwork, writes job references, and searches for homes for those who will soon walk through the door.

As Moussa opens the doors at 8am, the church hall and courtyard fill as breakfast – a variety of eggs, toast and cereal – is served. Nicole Anderson has just sat down on a bench. She arrived at Parramatta Mission after beginning to deal with the trauma of having family members killed. She’s in her third year of studying social work, and says the community has given her a sense of stability in life.

“It’s a place where everybody interacts with everybody,” she says. “This is a place where people, whether they’ve got mental health [issues], are drug addicts, alcoholics, whatever, they always know this is a safe place to come.”

A painted banner above the bains-marie highlights the charity’s values, including grace, dignity, faith, and hope. “Everyone is welcome,” Moussa says. “You haven’t got to fill out a form, ‘you’re suitable, you’re not’.”

Faith? “Church can conjure up trauma,” he says. “We don’t use the word faith, we use the word trust. You build someone’s trust … with hospitality. So if you’re looking for KPIs: somebody comes in hungry with their head down, they walk out with a full stomach and their head up. And when you feel comfortable, you might invite us on your journey.”

Despite Parramatta’s economic rise, those who have been left behind are struggling. Last year’s street count identified 222 sleeping rough in the area, up from 156 a decade ago, although down from its 291 peak in 2024.

“Behind every statistic is a person,” says Geoff Smith, the charity’s chief executive and lead minister of Parramatta Community Uniting Church. The group launched a campaign this week to highlight the reality of life on the street through the use of a mock real estate ad, with Ray White real estate agent Peter Vines fronting a video advertising a “brutally authentic opportunity” for sleeping rough.

0:51

Parramatta's 'unliveable listings'

Western Sydney real estate agent Peter Vines advertises the "brutally authetic opportunity" facing rough sleepers in Parramatta for Parramatta Mission's homeless charity.

Western Sydney’s homeless population has no trust in governments nor many of the non-government organisations that want to help, Moussa says. “People don’t choose to be homeless, but they choose homelessness because they have no confidence in the system. And to manage the system, you need to be Einstein.”

Volunteers are clearing breakfast plates away when 25-year-old Ashool arrives at the door. Moussa conjures up some extra toast and leftovers of the breakfast service and sits him down to enjoy the meal.

You wouldn’t know it from his neat black T-shirt and blue business shirt, but the Fijian national has been sleeping on the edge of Prince Alfred Square for almost a month. His housemate with mental health issues kicked him and a friend out earlier this year. He’s since learnt the locations of every outdoor power socket in Parramatta. He needs to charge his phone to work late at night delivering food on Uber Eats, for which he spends $80 a week renting an e-bike. He turned up after an outreach worker approached and told him about a place for free meals.

“We’re going to work this out,” Moussa tells the young man as he puts his arms on his shoulders, peppering him with practical questions. Does he have a visa? Does he have any training? Does he need a resume? “First thing, let’s get you some clothes.”

“You’re going to make me cry,” Ashool says. It’s the first time he feels cared for, he says, in more than three years of living in Australia. But the 71-year-old won’t allow tears. “If you cry, I cry,” he says.

It is now almost noon. In the kitchen, the final preparations are being made for the lunch service. Hayley Dickerson, a longtime chef who joined the group this year, is overseeing the serving of some vegetables and meat.

“Everyone’s pretty rapt about what they’re getting, a nutritious meal,” she says. The fact that two delicious, healthy meals are being served to hundreds of guests each day is remarkable: the group relies almost entirely on donated goods, meaning there’s little consistency in what they can cook with. Twice a week, OzHarvest delivers fresh food. Other times, the City of Parramatta drops off leftover catering from its events, and the local Buddhist temple brings in 50 vegetarian meals.

Before the lunch service begins, in a bright room at the front of the building, about a dozen government agencies, other charities and not-for-profits have set up tables for a community hub to connect guests to essential services.

Jenny Oates, a staff member at the charity, helped establish the hub when trying to get help for someone who was homeless.

“They couldn’t get housing because they didn’t have Centrelink. They couldn’t get Centrelink because they didn’t have a bank account,” she said.

“They couldn’t get a bank account because they had no ID. If you’re on the street or you’re escaping DV, you don’t have that stuff.

“So we thought about the hub to bring together: Births, Deaths and Marriages, Centrelink, Service NSW and Housing, so that we could fast-track people … rather than having to send them out to different situations.”

Centrelink found it so useful that the agency has employed a staff member to be on site every day.

“I wouldn’t be where I am now without it,” says 59-year-old Julie Sutherland of the community she has formed at the centre. She’s attended daily for years.

“Paul is down as my next-of-kin. I call him my stepdad. When I [was] in hospital, when I lost it taking ice, I came here. He rang the ambulance and talked me into going to Cumberland [mental health facility]. He sent someone in with underwear and clothes. He’s just a really caring person.

“Without this place, there’d be a lot more people hungry, there’d be a lot more shoplifting, there’d be a lot more fighting on the streets … Parramatta would be a sad place without this.”

The reason for the success is partly in the group’s approach to its community members. “We help people achieve what they want,” Moussa says. “We journey with someone. We don’t walk behind them, pushing them to where we think they should go. We don’t walk in front of them leading them to somewhere they don’t want to go … Personally, I value a community response rather than a government response.”

But the organisation is still pushing for government funding, especially as services, including Centrelink and Homes NSW, refer clients to Parramatta Mission – when it should be the other way around. The group has plans in with the council for a renovation that would turn the community space into a modern centre with office space above it to bring in revenue. But money right now is tight.

Many politicians come and visit – some say they’ll come but never do. “The only good one is [state MP for Parramatta] Donna Davis,” Moussa says. She often rings them if someone is in need.

Moussa’s approach to guests is hospitable, but firm. He yells at guests not to take too much food from the community food collection held in the afternoon, and, on occasion, has to break up a fight. His work earned him a Medal of the Order of Australia in 2025.

“I had an argument with one of the ministers [a decade ago]. They used to charge people for meals, $1 for breakfast and $3 for lunch … so when a bloke owed $400, they wouldn’t feed him. I said, ‘Take that cross out of the church and put in a cash register, and you can bloody well pray to that.’”

The meals are now free.

“I’m a dinosaur and a control freak and all those negative things,” he says with a grin. “But it is the energies of many – our volunteers, our community and our clients. We are a community within a community.”

It might be the serious lack of sleep, but Moussa says he has two regular dreams: one is where no one turns up to Parramatta Mission because no one is hungry. The other is where the street outside is full of people trying to get in. “Let’s do this,” Moussa tells his volunteers in his dream. “Either way, I’m happy.”

Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz as deal still out of reach

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 21:01:28 GMT

Tehran urges US to ‘correct its behaviour’ as UAE says one of its ships targeted by Iranian missile

Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, while the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach on Saturday.

Iran’s politburo-like body known as the supreme national security council said the strait of Hormuz will not open until the United States “corrects its behaviour”, and its state broadcaster published a statement from the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The US must never threaten Iran again, the statement said, and must permanently end the war with Iran and its armed allies in the region. The US must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. It also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets.

There was no immediate comment from the US, which has wanted an acceptable deal on the strait before ending the blockade. According to the interim deal signed in June, a schedule to end sanctions and a plan for compensation would be part of the final deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets.

The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on Saturday that they were close to reaching an agreement on navigation, “specifically the determination of a transit route”. But the waterway’s reopening is contingent on other conditions, he said, in remarks shared on social media, and blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the interim deal.

Oman, which is mediating and has made relatively few comments on the talks, said in a statement on Saturday that the discussions were continuing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”, and condemned attacks on ships on the strait.

Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait and wants to charge users for passage, repeatedly attacking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route.

The US opposes any Iranian tolls in the strait, though the June deal allows Tehran to hammer out arrangements for the “future administration” of Hormuz in conjunction with fellow coastal state Oman.

The 60-day period to negotiate a final deal will end in just over a week but could be extended.

Iran has said it was close to reaching a separate deal with Oman to manage the strait, which runs between the two countries.

Continued attacks in the strait, which was free to sail through before the war, led to the collapse of an April ceasefire, and mediators have since urged both sides to return to the terms of the June memorandum.

The strait, which is crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, had been considered an international waterway before the war. Ship transits remain low.

Meanwhile, a vessel owned by Abu Dhabi’s state-owned Adnoc oil and gas company was attacked while sailing through the strait of Hormuz, Emirati authorities said earlier on Saturday. The foreign ministry said Iran fired the missile as part of attacks on commercial shipping.

Adnoc said in a statement that there were no casualties following the attack early on Saturday. The company said more than a dozen of its vessels have been attacked by missiles and drones while using the strait since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. One crew member has been killed and 20 others wounded, it said.

Adnoc did not elaborate on the location of the attack or any damage.

Later, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said a vessel east of the town of Khasab, Oman had been struck by a projectile that caused a fire that was put out, and the vessel and crew were safe. It was not clear whether this was the Adnoc incident.

Navy says it is spending 25% more time monitoring Russian vessels around UK waters

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 20:03:34 GMT

Warning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North Sea

The Royal Navy has warned of increasing Russian activity around the UK’s waters after it spent 21 days in July monitoring Moscow’s ships.

Naval operations to monitor Russian vessels increased by 25% last month compared with the previous year, with warships making repeated voyages through the strait of Dover and the North Sea.

Offshore patrol vessels HMS Tyne, HMS Mersey and HMS Severn, alongside Wildcat helicopters from 815 Naval Air Squadron and Merlin submarine-hunting aircraft, were deployed throughout the month to shadow Russian frigates Neustrashimy and Admiral Grigorovich, which are tasked with escorting so-called “shadow fleet” tankers.

Last month, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in its annual report that Royal Navy vessels had been “activated” 116 times in the year to March 2026, shadowing 61 Russian warships and 28 merchant vessels around the UK’s waters.

This reflected a 30% increase in Russian naval activity over the previous two years and included operations to deter the spy ship Yantar, which was spotted near undersea cables off Scotland last November.

Vladimir Putin has been accused of using the Kremlin’s shadow fleet of ageing vessels to evade international sanctions on its oil and fund the war in Ukraine.

The increase in Russian naval activity follows the seizure of the tanker Smyrtos by Royal Marines in June, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel.

The MoD said the diversion of ships from Russia to escort shadow fleet vessels meant the country was “using up valuable operational capacity to constantly guard cargo”.

The UK has already imposed sanctions on more than 500 vessels, and Russia’s oil and gas revenues fell by 24% year on year in 2025.

HMS Tyne was also tasked with monitoring the Neustrashimy as it carried out a live-firing exercise outside British and French waters on 20 July.

Another ship, the frigate HMS Somerset, has been involved in monitoring Russian activity in the North Atlantic as part of a four-month Nato deployment searching for submarines, alongside helicopters from the Navy’s Fleet Air Arm.

Somerset’s commanding officer, Cmdr Matt Millyard, said on Saturday: “This deployment demonstrates exactly what the Royal Navy exists to do: protect the UK and our allies from wherever our interests are threatened.

“I am immensely proud of every single member of the ship’s company for what we have achieved over the past four months.”

The moment I knew: As I packed, our future looked uncertain – then he gave me his fluffy pyjamas

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 20:00:09 GMT

Stephanie Casey was an exchange student in Ireland when she met Jack. They quickly became close but as the year drew to a close, her departure loomed

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

In 2016 I was an Australian student on exchange in Dublin, plotting to fall in love at Trinity College before Normal People made it cool. My housemates had swiped on Jack’s Tinder profile on my behalf, and we met in October for the first time under the Spire on O’Connell Street.

Jack couldn’t quite believe I had actually shown up; I was just glad he wasn’t the other lad standing there with the Peaky Blinders haircut and matching tracksuit. We went to a bookshop cafe, where Jack spilled his tea due to nerves and I waxed lyrical about the importance of compulsory voting due to mine. It was sweet, genuine, interesting conversation. When we parted ways, we both did the classic over-the-shoulder, cow-eyed glance back. Jack kept his cool; I panicked and walked straight into a line of kindergarteners on an excursion in the city.

Soon we were seeing each other every week, which quickly turned into every day. My room had a view out onto Pearse Street, and Jack would wave to me out of the train window as it pulled into Pearse St station. I’d sign him into the “overnight visitors” book at my dorm (sorry Mum) where we’d watch Australian horror films (Wolf Creek) and Irish comedies (Father Ted). We walked all over Dublin in the cold afternoons that were bluey-gold in the light and smelled like peat fires, Jack taking me to his favourite parks and pubs. We ate spice bags and Vegemite, drank tea and Guinness.

My uni friends put my phone on time-out so I could stop texting Jack about the “season finale of America” – Trump 1.0 had just begun – and start studying for exams; my Australian friends wondered if I’d finally cracked and made the whole boy up, given the romantic disaster I’d been at home.

But as the year drew to a close, reality loomed. My visa meant I had to come home in January and Jack still had two more years of study to complete in Dublin. We hadn’t talked about what we were going to do, or what our future looked like.

Our relationship status remained undefined, at least by us. To everyone else, from my mum who gently advised me to “give it a chance” to Jack’s family who I joined for Christmas Day, it was clear we were serious about being together.

On the night I was leaving my university accommodation, Jack helped me pack my life – which had quickly become our life – into a straining suitcase. He picked up a pair of his pyjama pants that I coveted and had claimed as my own. They were thick, fluffy, in a blue and green plaid; no Irish clan connection, no fancy label, just a budget pair from Penneys, my other great Irish love. He packed them into my bag, but I protested: “You can’t do that, you love these pants”. He looked at me steadily and said: “Yes, but I love you more.” His words were a simple gift, one that I had never received before, which gave me the answer I didn’t know I was looking for: that we would give it a chance, together.

I flew back to Australia a few days later and cried the whole way home. We didn’t have a plan, but we knew we wanted to be together. We talked in the mornings, sent memes to each other during the day and called to say goodnight. We did this for three years. Life might have shrunk to the size of a phone screen, but it had also never felt so large.

I visited Jack in Dublin in 2017; he spent six months in Australia doing his own exchange in 2018; we reunited halfway in Vietnam in 2019. In early 2020, Jack moved to Australia – he really took “locking it down” seriously, even before Covid.

Since then, Jack has become a citizen, and we’ve bought a house and a puppy together. We married last year, in Dublin, around the corner from our first date.

Our love is something I’m so proud of, and it brings me joy every day. There have been sacrifices, hard conversations and long lonely days, but I would do it again. I’m pretty sure Jack feels the same. But perhaps he has just been trying to get his pyjamas back this whole time.

Hunter Biden talks about how his father’s cancer has spread and is causing him pain

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 19:17:01 GMT

Former US president Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread to other parts of his body and is causing him pain, even as he continues to speak out on public issues, his son Hunter said in an interview.

In a wide-ranging interview with the BBC broadcast late on Friday, Hunter Biden grew emotional as he discussed his father’s condition, describing it as very sad to watch.

“The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” he said. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects.”

Joe Biden, 83, was the oldest man to serve as US president and his age was a source of concern for much of his four years in office. He and his White House advisers have faced intense criticism for allegedly concealing the extent of his health issues, especially after he was forced to abandon his bid for re-election after a disastrous debate with his eventual successor, Donald Trump.

The former president revealed his cancer diagnosis in May of last year, less than four months after he left the White House.

Hunter Biden said the diagnosis had been tough on the family.

“It’s really sad to watch,” Biden said. “The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good.”

But Biden said his father remains “out there”, speaking publicly about the issues that are important to him.

“He’s still doing his thing,” he said. “He so believes in this country.”

Biden also expressed gratitude for the pardon his father granted him because if he had not, Trump would have sought retribution against him, he said. But he also acknowledged that it was not good for the former president’s legacy or the American people.

“It is something that is easily criticized and for good reason,” Biden said. “All I know is that I’m grateful he did it for me, and all I can say to anybody out there is, what would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me?”

Joe Biden will publish a memoir, Promise Me, America, after the midterm elections.

Premier League managers have never been less English, title-winning or secure in their jobs

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 19:00:05 GMT

Huge turnover between seasons means 11 clubs start 2026-27 led by people with under a year in their dugout

Nine of the 20 Premier League clubs will begin the 2026-27 season with a different man in the dugout than the one who ended the last campaign. Opta recently revealed that the only other seasons which started with so many men making their managerial debut for top flight clubs were 1888-89 and 1946-47; the inaugural season of league football and the first following the second world war. Neither occurred under normal circumstances yet the level of turnover this summer does not feel unusual. Job security has never meant less in the Premier League.

Adding in the recently appointed pair of Roberto De Zerbi and Michael Carrick – confirmed in March and May respectively – means this season will start with 11 teams led by coaches with less than a year in their hotseat. The median tenure of Premier League managers at the start of each season has never been so low.

The most recent similar season was 2016-17. Heading into that campaign, 10 clubs had managers with under one year in the role. But with respect to the current Premier League crop, the relatively new head coaches that summer included Antonio Conte, Pep Guardiola, Jürgen Klopp and José Mourinho. All had either already won the Premier League or would go on to do so.

With Arsène Wenger still at Arsenal, four of those considered the five big beasts of Premier League management were competing, with the other (Alex Ferguson) having retired three years earlier. By contrast, Mikel Arteta is the only man who has won the English league who will be starting 2026-27 with the chance to do so again. There was also only one such manager two years ago, albeit it was Guardiola with his bulging trophy cabinet.

As Arteta has a single championship win, this season begins with the fewest English league titles on the division’s collective CV in the Premier League era. The previous lowest at the beginning of a campaign was three in 1995-96 (thanks to Ferguson having two and Howard Wilkinson one) and 2019-20 (Guardiola two, Manuel Pellegrini one).

This is a natural byproduct of managers being younger and less experienced. The median age of Premier League managers is 46.9 years old. It was the same heading into 2024-25 but was last younger 20 years ago. The drop in age has not led to further opportunities for Englishmen.

Eddie Howe’s departure from Newcastle means there will be three English managers when 2026-27 gets under way. The total was the same at the start of the last two campaigns, though interestingly it will be a different trio this year (Carrick, Frank Lampard and Gary O’Neil) than 12 months ago (Howe, Scott Parker and Graham Potter). The standing of the six clubs led by these men is worth considering. Two of the current coaches are at teams that have just been promoted, while two from last season’s group were with sides that went on to be relegated. Opportunities with even relatively secure Premier League clubs are now rare for English managers, never mind at those with realistic title ambitions.

The top end of the division is likely to have a Spanish feel. The Basque region of Gipuzkoa is providing more head coaches to England’s top division than England, with Arsenal, Aston Villa, Chelsea and Liverpool led by men from that relatively small area of Spain. It’s plausible none of them will win the league given the presence of Manchester City (who themselves are under new management after a decade of Guardiola) but Arteta, Xabi Alonso and Andoni Iraola are in charge of three of the leading four clubs in the title betting market, with Unai Emery’s Villa seventh.

Managers from overseas lessening opportunities for English coaches in the Premier League is simply following the trend on the pitch. Just 8.6% of available minutes went to players from outside Britain or Ireland in 1992-93 yet a new high of 69.6% was reached last season. It is a truly global competition at every level, including ownership and sporting directors.

The influence of the latter on recruitment decisions has blurred the line between being a head coach and a manager. Liam Rosenior said he was “extremely humbled and honoured to be appointed head coach of Chelsea Football Club” when he was appointed by the Blues in January. “It fills me with immense pride to become manager of this great club,” was Xabi Alonso’s line when he secured essentially the same gig less than six months later. Based on the announcements clubs made to herald news of their appointments, the Premier League currently employs 14 head coaches and six managers.

Regardless of what the sign says on Alonso’s office door, he should reflect upon his new club giving him a four-year contract when they haven’t kept a manager for as long as two years since Conte left in 2018, or three years since Mourinho’s first spell in charge over a decade earlier.

Rosenior learned this the hard way. He signed a six-and-a-half year deal yet Chelsea previously employed both Rafael Benítez and Guus Hiddink on interim bases for longer than the young Englishman lasted at the club. Head coach or manager, call it what you will. The profession has never offered shorter-term employment, or felt less English, in the Premier League.

If there was one of his many assets Newcastle supporters grew to love above all about Bruno Guimarães then it was best summed up by the man himself after being unveiled as Arsenal’s new £75m signing. “That’s a tough one,” said the Brazil midfielder when asked what fans in north London can expect from him. “I would say I can pass the ball, run a lot and play like a warrior. I’ll never give up.”

After more than four years on Tyneside and having seen Alexander Isak, Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali precede Eddie Howe’s departure, Guimarães – who was devastated after missing a penalty for the Seleção in their defeat against Norway in the last 16 of the World Cup – was determined to seize his opportunity.

While his emotional statement released by Newcastle as his move to Arsenal was confirmed on Saturday said they “did everything they could to keep me”, at the age of 28 he clearly felt it may never come again.

Andrea Berta’s pursuit of Vinícius Júnior came up short this week after the Brazil forward signed an improved six-year deal with Real Madrid. But at least Arsenal’s sporting director was finally able to bring in a player who was first courted by the club in the early days of Mikel Arteta’s reign, and who will add to the outstanding crop of central midfielders at his disposal.

Edu Gaspar, Berta’s predecessor, is understood to have first enquired about Guimarães when he was still at Athletico Paranaense in Brazil before he joined Lyon in the January 2020 transfer window – a few weeks after Arteta’s arrival at the Emirates.

They were also interested when Newcastle won the race to sign him in January 2022 for €40m, which came back to haunt Arsenal when he scored in a 2-0 win that went a long way to them missing out on Champions League qualification that season.

That first of nine appearances is the only time he scored against Arsenal, but Guimarães always impressed in a variety of roles whenever he came up against them, including in the Carabao Cup semi-final Newcastle won 4-0 on aggregate in 2025. He has covered more distance, won more duels and committed more fouls against Arsenal than any other side since making his Premier League debut.

It was no surprise that Declan Rice – the only player in the division to have covered more distance than Guimarães in that period and who enjoyed their fair share of battles – was one of the first to welcome him to Arsenal with a message that said “come here and please no more fights, now we’re friends”.

It is hard to argue with Guimarães that Arsenal have “one of the best midfields” in Europe because last season proved it. Yet having gone all the way to the Champions League final before spending the summer with England, after suffering with neural pain in his hamstring and lower back since December, Rice must be treated with the utmost care in the coming months. Guimarães can provide cover for him in a box-to-box role and gives Arteta options to rotate his other midfielders more frequently.

He did not seem to trust Christian Nørgaard, who has joined Everton, to deputise for Martín Zubimendi in the Premier League last year, and that led to the Spain midfielder running out of steam in the spring.

Water Colour review – an elegant, expertly handled study of depression

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 19:00:04 GMT

Traverse theatre, EdinburghMilly Sweeney’s award-winning two-hander about an art student and a kitchen porter draws power from its clever structure and light touch

It is rare to come out of a show raving about the structure, but the unusual plotting distinguishes Milly Sweeney’s two-hander. The young playwright’s theme is the way everyday social pressures – the stress of completing an art degree show, the anxiety of starting a job – can take a toll on mental health. With sensitivity, she traces the step-by-step process that might take someone from depression, compounded by circumstance, to thoughts of suicide.

Her characters are Esme (Molly Geddes) – friendless at Prestwick Academy, isolated at Glasgow School of Art – and Harris (Ryan J Mackay), seemingly on the up after landing a job as a kitchen porter in a Michelin-star restaurant.

The novelty in Water Colour, named best new play in the 2026 Cats awards, is that the two young people are unknown to each other. Their stories play out independently, except for the significant moment when they cross, one inadvertently helping the other at the point of greatest need. It is built with the elegance of a figure of eight.

A joint venture by the Byre theatre, Pitlochry Festival theatre and the Traverse, it is punchily performed by Geddes and Mackay, who help narrate each other’s stories to create the illusion of their happening at the same time. She plays his tyrannical head chef, while he plays her opinionated tutor, the two revelling in their malevolent caricatures in Sally Reid’s buoyant production.

This lightness of touch leavens the play’s serious intent. When Esme is suffering from debilitating inertia, still in bed at 3pm, Harris is the partying carouser with money to burn. The roles are reversed as the play loops round on itself, illustrating the fragility of our emotional health without overstating the case. It is a clever piece of writing, brisk and confident, portraying isolation even as it celebrates the power of mutual support.

At Traverse theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 August
