Tour de France Femmes: Vollering’s late escape for yellow leaves Niewiadoma fuming

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 17:09:14 GMT

Victory on penultimate stage secures eight-second lead

Previous leader claims she was blocked by rival’s team

Demi Vollering took the overall lead from Kasia Niewiadoma in the Tour de France Femmes with a vicious attack in the hills behind Nice to lead the race by eight seconds from the 2024 winner, with just one stage remaining.

“It’s very special to be back in yellow,” Vollering, leader of French team FDJ United-Suez said. “Tomorrow I start in yellow and I will do everything in my power to keep it. So much can happen – it’s still a big fight.”

It was Vollering’s fifth stage victory in the Tour Femmes and also her fifth yellow jersey and came after she had regretted failing to mount a meaningful pursuit of Niewiadoma on Friday’s summit finish to Mont Ventoux.

Vollering took the initiative on the final climb of the Cote de la Ginestière and after a breakneck descent, extended her lead on the long straight road to the finish on the Promenade des Anglais in Nice.

But Niewiadoma was critical of the tactics of Vollering’s team. “I was annoyed at the beginning of the climb because Gery, on purpose, just blocked me to the barriers where I had to stop pedalling,” she said of Célia Gery, Vollering’s teammate.

“They should compete fair play and not look to block me on the barriers because it is so childish. I lost all the respect for them for that.” Vollering responded by saying she had not seen the incident, which was studied at length by race commissaires after the stage. “I didn’t see anything, I just saw what was in front of me,” she said. “It happened behind me. I don’t have eyes in the back of my head. Celia probably didn’t see Kasia and I’m sure she didn’t do it on purpose. I’m sure Kasia knows deep in her heart that those kinds of things just happen sometimes in racing. It’s the shit part of racing.”

While the critical attacks came in the suburbs of Nice, the stage was animated by a two-rider breakaway, featuring Breton rider Maëva Squiban and Loes Adegeest, of the Netherlands.

The duo might have hoped to remain clear to the finish, but Squiban, winner of two stages in last year’s race, crashed on a left-hand bend on the descent of the Côte de Colomars and howling in pain, was swallowed up the peloton.

That left her former companion riding alone at the front of the Tour, but her escape ended nine kilometres from the finish as Vollering’s team attacked the bends leading to the Cote de la Ginestière.

It was there that Vollering attacked, and while Niewiadoma stuck to the task, she lost ground in the final cruel metres of the short steep climb.

Now only eight seconds separate the pair. Every second will count in Sunday’s final stage of the Tour, based around Nice, which takes in four climbs of the Col d’Eze, overlooking the corniche roads of Villefranche-sur-Mer.

The rivalry between Vollering and Niewiadoma goes back to the 2024 Tour, when the Dutch rider lost to the Pole by just four seconds, the narrowest margin of defeat in the history of any Tour de France, after an epic duel to Alpe d’Huez.

Meanwhile, French favourite Pauline Ferrand-Prévot’s title defence came to a predictable end. From her listless performance in the stage four time trial, to her major losses of time on Mont Brouilly and Mont Ventoux, her performance has been a stark contrast to that of a year ago.

The Olympic gold medallist’s exit from the race was sudden and dramatic. Her bike was prepared and readied outside the Visma Lease-a-bike team bus at the start of stage eight in Sisteron, when she was reported by French TV crews to have told team staff “I can’t do it, I can’t do it.”

Ferrand-Prévot’s vulnerability was evident as early as stage three, something her trainer, Rutger Tijssen, acknowledged.

OpenAI to pause some work on AI model Astra due to security concerns

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 17:00:41 GMT

Agent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacks

OpenAI will pause some work on an artificial intelligence model because of security concerns, the company stated on Friday, following a series of incidents in which AI agents have escaped containment.

The company had evaluated the agent, Astra, and found “significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity”, which had moved to a “critical” threshold where it can find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, or devise and execute cyber-attacks when given only a “high level desired goal”.

OpenAI stated that the model was not involved in an incident in which one of its AI agents went rogue during a test, accessed the open web and hacked a startup, Hugging Face. The company discovered other instances in which autonomous agents had escaped containment, Reuters reported in July.

The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them. Still, critics of the AI industry have warned that such disclosures from OpenAI and its competitors Anthropic and Meta could be designed to generate hype about the technology’s power and thus spur additional interest from investors.

To prevent potential rogue behavior from AI agents, OpenAI is “implementing stricter security controls for higher-capability models and associated activities, including isolated testing environments, restricted network and tool access”, the company’s blogpost stated. It will also install “enhanced model weight protections and encryption, additional monitoring and detection capabilities”.

The company will pause internal activities involving Astra that do not meet these new requirements.

“We’re committed to working alongside governments, safety institutes, and civil society to ensure that the frontier capabilities of models like Astra, and those that follow, are deployed responsibly and broadly for the benefit of all humanity,” the company stated.

Meta also disclosed this week that one of its models hacked another company during cybersecurity testing. And the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) announced on 4 August that agents powered by OpenAI and Anthropic had sent targeted emails to software developers in an attempt to pass a cyber challenge.

“These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world,” the institute stated in a blogpost.

The organisation cautioned that the models’ sending of harmful software was not a case of a “model escaping its secure test environment” but rather that the group had intentionally permitted internet access to “best assess the maximum capability of models”.

Still, the “behaviour was possible, sustained and new; that alone warrants attention”, the AISI said.

The reports emerged while the Trump administration was finalizing a framework on how to test AI models for safety and cybersecurity risks. OpenAI and Anthropic, which have increased competition from China and other tech firms, have argued that open-source models, meaning those that allow anyone to see and modify the underlying program code, pose a security risk and pushed for additional federal regulations on them.

West Ham sink Pompey in Carabao Cup as Sullivan ignores advice to stay away

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 16:38:20 GMT

In an unseasonable black bomber jacket, with heavy duty company beside him, David Sullivan took his seat. Against the advice of the stadium’s operators, unbowed by serious allegations placed against his name and the weight of public opinion, West Ham’s major shareholder, the former co-chair, sat with arms crossed, always conspicuous by his presence.

By beating Portsmouth in relative comfort, West Ham, the club where Sullivan’s name is no longer above the door, had secured a heartening Carabao Cup passage to the second round. There, they will be reunited with their former Premier League peers. The serious Championship business begins next Sunday at Burnley. Whether Sullivan travels north for that remains to be seen. It cannot be ruled out.

“Neither me nor the players,” said Nuno Espírito Santo when asked about the effect of the uninvited guest’s presence. “We’ll focus on the pitch. The noise that comes from outside cannot distract at all; we’re going to find a lot of noise. We focus on the game, they do their job, they did it well.”

Before kick-off, the London Stadium big screen showed a “countdown to walkout”, referring to the players’ arrival rather than to fans deserting the scene in protest. This being West Ham in 2026, any confusion would be understandable. Taking previous mutinies into account, and despite a summer of intrigue and anger, there were surprisingly few audible or visible signs of insurrection as season 2026-27 began, and an extended 90 minutes was played out.

Even with Sullivan’s arrival expected, the gate to the directors’ car park did not stage a welcoming committee, the lanes around the London Stadium quiet. Protests there have been a regular sight, targeting Sullivan and his departed associate Karren Brady.

Even once Sullivan’s presence was confirmed there was nothing resembling the barracking of last season. Instead, the loudest boos of the first half came at a hydration break at its midway point, with an odd choice of 90s rave musical accompaniment. The legacy of a North American World Cup continues to darken.

Perhaps still-searing temperatures and a dose of early optimism had doused the fires raging when the Hammers’ drop was confirmed in May. Time-served Irons know plenty about relegation; their club has dropped down each decade since the 1970s; West Ham heritage indeed.

The kick-off chorus of I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles drowned out the Pompey Chimes ringing out from 9,000 away fans. As is usual at the London Stadium, the visiting contingent decried their surroundings and the Faustian pact struck for West Ham’s tenancy.

Football has rarely been in focus during West Ham’s summer of tumult, boardroom battles after Sullivan’s defenestration. So what of football? Carabao Cup Saturday served as a decent dry run for their attempt at a promotion campaign. The new West Ham closely resembled the former West Ham, though shorn of the £151m worth of player sales that took in Mateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville and Freddie Potts. Joël Veltman, the sole summer signing so far, came on with three minutes left.

In midfield, Edson Álvarez, who spent last season on loan to Fenerbahce, lined up alongside Lewis Orford, a 20-year-old it is hoped can follow the path of Frank Lampard, Michael Carrick and Mark Noble, the latter a mentor, into becoming a first-team regular. His was a successful introduction into the first team.

“The energy of the young players is really really important for us,” said Nuno. “It’s up to us to develop the young academy players. That’s the vision for the future.”

The torpor of a first 30 minutes of little footballing consequence was broken by a Portsmouth goal, scored by Adrian Segecic, via a deflection off Maximilian Kilman, an expensive purchase far too regularly on the crime scene.

It took 10 minutes for West Ham to awaken before Mohamadou Kanté’s pirouetting feint laid up Taty Castellanos to equalise. Mere moments later, Jarrod Bowen, the club captain staying on to lead his club back up, a rare adult in the room last season, lashed in their second. “Jarrod shows us every day his commitment,” said Nuno.

The goals evidenced a quality that ought to guide the club back to the Premier League with some comfort, though nothing should be taken for granted. “If you give them a slight opening they’re going to take it,” said the Portsmouth manager, John Mousinho.

Sullivan kept any celebrations to himself and returned for a second half that began with Castellanos nodding in Bowen’s cross. An afternoon that might have descended into a familiar seething pit of rage and resentment now offered grounds for optimism. Though just beyond the hour, a chorus of “Stand up if you hate the board”.

If Sullivan is no longer a board member he was its undoubted target. He has turned many a deaf ear down the years and continues to do so.

One of UK’s best fossil collections sold overseas in ‘loss to the nation’

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 16:00:02 GMT

Exclusive: Lack of funds left British museums unable pay eight-figure sum for collection, which went to Abu Dhabi institution

One of the most important collections of UK Jurassic fossils ever compiled has been sold to a museum in Abu Dhabi, the Guardian can reveal, in what British experts have described as a loss for the nation.

The collection, which was amassed by a private fossil collector, consisted of 318 specimens, including ichthyosaurs, fish and crustaceans among other creatures, some of which could be new species.

The fossils were initially offered for purchase to the Natural History Museum (NHM) in London and to Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales) for what was described by one source as an “eight-figure sum”.

Neither institution bought the collection, with both citing a lack of funding. An email seen by the Guardian suggested the NHM had “no money at all” for acquisitions.

One curator said that while there had long been a hope that the collection could be kept in the UK, it also posed issues around storage space, curatorial time and packaging materials.

“I don’t blame the collectors at all. That’s all they can do. They can’t sit on these things forever,” the curator said, adding that the issue was expected to occur again and again as collectors get older and look for a suitable home for their life’s work.

“Whose responsibility is it to fund our heritage and the preservation of our heritage? Because otherwise it could get lost,” they added.

The extensive collection is understood to come from a sequence of rocks known as the Lower Lias, from Lyme Regis, Charmouth, and the south-west of the UK.

It was compiled by Chris Moore, a private Dorset-based collector with experience of hunting fossils in the area. In emails seen by the Guardian the collection is described as “stunning”.

Some countries, including Mongolia and Brazil, consider all fossils found in those countries in recent decades to be property of the state – a situation that has led to international disputes over repatriation of fossils housed abroad. However, this is not the case in the UK.

Richard Butler, a professor of palaebiology at the University of Birmingham who was not involved in the sale, said the collection was of national significance. “This is one of the most important collections of fossils ever made on the world-famous Jurassic Coast of Dorset. It would have been wonderful to see these fossils on display and engaging the public in a UK museum.”

He added: “This sale raises important questions about whether more should be done to preserve important and irreplaceable natural heritage such as this for the benefit of the UK public.”

In the United Arab Emirates, the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi confirmed it had bought a collection from Moore, which went on display in November 2025. A spokesperson for the museum said the Lower Jurassic rocks of the UK preserved some of the best examples of marine life from when what is now the Dorset coast was roughly at the same latitude as north Africa.

“All natural history museums around the world tell this story, often using fossils from multiple countries to help narrate their journey through time. If we are to tell a 4.2bn-year story of the evolution of life on Earth, all museums must travel both spatially and temporally with their collections,” the spokesperson said.

“A large majority of the Chris Moore collection is already on public display in the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi in the Mesozoic Gallery (Age of Dinosaurs Gallery).”

Lyme Regis is part of the Jurassic Coast, a Unesco world heritage site, that is rich with fossils that date back to between 200m and 145m years ago. The area has a long history of private fossil collecting, with notable figures including Mary Anning – a pioneering palaeontologist and fossil dealer whose triumphs included the discovery of the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaurus in 1823.

While approaches vary across the UK nations, modern fossil collectors along England’s Jurassic Coast are encouraged to follow the west Dorset fossil collecting code and the Undercliffs national nature reserve fossil collecting code.

Fossils initially belong to the owner of the land on which they are found, legal ownership is typical transferred to collectors who adhere to such codes and recording schemes – a situation that reflects the valuable role collectors are deemed to have in finding fossils that might otherwise never be recovered.

But while highly valuable archeological finds turned up by activities such as metal detecting can be classified as treasure – and therefore must be reported to the relevant authorities within 14 days of discovery – the same is not true for fossils, even those deemed to be key scientifically important fossils, known as category 1.

According to the west Dorset fossil collecting code of conduct, collectors “who intend to sell or otherwise dispose of their category 1 specimens must first offer them to UK registered museums for a period of six months. If no purchase has been agreed by this time, the collector will be free to offer the specimen elsewhere.”

However, such codes are not legally binding and even if followed, as Moore did, fossils found in the UK can be sold by collectors to private individuals, museums or other buyers – including those overseas. Moore was approached for comment.

According to the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DDCMS), only objects that are over 50 years old and are manufactured or produced require an individual cultural property export licence, and there are no export requirements specific to the sale of fossils.

A quick search of online marketplaces reveals a plethora of fossils, with small ammonites selling for as little as a few pounds.

But some fossils can also fetch colossal sums: in 2020, Stan the T rex, now also housed at the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, was sold for a then record-breaking $31.8m (£23.6m), while in July this year another T rex skeleton nicknamed Gus was sold at Sotheby’s for $50.1m.

These figures are far beyond the budget of most museums, with such specimens instead snapped up by private buyers – including business people and celebrities. Among those known to have bought dinosaur fossils are the actors Leonardo DiCaprio, Nicolas Cage and Russell Crowe – although Cage later returned the rare dinosaur skull he had bought to Mongolia, after it emerged it had been illegally removed from the country.

Fossils have also become popular on social media, with hunters using platforms such as TikTok to share videos of themselves cracking open rocks in a “fossil or no fossil?” reveal. Some accounts have several million followers.

Finding a fossil is only the first step on the road to a sale: as the NHM in London notes, painstaking mechanical and chemical preparation is needed to turn it one into a museum-grade exhibit. Only dedicated fossil hunters have the tools and skills to prepare fossils – and Moore is among them.

Many experts support the status quo for fossil collecting and sales, arguing that a ban on collecting would mean many important specimens would remain undiscovered and could result in a black-market for fossils – rather than allowing collectors to work with academics.

There is no suggestion the sale of the Moore collection to the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi has broken any rules.

Yet Dr Erin Maxwell, an expert in Early Jurassic marine vertebrates based at the State Museum of Natural History in Stuttgart said the sale was a blow. “Such a sale in my opinion represents a loss to the UK, as fossils represent part of the natural [or] cultural heritage of the region and country from which they originate.

“The loss is somewhat offset by the fact that these fossils are going to a museum rather than into the collection of a wealthy individual.”

Maxwell added that there were other options for countries such as the UK where fossils are not automatically considered property of the state.

“I think it is important for the state to have the right of first refusal on acquiring the collection on an at-cost basis prior to export – rather than the currently grossly inflated market price,” she said. “However, if the state declines, then sale to a foreign museum is a best-case scenario.”

Phil Davidson, a palaeontologist at Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre in Dorset, said the priority was that fossil specimens of key scientific interest were in public collections, such as museums, so they could be described by teams of international experts, noting most scientific journals did not allow specimens to be described if they were within a private collection.

“All the researchers I have talked to have said the same thing: the location of where the museum collection is housed is secondary,” Davidson said.

“Countless specimens of scientific importance are housed outside their country of origin. Often this was because the specific researchers are based in other countries, or that they do not have the capacity or need to focus on other pressing priorities”.

Davidson also stressed the importance of keeping the Moore collection together, adding the specimens come from a world heritage site “and this heritage is for everyone and not limited to lines on a map”.

Britain’s Jurassic gold rush: the fossil hunters chasing fortunes on Dorset’s beaches

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 16:00:01 GMT

Social media and soaring prices are fuelling a fossil-hunting boom, with rare discoveries worth thousands of pounds

Bent double at the waist, Martin Curtis combs a stretch of a Dorset beach with the concentration of a man searching for a lost cufflink or wedding ring.

The search is meticulous – and with good reason. What he hopes to find could be far more valuable than an errant piece of jewellery. Curtis is searching instead for the telltale spiral of an ammonite, the star-shaped rod of a crinoid or rocks of a particular shape and colour that suggests there is something very special inside. He is hunting fossils.

Along Charmouth beach and elsewhere on the Jurassic Coast, families with children, seasoned collectors and lone day-trippers peer intently at the ground in search of traces of creatures that lived 190m years ago. While some are here for fun, a growing number are here for business.

That growing professional interest reflects the rising popularity and value of Jurassic fossils, creating a thriving marketplace that has made some collectors social media celebrities and others very wealthy.

A Guardian investigation this week revealed that one of Britain’s most significant collections of Jurassic fossils was recently sold to a museum in Abu Dhabi for what is believed to be an eight-figure sum.

The collection, amassed by the private fossil collector Chris Moore, included 318 specimens, some of which may represent species previously unknown to science. The sale was described by some experts as a loss for the nation.

Yet while British museums lacked the funds to acquire Moore’s collection, wealthy institutions in the Gulf did not. For the fossil hunters combing Charmouth beach, it is another reason to scrutinise every promising item of unusual shape, colour and texture.

Fossil hunting – and the industry that has grown around it – is not a modern pursuit. Perhaps England’s best-known fossil hunter and dealer, Mary Anning, was born at nearby Lyme Regis in 1799 and made breathtaking discoveries along this coastline, including the first complete plesiosaur skeleton – a huge long-necked marine reptile that lived during the Jurassic period before becoming extinct alongside most dinosaurs 66m years ago.

Anning has not been forgotten. Her name and image are everywhere, from information boards along the seafront to the colourful Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre overlooking the beach. Here, fossil collecting is largely encouraged.

“On the rapidly eroding West Dorset coast, fossil collecting is essential if specimens, some of which may be of great scientific value, are to be saved from damage or destruction by the sea,” notes the West Dorset fossil collecting code of conduct.

And just as Anning sold many of her discoveries, fossils are still bought and sold today. Downstairs is a shop where small ammonites can be picked up for a few pounds, while larger specimens, painstakingly prepared within their surrounding rock, sell for several hundred. Provided hunters follow the code of conduct, ownership of fossils passes to the finder.

“Professional collectors have the most time, are able to react quickly to events that uncover the fossils – ie: storms and landslides – and have a great deal of local knowledge. But they need to sell their finds in order to earn a living,” the code notes.

It is easy to understand how fossil hunting becomes addictive. As we comb the beach, Curtis points to a smooth, brown, bullet-shaped object: the fossilised remains of a squid-like creature known as a belemnite.

“That belemnite’s 190m years old. And we are the only three people to ever see that creature,” he says.

A little later, I spot a sparkling curve nestled among the pebbles and prise out a tiny ammonite, glittering with iron pyrite. It is the size of a penny and, though it is probably worth very little, I feel as if I have won the lottery.

As a professional guide and fossil hunter, Curtis knows these beaches intimately. “I spent a lot of my childhood on the beach with my father, finding fossils a bit further down the coast that way in Kimmeridge,” he says.

As an adult, he returned to the coastline while caring for his eldest daughter. “I could take her out on the beach, walk along for two hours looking for fossils [while she was] fast asleep in the backpack,” he says.

He later turned his hobby into a business, using his mountain leader qualifications to run guided fossil walks and selling specimens he has painstakingly revealed from the surrounding rock using air chisels and iron-powder air abrasion.

“I’m a big ammonite fan. They are my favourite fossils, and I’ve got loads of rocks at home with some really nice big special ammonites in, waiting to be prepared,” he says.

Progressing along the beach, we pass the remnants of huge mudslides, where it is clear there are many for whom fossil collecting is a more than a casual pastime. Hammers are swung, chunks of sticky mud broken apart and carefully examined. This is fossil hunting in earnest.

Curtis says TikTok and Instagram have transformed the activity in recent years. Social media is awash with videos of fossil hunters cracking open rocks on Britain’s beaches.

“It’s really changed the scope of fossil hunting down here. It’s now making it a lot harder because it’s introducing a lot more people to fossil hunting. I’ve been running walks here for 10 years now and the change [during that time] is quite significant,” he says, adding that the influx of fossil hunters during Covid staycations accelerated the trend.

Curtis believes parts of the coastline are being over-collected. “The erosion rate is struggling to keep up with the amount of people on the beach, because of the conditions,” he says, noting that fresh material is not being exposed quickly enough. And when new material does appear, word spreads quickly on social media. “So even on a[good day], there’s going to be twice as many people here.”

Competition among professional fossil hunters is intense, with experts keeping an eye on one another as they inspect new falls and vie for the finest discoveries. It is perhaps not surprising that rare finds or beautifully prepared specimens can command substantial sums.

“As fossil hunters, [when] we come to the beach, we are collecting to try to earn money. Maybe selling a few bits … online. But generally, we are collecting for ourselves. And if we find anything good, we keep it,” Curtis says.

Some fossil hunters have amassed remarkable collections. Figures such as Moore have become big names in the fossil-hunting world, with his specimens displayed in museums locally and beyond, and counting David Attenborough among his friends.

The recent sale has cemented Moore’s status as one of the Jurassic Coast’s leading collectors. But his collection is unlikely to be the last to leave Britain. As the country’s professional fossil hunters grow older, more private collections are likely to be in need of new homes.

Perhaps unsurprisingly for a man used to handling relics from millennia gone-by, Curtis is philosophical about his friend’s collection being sold overseas. “It’s always sad when things like that go abroad” said Curtis, adding that Moore had worked hard on his collection. “The key thing is it’s being enjoyed by someone,” he said. “It’s all well and good having a good collection, but it’s no good stuck in a box somewhere.”

There is a striking irony here. The remains of creatures that have been hidden in these shores for 190m years are now being sold to countries whose modern wealth is derived from plumbing their own oily depths.

Yet down on the beach in Dorset, the international marketplace feels a long way away. For Curtis, size isn’t everything – it’s all about the next swirl in the sand. “[A discovery] doesn’t have to be big. It just generally needs to be special. And the more you get into fossil hunting, the fussier you become,” he says.

Where in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse?

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 15:08:31 GMT

When, where and how to get the optimal view of the first solar eclipse to be visible across the country this century

For the first time this century, people across the UK will be able to see an almost total solar eclipse in the evening sky on Wednesday.

A solar eclipse occurs when the moon moves between the sun and the Earth, blocking the sun’s light either partly or fully. This year, people in the UK and Ireland will see 90-96% of the sun covered by the moon for the first time since 1999 – and it’s their last chance until 2081.

Across north-western Europe, people will see about 88-95% coverage, while spectators in parts of Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain will see a total eclipse for up to two minutes and 18 seconds in duration.

In the UK, viewers in the west will see the most of the sun obscured: 95% in Plymouth, 93.2% in Cardiff and 93.1% in Belfast. Spectators in Manchester will see 91.9% and Londoners will catch 91.4%. Farther north and east people will see smaller proportions, with Edinburgh at 90.7%, Newcastle at 90.2%. Shetland will have the lowest coverage at 88%.

Royal Observatory Greenwich astronomer Jess Lee said that these are small differences, and all “will still be impressive sights”. She recommended finding hills with clear views to the west, for example Parliament Hill, Alexandra Palace or Primrose Hill in London, or rooftop venues.

Because the eclipse takes place in August, there’s a stronger chance of clear skies. Tom Morgan, a Met Office meteorologist, said it was too early to be confident, but “given the summer we’ve had a lot of the UK will have reasonable viewing conditions”.

At present, there is a higher risk of thick cloud and rain in Scotland and Northern Ireland, while the clearest skies are likely to be towards the south and the east of the UK. “For many it’ll be quite a spectacular and rare event,” he said.

For Scotland’s astronomer royal, Catherine Heymans, keeping an eye on the clouds is the secret to scoring the best view, since these could partly or entirely obscure the eclipse. “I plan to check the Met Office’s fantastic online cloud cover forecast as we get closer to the day. I’m ready to hop on a train north, south, east or west to find some cloud-free skies,” she said.

Getting to a high point with a clear view of the horizon also helps. “I’d recommend a dress rehearsal in the days before. If you can’t see the sun from your planned viewing spot at 7.30pm because your view is blocked by a hill or a house, then you’ll want to find yourself a different location for the real event,” Heymans added.

The most important thing, she stressed, is to wear eclipse glasses and avoid looking directly at the sun.

During an eclipse, the sun appears dimmer, making it easier to look at directly. However, solar radiation can still reach and damage the retina, often without causing any pain, so viewers may not realise harm is occurring until it’s too late.

Following the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reported about 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching the eclipse.

The UK Health Security Agency advises that there are two safe approaches: specialist eclipse viewers or indirect viewing methods.

Eclipse glasses or handheld solar viewers must be genuine and sold by a reputable retailer, and should have specially designed filters that meet the international safety standard ISO 12312-2:2015(E), and no scratches, tearing or damage to the lens. Old pairs may not be reusable and sunglasses should never be used.

Indirect view methods include viewing the sun’s image projected through a colander or the gaps between tree leaves on to white paper, or using a pinhole pierced in one sheet of card and projected on to another.

Sarah Crowther, an astronomer at the University of Manchester, said it was important to remember that the solar eclipse would take place at different times across the UK.

It starts at about 6.08pm in Edinburgh and Glasgow, 6.10pm in Belfast, 6.13pm in Manchester and Liverpool, 6.15pm in Birmingham, 6.17pm in London and 6.18pm in Cornwall. Maximum eclipse follows roughly an hour later, ending about 8pm.

People might observe the surrounding area going quiet during the solar eclipse, “when animals think it is night because it is darker, which gives a sense of calm. And then there’s an awakening as it gets light again, birds think it is dawn so there could be a dawn chorus,” said Crowther.

She added: “I think many people feel a sense of awe when they see an eclipse. It can put the vast scales of the solar system into some kind of perspective.”

Private pensions are a publicly subsidised gift to the wealthy

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 15:00:48 GMT

John Healey should equalise the tax break on pension savings to stop inequalities from widening

Private pensions are a privilege for the lucky few and a curse for everyone else. Sold as a saviour for what would otherwise be a ruinous old age, they have become pernicious financial vehicles that allow an older generation to hoodwink younger generations, who also seek security in their latter years.

To make matters worse, saving by the better off is enhanced by state subsidies, widening the divide between rich and poor in retirement while driving a wedge between the generations.

As John Healey scours the public finances for ways to boost spending on defence, social care (and the rest) before the autumn budget, he should put considering equalising the tax break on pension savings top of his list.

Do standard-rate taxpayers know that they get half the subsidy for pension saving that higher-rate taxpayers receive? Probably not.

Official figures published last month show that the cost of income tax relief on pensions soared from £48bn in 2022-23 to £60bn in 2024-25, an increase of a quarter in just two years. About £40bn is swallowed up by higher-rate taxpayers. That’s because higher earners get a 40% tax break while everyone else gets 20%.

At the heart of the problem, and why Healey will find it difficult to confront, is the concept of retirement itself, the purpose of which has changed dramatically over the past 80 years.

Once a safety net for later life when workers and carers were too infirm or too ill to continue caring or working, it has become something that should involve three, four or five holidays a year, and last for 35 years or more. It’s why many of the people standing outside pubs on a Thursday evening – a ritual Westminster council would ban – are grey heads celebrating their early retirement, and a long one to boot.

Someone aged 60 in the UK will live, on average, to 84 and have a 33% chance of living to 90, according to the Office for National Statistics’ life expectancy calculator. And that predicted lifespan is longer the more affluent you are.

There is a growth industry among consultants who not only plan the finances of those who retire with big pension pots, but also design a life for those who were senior in some way in the latter part of their working life and feel lost without anything to do.

While many people will devote their retirement to charity work or looking after children, for too many living the retirement dream is to inhabit a comfortable cocoon. Why? Because those who have saved deserve another entire lifetime of R&R after so much hard graft, they say.

Of course, those people who have actually grafted tend to have meagre pension provision. White-collar workers, and especially those in management or aged over 50, have the best of it.

The scandal of baby boomers and gen Xers hoarding their pension savings can be seen in the industrial disputes of the 2010s, when almost every strike was called to defend the pensions of older workers.

Shop stewards, mostly over the age of 50, would negotiate deals with managers in a similar age bracket to secure guaranteed defined benefit pensions for themselves while younger workers and new joiners were offered the much cheaper, stock market-dependent defined contribution schemes.

Over time, these shop stewards and their contemporaries on both sides of the management divide have walked off into the sunset, taking their gold-plated pensions with them.

It is damaging to the economy when so many experienced and skilled workers prefer buying an even bigger SUV and a cruise ship holiday to finding a way to contribute into their old age, at least while they have their health. This is especially true in a society like the UK where, since Nigel Lawson’s reforms in the 1980s, pension provision is largely privatised.

Global studies of state pensions show they encourage workers to stay employed for longer, either because the payout is too low to sustain a decent standard of living, or because governments have “moved the goalposts” and delayed the state pension age.

However, as the state pension has faded into insignificance for many better-off workers, the incentive changes. A defined benefit scheme, more commonly referred to as a final salary pension, has a default retirement age of 60 and anyone who has accrued all their rights has little incentive to carry on.

Analysis by the Institute for Fiscal Studies shows that those people with the lowest and highest wealth are least likely to be in work aged 65; the lowest due mainly to ill health and a lack of skills, the better off because they have lucked out with their pensions.

Chief among the winners these days – those with guaranteed pensions linked to their salary rather than to the stock market – are public sector workers. They regularly attended retirement parties for colleagues who think it reasonable to retire at 60 after 35 years of office life with a pension lasting another 35, believing the failed economics of this outcome is someone else’s problem.

Professional baby boomers may have escaped with their winnings to live the high life, but Healey can stop gen Xers perpetrating the same heist. Of course there will be complaints. But the judges, doctors, marketing executives and company directors who will shout loudest should ask themselves why 40% of their pension pot should be provided by other taxpayers, most of whom are much poorer than they are.

Nicola Sturgeon ‘has not spoken to’ estranged husband, Peter Murrell, since he was jailed

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 14:50:25 GMT

Scotland’s former first minister says she will not visit Murrell in prison, where he is serving five-year sentence for embezzling SNP funds

Nicola Surgeon has said she will not visit her estranged husband, Peter Murrell, in prison, has stopped speaking to him and views herself as a “mug” for worrying about his wellbeing and mental health earlier this year.

During a podcast recording at the Edinburgh festival fringe, Scotland’s former first minister said Murrell had lied to her until the day he pleaded guilty to embezzling more than £400,000 from the Scottish National party.

He was imprisoned for five years in June, and Sturgeon revealed she had not spoken to him since then. She told the broadcaster Iain Dale she had only discovered Murrell was due to plead guilty a week before he appeared in court.

She later found out he had been negotiating his plea for months.

“[That] hit me like a tonne of bricks,” she said. “He was still lying to me right up until the day he pled guilty.”

She added: “He was very isolated over that period, he very rarely left the house, he wasn’t communicative, I was a bit worried about his wellbeing and his mental health.

“And then, now I think: ‘What a mug, why were you worried about him?’ He didn’t worry about me. He didn’t worry at all about what he was doing.

“What he has subjected me to is beyond anything I could ever have comprehended. I don’t understand why he did it, he had no need to do it. I don’t think I will ever understand his motivations.

“But whatever that motivation was, he could not have stopped and ever thought about me. But I was, until recently, still worrying about him.”

Asked if she would visit him in prison, Sturgeon replied: “No. I’m not going to speak to him, I’m not going to visit him.”

The former first minister said that when Murrell was in court she was still finding out details of the purchases he had made using party funds.

“Over the years, he never really levelled with me,” she said. “The day he pled guilty, I was still learning about some of the detail of what he had done for the first time. I suddenly realised I had been living with somebody that I never really knew properly.

“That’s something for me to come to terms with, and I don’t think I’m there yet, but also for my family to come to terms with. It’s a really difficult process.”

Murrell, 61, spent the money on items including a motorhome, a Jaguar SUV and a VW Golf, boutique cosmetics, iPads and a pair of Lalique Feuilles salt and pepper grinders worth £2,618.

Sturgeon, 55, has consistently denied knowledge of his crimes, which spanned the years 2010 to 2022, and was not charged after a police investigation.

She has previously said she made an error of judgment by keeping Murrell on as SNP chief executive when she became party leader in November 2014, but refused to apologise for his crimes and denied ever “consciously” seeing the motorhome he bought and stored at her mother-in-law’s house.

‘Old racist wine in a new bottle’: Black academics respond to Jason Arday affair

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 13:00:46 GMT

Figures in higher education feel double standards are being used to delegitimise work of minority groups

“Jason has to take responsibility for what he did. But when a white person makes mistakes, it’s just a story about them as an individual. When a Black person makes a mistake, it’s treated as collective – and used to undermine the very principle that Black people should be in these spaces,” one Black academic said this week, describing the impact of Jason Arday’s case on his peers.

Arday, who was the University of Cambridge’s youngest Black professor when appointed in 2023, stepped down this week amid allegations of plagiarism and embellishing his CV.

As well as allegations about his academic credentials, there have been questions raised about his claimed sporting achievements, his charity work and some of the abuse he says he received. Arday, 41, has admitted “mistakes”, but says he has been falsely framed as “this kind of liar and fantasist”.

Whatever the truth of the claims, days of reporting describing sociologist Arday as a “diversity poster boy” have had a chilling effect on the UK’s Black academics, already demoralised by the impact of cuts on Black scholarship. Many compared the response to the academic criticism with accusations against white academics that have passed with little fanfare.

While views among Arday’s peers vary on the gravity of the accusations about his academic work – no formal investigation to date has found him guilty of plagiarism – opinion is united that Arday’s story has provoked a rightwing backlash against Black progress in academia and public life.

“I think there’s a real question about whether these spaces are safe for us and whether we just have to start doing this outside universities,” says Kehinde Andrews, who was the first Black Studies professor in the UK but was recently made redundant from Birmingham City University.

Andrews added: “No matter how many cracks have appeared in [Arday’s] CV, it doesn’t change the fact that this is a dedicated, coordinated smear campaign from the right, based on the premise that Black people should not be at Cambridge. There’s so many other things that happen in higher education that are never discussed.”

Andrews believes there were “problems with some of [Arday’s] scholarship,” but that they stopped short of plagiarism.

For the eminent sociologist Paul Gilroy, responsibility for the row lies with the “culture warriors” who appointed Arday, as well as “racist critics” – and comes at a critical time for the sector.

“Reckoning with Jason Arday and his impact-chasing enablers should not be allowed to obscure the vicious, irrational cuts to humanities that are wrecking UK universities,” Gilroy added.

“The unthinking culture warriors who have supported [Arday] unconditionally share responsibility with his racist critics for making life harder for Black academics and dragging UK higher education deeper into the mire.”

Few black academics are happy to speak about Arday’s case publicly. One academic said: “I can’t say anything on the record or I’ll be the right’s next target. The [right] have set their sights on pushing Black people out from all these institutions.

“There’s a white Cambridge academic who was accused of plagiarising a student’s work, kept his job and didn’t receive the same amount of media attention.”

The row erupted this month after another academic – self-defined “race realist” Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 – alleged he had found plagiarism in Arday’s work. Cofnas had previously suggested in a blogpost that, in a meritocracy, there would be “close to zero” Black professors at Harvard.

“It’s not just about Black people – any minoritised group, our success is generally seen as not being genuine,” said one academic, speaking anonymously.

“[The row] will make the small number of Black people in the field feel much more vulnerable. It will give licence for a while to people who don’t want Black people in the academic space and it may give pause to people who want to redress the massive [racial] imbalance in academia.

“But it’s a mistake to think of any of this as a meritocracy – there’s lots of people in academia who don’t deserve to be where they are, and there’s lots of people who should be more advanced in their careers than they are.”

Andrews said he was setting up an independent Black Studies centre, describing the university sector as “toxic”.

“Academia is set up so that there’s these few places and we’re all fighting over scraps to get into these places,” he said. “It might just be time to say, let’s do it ourselves and let’s not keep relying on these institutions.”

But while Arday’s case – and cuts to the humanities – negatively affect morale, many academics emphasised the proud history of Black scholarship, insisting the Arday affair must not be allowed to tarnish it.

“Black British academics – like Stuart Hall, Paul Gilroy, Hazel Carby and Isaac Julien – punch way above their weight globally. The idea that this one incident in some way reflects Black British academia in general is bonkers,” one academic said.

“There’s a bunch of people out there who think Black people are less intelligent than white people, and that the only way they can get anywhere is by being forced into situations that they are unqualified for. For those people, being Black is the definition of being unqualified. It’s an old racist wine in a new bottle.”

Rest assured, the new CDC director thinks ‘abortion surveillance’ is essential

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 12:00:46 GMT

An exchange between Dr Erica Schwartz and Senator Josh Hawley during her confirmation hearing is alarming

Robert F Kennedy Jr’s new cooking show isn’t the only big news out of the public health world this week. On Wednesday, Dr Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), making her the first Black woman to hold the position. This is the first time in almost a year that the agency has had a permanent leader; the previous director, Susan Monarez, only lasted 29 days before she was ousted for butting heads with RFK about US vaccine policies. Translation: she was a little too keen on following accepted science for the Trump administration.

So is Schwartz an RFK-approved vaccine skeptic who thinks you can cure cancer by praying to trees? Surprisingly: no. Schwartz, who served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term, actually has government experience and a public health background. During her confirmation hearing in July, she walked a careful tightrope when asked about her stance towards vaccines. Schwartz said she “will never betray the science” but also dodged questions about how she would handle pressure from Kennedy.

But don’t breathe a sigh of relief quite yet. During that same confirmation hearing, Schwartz made some chilling remarks about abortion surveillance when quizzed on the issue by Missouri senator Josh Hawley, an anti-abortion lawmaker who wants to ban the abortion pill mifepristone nationwide.

“The CDC collects data on abortions that are committed in the United States of America through a system called the Abortion Reporting System,” Hawley said when asking Schwartz whether she would commit to collecting detailed data on abortions. “This system is voluntary, and so a number of states, not coincidentally large blue states, do not turn over any data, so that it’s difficult to get a picture of just how many abortions and under what circumstances are committed in this country. We do know the numbers are going way up.”

“Senator, you have my commitment,” Schwartz replied. “Abortion surveillance is absolutely a critical component of what the CDC is currently doing.”

“I also want to make sure that certain states are not conflating emergency services and hiding abortions in that emergency services case definition,” she added. “We need to make sure we’re pulling out true abortions and making sure that we’re really having clear case definitions regarding abortions so the data is actually accurate.”

“Tremendous,” Hawley replied. He seemed very happy with her response.

If you are concerned about the growing criminalization of abortion and surveillance of pregnant women in the US, then absolutely nothing about this is tremendous. I’ve quoted the majority of the exchange between Hawley and Schwartz instead of paraphrasing it, because the choice of language is so alarming. First, look at the way in which Hawley frames the issue. He talks about abortions being committed: a loaded word which makes you think of murder. (Imagine it in another medical context: I’m having a mammogram committed tomorrow!) Then he insinuates that blue states are hiding abortion data for nefarious reasons. As it is, 44 states plus Washington DC have some form of mandated abortion reporting, according to the Guttmacher Institute, and there is no evidence that these states are hiding anything. New York is an outlier in that it only requires abortion reporting when a patient makes a request related to the disposition of the fetus’s remains. Which seems like a sensible policy that protects the privacy of people who have had abortions.

Now look at Schwartz’s reply. Why would abortion surveillance be “a critical component” of what the CDC is doing? Data collection around abortions can serve legitimate purposes, sure, but isn’t it rather more important for the CDC to be, I dunno, controlling and preventing diseases? Her reference to “true abortions” (as opposed to fake ones?) and to states “hiding abortions” is also worrying. Pregnant people are already dying preventable deaths because providers in states with abortion bans are terrified of treating them. This sort of language from the CDC director is going to make the situation even worse.

Donald Trump has called Schwartz “a STAR”. If her exchange with Hawley is anything to go by, however, she seems to be yet another stooge: happy to facilitate the Trump administration’s anti-abortion agenda and politicization of public health.

“Erica Schwartz’s testimony … should alarm everyone who believes private medical decisions belong to patients, not politicians,” Mini Timmaraju, the president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, said in a statement. She added that, under the Trump administration, “abortion surveillance could be expanded or weaponized to collect more intrusive information, spread disinformation about reproductive health care, and support efforts to investigate or criminalize patients and providers”.

As activists and experts have repeatedly said, overturning Roe v Wade was just the beginning of the new war on reproductive rights in the US – a war facilitated by an unprecedented network of surveillance technology. The convicted felon in the White House seems intent on treating every pregnant woman as a potential criminal.

During a private call with religious groups, the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, said efforts to reverse the Biden administration’s efforts to protect abortion were “taking longer than we want”. He seemed to suggest that the administration was working to restrict access to abortion pills and said: “We don’t have complete victory yet, but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and it will be permanent.” Blanche has faced a rocky road to confirmation as attorney general. The bad news is that the government’s anti-abortion agenda will continue whether he gets the role or not.

That’s according to a new ruling by the state’s supreme court. No doubt they’ll soon be forced to report abortions, though!

after newsletter promotion

“If you’ll notice, women don’t method act because we have things to take care of,” Taylor-Joy said in an interview promoting her new Apple TV show Lucky (which is extremely good, by the way). Back in 2024, Natalie Portman similarly described method acting as a “luxury women can’t afford”. She added: “I don’t think that children or partners would be very understanding of, you know, me making everyone call me ‘Jackie Kennedy’ all the time.”

More than a million people watched Towle navigate her cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer of the bile ducts. She raised awareness of the disease and built community. However, because the internet is often toxic, she was also accused by trolls of exaggerating or even faking her cancer. It even got to a point where Towle’s doctor had to confirm to the New York Times that she had stage 4 cancer.

This is not some unfortunate byproduct of war; it is by design. Last year, a UN report found that Israel’s systemic attacks on women’s healthcare in Gaza amount to “genocidal acts”. The report noted that Israel’s destruction of maternity wards, an IVF clinic and control on essential supplies into Gaza “destroyed in part the reproductive capacity of Palestinians in Gaza as a group”.

A cat called Toast Malone survived a fire that destroyed an apartment complex in Utah by hiding in a closet for three days. Toast did not get burned, and has now been reunited with their family. Now they’re the toast of the town.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Creamy, high-protein and all over our socials, cottage cheese is having a moment. We test the best …

The best supermarket vine tomatoes

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

When I was growing up, cottage cheese was tasteless and mostly only eaten by dieters. Its recent revival in the UK, most likely driven by social media, has similar health reasons at its root – the current protein obsession in gym bros and weight watchers alike – but cottage cheese has become cool. The flavourless squeaky varieties of yesteryear are still around, but a whole new category now exists on supermarket shelves that is unabashedly fatty, rich and full of flavour, with artisanal complexity and a lacto-fermented sour twang.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

I scored these based on flavour; the more complex and sour, the better, especially when balanced with a rich, sweet and creamy suspension. None of these products were bitter.

Texture is also key. I find tough, squeaky curds a bit unappetising, but I do enjoy them with a bit of size, and the silkier, the better. Some of the products were less like cottage cheese and more like a grainy yoghurt. It’s rare I give five out of five, especially when a product is not organic. However, there was one today that was so good it deserved the award.

As usual, marks were also given for transparency, traceability and provenance; plus sustainability certification and, importantly, value – though even the most expensive products were relatively well priced. The quality, taste and range of cottage cheese on the market is now exceptional.

★★★★★

A wonderfully rich, unctuous and creamy cottage cheese made with live cultures, and the milk and cream of jersey cows on the Cholmondeley estate in Cheshire by this B Corp-certified dairy. A dense mixture with large, firm and plentiful curds. Protein content 10%.

★★★☆☆

Very creamy, extra-large, super-soft curds. Made with British milk and salt. Wonderfully silky and soft with a rich, creamy quality and classic sour edge. Protein content 9.1%.

★★★★☆

An excellent and consistently thick and creamy cottage cheese with large, silky curds. Sweet, rich and sour. Made with British milk and salt only. Protein content 10.3%.

★★★★☆

An extra-thick cottage cheese with large-to-small curds that make up the sauce. Very creamy and stiff, but with lovely soft curds and a fresh taste. Made with British milk and enriched with cream and creme fraiche. Joint highest protein content: 12%.

★★★★☆

Large, very firm curds with a thick layer of cream on top. Made in Yorkshire by Longley Farm, established in 1948, from milk and salt. It has a high fat content, making it rich and creamy. Protein content 10.3%.

Parenting is hard. Should we let AI do it for us?

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 11:00:47 GMT

Tech companies offer eye-movement trackers, personalized podcasts and ‘optimized nap predictions’. Who actually needs this?

What job in our world is less lucrative than being a parent? A Hollywood internship? Volunteering at a soup kitchen? Professional writer? Parenting is the only job you have to pay money to do. Lots of money. Lodging, clothes, food, school, Pokémon cards – it really adds up. And it’s getting worse. According to the tech industry, I have to strap my drooling offspring to a computer in order to ensure the baby’s survival.

Parents are being offered life-altering advancements in artificial intelligence that purport to make this taxing endeavor a tiny bit easier. OpenAI is suggesting its latest products can make child-rearing more efficient: its boss, Sam Altman, suggests generating a podcast about your kid’s life that you can listen to in the morning on the way to school. How entertaining would a podcast “that talks about one kid’s soccer game that afternoon, one kid’s upcoming birthday, some news, etc” actually be? “Jimmy needs to work on his dribbling.” Great. I think he knows already. He’s not going to be the next Messi, so how about we switch back to music?

Presumably, this idea renders the need for conversation moot. The computer already knows everything about our lives and has now regurgitated it into digital mush delivered by a generically cheery voice. But why I would find it helpful to have a machine reiterate information I have at my disposal already is a grand mystery even Philip Marlowe couldn’t solve. I’m a functioning, alive adult human being. This is like giving me an extra tooth with the promise that I can chew my food faster.

But what about the eight to 10 hours a day when your child has the gift of blissful solitude? Surely, they can’t be left alone at bedtime, lest they swallow a Hot Wheels car or open your favorite jar of loose razor blades. That’s where Nanit comes in – a startup that promises the kind of 24-hour surveillance that would make the Department of Homeland Security salivate. Nanit sells a camera and monitor set that observes your kid during sleep, tracking eye movements, “sleep efficiency”, and breathing patterns. Nanit’s rival, a company called Owlet, attaches a pulse oximetry tracker to your child’s foot through a sock. That’s not quite hooking your kid up to a terminal from the novel Neuromancer, but it feels like a decent first step in that direction. An app called Huckleberry offers “optimized nap predictions” and a chatbot assistant.

Of course, all of this costs money. A Nanit kit is $474, plus $100 a year in subscription fees. Owlet’s robo-sock is $300. Huckleberry’s app is free, but its nap predictions, like expert sports betting advice, will cost you. For $120, you can be told when your kid might go to sleep. I doubt there’s a money-back guarantee if they get it wrong, and the kid ends up spilling Legos all over the floor instead of going to bed.

These services promise to save lives by identifying health issues early in a child’s development. Nanit claims it offers more sleep and peace of mind, so parents can move their babies into their own rooms, thereby giving mom and dad a chance to go back to having regular intercourse. Yes, Nanit has looked into parents’ sex habits, too. If you went back to when I was married, you’d find there wasn’t much to look into.

None of this is anything people actually need to be parents. Babies need food, toys, diapers and a regular bath. Those all cost money. If I have to choose between saving for my son’s college and a spreadsheet with a bunch of biometric data, I’m skipping the spreadsheet. I realize, of course, these products are not for me. I don’t have an unlimited supply of disposable income. I have to prioritize and be practical. These devices are for people who optimize every single shred of their daily lives, thinking it will protect them from the reality of failure, illness and death. I’m sorry to report that a $400 camera isn’t going to fix any of that.

Society has been trying to offer solutions to solve the conundrum of parenting for decades: self-help books, classes, the legendary (and expensive) Snoo crib that shakes your child like it’s a gin martini until it stops crying. In every case, these aids cost money, turning parenting into a lucrative sector of the economy. If you can’t afford these modern “miracles”, where can you turn?

Parenting is hard, and we all need help. But there was a time when grandparents lived with their kids and grandkids, or at least lived close enough to help. I grant that the idea of living with my mother is akin to pitching a tent next to a cave filled with grizzly bears, but I’d do that before I got an AI-powered camera system to take a video of my kid sleeping. The best part of extended family childcare is that people can do something an AI can never do. It can teach children about someone besides themselves.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

‘She’s the voice of a really particular moment’: how Phoebe Bridgers became her generation’s defining songwriter

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 11:00:45 GMT

The US songwriter’s third album has drawn rave reviews, she counts Taylor Swift as a fan and pop bears the imprint of her wit and pathos. Her peers explain how she did it

This week, indie star Phoebe Bridgers releases her long-awaited third album, six years since her pandemic-era breakthrough. Alongside a slew of glittering reviews for Lost Weekend, including five stars from the Guardian, with it comes her first solo charting single in the UK – although the Californian musician’s influence runs far deeper than reviews or record sales could measure. Just how did a RuneScape-referencing, Halloween-costumed Berklee drop-out become the most influential songwriter of the 2020s?

Bridgers’ idiosyncratic writing has shaped the sound of the decade. Her second album Punisher, released in June 2020 (and recorded many months before), spookily anticipated that strange, lonely year: in her eerie double-tracked vocals (a nod to Bridgers’ musical hero, Elliott Smith), Bridgers sang of empty shopping malls and conspiracy theories over lush, unsettling music made from watery electric guitar, Mellotron, strings, screams and birdsong. Today, Bridgers’ distinctive mix of dry wit and pathos is traceable in the lyrics of pop’s new chart toppers, such as Olivia Rodrigo and Gracie Abrams, while heavyweights across generations and genres, including Paul McCartney, Taylor Swift and SZA, have clamoured for collaborations. “She is the reference now,” Swift told the Guardian in 2022.

“She’s the voice of a really particular moment,” says author Carmen Maria Machado, who first met Bridgers when she attended an event for Machado’s prize-winning memoir In the Dream House. There is a kinship between Machado’s prose and Bridgers’ lyrics – both are candid, haunted, unafraid to get gruesome – and it resulted in Machado publishing a short story to accompany Punisher. “Phoebe’s never looking directly on, rather looking askance,” says Machado. “Her music is so precise and weird and beautiful; it’s a prayer or an ode to this place that we’re living in, while also watching it fall apart.”

Reviews for Lost Weekend have highlighted the album’s deeply personal subject matter – it discusses the death of Bridgers’ father, and the end of her engagement to actor Paul Mescal – but also Bridgers’ enduringly surreal sense of humour. When performing single Lost Boys on the Tonight Show, she played it first with a band of children, who were fizzing with excitement, and then again in an acoustic arrangement with veteran folk legend Dan Reeder. The effect was trippy, sweet and faintly morbid: distinctly Phoebe.

For Naomi McPherson, a member of synth-pop three-piece Muna, it’s this mixture of matter-of-fact and magical that makes Bridgers so distinct. “It’s infuriating and inspiring how good she is,” McPherson says, pointing to a forthcoming Lost Weekend song with a line about turning down the stereo volume to better parallel park: “To be able to put that in a song in a way that isn’t stupid, but is actually brilliant and somehow deeply touching, is an enormous feat.”

Muna signed to Bridgers’ record label Saddest Factory in 2021, joining a cohort of imaginative, predominantly queer musicians united under Bridgers’ mentality of “getting cool stuff out to people as fast as possible”. Singer-songwriter Claud (whose song A Good Thing soundtracked the finale to queer romance series Heartstopper) was the label’s first signee. They emphasise the value of Bridgers’ support at a vital time for both artists: “I knew I could trust her opinions and instincts for my project, because I love everything she does with hers.”

The label was rolled into parent company Dead Oceans earlier this year after a trademark dispute, but its lasting influence reflects Bridgers’ determination to change the music industry for the better – as did her supergroup, Boygenius, formed with songwriter friends Lucy Dacus and Julien Baker. Together the trio played their biggest stages to date and clinched three Grammy awards, while Bridgers took the award ceremony as an opportunity to condemn former Recording Academy boss Neil Portnow, who had been accused of sexual assault, for his disparaging “step up” comment towards women in music: “Rot in piss!”

Bridgers’ plain-talking has won her a passionate fanbase, many of whom are easily spotted by their matching ghost tattoos – a reference to the cover of her 2017 debut Stranger in the Alps – and her concerts are intense: Claud, who has toured with Bridgers, describes “crowds of tens of thousands where you can actually hear a pin drop”. It tracks, then, that Bridgers decided to promote Lost Weekend not with sit-down interviews but a series of secretive pop-up shows across the US, taking the new songs straight to fans.

Fan Baleigh Epperly, an environmental advocate, DJ and co-founder of queer, female-led local DJ collective Their House, “freaked out” when Bridgers rolled in to play at the Loud, a 500-capacity venue in her home town of Huntington, West Virginia. “We never get shit,” she laughs, saying it meant “everything” that Bridgers was visiting “the overlooked places, the places where she knows her fans are”.

The tiny shows were first come, first served, capped at $50 a ticket, and mobile-phone free. Epperly says they all sat cross-legged, watching Bridgers play as if it were a house show. “It was the talk of the town, literally,” she marvels, predicting that the performance will have a lasting impact on young musicians who may have internalised damaging stereotypes about Appalachia: “If Phoebe is good enough for West Virginia, then you’re good enough to play here, to live here, to be from here.”

Muna’s Katie Gavin describes Bridgers’ influence in similar terms. “She’s an aspirational songwriter for me. Seeing her make art makes me want to do it, which is what the best music does.”

Stretchy, supportive and completely chafe-free: the sportswear real people swear by

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 11:00:45 GMT

From leggings that don’t roll down to bras that keep everything in, keen amateur cyclists, weightlifters and swimmers reveal the bits of kit they can’t do without

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

What is the perfect sports kit? That is the question we set out to answer, talking to sport and fitness enthusiasts all over the country. From Zumba dancers in Bristol to marathon runners in Leeds and gym bunnies in Thurrock, we asked different groups for the activewear they swear by and why it works for them.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Sea swimmers in Felixstowe had conflicting views about wetsuits, but all swore by brightly coloured tow floats and swim caps. Boxers in east London were united on the best kind of glove, but had different takes on clothing choices. Cyclists in the Wirral had differing levels of bike-collecting addiction, but agreed on the benefits of being Mamil (middle-aged men in Lycra).

Finding the right kit is a matter of trial and error, and what is comfortable for one person can be sensory torture for another. Cost can also be an issue, but spending more doesn’t always equate to a better experience, as these interviews show.

Above all, what is clear is that when you do find perfection, it can enhance how you feel about yourself when participating in any given sport. All that’s left to do iseither bulk buy or devise a very efficient washing system.

Here is some inspiration to get you started …

When Sally Gulliford first plucked up the courage to start going to Zumba in Bristol in 2019 with her daughter, she didn’t want to stand out. “I wore baggy clothes and stood at the back,” says Gulliford, 57, who is a civil servant and lives in the village of Backwell near the city.

Amy Smith, who takes the class, reassured Gulliford that everyone would be focused on the instructor doing the moves at the front. The 38-year-old from Bristol had herself only recently regained the confidence to teach, and to wear tight-fitting workout clothes, having started leading classes after the birth of her two daughters. She decided her sessions would be held in a nightclub in the dark: “This creates an atmosphere where people not only feel like it’s a party, which it should be, but lose their inhibitions more. It is like a girls’ night out – we compare outfits and ask where things are from.” The clothing choices of attendees reflect this disco atmosphere. “I wear bright colours now,” Gulliford says. Her daughter still goes, too: “And borrows my gear.”

“You want to completely submerge in the workout,” says Lucy Law, 35, a psychological therapist from Yeovil, who has been going to classes since 2024. This is why the right attire is key: “You don’t want to be worrying about your back fat or your side boobs, or anything rubbing.”

With all the jiggling about, a sturdy bra is crucial; all the women agree that M&S’s Goodmove ultimate support non-wired sports bra (worn by Smith and Gulliford, above centre and right, £15) is the best. The zip-front design ensures “you’re not going to fall out”, Gulliford says. Law also rates the F&F active zip-front high support sports bra (seen on her above left, £18), “because it’s so soft”.

Gulliford says Zumba Wear’s mesh tops (worn by Smith, above centre, from £24.70) are popular to keep cool and Halara’s skorts and skort dresses (worn by Law, above left, from £17.95) work well for bum-shaking. “You don’t want something to feel like a wetsuit,” Law says, “but you want it tight enough that it flows with your body. A massive one for me, especially with trousers or shorts, is rolling down at the top. I pull them up to suck the belly in and I don’t want to be spending the workout pulling them up.” Gymshark’s Light Hold Leggings (£38) and Matalan’s Souluxe leggings (from £12.50) do the job: “They do not move on your tummy.”

Dressing up for Zumba has helped the women to feel good about themselves. “It has definitely given me a lot more confidence in how I look at myself and what I wear,” Gulliford says.

To find Amy Smith’s online and in-person classes, follow her on Instagram at ZDP_Amy

“I’m not going to lie and say that I don’t feel the heat; I absolutely do,” says Habiba Hassan, 26, of pounding the pavements of Leeds with the Lost Culture running club. “It can be quite difficult at times, especially when we are doing long distances, and in the summertime.”

Hassan, an NHS dietitian who completed this year’s London marathon, says that her running look has evolved as modest activewear has improved. “What was available five years ago is very different to now,” Hassan says. “I’m not in a position where I have to wear a men’s oversized T-shirt any more. There are brands that cater for me.” Hassan sources breathable tops that are intentionally loose-fitting, such as her Haya Active essential training top (above centre, £39). She is always being asked where she got her loose trousers: they are Promover yoga trousers with pockets (above centre, £27.99).

The founder of the club, André Lance, 35, says that while they are an undeniably stylish group, participants are encouraged to prioritise more practical considerations when dressing for training sessions and races. He wears Kiprun’s 2 in 1 long-distance trail running shorts (seen on Nico Junior, above left, £39.99) – which have an inner layer “that feels like it stops chafing, which is a positive” – and an oversized, aerated T-shirt, along with basic running shades or a skullcap in winter.

Chafing is a concern for Hassan, too, especially as “where I chafe changes year on year”. She finds “softer, buttery fabrics” are better. Adidas’s cushioned socks (£8 for three pairs) help on long runs.

Junior, 28, who works in tech and runs with the group, sings the praises of his Coros Pace 4 GPS sport watch (above left, £229): “You can determine on a run whether you’re doing too much and it helps you to pace yourself.” Hassan has just moved from an Apple Watch to a Garmin Forerunner 55 GPS (£111.99), saying it is more tailored to running. Lance uses JBL’s Endurance Race 2 earbuds (£59.99), which “stay in my ear all the way”; Junior prefers Beats By Dre’s Powerbeats Pro 2 (£249.99). They go around the ear and, he says, stop his head feeling heavy on long runs.

Vests are handy for trail runs and races, to carry gels and other items. Hassan loves the Salomon Active Skin 4 running vest (£95). “It has lots of zips, which are really good for your keys,” Hassan says, “and deeper pockets for your phone. At the back, there is a really deep pocket if you want to carry extra layers or a coat. It distributes the weight, which is why I love it so much, because I found that belts hitting against your tummy can cause abdominal pain. It comes with soft water bottles that are like pouches.”

They all save carbon-plated trainers for racing. “I wear Puma Deviate Nitro 4 running shoes (as does Junior, above left, £150) for training,” Lance says, “as they are more centred on comfort and stability. For race day, Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4 shoes (above right, £154) have knocked minutes off my time. It feels like I’ve got magic powers.”
