“The high you get from sparring is like nothing I’ve experienced before,” says Mackenzie Qu, a 23-year-old from Hackney who works in retail, “and I’ve played a lot of sports.” One of the downsides is that boxing involves a lot of gear, explains Qu, who took up the sport last October, signing up to Hot Girl Boxing in east London. “I’ve survived OK so far without a lot of it, but if I take it any more seriously, I’m going to have to invest in gloves at least.” It is definitely worth borrowing gloves to start, says Ailsa Mullins, 34, the coach at Hot Girl, but you need to be “prepared for the stench of putting on gloves that 30 people sweated in before you!”

For Qu’s first fight in November, they plan to wear Muay Thai-style shorts (with a high elastic waist and silky flared leg openings) with a bright yellow waistband, found at a branch of Traid. “I thrift most of the sportswear I own,” Qu says, adding that Oxfam, Crisis and British Heart Foundation shops are the best for unearthing treasures.

Also preparing for the November fight is Manuela Campbell, 43, who lives in east London and works for a trade organisation. As the name of the club suggests, “I get really hot, so at this time of year I am usually in something sleeveless. If it’s not sweltering, I prefer a baggy shirt: I don’t want my top to ride up. I like to keep it loose, so there’s a bit of airflow,” she says.

Mullins wears a sports bra: “I like something with high coverage that’s quite compact – anything that can push you in – because your chest is in the striking zone.” She rates Gymshark’s Everyday seamless racerback sports bra (£28), and Lululemon is another go-to brand.

Campbell is prepared to indulge in decent gloves – she just got new ones made by Rival – which last for around two years. “All the Hot Girls wear Rivals,” Mullins says. “They are a really good entry-level glove.” She recommends the RV7 Fitness Plus bag gloves (£54.99) she’s wearing above left.

Having a good supply of wraps – worn under gloves for extra protection – is non-negotiable. “I stockpile wraps,” says Campbell, who owns leopard-print Hot Girl-branded versions and Meister’s Semi-elastic hand wraps (£7 a pair). Gum shields are also a must if sparring. Head guards are always worn in fights, but Campbell feels safer wearing them more generally: “My brother has been doing martial arts for years and I don’t want my nose to look like his.”

When it comes to footwear, Campbell and Mullins favour boxing boots. “If you’re going to stick at it, get those first,” Mullins says. “You can borrow most other things but your own pair of boots will make such a difference.” Adidas’s Box Hog classic shoes (above left and right, £60) are her favourites.

The boxers all find the act of getting dressed to box inspiring: “There is something about the ritual of wrapping your hands before starting a session,” Campbell says, “that makes you feel very powerful, and capable of a lot more than what people have told you. I was told from a very young age that I wasn’t a sporty girl – turns out I’m actually quite athletic.”

Hot Girl Boxing holds sessions in Hackney, east London, on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

Amanda Bowden, 59, from Felixstowe, Suffolk, got into sea swimming on “a bit of a whim”, when someone invited her to do it to mark her 50th birthday: “I lasted about seven minutes, then didn’t do it again for a year.” After getting the bug properly, though, Bowden signed up for a 6km swim and it took off from there.

There was one slight problem: she struggled to find swimwear “in colours and coverage that reflected how I wanted to present myself”. As a sewing school owner, the obvious thing to do was to make her own swimsuit – using specialist material, sourceable from companies such as Funki Fabrics. She wore it when she swam the Channel solo at the age of 56 – “It had a teal background with white polka dots and red crabs all over it” – and has made others since (above left). If buying a costume, she says, it’s essential to try it out first: “Rotate your arms and move about in it. Bend over and see if your boobs come out. If you’re an endurance swimmer, look for something lined, with well-finished edges. The more bands and straps there are, the more risk of chafing.”

Bowden is part of the Swimscapes club in Felixstowe, as is Jenny Saltmarsh, 52, a health and safety consultant. Saltmarsh is a fan of Funkita swimsuits, which come in fun patterns (like the one above right) and fit her well. In winter, she opts for a Zone3 Ti+ thermal high neck swimsuit (£75). Neither swimmer wears a wetsuit: “Too much faff,” Saltmarsh says, though, without one, Bowden laughs, “it can be a bit brutal”.

Seamus Bennett, 61, a swimming coach and councillor who set up Swimscapes in 2012, wears an Orca wetsuit (above centre, from £149) from March to June. He recommends a proper, flexible swimming one: “A general surfing or sailing suit may actually hinder you.”

In summer, he likes Funky Trunks’ Jammers (£39.95). He feels the cold in his hands, so wears Lomo Tri-X neoprene gloves (£21), but avoids boots, which he says “slow you down”.

There are safety concerns to swimming all year round. To help, Bowden uses “a highly visible tow float and a bright cap, so people can see me”, while Saltmarsh wears SurfEars 4.0 vented earplugs (£54.95) to avoid surfer’s ear, “bony growths, from cold water coming in”. Bennett recommends Garmin’s epix Pro Gen 2 watch (above centre, £299.99), which he says has a better battery life than others, and Bowden favours Crocs for navigating the stony shore. As for goggles, Bennett wears Arena Cobra Tri Mirror triathlon swipe goggles (above centre, £68.99), because “the anti-fog lasts a long time and they’re really clear and comfortable”. In open water, Saltmarsh wears “polarised Zone3 Venator-X swim goggles (above right, £35) and a “necessary evil” swimming cap – the brighter the better.

How do they feel about the divisive issue of changing robes? Saltmarsh says she loves her Dryrobe (above right, £175). “Everybody in my house has one – even the dog. My friends got me a badge: ‘All dry robe, no knickers.’” Bowden, of course, made her own.

Swimscapes meet on Saturday and Sunday all year round, plus Monday May-Oct; facebook. com/FelixstoweSwimscapes

Lauren Briggs, 30, from Thurrock in Essex, hadn’t been to a gym before she lost both her legs after having sepsis in 2021. “I’d never done any sport before,” says Briggs, who also lost her admin job in the aftermath of her illness. Now she goes to Alternative Movement, an adaptive gym five minutes from her home, four times a week for group and individual PT sessions. Briggs is able to deadlift more than her own weight, and has taken part in a triathlon and an adaptive competition.

“Being a bilateral amputee, I really overheat,” she says. “Because I’ve lost two of my extremities, the heat doesn’t dissipate; it all comes up through my body and head. I find that tight clothing insulates you more, so I try to wear airy clothes that don’t cling to me too much.” She opts for loose and light materials, and wears “quite a lot of Adidas” (such as the T-shirt above centre) because she likes their sweat-proof material. Shorts work better than leggings with her prosthetic legs – she’s a fan of these Halara SoftlyZero Airy super high waisted 2-in-1 yoga shorts (£19.95). “They’ve got tight shorts inside but they are still loose, so it’s good for when you are getting up and down off the floor. Sometimes with baggy shorts, being female, I feel a bit exposed.

“I have very sweaty hands,” Briggs adds, which can make lifting tricky, “so gloves do help. But I also use chalk, such as Bear Grip’s liquid chalk (£8), because with the gloves, when you’re sweating in them, it can sometimes cause friction and you get blisters. With the chalk, you don’t.”

Another Alt Movement gym-goer, Wilf O’Donoghue, 17, who is a student, says he prefers sweat-proof T-shirts and elasticated shorts, and Uniqlo is his go-to: “It’s affordable and easy to work out in.” He likes these shorts (above left) and the Dry-Ex T-shirt (£19.90).

George Barrett, 24, believes having a uniform for the gym helps him to stick with it, as a person with autism spectrum disorder: “Comfort and routine is baked into our identity.” M&S shorts and Under Armour vests meet his sensory needs, and he uses Sennheiser in-ear headphones (above right, from £34.99) to cancel out any noise: “I mainly listen to music with a lot of power behind it.” As for footwear, Barrett says his Skechers Slip-ins trainers (above right, £90) are “loose and breathable”.

Briggs has found the best gym shoes for her are RAD’s One V2 (£130), which she’s wearing above and says are good all-rounders. “For weightlifting, I’ve realised that your footwear is crucial.”

There are adaptive clothing ranges, including at Primark, but not all offer sportswear and most are on the pricey side, according to Briggs. “As soon as you market something as adaptive or for the disabled community, the prices do seem to hike up quite drastically,” she says. “A lot of disabled people, we’re not working, we’re on benefits, and we’re paying premium prices for something just to be able to live our day-to-day life – that’s not really fair.”

Alternative Movement offers a range of sessions at different times across the week at its gym in Grays, Thurrock, Essex; altmovement. co. uk

In 2016, a group of friends from Bromborough, Wirral, signed up for the Liverpool-Chester-Liverpool bike ride. Most had not ridden much before, or not for a while, and their first training ride, which they were very proud of, was 11 miles. “We had mountain bikes and were wearing Aldi’s best gear from the middle aisle,” laughs John Moore, 62, who works at the University of Manchester.

After the race, they agreed they had enjoyed it so much, they would go for weekly Sunday rides around Cheshire and north Wales. “We used to look at road cyclists and say we’re never going to be like them, we’re never going to be Mamils [middle-aged men in Lycra],” Moore says. “But six months later, we all started. I suppose it’s more aerodynamic.” Simon “Bob” Smith, 61, who is retired, agrees: “There’s no flapping.” Chris Weatherston, also 61 and retired, thinks it’s more comfortable. “Not to look at, admittedly,” Moore adds.

Over a curry at Wirral Tandoori, Brombay Bicycle Club was born. One member, Garry Swaby, a graphic designer, came up with a concept for the club jersey, converting the Indian flag. The curry house even sponsored the kit. They got the design printed on a L’Etape Jersey (above centre, £50). Quickly, bikes were upgraded and, inevitably, collections grew, turning it into an expensive hobby. “I’ve got six bikes,” Smith admits. “I’ve got seven,” Weatherston says.

Moore has just two and says he loves his Giant TCR Advanced 2 (£1,839): “It’s light, has a carbon fibre frame and handles really well.” If you are starting out, go for a main brand and read reviews, Smith says, and take it for a test drive if the shop will allow you to, Weatherston suggests.

Padded cycle shorts are a must, with the group rating the Castelli Endurance 4 Short (£140) – “You can ride for hours in it,” Smith says, adding that, when not in the club kit, “I like my Castelli Climber’s 3.0 SL2 Jersey (above left, £41.99). It looks great, is lightweight and breathable, and has UV protection.” As for helmets, Smith, who has “come off a couple of times”, favours Specialized’s Align II (£45).

Finding a decent saddle – the SLR Boost TM Superflow (£134.99) – for added comfort has been a gamechanger, Moore says, and his Mavic shoes with cleats (above centre, from £101.98) “make a massive difference”. Smith gets “sore palms after a few hours”, so needs gloves (above left, from £18), adding, “Glasses are important, not just to look cool, but to stop getting bits in your eyes.” Moore has “Oakley sunglasses that are brilliant”, the RSLV 141s (above centre, £188). The club’s local bike shop, K Cycles, is their first port of call for kit and advice.

This summer, the club marked 10 years of cycling together by returning to do the Liverpool-Chester-Liverpool again, in memory of Chris Lewis, a member who died in June. They proudly wore the Brombay Bicycle kit. “Our dazzling apparel definitely gets noticed,” Moore says. “At a time when flags can be divisive, it is great to wear something flag-based that gets such positive reactions.”

President Xi never wastes a good crisis. As Iran, Ukraine and Palestine distract the world, he tightens his grip

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 11:00:44 GMT

Ever the strategist, the Chinese leader is taking the offensive, both abroad and at home. That’s bad news for global order, and minorities in his country

Imagine what would happen if a British prime minister in London told the Scots they could not have their own parliament, national football team or fly the saltire. Or if the Welsh were told their language and poetry were banned and must no longer be taught in schools. The ensuing uproar would probably destroy the United Kingdom. Yet that’s exactly what Xi Jinping, China’s communist emperor, is telling the roughly 125 million members of the 55 ethnic and religious minorities who together comprise about 9% of the country’s (majority Han Chinese) population.

Xi claims his sinicisation policy, embodied in a new “ethnic unity” law, will boost national identity and integration and, by expanding compulsory use of the Mandarin language, improve life and work prospects. Minorities should “hug tightly like pomegranate seeds” to build a strong, united China, he says. But Tibetans, Mongolians, Uyghurs and others who value their separate language and customs fiercely object to what they see as forced assimilation into a conformist, intolerant monoculture dominated by the Communist party’s tunnel vision. For them, it’s ethnic cleansing by another name.

The new law has been condemned, though not too loudly, by western governments and more vociferously by rights organisations such as Amnesty International. The death of Lobga Rangzen, a Free Tibet activist who set himself on fire in protest outside the UN in New York last month, briefly drew international attention. But such tragedies are not new. Wholesale repression in Tibet and brutal “re-education” camps in Xinjiang are but two longstanding aspects of Xi’s intensifying nationwide war on dissent, difference and diversity. The law and its harsh penalties, which extend to Chinese citizens based abroad, adds legal weight to existing efforts to enforce his and the party’s will (much the same thing these days) by creating a politically compliant, cowed population that dare not answer back.

A debilitating fatalism has taken hold in the west about China’s behaviour, whether it involves persecution of minorities, evisceration of democracy in Hong Kong, vindictive prosecutions of pro-democracy activists such as the former Apple Daily publisher Jimmy Lai, or vicious suppression of independent Christian churches and “unapproved” religious groups. It’s as though Xi’s China is now seen as simply too big, too economically powerful and too militarily threatening to influence, let alone contain or control. When China’s internal affairs are the issue, it’s easier to steer clear. Awkwardly balancing trade against security, and culpably silent on human rights, Britain is far from alone among western democracies in failing to articulate a coherent China policy.

But Xi’s increasingly aggressive, uncompromising policies are not confined to domestic matters. In power for nearly 15 years, Xi, 73, is growing ever more confident and abrasive in pursuit of his international legacy bucket list: establishing China as the dominant global power, relegating the US to second place and making his country the essential hub of a new multipolar security, economic and diplomatic order. His legacy list includes a takeover of Taiwan before he stands down, and unchallenged supremacy across the Asia-Pacific region. It all points one way: to Xi’s coronation as the greatest Chinese leader since Mao Zedong.

With the 21st party congress approaching, 2027 could be a big year for Xi – and he is already getting his ducks in a row. His dictatorship looks unassailable. Top regime cadres, meeting this week in secretive conclave at the Beidaihe seaside resort in Hebei province, are expected to endorse his redoubled drive to enforce loyalty and discipline in the ranks – the official phrase is “sustained advancement of full and rigorous party self-governance”. The Beidaihe gathering, and another meeting due in October, come amid almost Stalinist purges of senior political and military figures.

Signs of a more assertive international posture are everywhere. In recent months, China has stoked nationalist tensions with Japan and deliberately provoked the Philippines in disputed areas of the South China Sea. Its intimidation of Taiwan is unceasing. This week, Japan’s latest defence white paper singled out China as presenting “an unprecedented strategic challenge” and warned the threat was moving closer to home. Admiral Samuel Paparo, head of US Pacific Command, fired a broadside at China’s “coercive actions” in pursuit, he said, of regional dominance.

Xi is now actively challenging the US and the west on several other fronts. China is reportedly planning to provide Iran with up to 400 shoulder-fired missiles and new air defence systems. It is already materially assisting Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. And an emboldened Beijing is deploying the sort of trade weapons beloved of Donald Trump. Last year it restricted exports of vital rare earth minerals, to Washington’s great alarm. Only this week, China hit back at Trump’s new tariffs by blocking sales of drone technology.

Xi’s ever more bullish stance owes much to Trump’s trashing of the post-1945 global order, disdain for international law and national sovereignty (as seen in Venezuela and Greenland), and strained relations with traditional allies such as Japan, South Korea and European Nato countries. Many now view the US as an unreliable partner. For China, Trump’s shifting focus away from Asia and towards the western hemisphere is a golden opportunity to be exploited while it lasts. That may be one reason why Xi has taken the unusual step of agreeing to visit Trump in Washington next month, so soon after their May meeting in Beijing.

The main focus of the summit is expected to be artificial intelligence, amid US worries that it is in danger of losing the AI race. According to Chinese commentators, at least, Trump asked for the meeting after China agreed AI partnerships with 28 countries, mostly from the global south. AI is “probably the biggest thing anybody’s ever seen”, Trump said last month. “Whoever wins that race is probably going to win, period.” By which he presumably means, win the 21st century’s superpower crown.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The summit is likely to confirm the impression left by the last one: that Xi, outmanoeuvring Trump on Asia-Pacific security and Taiwan, accumulating geopolitical clout, and winning trade and tech wars, is well on the way to fulfilling his ambition of gaining the upper hand over the US. Yet in the end, Xi is still an unelected autocrat, a thug in a suit who relies on force to stay in power. He’s failing to deliver economically and, as in India and elsewhere, young urban Chinese may not tolerate his old-school brand of suffocating authoritarianism indefinitely. Who knows? Perhaps his ethnic unity law may ultimately prove a step too far – as it certainly would in Britain.

All should be on their guard. Xi, no friend of the west, may be morphing into an outright enemy while all eyes are on Iran, Gaza and Ukraine. Symbolically if not yet physically, a dangerously unconstrained Xi is shutting the door on peaceful coexistence at home and abroad.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

The Bond effect? How MI6 fascinates spy watchers around the world

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 11:00:44 GMT

Britain’s spooks take quiet satisfaction from survey ranking Secret Intelligence Service Europe’s top espionage agency

MI6 has the swagger of James Bond; its French equivalent, DGSE, the complexities of the television drama Le Bureau. The film and TV shows may be fictional, but a survey run by a French magazine that placed the British spy agency above the French as No 1 across all of Europe this week is not.

L’Express, a news weekly, conducted a Eurovision-style poll of 60 current and former spies from across the continent, plus the CIA and Israel’s Mossad. Each was asked to rank their top five foreign intelligence agencies, in secret, naturally enough. MI6 was first with 251 points ahead of DGSE on 169, with other agencies trailing behind.

The result did not surprise Alexandra Saviana, a deputy editor at the publication, specialising in defence and intelligence, but the margin of victory did. “It is a huge point gap,” she said, reflecting the opinions of insiders and allies, 17 of whom are or were agency chiefs in a interconnected, covert ecosystem.

At MI6’s headquarters in Vauxhall, London, there has been no sign of a public reaction from its chief, Blaise Metreweli. But there is a quiet satisfaction at the unexpected verdict, not least because the agency values how it is perceived by both allies and adversaries. “Reputation matters a lot in the espionage game,” said a former Whitehall insider.

“British spies fascinate Europe, and beyond,” L’Express explained in its cover story. Saviana added that MI6’s success in the poll was principally down to its record in recruiting and running high-level human sources over generations: a focus on human intelligence in an era dominated by technology, intercepts and satellite monitoring.

“The British have the ability to play the long game, to bet on sources over 10 years, a bit like the Russians,” a former French DGSE spy told the magazine, adding “and they have a penchant for underhand tactics” without revealing what they meant.

One ex-spy voiced scepticism about the survey and added that a human intelligence service such as MI6 was only as good as the high-value agents on its books. Under Richard Moore, MI6’s previous chief, there were worries that it no longer had enough. Others, including Saviana, accept that greater credit might have been given to MI6’s sister agency, the signals intelligence experts at GCHQ, but it was not in the poll.

MI6’s reputation among its peers, the French publication said, was built on “long standing tradition”, including recruiting cold war assets, most notably the KGB’s Oleg Gordievsky, a double agent through late 1970s and early 80s, who helped convince Margaret Thatcher to take Mikhail Gorbachev seriously before he had to be dramatically smuggled into Finland in 1985, his cover finally blown.

Not every mole evaded capture. Alireza Akbari, a former Iranian deputy defence minister who had become a British citizen, was arrested on a return to Iran in 2019 and executed in 2023. Prior to his death, he confessed to being an MI6 agent. Though the confessions appeared coerced, spies from a number of countries indicated he was the person who had passed on the existence of the Fordow nuclear enrichment site in 2008.

In the run-up to the 2003 Iraq war, MI6 was accused of simplistically supporting the case for war, promoting what turned out to be false sources, claiming that Iraq’s leader, Saddam Hussein, could attack UK targets within “45 minutes”, and relied on one source who described supposed chemical weapons devices that were remarkably similar to one in the Hollywood movie The Rock. It was a low point.

L’Express argued that MI6 had rehabilitated itself in the run-up to the Ukraine war in February 2022, correctly warning in conjunction with the CIA that Russia was about to invade, while French and German counterparts were sceptical up until the last minute, having misjudged the situation. The chief of the German BND agency even flew into Kyiv the day before the invasion, seemingly unprepared.

It reflects MI6’s close and longstanding relationship with the CIA, part of the wider Five Eyes arrangements for intelligence sharing, between the US, UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, that are the envy of continental Europe, even allowing for the complexities posed by Donald Trump’s chaotic presidency. “Every other country wants to say they are the sixth eye,” Saviana said.

Fiction also has its advantages. Gordon Corera, a co-presenter of The Rest is Classified podcast, recalled that a former MI6 chief once told him a story of a young officer going somewhere far flung, not knowing whether the person he was trying to cultivate spoke English. “As he walked into the room the contact extended his hand and said: ‘Hello, Mr Bond.’ The former chief remarked: ‘I doubt if he would have received such a warm welcome if he’d been from the Belgian secret service.’”

Train operators to crack down on ‘donutters’ and other digital ticket cheats

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 10:00:42 GMT

South Western and GTR announce fightback after move away from paper tickets increases fare dodging

There is more than one way to commit fraud and, for some rail travellers, it has been as simple as a couple of taps on their phone as their train approaches its destination.

That telltale last-minute purchase of a digital ticket – for the shortest journey that will allow them to bleep through the gates, regardless of how far they have travelled – is one of a number of illegal wheezes that train operators are trying to eliminate, with the enthusiastic backing of the government department that will directly oversee most of England’s rail services when they are renationalised next year.

Two rail companies, South Western Railway (SWR) and GTR, which operates Thameslink, Southern and other services, this week introduced measures to clamp down on “short-faring” – a trick by which passengers buy a last-minute digital ticket only for the final part of their journey, even if they boarded in a station without barriers much further away.

Don’t bother trying to download a digital ticket from Vauxhall to Waterloo, the terminus for many trains to London from the west – or on a number of other routes, apparently including from Norwood Junction to London Bridge, where many services from the south coast hit the capital. For those and some other routes, you will now need to collect a physical ticket from a physical ticket machine, after operators found that up to 95% of tickets on some short routes were being used fraudulently.

Fare evasion on Britain’s railways did not begin with digitisation – you don’t need a QR code to vault a barrier or hide in the toilet from a ticket inspector. But the increasing reliance on digital ticketing has widened some of the loopholes for those minded to cheat – and added to an ever-growing problem for train companies.

Up to £400m is lost to fraud each year on the rail network, according to the Department for Transport, through high-tech and decidedly low-tech methods. As well as short-faring, operators point to “quick scanning” (buying a ticket on your phone seconds before being approached by an inspector), “tailgating” (squeezing behind a paying customer as they pass through a ticket gate) and “donutting”, a scam by which a passenger buys a cheap ticket covering the first part of their journey and another covering the last, but avoids paying the higher cost of the full trip. A former senior executive at HSBC, Joseph Molloy, received a suspended sentence earlier this year for using this technique 740 times to commute between Orpington in Kent and London Bridge, saving him £5,911 over 11 months.

“It’s quite a big problem, because we’re coming to terms with a completely different form of ticketing,” said the railway commentator and author Christian Wolmar. “No longer do you go to the ticket office and buy little red and yellow cards. You now buy online, and that affords these new opportunities. The system is clearly open to abuse.”

Though a push to reduce staff numbers has been a factor, he says, “how you tackle this is very difficult because you can’t have guards at every stop. It’s through digital analysis that they are going to find a solution to this.”

The government appears to agree, widening the introduction earlier this month of an app that calculates ticket fares by tracking the user’s phone. While currently being trialled on a number of routes in the East Midlands and Yorkshire, the technology could eventually be brought in across Great British Railways, the public body that will take over the running of the soon-to-be renationalised network, expected to be up and running next year.

“Fare evasion is illegal and selfish – it actively makes journeys worse for all rail passengers by diverting money that could otherwise be used to improve services,” said the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander. “We are committed to tackling ticket cheats, and that’s one of the expected benefits of expanding our digital ticketing app to more people across the trial areas.”

Her department has also recently given £33m for new or enhanced ticket gates at “fare dodger hotspots” across England, and has closed a loophole that allowed some passengers to dishonestly claim a refund even though they had used a service.

SWR said its introduction of new anti-fraud measures came after one intervention at Brighton station found that half of those travelling on the wrong ticket were using the short-faring scam.

To passengers disembarking at the station on Friday morning, a clampdown on cheats was very welcome. “Obviously fares go up anyway because of inflation, but they are probably pushing up our fares as well, so we all suffer,” said Deanna Smith, who had travelled on Thameslink with her partner to visit a coffee festival. “It’s just like tax dodging – we all fall victim to their behaviour.”

Nicola Garrett, who was on a day trip to Brighton with a friend from her home town of Leigh-on-Sea, said: “I’m someone who has always paid for everything, so I get a bit pissed off [by fare dodging]. Nobody seems to think that they have to pay for anything these days. It’s just like, if you can get away with doing it, why wouldn’t you?”

Fifa president Gianni Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged ‘lover’

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 09:27:46 GMT

Infantino was Uefa general secretary from 2009 to 2016

‘These allegations … are categorically untrue,’ says Fifa

Uefa has confirmed a “departure payment” was made to a female employee who is alleged to have been in a relationship with Gianni Infantino while he was the organisation’s general secretary, allegations Fifa has dismissed as “categorically untrue”.

The Daily Telegraph reported on Friday night that the woman received a six-figure sum following the alleged relationship with Infantino. In a statement, Uefa confirmed a payment was made along with covering the fees for an MBA course, which it said was “in line” with regulations at the time.

However, Fifa has responded to the reports. “Fifa president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory,” a Fifa spokesman told the Telegraph. “No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino’s behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved.”

The report comes as pressure mounts on Infantino following his plan to seek private investment in a company which would run Fifa’s competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cups. Infantino worked at Uefa for 16 years and was its general secretary from 2009 before being elected as Fifa president in February 2016.

A Uefa spokesperson said: “We are aware of the allegations and can confirm a departure payment was made to the individual in question, coupled with the payment of fees for a MBA course at a local business school.”

The payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time. “Such regulations have been tightened since 2016 and the current staff regulations – which apply to all Uefa employees at whatever level – reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation.”

Infantino has found himself at the centre of a storm for two weeks following his controversial plan to sell stakes to private investors in a company to run the World Cup. The plan was rejected by Uefa and two other continental confederations. On Wednesday, Infantino was backed by Fifa’s management board following a meeting in Morocco and issued an apology over the process.

Uefa’s threat for its 55 member countries to boycott Fifa competitions until the plan was scrapped remains, with the European confederation saying on Thursday that Wednesday’s announcement “changes nothing”.

Is it OK to talk about Ariana Grande’s body? There is no right answer

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 09:00:43 GMT

I wish I could say that expressing concern for the pop star’s health is helpful – but I know from experience it’s not that simple

The last time I opened X, a photo of Ariana Grande leaning over in a low-cut black dress, clavicle showing, was at the top of the feed. The post read: “hey @grok make Ariana Grande healthy and fat”.

Images of celebrities at their most skeletal regularly rise to the top of social feeds because they generate enormous, dissenting engagement. Social media platforms have made half-hearted efforts to suppress explicit pro-eating disorder content; Instagram and TikTok redirect searches for “thinspo” toward support resources. Yet over the past couple weeks, Grande has sent users into a frenzy that outstrips the platforms’ attempts.

The screenshot the user posted was taken from Grande’s music video for Petal, the title track from her latest album. Grande and her team have not said that she lives with any kind of eating disorder. Nevertheless, promotion for Petal has been thoroughly overshadowed by discussion of the singer’s ultra-thin body.

Other replies to the screenshot ranged from vicious attacks on Grande and other users’ bodies, to earnest, almost desperate pleas for empathy. Having lived with an eating disorder as a teenager, I recognize in these reactions a familiar pattern. People often respond to the visibly suffering body with a visceral pity intertwined with a kind of disgust. Whether that response actually protects anyone, or instead solidifies the very dynamics it seeks to resist, is a question worth returning to.

Those of us who have lived through eating disorders and are witnessing this news cycle feel compelled to offer our own interpretations – to explain what this moment means, and to argue for the “right” way to speak about it. But precisely because disordered eating is so idiosyncratic and so forceful, there may be no single correct language for confronting it. The only honest response may be to acknowledge its contradictions.

In the case of Grande, all of the prayers, best wishes and outcries so far haven’t provoked the public response so many have hoped for. Instead, it appears to have pushed her in the opposite direction. Over the weekend, just days after the release of Petal, a representative told People magazine that Grande would be “taking a step back from visibility” after her current tour, cancelling future promotional plans and withdrawing from an upcoming West End revival of Sunday in the Park With George. At a recent concert, Grande explained to fans that stepping back from the spotlight was something she had planned “a long time ago” and that it came from a “thoughtful and empowered place”.

If this were a case of disordered eating, a retreat from public life might seem like a positive step towards recovery. But I know from experience that someone who is suffering can mistake isolation for self-preservation. The cruelty of an eating disorder is how easily it convinces you that it is the only thing standing between you and a world trying to take control away from you.

Concerns over Grande’s body have hovered since the beginning of her teenage acting career. In 2013, the year she released her debut album, Yours Truly, she took to her old Tumblr account – which has itself been accused of “pro-ana” content, or content promoting disordered eating – to address “the rumors going around.” In a blogpost she wrote that reports of “this whole ‘eating disorder thing’” had been “a bit blown out of proportion”.

“Yes, I lost a bit of weight last year,” she continued. “It’s because I stopped eating junk food and started making healthy choices. I was happy with the way I was before and I’m still happy now! Just healthier!”

More than a decade later, she made much the same point in a TikTok after people posted side-by-side photos of her during the Wicked press tour and the years when she acted on the Nickelodeon show Victorious. “The body you’ve been comparing my current body to was the unhealthiest version of my body,” she said in April 2023. “I was on a lot of antidepressants and drinking on them.”

Her response reminded me of something the singer Fiona Apple said in 2013, after years of speculation about her weight. While performing on stage, Apple exploded at a heckler who shouted: “get healthy”. “I’m healthy and I shouldn’t even have to say any of that,” Apple told Pitchfork the next day. “What makes me unhealthy and puts me in danger is that kind of scrutiny itself.”

Avoiding scrutiny can become part of an eating disorder itself. I know this because I suffered for many years with bulimia, and I now realize my years spent hiding in the bathroom after every meal was an attempt to withdraw from any kind of outside opinion. When friends hugged me and recoiled at the touch of my bones, that only influenced me to raise the wall between myself and the rest of the world. It was an untenable and, frankly, devastating attempt to cope with the terror of puberty, trying all I could to stay both in control and independent of my body and its radical changes.

On several levels, disordered eating is built on irreconcilable tensions. It requires relentless self-control while submitting to an all-consuming fixation. In seeking to disappear, the thin body only becomes a spectacle of morbid curiosity. What usually begins as an effort to master the self soon becomes an act of self-destruction. The confused discourse surrounding Grande’s weight mirrors the paradox. Every word feels stuck in place, because we don’t yet have a cultural script capable of holding all these ambiguities.

It is obvious and true that the bodies of female celebrities are uniquely surveilled. It’s why Billie Eilish resisted that surveillance by wearing oversized clothing and criticizing the public’s sense of entitlement to judge her body – a tactic Grande employed, too, in 2018, a year after the devastating Manchester Arena bombing.

For much of the 2010s, the body positivity movement supplied a simple injunction against prying eyes: don’t comment on women’s bodies. It corrected for the smarmy and misogynistic tabloid treatment of celebrities in the aughts, discouraging public discussion of other people’s bodies as intrusive, harmful and unnecessary.

But it might have been an overcorrection. Grande’s appearance presents a case where that consensus no longer feels entirely adequate, or ethically tenable. But it’s complicated. Two feminist arguments are at odds. The first is that women should not have to submit their bodies to public interpretation or explanation. The second is that eating disorders thrive in secrecy and denial. We do not want a culture that treats visible suffering – and conversations around them – as too taboo to acknowledge.

After all, Grande has long featured in thinspo Pinterest boards. On private pro-ana message boards, users have found recognition in her public statements. “The whole ‘don’t worry about me’ and ‘the old me was sad and unhealthy’ sounds like people responding to an intervention lol,” one user wrote. On the pro-ana internet, Grande’s body is both hailed as aspirational and a huge trigger. In eating-disorder recovery Reddit communities, users describe her as the reason for their “relapse”, putting them back into the mindset of their illness. Beneath the now widely circulated photograph of Grande bending over, users in the underground X community known as EDTwt have openly compared themselves to her body and wondered how they might achieve a similar appearance.

More broadly, her body has also become a proxy on to which wider cultural anxieties are projected. In a moment of GLP-1 drugs reinstating the aspiration of thinness, body positivity in retreat, bonesmashing still on the up, and Maga tradwives once again moralizing fatness, fears about the return of aughts-era anorexia have settled on to Grande herself. Whether or not those fears belong to her alone is almost beside the point. Her body has become the site through which the culture argues with itself.

She is hardly the first celebrity on to whom those anxieties have been projected. From Karen Carpenter’s collapse from starvation at her parent’s home in 1983 to the many stars who have since publicly disclosed eating disorders – including Demi Lovato, Taylor Swift and Kesha – it is almost assumed that a significant portion of the female entertainment industry has, or has had, some form of eating disorder. The illness is simultaneously embedded within ordinary culture and yet treated as an aberration whenever it becomes visible.

The desire to resolve those contradictions might even keep us at the distance the illness relies on, allowing us to imagine that a single correct response will absolve us of having to deal with it in the first place. Instead we could try broadening our concern towards the millions living with eating disorders by petitioning to improve a medical system that has so often failed them; insurers that routinely deny care if the patient’s BMI is anything other than extremely emaciated; and clinicians who still stigmatize the illness.

Grande’s visibility isn’t moving down the feed. People are continuing to debate it, defend it, plead for us to find another way to talk about it. But ultimately, another person’s physical and mental reality is out of our control; no one person’s recovery can be crowdsourced. If only it were all as simple as Grok editing Grande into health.

In the US, help is available at nationaleatingdisorders. org or by calling ANAD’s eating disorders hotline at 800-375-7767. In the UK, Beat can be contacted on 0808-801-0677. In Australia, the Butterfly Foundation is at 1800 33 4673. Other international helplines can be found at Eating Disorder Hope

Scratch of the day: local football season postponed due to ‘rock hard’ pitches

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 09:00:43 GMT

Drought and record heat have forced the Norfolk and Suffolk league to move kick-off to the end of August as the ground is deemed too dangerous to play on

This summer’s record drought has forced a football league to delay the start of its season because “rock hard” pitches are a danger to its players.

The 2026/27 season in the Anglian Combination League of 85 amateur teams in Norfolk and Suffolk was due to start next weekend.

But on Friday after an urgent meeting, the league’s board announced it had unanimously decided to postpone the start of the season until the end of August, because most of the clubs’ pitches are dried out and too dangerous to play on.

It said a number of pre-season friendlies have had to be cancelled because of the drought and matches that have gone ahead have led to “many injuries”.

In a statement addressed to all leagues clubs, players and officials, it confirmed the start of the season will be delayed until 29 August.

“The rationale behind this decision is to protect the welfare of players, officials and all associated with the match day, in what has been the driest and hottest July since records began in 1836,” the league chair, Dale Brown, said in the statement. “Most of our league clubs pitches are grass and the ground conditions are extremely dry and pitches rock hard.”

Brown added: “This was a very difficult decision to reach and one that will not please all clubs.”

The league’s decision comes after a series of record-breaking heat waves and exceptionally low rainfall have left much of England and Wales visibly parched and the ground as hard as concrete.

Record temperatures were experienced in May and June, and July was the driest month since records began. A drought was declared in half of England last month with many water companies imposing hosepipe bans. Such a ban by Anglian Water which covers Norfolk and Suffolk, has been in force since 11 July.

Aerial images have shown dried out parks and sports fields devoid of any signs of green, with the exception of golf clubs, some sports clubs, and private schools who enjoy controversial exemptions from hosepipe bans.

The Met Office forecasts another heatwave next week, with temperatures set to reach 36C in parts of East Anglia and south-east England by next Thursday. There is no sign of much-needed rain, although humidity is expected to increase next week.

The FA does not hold figures on the number of leagues that have been forced to postpone the start of next season because of the drought. It said it was a matter of individual leagues and county football associations.

‘The market is dead’: why aren’t flats in England selling?

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 09:00:42 GMT

Figures show most leasehold flats in England do not find a buyer within six months, despite slashed prices

‘The market is dead for flats,” says Susan Young*, who has been trying for some time without success to sell her two-bed flat in a popular Devon seaside resort.

The first-floor property is in “immaculate condition”, Young says, thanks to the £15,000-£20,000 spent on renovations. It has “superb views” across the beach. And, perhaps most crucially, it is a freehold flat, so is untainted by the controversies associated with the discredited leasehold system.

“Despite not needing to buy (that is, no chain) and dropping the price to well under what I paid for it, I have only had four viewings in nine months,” says Young, a former teacher, who moved in 2023 but now needs to relocate for family reasons.

She paid £300,000 for the property and currently has it on the market for £280,000.

She does not want to reduce the price any further and, if there are no viewings by the end of the summer, she intends to take the flat off the market and put it back on next year when, hopefully, there will be more interest from buyers.

She says the flats market is moribund even though hers is in a block of six where each flat owns a sixth of the freehold and they set their own management fee. “It is very dispiriting.”

Meanwhile, Louisa, who lives in London, has been trying to sell her leasehold flat for two and a half years. The sale recently fell through for a third time after several months of negotiations when the buyers demanded she knock £10,000 off the price.

She initially feared having to “sell at a massive loss, losing all my deposit and preventing me from buying in the near future. My property is above a barber shop, and I have been told that banks will not lend mortgages above these, leaving me in a position looking for reasonable cash offers.”

However, there is now some hope as she has found a cash buyer. “So I’m currently going through the process again, but I’ve stated that I will only give the sale a few months before giving up and trying to rent it out. This will be attempt number four.”

Louisa bought the flat for £200,000, and the sale that fell through recently was for £145,000.

“It’s a one-bed flat, and I now have a two-year-old daughter. This situation has meant we are unable to leave my family home, where we have been staying. I just want to move on and give my child a bedroom.

“I’m not buying again in the near future. I’m quite traumatised from the experience.”

Young and Louisa are just two of the Guardian readers who responded to a recent call-out asking about their experiences of trying to buy or sell a flat in recent months.

Many of the respondents said the same thing: they have been trying – and trying – to sell a flat. Some have cut the price several times but to no avail; others have been left in the lurch when buyers pulled out.

Some are owner-occupiers; others are small landlords who are trying to leave the rental sector.

So what’s happening?

In June, the property website Zoopla issued data showing that the average price of a house was up 43% since 2016 across the UK, but flats had increased by 10% over the same period.

Zoopla said “uncertainty around leasehold in England is affecting the pricing of flats versus houses” and that flats were taking longer to sell as a result.

Most flats listed for sale in England are leasehold. And the long list of scandals and controversies associated with this form of ownership – from high service charges and ground rents and hefty one-off bills to cladding issues, costly lease extensions and difficulty buying freeholds – has prompted government action.

However, a ban on new leasehold properties in England and Wales is unlikely to come into force until after the next election, and concerns about cost and complexity are clearly having an impact now.

We asked Zoopla to crunch the numbers on flats not selling and why. It found that across most of England, the majority of leasehold flats listed for sale in 2025 had not sold within six months.

“London was worst – about 87% unsold – followed by the south-east (85%) and the east of England (84%),” Richard Donnell, the Zoopla executive director, says. The average was 80.5%.

As to why many flats are struggling to find buyers, Donnell says it is not only the leasehold issue, which reinforces the preference for buying a house where possible. It is also to do with who is buying and who is selling.

“Flats take longer to find buyers because the natural buyer (the first-time buyer) and the natural seller (often an investor with no urgency to move) may want two different prices,” he adds.

For example, in London, most first-time buyers are looking for flats, not houses, as flats are their main route into ownership, Donnell says. “But investor-owned flats are being priced above the typical first-time buyer budget (£450,000 v a £425,000 budget). So even though flats are what buyers there want, the ones investors are selling are out of reach.”

In addition, thousands of aspiring homeowners are finding themselves shut out of the flats market owing to banks’ increasingly restrictive mortgage lending rules, says William Coe at the mortgage broker Cleerly. At the same time, he adds, surveyors are increasingly “down valuing” flats – creating yet another barrier for buyers.

Barbara Doolan*, who lives in Sussex, has owned a flat in a small block in Croydon for 20 years, and has always rented it out.

She tried to sell the flat in 2024 but had no joy, despite cutting the price twice. She says she had no choice but to rent it out again, and had a “terrible experience” with the tenant, who defaulted on the rent and illegally sublet it.

“I’ve considered selling again … and the market is even worse now. Three agents have said I’d need to drop the price by another £30k to get some interest as small flats like this just aren’t selling.”

Angie West and her wife own two flats in London, one of which they bought 20 years ago as a buy-to-let investment. At the time they both worked in the voluntary sector and neither had a private or workplace pension, so they hoped the flat would provide them with some financial security in retirement.

West, who is now semi-retired, says that in late 2024 they put it on the market for £325,000. There followed a difficult period during which they reduced the asking price several times and had two separate buyers pull out.

With costs mounting, they later decided they would have to rent the property out again. More costs were racked up, and the current tenants recently gave notice and are due to leave this month.

“We intend to try selling the flat again but are very worried about what will happen if it does not sell … What concerns me most is that the combination of falling flat values, repeated failed sales, leasehold costs, licensing requirements and increasing complexity in the rental sector has left ordinary small landlords like us trapped,” says West, who lives in south London.

“The whole process feels incredibly insecure. Buyers can pull out at any stage for almost any reason, with no financial consequence to them, while sellers are left paying legal fees, management pack costs and other expenses.”

Know your market “Chat to your agent about what local first-time buyers can actually afford and who is buying flats and what they are prepared to pay,” Zoopla’s Donnell says.

Price realistically from day one Buyers have a lot of choice, so getting the asking price right is crucial. “The key to selling a flat successfully in the current market is pricing competitively from day one,” says Colleen Babcock, Rightmove’s property expert. “Our research shows that nearly three-quarters of homes that have sold so far this year have done so without a price reduction.” So if you list a property at an optimistic price, thinking you can always reduce it later, “you’re putting yourself at an immediate disadvantage”.

Major on all the benefits The buying agent Henry Pryor says that aside from the obvious – “make it clean, make it tidy, make it desirable, make it smell of freshly baked bread and coffee …” – sellers should also emphasise the property’s “lock up and leave” benefits. Lock up and leave means requiring very little in terms of daily maintenance – for example, a flat that doesn’t have a garden or lots of rooms or areas to clean.

Be on top of your service charge history Some potential buyers will ask for (at least) three years of service charge accounts (where relevant). So sort these out before you list the property and be ready to explain the trend, Donnell says. A recent Zoopla analysis showed that the typical leaseholder pays £1,900 a year in service charges, plus £200 a year in ground rent. If your service charges or ground rent are relatively low, then point this out, Rightmove says.

Lease length matters About a fifth of leasehold listings have less than 100 years left on the lease, according to Zoopla. Leaseholders have the statutory right to extend their lease at a cost that rises quickly once a lease drops below 80 years, it adds. “For flats with less than 85 years remaining, consider applying to extend the lease before listing,” Donnell says. The Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024 will make it cheaper and easier to extend a lease, but it’s not yet clear when these measures will come into force. The government last month said the changes would go live “as soon as possible”.

Six may be the magic number “You should always be able to attract an investor by pricing your property so that a buyer would generate a 6% or better yield,” Pryor says. You need to work out what your flat would rent for (local estate agents should be able to provide that information), he says. Then work out what capital value would generate a 6% or better yield. To do this, take the annual potential rent – the per calendar month figure x 12 – then multiply this by 100, then divide by 6. “That’s where you need to pitch your asking price,” Pryor says, although he adds “hopefully you will do better” than that and actually find a buyer who really likes your flat.

* Name has been changed

This burning summer is the proof: the voices of climate denial aren’t just delusional, they’re deadly

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 08:00:41 GMT

Look at our blazing forests and parched cities. Green policies aren’t a ‘luxury’, and we can’t burn more oil and gas. People need the truth

Report: Sadiq Khan calls on Andy Burnham to commit to climate action as pressure grows over North Sea oil

Europe is burning. This summer, an unprecedented series of heatwaves has swept through the continent and across many parts of the globe. The consequences have been nothing short of catastrophic. In recent weeks deadly blazes have torn through France, Greece and Spain, killing firefighters, forcing people from their homes and robbing them of their livelihoods.

With Tuesday marking Britain’s 34th day of temperatures exceeding 30C (86F) this year, the UK has also found itself reckoning with ferocious heat. Wildfires have forced evacuations in Suffolk and the Cairngorms. In London – where parks have become burnt, brittle and brown – hundreds of grass fires have put our firefighters under pressure like never before. In July, the weather station at Kew Gardens recorded its first ever month without rain since it started operating in 1871. As rivers run dry and reservoirs run low, farmers are warning of food shortages amid the deepening drought. With thousands of deaths already estimated to be linked to the extreme heat we saw in May and June alone, it’s likely this figure will climb higher still.

The terrifying scenes we’ve seen so far this summer are the latest part of a pernicious long-term pattern. This is the third drought London has experienced in the past five years. Across the world, the past 11 years have been the 11 hottest ever recorded – and with a super strength El Niño forming in the Pacific which could pour yet more fuel on the fire, that trend is all but certain to continue. The climate emergency is here – and no one can say they didn’t see it coming.

When I was first elected mayor back in 2016, I warned that our rapidly warming world would be the defining challenge of our time. I was the first mayor of a global city to declare a climate emergency. Since then, a coalition of climate deniers and delayers has been relentless in condemning the green policies I’ve introduced. When I announced my intention to expand the Ulez – creating the largest clean air zone in the world – they unsuccessfully attempted to drag down the debate and whip up a crude culture war. On social media, people were blinded by a dark blizzard of disinformation designed to discredit climate action. Radicalised by what he’d seen online, one man even detonated a homemade bomb, destroying a Ulez camera in a shocking act of domestic terrorism.

Looking back now, it feels like the fierce fight over Ulez marked the beginning of something else: a new age of extreme climate scepticism. In the years since, the horrifying reality of the climate crisis has come into sharp relief – and yet somehow the clamouring voices of denial and delay have grown louder than ever. Having dismissed climate change as a “con job”, Donald Trump has sought to sabotage global climate action, withdrawing the United States from the Paris agreement for the second time, cutting support for clean energy, and boosting oil and gas production. In the UK, where cross-party consensus on the climate crisis has collapsed, his ideas have been echoed by opposition politicians and rightwing populists who veer wildly between denialism and fatalism. As some claim the climate crisis is a hoax, others insist it’s too late to act.

Both arguments are bogus. The climate crisis is getting worse, but in London we’ve shown that – with courage and creativity – we can prepare ourselves for its impacts. We’ve planted more than 640,000 trees across the capital, shading our streets from the summer sun. We’ve embraced rewilding while creating and improving more than 2,000 football pitches’ worth of green space, providing natural drainage to prevent flooding. And just last month, we set out a plan to clean up our rivers and create safe swimming sites where Londoners can cool down in the heat. We have more zero-emission buses than any city in Europe and about a third of our country’s electric charging points.

At the same time, since I’ve been mayor our city’s carbon emissions have fallen by about a quarter, while our economy has continued to grow. And last year the Ulez helped us to get levels of nitrogen oxide – one of the most toxic pollutants in our air – within legal limits almost two centuries before experts predicted we would. Between 2019 and 2024, estimated deaths associated with air pollution in London fell by an estimated 40%.

Through C40 Cities, a network of almost 100 global cities I co-chair, London is working side by side with cities around the world to take on the climate emergency – from rolling out new green buses to boosting the supply of renewable energy – but we cannot do this alone. National governments across the globe must step up and meet the gravity of this moment with renewed focus, funding and resolve. This includes our own government, which should reassure the public by reaffirming its commitment to net zero and making clear that it will continue to reduce our reliance on oil and gas and to invest in green projects.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The most common refrain I hear from climate deniers is that green policies are some kind of luxury divorced from the worries of working people who are just trying to get by. But the idea that you can separate the climate crisis from the cost of living is patently absurd. What happens when droughts cause food prices to rise and when oil-price shocks squeeze household budgets? When hospitals are overwhelmed by vulnerable people struggling in the heat? When railways and roads buckle, workplaces close and schools are shuttered? The notion that climate action represents “woke nonsense” relies on the ridiculous premise that the climate crisis isn’t real – or that if it is, we won’t feel its impact on our lives. This year has proven just how wrong that is.

We are living in an era of extremes, and my fear is that – without urgent action – the worst is still to come. In this context, climate denial and delay isn’t just delusional – it’s deadly. Because it won’t be President Trump and the fossil fuel companies paying the price for failure – it will be the rest of us. If we are to protect our planet and the people who call it home, we must turn the tide on climate denial by preparing for a hotter future and embracing net zero like never before.

Sadiq Khan is mayor of London

Planting seeds of peace: teenagers from conflict-torn world build bridges at summer camp

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 08:00:40 GMT

UK hosts decades-old event for first time where many participants are from opposite sides of global disputes from Israel and Palestine, to India and Pakistan

On the surface it looks like a normal summer school in the Devon countryside, with teenagers playing volleyball in the sun, doing arts and crafts in the hall, and preparing for the night’s talent show.

But behind the scenes, intensive discussions are taking place. Many of these teenagers come from opposite sides of historical national conflicts – from Israel and Palestine, India and Pakistan.

Every day at Seeds of Peace they spend two hours in dialogue sessions with each other, sharing their personal experiences, their pain and trauma, and trying to find the common ground that unites them. Over the course of three weeks, that is 32 hours in a room discussing heavy topics and trying to build bridges.

“You won’t find them sitting with maps and facts and books,” said Eva Armour, Seeds of Peace’s executive director. “They’re talking about their own lived experiences – that’s how the learning is happening. You can’t debate someone else’s lived experience the way that you might debate what happened in the war.

“It’s almost embarrassingly simple how well this model works, but we need to invest in this work even a fraction of what we’re investing in the aftermath of war.”

The Seeds of Peace summer camp, for teenagers aged 14 to 17 from eight different countries including the UK, has been running for 30 years but this is the first time it has been held in Britain.

Founded in 1993 by the American journalist John Wallach, it usually takes place in the US but political uncertainty meant organisers felt the UK was a safer bet this year.

“Picking a country to host this is one of the enormous challenges,” said Qasim Aslam, the global youth programme lead. “If you pull up a map, there are very few countries where all parents from all eight countries would be comfortable sending their kids, and where we can get visas for all participants.”

Coming to the end of their three-week stay at a Devonshire boarding school in Tavistock, many of the campers – known as “seeds” – said the experience had been challenging but life-changing.

Mika, a 17-year-old from Israel, said she was glad she attended even though she had not come closer to answering her questions about peace. “Now I’m thinking, did I really expect three weeks to fix it all?

“Facing someone who is supposed to be my enemy, but she’s just a girl like me – it’s difficult,” she said. “I could just not know about it and go and have fun in another summer camp and it would be way easier. But I prefer knowing it and starting to work through it for what I believe.

“If one day maybe I have the power to change something, I don’t want to be ignorant. I want to know the pains of everyone.”

Hala, a 16-year-old Palestinian from Jerusalem, said it was the first time she had met Israelis “outside of checkpoints, raids and IDF uniforms”.

“It was hard at first, I thought I was betraying something deep down inside of me,” she said. “But when I got to know these people, I realised they have very different views about their government. And we like the same movie. We have so many things in common.”

Even for those coming from outside the main conflict zones, the experience has been enlightening. “I have never had the chance to speak to people from different countries like Israel and Palestine before – you never know how the media censors stuff so it’s really powerful to hear from people themselves,” said Esther, a 17-year-old from Belfast. “I feel like I’ll be much less quick to judge people now.”

For some participants, the act of attending is fraught with difficulty. Ahmad, a 26-year-old Palestinian camp counsellor who previously attended as a teenager, said he would not be speaking about his summer trip back home.

“For some people, it feels like you’re betraying your country, because you’re trying to make peace with the people who are killing you at the same time,” he said. “You can’t just go home and expect people to understand Seeds of Peace in a second. You need to be here to understand that.”

While camp organisers aim to get a diverse range of teenagers, they admitted there were limits to how accessible they could be – English language skills are required so the dialogue sessions can be most effective.

The cost to attend the summer camp is $9,000 (£6,700), although many of those attending receive scholarships to cover the vast majority of this fee. And in some countries there is a competitive application process. “We’re trying to identify young people that could be influencers in their respective communities in the future,” said Aslam.

Many past attenders have gone on to become politicians, ambassadors and business leaders, taking the skills they learned at Seeds of Peace with them into their work.

Over the past three decades, the organisers have worked in areas such as the Balkans, Cyprus, Greece, Turkey and Afghanistan, tailoring their camps to respond to geopolitical events. They also do year-round work and regional camps in place where need is greatest.

“It feels like it’s getting harder for people to be able to talk to each other across differences,” said Armour. “After 7 October [attacks on Israel by Hamas], we actually got a lot of calls from schools and institutions saying we don’t really know how to talk to each other about this, can you help?”

Joud, a 17-year-old from Jordan attending for the second year, said the camp had enabled her to have healthy debate with her family for the first time, and she had become good friends with a Jewish girl from the US, which she “never expected”.

“Our social identities are complete opposites. But we connected in many different ways, and I learned how to listen and understand, not just respond,” she said.

“In what situations are 14- to 17-year-olds with very opposing ideologies and opinions sat down together in a room for two hours talking about things that maybe the leaders of their own countries don’t have the courage to sit down and talk about?”

US accused of meddling in British politics with $500,000 grant for ‘public education’ courses

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 07:00:41 GMT

Documents published on US embassy’s website prompt claims of attempt to export Maga propaganda to UK

The US embassy in London is offering grants of up to half a million dollars for new “public education” programmes in what has been criticised as interference in British domestic politics.

Using language that the pro-Trump Maga movement has sought to appropriate, a funding notice identifies a goal of fostering a “national conversation” about “shared civilizational values” underpinning US-UK ties. Priority will go to applicants aiming to celebrate “freedom of speech” and “limited government”.

It comes after senior Trump officials voiced sharp criticism of British authorities and repeated misinformation on a range of fronts including abortion and digital regulation, and allied with European far-right movements in attacks on hate speech and immigration policies.

The grants appear to be separate from other grants of $12m which the US state department is planning to allocate to organisations in the UK founded by the prominent Conservatives Jacob Rees-Mogg and Toby Young.

Those intended grants, revealed in US government documents leaked to the Guardian, are part of a package of support for European groups viewed favourably by the Trump administration.

However, the US government has now been accused of “meddling in British democracy” after documents published on the US embassy’s website invited charities, non-profit organisations and others to apply for grants under a scheme labelled “Liberty Under Law: The Shared Anglo-American Tradition”.

It seeks “innovative, high-visibility public education and civic-engagement programs” that “deepen public understanding of the shared Anglo-American common law tradition” and to commemorate the 70th anniversary next year of the American Bar Association (ABA)’s unveiling of the Magna Carta memorial in Runnymede.

The ABA – which is not involved in the grant scheme – is suing the Trump administration over alleged intimidation of lawyers and legal firms. European counterparts including the Law Society and the Bar Association in Britain have voiced support for US lawyers claiming that the US president’s attacks on law firms bear similarities to events in Nazi Germany.

A notice offering the funding states: “Priority will be given to ambitious initiatives that connect foundational principles, such as freedom of speech, due process, trial by jury, limited government, rule of law, property rights, taxation by consent, and ordered liberty to contemporary civic life.”

Proposed projects must meet one or more of a number of objectives, including the need to “demonstrate measurable impact on public discourse, media coverage, and civic engagement regarding the rule of law and democratic norms”.

Lisa Smart, a Liberal Democrat MP and the party’s Cabinet Office spokesperson, said: “Magna Carta aimed to limit the powers of tyrants and said everyone was subject to the rule of law, something for which Trump has repeatedly shown utter contempt.

“We have a proud tradition of liberty and freedom of speech in this country and we don’t need Trump’s Maga money meddling in our democracy.”

There is also deep unease among serving and recently departed US state department officials. One told the Guardian: “While it’s not unusual to support public diplomacy efforts to showcase the special relationship between the US and UK, to specifically fund topics related to a narrow vision of America First is highly unusual.”

The same person accused the US government of trying to “create UK-originated narratives to support Maga propaganda”.

The notice states that the funding is not intended to support partisan political activity or lobbying.

A spokesperson at the US embassy in London said the funding initiative aimed to strengthen US-UK ties “and deepen public understanding of the constitutional principles, rule of law, and democratic norms that underpin both nations”.

Responding to Smart’s allegation of “meddling”, they added: “The Embassy is mindful of such concerns, and has discontinued Biden-era public diplomacy spending on divisive ideological projects such as ‘climate justice,’ LGBTQ activism, and race-based hiring initiatives – none of which, to our recollection, raised such complaints from officials.”

Eyebrows have also been raised by veteran former state department officials at some language used in a second grant opportunity being offered by the US embassy’s website under its Public Diplomacy Section program, an annual grant scheme.

Applications, including those intending to run “Educational and public awareness initiatives”, are invited to submit proposals for goals including strengthening US prosperity and UK economic resilience, securing UK support for US policy including “ensuring support for Israel’s right to defend itself” and countering competition from China.

A former state department official said: “In the past the language for this stuff would be more like ‘increase understanding of US policy’. This is very openly saying more ‘persuade people to agree with US policy’.”

“Increasing support for Israel in a third country is weird. Can’t say if it’s ever been done, but it’s weird.”

A tale of two Murrays: when Ewan met Ewen to talk Tiger Woods, stiff gins and 15 years of mistaken identity

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 07:00:40 GMT

Guardian journalist Ewan Murray and Sky Sports Golf commentator Ewen Murray on being mixed up by irate fans and ‘canteen commandos’

It started with an email in early 2011. “I don’t know what it is like in your country, sir,” wrote angry of Arizona. “But here in America we SPIT!!!”

The penny eventually dropped. Ewen Murray’s commentary on Sky Sports about Tiger Woods emptying his mouth on a putting surface in Dubai triggered a reaction fired directly towards Ewan Murray of the Guardian. Murray of Sky fame can still recall it.

“Tiger spat on the green with three groups playing behind him,” Ewen says. “I remember my words. ‘For a person who is an inspiration, not just to golfers but to everyone, there are times when he is arrogant and disrespectful.’ I switched the mic off straight away. I knew there would be trouble. But if I don’t say anything, people close to me are going to ask why I didn’t comment.

“There was no bigger supporter of Tiger than me but the email you got, I got an awful lot more of ‘Who the hell are you to tell …’ I wasn’t telling, I was only saying it wasn’t acceptable.”

Months later, at the Scottish Open, I explained the email episode to Ewen. He was concerned at the impact of this tirade on me. My response related to my ongoing coverage of Scottish football, a domain where even mild opinion fuels abuse. Water, duck’s back.

Fast forward to 2026 and we are together again, this time in the Open Championship’s media centre. “If only we knew,” says Ewen. Indeed. If only we knew.

It is coincidental enough for two individuals whose names are one letter apart to work in media coverage of the same sport. Freakish in this instance is that we both joined Twitter in October 2010. Before long, confusion reigned. We may be almost three decades apart in age and of totally different stock – Ewen a former professional golfer who competed in the Open, me an erratic amateur – but social media criticism (plus the odd element of praise) intended for Sky’s esteemed commentator flew this way. Lots and lots of it.

My response was to fight fire with fire in an alter ego; to take on the canteen commandos in a manner that is considerably more pretentious than Ewen in reality. The man himself soon roared with approval.

“I think if you don’t have humour in life; and let’s face it, there isn’t much nowadays … ” he says. “Laughter is the best medicine. I have found it all very funny and everyone I have spoken to about it is the same. What I should have been doing is answering some more of the messages meant for you but the trouble was the language was so bad. People just Google the name. ‘That’s him, there he is, Ewan Murray!’

“Some of your answers are very, very funny. Darren Clarke had tears coming out of his eyes when I showed him a few of them. He used to collapse with laughter. ‘Look what he has written now.’ Something about buggers upstairs not paying you properly, sinking stiff gins and dancing on the table. People started looking forward to the next one. I certainly do.”

Just for clarity: “I don’t drink stiff gin any more. And I found dancing on tables was bad for the hamstrings.”

When the Guardian's Ewan masquerades as Sky's Ewen
