"Good to hear you on commentary, hopefully we will see @ShaneLowryGolf in green tonight." The Masters, 2026Niall, you are a fine man. Perhaps 24 hours early but I was atop the piano in Surrey Tavern at 1am, belting out "When Irish eyes are smiling." Enjoy the finale

There have been high-profile victims. Mick Fitzgerald, the famed jockey, praised my television commentary on a recent major. Rory McIlroy sought me out mid-round at the 2018 Open having been so tickled that a multiple world champion in another sport (who shall remain nameless) asserted, “you’re not Ewen Murray” when we first met.

Other moments have flirted with danger. One punter threatened to seek me out in a public house close to Hoylake after some Ewan/Ewen antics during the Open of 2023. “He was going to find me,” Ewen says. “If people don’t find it funny, if people take offence to that, I think they have a major problem. It’s actually quite lucky to have this because so many people are involved; the players, the fans, the press, the TV. Because it is funny.

“If I say something wrong on air, I know what is coming to you. You get the brunt of it but you also get the joy of answering them. ‘Do you know how many Opens I have played in? I have played with Arnold Palmer, you know.’” He is spurting with laughter once more.

This frivolity is a mere footnote on Ewen’s rich career. He combines commentary skill with an unrivalled, intense knowledge of golf and its courses. Now 71, he is still going strong in the booth and intends to do so for some time.

Ewen’s time in broadcasting began almost by accident in 1990, after an executive at Emirates airlines called a professional’s shop in Sussex looking to offer Brian Barnes the gig at the second edition of the Desert Classic. “I said, ‘I’ll do it,’” Ewen says. “That was the start, a two-minute phone call. They sent me an air ticket and £500. I was lucky in that I had just finished playing so I knew all the players. I knew their strengths, their weaknesses and their characters. I still have the tapes.”

He had lost his European Tour card a year earlier. Ewen’s confidence, primarily on the greens, had left him. “Too much negativity,” he says of his mindset. “When I was a kid, it was the other way round. I would dream then about hitting shots and they were all good shots. As I got older, that changed. I could see the end coming; then there was a big problem. What do you do now?”

He left home in Edinburgh at 18 for an assistant professional’s job at Walton Heath. “I sat on the bed and thought ‘What the hell have I done?’ I had no car. My wage was £5 a week, my digs was £5 for the week.” Teaching, playing, commentating. A life in golf was colourful enough before online mischief-making. Not that all condemnation is swatted aside.

“I ignore it unless I think they might be right,” Ewen says. “Constructive criticism is vital in life. I haven’t had it too bad, though. Nowhere near as bad as you.” Long may it continue.

Spanish mountain village braces for astrotourists lured by total solar eclipse

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 07:00:40 GMT

Somosierra will be prime spot to view celestial alignment on 12 August, an event that poses logistical challenges

Little stirs in the mountains above Somosierra beyond the wind that lashes the flat peaks, the cows that graze on parched grass and the sun that beats down on the abandoned aerodrome where generations of glider pilots learned to ride air currents alongside squadrons of vultures and red kites.

But all this stillness will disappear, albeit temporarily, on the evening of 12 August, when swathes of northern and eastern Spain and the Balearic islands experience a total solar eclipse, the likes of which has not been seen here for more than 120 years.

The rare celestial alignment has suddenly turned Somosierra – a small village that sits at an altitude of 1,440 metres where the northernmost reaches of the Madrid region fade into neighbouring Castilla y León and Castilla-La Mancha – into a prime astrotourist destination. No site as close to the Spanish capital will enjoy what Somosierra will: one minute and 29 seconds of pure, clear-skied total eclipse.

Awe-inspiring as the event promises to be, however, it has thrown up all sorts of unexpected but pressing questions for the village and its 93 inhabitants.

With as many as 2,000 visitors expected, where will everyone park? Will there be enough water? And, last but not least, how many batches of paella will the local restaurant need to prepare for the invasion of hungry sky-gazers?

“The fact that we’ve been selected as the best place in the Madrid region to watch the eclipse has led to a huge amount of media and social media coverage,” said Somosierra council’s tourism manager, Irma López Muñoz, as she looked out across the eclipse observation site, a 10-minute drive up past the village.

“That’s generated a lot of interest among people in Madrid – and some from abroad. So we’re anticipating a large influx of visitors because it is a unique event that hasn’t been seen for over 100 years.”

Even before the recent massive wildfires broke out to the west of Madrid, Somosierra council was thinking about how to minimise risk factors on the day of the eclipse and has been coordinating its efforts with police and civil protection authorities.

Although the village council has offered 400 official registration slots, it believes five times as many people could turn up on the day.

“We’re very close to a major European capital with a huge population, and many people are going to come without seeking out information beforehand,” added López. “That’s beyond our control. We can’t predict that someone might be watching television and say, ‘Well, I’m going to make some sandwiches and go see the eclipse with my children.’”

With that in mind, the council is scrambling to recruit and educate volunteers to help steward events on 12 August. It recently hired El Nocturnario, a company of astrotourism experts, to deliver a day’s training to the volunteers who had gathered in Somosierra’s tiny cultural centre to learn about the joys and dangers of eclipses.

One of the volunteers, María Gradaille, said she was delighted to help out with what she called “a once-in-a-lifetime event and a historic scientific milestone”. She was also grateful for the knowledge and the tips she had picked up at the training session.

“I’ve learned so much about the eclipse,” she said. “I didn’t know it could burn your eyes so badly or just how dangerous it can be.”

after newsletter promotion

According to Sarai de la Hoz, one of El Nocturnario’s co-founders, local and regional authorities around Spain are belatedly beginning to wake up the potential benefits of all things astronomical. The looming total solar eclipse will be followed by a six-minute-long “eclipse of the century” in August next year, and by a spectacular “ring of fire eclipse” in January 2028.

Little wonder, then, that the Spanish government has set up a special committee to oversee the trio of eclipses. As the government spokesperson Elma Saiz Delgado pointed out on Tuesday, the events will put Spain “at the centre of global astronomical observation and astrotourism”. This first eclipse alone is expected to attract 446,000 additional visitors in a year when tourist numbers in Spain could pass the 100-million mark for the first time. The event is also forecast to bring in an extra €342m (£292m) in tourist revenue.

“When we started talking about the eclipse a year ago, people kind of thought we were mad. They were like: ‘It’s not going to be that big a deal’ and: ‘Not that many people will come,’” said De la Hoz, “But as time’s gone by and the authorities have realised what’s to come, we’re been getting calls from people who need our help.”

While much of the training she and her colleagues provide is about eclipses and how to watch one safely, the classes also involve a lot of logistics and organisation: “How’s the event going to be organised; who’s going to liaise with the local police and the civil protection authorities, and how will you deal with parking and people at the venue?”

Authorities in the Balearics, which are bracing for huge numbers of extra visitors, have already announced that restrictions will be introduced on 20 main roads across Mallorca, Ibiza, Menorca and Formentera from 3pm until 9pm on the day of the eclipse to prevent gridlock.

Practicalities of a rather different nature are on the mind of Yolanda Cerezo, who has run the Hotel Restaurante El Puerto de Somosierra for the past 26 years. Sitting on the shady terrace of the hotel and restaurant, Cerezo pondered the possibility of a tenfold increase in the 200 to 300 customers she would normally serve on a busy day.

“We’ve had some big one-day events and parties, but we’ve never seen this kind of volume,” she said. “The eclipse is going to be a long day, but we have to make the most of it. We’re not going to see another day like it, are we? It’ll be unique.”

Cerezo, who also caters events, is hoping to get the necessary licences to set up a stall and a bar at the observation site. If she succeeds, she will need to hire another eight or nine people to supplement the restaurant’s regular workforce of nine people. Menu-wise, she’s thinking lamb stew, paella and an assortment of hot and cold sandwiches, all of which can be prepared in the hotel kitchen and driven up the mountain.

“If I do a massive paella and it runs out, I’ll ring down to my people in the kitchen here and they’ll prepare another one and bring it up,” she said. “We can’t leave people stuck halfway up a mountain with nothing to eat.”

Why Super Furry Animals joined music’s dash to cross over football’s vinyl frontier

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 07:00:39 GMT

The sponsorship deal between Cwmbran Celtic and the Welsh indie-rockers is part of a trend to monetise ‘adjacent audiences’ as much as it is a nostalgia trip

As someone born on the cusp of the gen X-millennial divide, I am the perfect target for today’s 90s nostalgia. I played my modest, teenage part in the Battle of Britpop (verbal skirmisher, Blur division); I fervently sang – and, God help me, believed – that Things Can Only Get Better. Super Furry Animals were a band I knew only distantly, via the transgressive thrill of that song they had with all the swearing in. And yet the news they’ll be shirt sponsor for a Welsh football club this season has managed to whisk me straight back to a time when things seemed simpler, kinder and more hopeful.

Nearly three decades have passed since Super Furry Animals last had their logo on a football kit. Back in 1999, their frontman Gruff Rhys and bassist Guto Pryce, both Cardiff City fans, persuaded their Bangor-born bandmates to lay down their north Wales allegiances for the duration of the Bluebirds’ Welsh Cup run – which was, incidentally, all they could afford. The cup shirts cost them £2,000 and were, according to Rhys, knock-offs made for ice hockey. This year’s beneficiaries are a more modest outfit: Cwmbran Celtic, just relegated from Wales’s second tier. Cwmbran is the town where the band send their stage props for repair, and given the props in question are giant inflatable bears, you wonder whether they could get one installed in goal.

Super Furry Animals aren’t the only 90s band involved: Scottish post-rockers Mogwai have sponsored the men’s away strip, with 10% of the profits from all shirt sales going to a grassroots music charity.

There has traditionally been an element of patronage when famous musicians do football, from Elton John’s time as chair of Watford, to Robbie Williams’s 2024 elevation to Port Vale club president. The pattern is a repeating one: local lads (they’re usually lads) make good, and want to give back to the team they’ve followed since they were little. Wet Wet Wet were the first to go down the shirt-sponsorship route with Clydebank in 1993. The team’s shirts turned out to be a more timeless design than the loud, oversized suits that Marti Pellow’s crew wore the day they unveiled them.

Slapping your logo on your home side’s shirt was a charitable endeavour, rather than an investment. Nothing underscored this point better than Fatboy Slim’s relationship with Brighton & Hove Albion. The DJ’s record label first sponsored their shirts in the late 90s, back when the team’s financial straits had left them flirting with extinction, and Tony Bloom’s billions were still waiting to be won. It was particularly appropriate back then that Micky Adams’s men should run out on to the field with their chests declaring them SKINT.

Musical match-ups have tended, therefore, towards the endearing, not the cool. Jake Bugg sponsored Notts County not to market his own music, but to evangelise the Midlands team on his global tours. And it’s even cuter when bands have sponsored kids’ teams. The late Lemmy of Motörhead was tickled by the thought of a Lincolnshire under-10s team sporting his Snaggletooth skull mascot on their fronts; unfortunately the resultant all-black kit too closely resembled referees’ uniforms and the children were banned from wearing it in league matches. Still, the idea had an enduring appeal: the Prodigy, Biffy Clyro, Sleaford Mods and Franz Ferdinand have all paid for youth kits.

In the last couple of years, though, the relationship between bands and football teams has turned serious. The move to monetise the “adjacent audiences” of pop and sporting fandom means shirt sponsorship is no longer a way of artists showing their support, but a marketing and merchandising opportunity in its own right.

Spotify’s deal with Barcelona got the ball rolling, with Coldplay, Karol G, Rosalía and Travis Scott each briefly appearing on the shirtfront, and limited-edition replicas costing more than £340 a pop. The footie-kit-as-streetwear trend means bands aren’t “sponsors” any more, they’re “collaborators”. Hence Manchester United’s pre-match shirts don’t bear the name of the Stone Roses, just their album artwork. And while that may have baffled a few younger fans – the club’s website ran a post explaining who the Madchester group were for the gen Z-ers – it still reflects a genuine connection. Ian Brown is a lifelong Red, and the team has walked out to This Is the One since Gary Neville first requested it two decades ago.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Whereas a year ago, if you’d been asked at a pub quiz what Paris Saint-Germain had in common with a K-pop band, or what Pink Floyd had to do with a Serie A team, you’d have been within your rights to say “nothing”. The answer, now, is clothing ranges – PSG teamed up with the girl group Blackpink to optimise fan engagement in Asia, while Inter marked the 50th anniversary of the album release of Wish You Were Here.

All this can be confusing for the simple-minded sports lover like me. What is a culture-forward lifestyle capsule, anyway? It sounds like something Musk and Bezos want to blast to Mars in. Creating a sporting look now involves an advanced understanding of fashion arithmetic: at last year’s Euros it was Admiral x Spice Girls, now it’s the Rolling Stones x England Cricket x Castore. These are powerful equations, as when a 2025 Bohemian FC x Fontaines DC shirt (raised to the power of Greta Thunberg when she wore it on her flotilla to Gaza) = £££££ for charity. Maybe Ed Sheeran’s Mathematics tour top for Ipswich was an omen. Or perhaps this is a fad, and the music industry will soon move on to something new. GQ, which has declared “blokecore” over, says we’ll be wearing classic rugby tops by autumn/winter. Sounds delightfully 90s to me.

The night Belfast burned: how the Northern Ireland race riots unfolded

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 06:00:39 GMT

A horrific knife attack on a street in June sparked another summer’s night of racial violence, stoked by loyalist groups. How did the unrest erupt – and why do many fear it will happen again?

Shortly after 10.30pm on Monday 8 June, as a summer twilight lingered over Belfast, a horrific scene unfolded on Kinnaird Avenue: a man straddled and repeatedly stabbed a figure lying on the ground in a bloody assault that ended only after onlookers intervened.

Others captured the drama on cameraphones and uploaded the footage to social media. Once seen, the grainy images were hard to forget, and by dawn on Tuesday 9 June they were ricocheting around X, WhatsApp, Facebook, Telegram and other platforms.

Many commentators highlighted one aspect: the assailant was black, the victim white.

Police had a suspect in custody – he was initially identified as a refugee from Somalia, later corrected to Sudan – but this did not stem a cascade of outrage. What, commentators demanded to know, about other foreign men of “military age” in Northern Ireland? Had they been “vetted”? What “alien culture” had they imported?

By 9.30am a message – an exhortation – was being widely shared. “All business to close at 5.30pm tonight. No excuses.” It listed 25 locations around Northern Ireland for people to gather at 7pm. “Please forward [to] all men of the age of 18 and over. Wear dark clothing … and be prepared to fight or be arrested.”

It was an invitation to a pogrom.

Far-right agitators, such as Elon Musk and Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known by his alias Tommy Robinson, amplified calls to protest, and those interventions were prominent in the coverage that followed.

Through a combination of interviews with witnesses and people who responded to the unrest, on-the-ground reporting in loyalist strongholds and at far-right rallies in Northern Ireland, and analysis of messages sent by figures connected to the extreme right, the Guardian has established the most complete picture yet of how a single incident of horrific violence precipitated the crisis. And it suggests that organisers in Belfast needed no encouragement or direction. This was their show.

Drawing on previous eruptions of violence – this was to be the third consecutive summer of racial disturbances in Northern Ireland – the organisers issued further instructions: leave mobile phones at home and deactivate dashcams and doorbell cameras.

By early afternoon, schools were sending children home, public transport was halting and steel shutters were clanging down over foreign-owned barber shops, supermarkets and other businesses.

As families sat down for dinner, crowds gathered at designated roundabouts and intersections in loyalist areas across the city.

At about 7.30pm a woman with a megaphone on the Shankill Road recited the Lord’s Prayer to several hundred people, some draped in union flags. They marched through terraced sidestreets and halted outside the home of a Romanian family. A nearby Black family, anticipating trouble, had already fled and asked neighbours to move their car.

The Romanian family’s windows had been “put out” twice before, but the family had refused to leave. The previous night’s stabbing had nothing to do with the Romanians but somehow alchemised into what one woman in the crowd called “the last straw”.

Dozens of boys and men wearing hoods and masks surged forward. Some launched bricks through windows, others shoved fireworks through the letterbox. A woman inside, visible to the crowd, watched helplessly as her home came under attack. The family’s car went up in flames, then men in balaclavas broke down the door.

Women and children in the mob observed proceedings. “There’s wee girls inside,” said one. In contrast to race riots in England and Belfast in 2024, and in Ballymena last year, the violence was not recorded or streamed on mobile phones. A teenage boy who ignored the injunction against filming was dragged aside and chastised.

Similar scenes played out across Belfast. In the east of the city, families from Ukraine, Romania, Poland and Sudan left. Properties and vehicles, including a Glider bus, were set ablaze and plumes of smoke rose into the night.

On arterial roads and by roundabouts, crowds lit bins and set up roadblocks to question and intimidate suspected foreigners. In Sandy Row, central Belfast, Ethiopian and Chinese residents fled and arsonists burned a Syrian supermarket. On Crumlin Road, in the west, Ugandan health workers and Nigerian families sought refuge. In some places the police were absent or stayed back and it was left to community volunteers to navigate the mobs and escort families to safety.

At around 10pm the violence abated and crowds began to disperse. Some whooped in jubilation, others surveyed the smouldering debris with satisfaction. A point, they said, had been made. Rain began to fall, helping emergency crews to douse the embers of gutted homes and vehicles.

The riot should not have come as a surprise. Northern Ireland was primed for it. “We could see it coming,” said Daniel Holder, the director of the Committee on the Administration of Justice (CAJ), a Belfast-based advocacy group. “It wasn’t unprecedented, it was an escalation of an existing pattern.”

An escalation, and a learning curve. Drawing on lessons from 2024 and 2025, the agitators refined their methods to hit more targets and reduce the chance of arrest.

Far-right allies in England and the US were taking notes. Enrique Tarrio, the former head of the militant US group Proud Boys, recently visited and interviewed activists for a documentary. And last month, the Advance UK-affiliated YouTuber Sarah White was streaming multiple events in Northern Ireland, including an Orange Order march and an anti-migrant protest in Portrush.

The Northern Ireland “model” is not necessarily transferable. It has taken a unique mix – the legacy of the Troubles, xenophobia, social media platforms and state acquiescence – to create the toxic climate.

Until the 1998 Good Friday agreement the region was almost entirely white and native-born. As sectarian violence eased, immigrants trickled in. By the 2021 census, 3.4% of the population was from a minority ethnic background – small compared with 19% in England, but the sight of people from Africa, Asia and the Middle East still came as a jolt.

Many immigrants settled in working-class loyalist areas where the population was declining, property was cheaper – and paramilitary groups endured. Despite a state-sponsored “transitioning” process, the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) and Ulster Defence Association (UDA) split into sub-groups that continued to deal drugs and coercively control communities.

“Peace” walls between Catholic and Protestant neighbourhoods still stand, underlining the persistence of traditional sectarian divisions, but the waning IRA threat weakened loyalist paramilitaries’ claims to be community defenders, prompting them to seek a new bogeyman to justify their existence.

“Loyalism has always been a reactionary ideology based on keeping out ‘foreign’ influence,” said Stephen Millar, an academic and author of Performing Paramilitarism: Loyalist Songs, Conflict, and Culture War in Northern Ireland. “The pivot from [opposing] Irish nationalism to anti-migrant rhetoric is, to some extent, internally consistent, and serves to keep loyalism ‘relevant’, trading one form of racism for another.”

Sporadic attacks and harassment against minority ethnic families – paint bombs, smashed windows, “locals only” graffiti, threatening posters – have proliferated over the past decade, especially in County Antrim, where healthcare workers from Africa were among those targeted.

That turned out to be the warm-up for a full-scale riot in Belfast in August 2024 – a copycat response to mayhem in England after the killing of three girls in Southport. Then in June 2025, Ballymena, 25 miles outside Belfast, erupted after two Roma teenagers were charged with rape (the charges were later dropped).

June’s eruption completed a grim summer hat-trick.

Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of the Police Service Northern Ireland (PSNI), said the overall picture of paramilitary involvement in the most recent trouble was “inconsistent” but that paramilitaries were present.

However, many say the police have been slow to recognise, at least in public, the role of paramilitary groups in controlling the violence. Holder said: “To anyone on the ground, that was very obvious from the start.”

The UDA and UVF are fractured. Some factions urged restraint – that is partly credited with keeping Ballymena calm this summer – but independent observers say other factions orchestrated much of the violence. Firefighters had no doubt about paramilitary influence and sought permission from their leaders before tackling blazes, sources said.

The ferrying of teenagers to and from flashpoints was further evidence of orchestration, said Chris Quinn, Northern Ireland’s children’s commissioner. “There’s been a long history of child criminal coercion and child criminal exploitation.”

Such children should not escape legal consequences but they too were victims, said Quinn. Some heeded the call to riot to service debts, including drug debts, he said. Another source, a youth worker, said paramilitary groups paid boys £100 to join the rioting.

Instead of Catholics, it was now people of colour in the crosshairs of loyalist groups, said Michaela Rafferty, of Anaka, a women’s group that helped escort besieged families to safety. “There has been a sectarian element, obviously, through our years of Troubles and violence. Now that focus has kind of moved to brown and black people.”

AI-generated anti-Islam murals have appeared in loyalist strongholds such as Moygashel and Newtownabbey. “Islam is Heathen, Islam is Satanic — A New Evil Has Arisen,” says one, “Not welcome, not wanted, not here,” says another.

Agitators have refined their methods. Most rioters in Ballymena last year wore masks or hoods but footage uploaded by participants and onlookers helped police identify and charge dozens of rioters. The lesson was not lost on the recent rioters in Belfast – they banned filming and made greater efforts to conceal identifying details, such as tattoos.

Through trial and error they also discovered that without a galvanising incident, such as a brutal crime allegedly committed by a foreigner, calls for mass mobilisation tended to flop, and this punctured morale.

Instead, they set up online community groups and joined existing ones to drip-feed anti-foreigner sentiment, said Dessie Donnelly of rabble. coop, a Belfast-based tech cooperative that tracks online xenophobia. “Ballymena was a watershed. You had loads of groups springing up online and a far-right network emerging.”

Before the most recent riot, posts about dark-skinned men in parks, and foreigners moving into houses of multiple occupation (HMO) on particular streets, proliferated. The tactic distilled Islamophobia to a hyper-local level, said Donnelly. “It prepares people for when there is an animating event.”

Activists in Belfast, Bangor, Coleraine, Derry, Newtownabbey, Portadown and other towns formed online “clusters” that shared and amplified posts and infiltrated online forums for loyalist bonfires and marching bands, said a researcher with Accountability Project Northern Ireland, a group that monitors online hate.

Last summer, the watchdog noticed that a Portadown-based Facebook group was circulating a screenshot of council-owned HMO properties – a ready-made hitlist of addresses that rioters used in June.

Burgeoning attacks – in the year to 31 March, police recorded 2,367 race incidents and 1,507 race crimes, the highest on record – created a sense of foreboding as summer approached, said Naomi Green, the Northern Ireland-based assistant secretary general of the Muslim Council of Britain (MCB). “We thought it was going to get quite scary very quickly, and it did.”

A week before the riot, anti-racism organisations convened an emergency meeting in Belfast because they feared trouble, said Holder. The marching season loomed and there was “a huge buildup” of racist activism on- and offline, he said. “For a third successive summer, it was waiting on an excuse.”

The attack at Kinnaird Avenue provided the spark. For foreigners who had been previously targeted there was a sense of inevitability, on the afternoon of 9 June, to what came next. “We’ve been sharing the same messages all day: go home early, stay inside, don’t go out,” Mohammed Mahmoud, 39, said as a crowd gathered near his Sandy Row grocery store.

The violence that night gave way to an eerie calm the next day. Central Belfast was like a ghost town, with most businesses remaining shut in expectation of fresh strife. A familiar message duly began to circulate on social media. “All business to close … wear dark clothing.”

In fact, Belfast remained largely quiet on the night of 10 June but in Glengormley, 7 miles north, a mob tried to march on the Chimney Corner hotel, which had been used to house asylum seekers, and fought against police in riot gear. The crowd hurled bricks and rocks, lit bonfires in the street and torched a vacant house. Police used water cannon and plastic bullets to drive them back.

Around 11pm the violence dwindled and stopped, as if someone had turned off a tap. That was the last disturbance in June. But in some ways the aftermath has been just as troubling.

In a poll by the thinktank More in Common, 8% of people in Northern Ireland said it was justified to burn migrants out of their homes and 11% agreed with intimidating them out of an area. Forty-one per cent said they sometimes feel like a stranger in their own country and three-quarters worry about asylum seekers entering Northern Ireland.

Conleth Burns, the associate director and Ireland lead for More In Common, said polling in England showed similar results. “You’ve got a similar number of people in lots of societies who think that this level of violence against migrants is justified.”

Northern Ireland, however, has far fewer foreigners and people of colour than England, which shows that even small numbers can have an outsized impact, said Burns. Most people expressed concern about immigration, racism and violence, he added. “People don’t see [those views] as being contradictory.”

The Institute for Strategic Dialogue, which tracks extremism and misinformation, said the unrest turbo-charged far-right activism online. Posts that promoted claims of anti-white police bias surged to more than 200,000 in the first two weeks of June compared with 104,000 in the whole of May, it said in a report published this week.

The main parties at Stormont strongly condemned the violence but critics say the executive failed to prepare for the crisis.

“This was the third time in two years,” said Donnelly. “They should have known something would happen, it was building up.”

Even though the Police Service of Northern Ireland had struggled to contain unrest in previous years it was still under-resourced, said Donnelly. “There was no acknowledgment that immigrants had been systematically attacked twice and that it would happen again.”

Holder said Stormont’s response had downplayed the gravity of the crisis. “You’d expect a racist pogrom to be the key issue for the institutions to deal with over the summer, and putting in emergency measures to prevent that happening again. But no, there’s no sense of urgency.”

Liz Griffith, the head of migration justice at the Northern Ireland Law Centre, said the devolved government had failed to update anti-racism legislation and downgraded a long-awaited policy document.

The strategy now focused on “race relations”, which Griffith said was “a discredited term now; it is woefully out of date and has been out of date since the 1970s”.

“It’s as if this was to do with somehow the relationships of people not getting on with each other,” Holder said. “That the people having the brick put through their window need to improve their relationship with those putting the brick through the window.”

The Stormont executive had failed to bring forward hate crime and race equality laws in line with the rest of the UK.

“The law in itself does not prevent racism but it’s the bedrock on which all your other initiatives rest,” Griffith said. “It’s been updated in England, Scotland and Wales, and ours is just antiquated. There’s constant talk of consultation after consultation to update this legislation, but it has just got stuck, it’s never moved.”

In the face of this inaction, many want Andy Burnham, the new prime minister, to step in. “Unless Westminster intervenes at this point and ensures that there are protections, and legal protections, and consequences for some of this behaviour, unless there is some accountability here, it’s going to continue,” Green said.

Many migrants and refugees think another eruption is likely but some try to remain optimistic. Suleiman Abdulahi, the founder and director of Horn of Africa People’s Aid Northern Ireland, has endured many attacks and reported 12 of them, most recently on 26 June. None have resulted in a prosecution but he did not wish to condemn his adopted home. “I’m not saying the Northern Ireland people – the majority – are racist. The majority are hospitable.”

The best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:

The Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.

If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.

Our guide at theguardian. com/tips lists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.

From Love Me Tender to Kevin Bridges: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 05:00:38 GMT

Vicky Krieps puts her heart on the line in Anna Cazenave Cambet’s romantic drama, and the Glaswegian comedy superstar is back on stage for a massive UK tour

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Love Me TenderOut now Vicky Krieps heads up Anna Cazenave Cambet’s drama about a woman who splits amicably from her husband to follow her dream of becoming a writer, but then falls for a woman – at which point, the ex-hubby files for sole custody of their child. Also starring Monia Chokri and Antoine Reinartz.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Edinburgh international film festivalVarious venues, 13 to 19 August The world’s oldest continuously running film festival returns with a programme that includes 10 films competing for a £50K prize; plus the UK premieres of I Want Your Sex by Gregg Araki and Lance Hammer’s Queen at Sea; and special guests doing talks including Kenneth Branagh, Ewan McGregor and Bruce Dern. There’s also a screening and club-night celebration for Trainspotting’s 30th anniversary.

Ice Cream ManOut now Eli Roth directs a slasher about an ice-cream man who turns children into homicidal maniacs. You’re probably either in or out by this point but, in case it makes a difference, the film stars Ari Millen of Orphan Black fame as the titular dispenser of summer treats.

A Child of My OwnOut now A true-crime docudrama based on the real-life case of a Mexican woman who abducted a baby from the hospital where she worked as a nurse. Chilean director Maite Alberdi’s factual account is interwoven with a telling of the story from the perpetrator’s point of view. Catherine Bray

JojiDublin, 11 August; London, 13 August; touring to 16 August The Japanese-Australian YouTube prankster turned serious musical artist arrives in arenas in support of February’s fourth album of ornate electronic ballads, Piss in the Wind. The night’s singalong moment is likely to be Glimpse of Us, which is now on 1.8bn Spotify streams and counting. Michael Cragg

John Grant with Richard HawleyKelvingrove Bandstand, Glasgow, 10 August Originally brought together in 2023 as part of the Manchester international festival, Grant and Hawley reunite for this unique collaboration celebrating the work of late country star Patsy Cline. With Cline’s songs steeped in romance and heartbreak, expect them to come to life anew on a Glasgow bandstand. MC

The Galloping CureFestival theatre, Edinburgh, 9 to 12 August Advertised as “an opera for the opioid age”, this is the latest collaboration between Missy Mazzoli, one of the most successful composers working in opera today, and librettist Royce Vavrek, dubbed “the indie Hoffmannsthal”. Its world premiere production by Scottish Opera is a musical must-see at this year’s Edinburgh international festival. Flora Willson

Denys Baptiste, Gary Crosby, Cassie KinoshiBristol Beacon: Lantern Hall, 8 AugustJoining the BBC’s wider Proms season, this live-broadcast Radio 3 Bristol concert showcases successive generations of African-Caribbean jazz artists who have transformed the UK scene over the past half-century. Soulful Coltrane-inspired saxophonist Denys Baptiste, Jazz Warriors co-founder Gary Crosby and saxophonist/composer Cassie Kinoshi highlight this diversely creative gig. John Fordham

Kira FreijeModern Art Oxford, to 16 August It’s your last chance to catch a clutch of exhibitions this week before they close, including strange, lifesize figures frozen in moments of emotional anguish created by Freije, who is nominated for this year’s Turner prize.

New Contemporaries 26Mima, Middlesbrough, to 16 August There’s no better place to spot the art stars of the future than the annual New Contemporaries exhibition, which brings together work by recent graduates and early-career artists.

Rachel Maclean: They’ve Got Your EyesFact, Liverpool, to 16 August This Scottish artist combines film and sculpture, fairytale and horror for a terrifying immersive exploration of AI and how it’s tearing apart the idea of art and authorship.

Flare-UpGoldsmith’s Centre for Contemporary Art, London, to 16 August Health and illness are the focus of this show about the body and disability, featuring a stellar lineup of artists including Derek Jarman, Félix González-Torres and Racheal Crowther. Eddy Frankel

A History of PaperPitlochry Festival theatre, 9 August to 19 September Oliver Emanuel and Gareth Williams’s thoughtful and romantic new musical charts a burgeoning relationship between a man and woman through the scraps of paper they leave behind – tickets, letters, menus and shopping lists. Alan Cumming and Shirley Henderson star. Miriam Gillinson

Love’s Labour’s Lost and Much Ado About NothingThomas’s College, Richmond, to 22 August This enticing Shakespearean double bill transforms his two comedies into a sweeping single love saga set around the second world war. MG

Kevin Bridges8 August to 20 February; tour starts York The Glaswegian comic’s gritty, relatable and masterfully constructed observational fare made him a standup institution in his homeland long ago. Now, more than two decades on from his debut, the (still only) 39-year-old heads back out on the road with new show Here If You Need Me. Rachel Aroesti

Tchaikovsky: Child of GlassOpera Holland Park, London, 13 to 15 August A music-dance-drama about the life and forbidden loves of composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. This is a real meshing of forms, the play written by Tama Matheson (artistic director of the Brisbane Shakespeare festival), with pianist Jayson Gillham playing live, and Royal Ballet soloist Téo Dubreuil performing choreography by Stephen Wicks. Lyndsey Winship

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

Warren’s VortexNow & Sky Comedy, 10 August, 9pm This sister show to the New Zealand comedy Wellington Paranormal (itself a What We Do in the Shadows spin-off) sees a teenage girl fall into the transdimensional wormhole her dad has been hiding in his shed, leading the pair into a host of absurd alternate timelines.

Hit PointU&Dave, 13 August, 9pm Misfits creator Howard Overman’s twisty romcom-thriller ramps up the standard-issue police procedural suspense with a hefty dose of sexual tension. Saffron Hocking and Nick Blood are two detectives trying not to get distracted by their mutual attraction while investigating a gangland robbery that doesn’t quite add up.

A House Through TimeiPlayer & BBC Two, 13 August, 9pm David Olusoga’s particular brand of braininess may not have made him much of a Traitor hunter, but the softly spoken historian is the perfect fit for this gently fascinating series which chronicles British life through the prism of a single dwelling. This sixth instalment focuses on an Edinburgh home that dates back to 1765.

MourinhoNetflix, 11 August The Special One (a nickname he loudly disavows in the trailer while standing in front of a huge self-portrait) and his 20-year winning streak is the subject of this new series from Joe Pearlman, director of arch documentaries on Robbie Williams and Bros. Ferguson, Terry, Lampard, Ibrahimović and Drogba are among the talking heads. RA

Agent 64PC, out 11 August Aimed squarely at those who played and loved GoldenEye 007 on the Nintendo 64 nearly 30 years ago, this homage keeps the lo-fi graphics and much-loved split-screen multiplayer mode but has its own story campaign and the ability to play online. Relive your youth – now with updated modern design.

Servant of the LakePC, out 13 August Eye-catching for its charming mix of bold line-drawn characters and muted sketched backgrounds, this point-and-click adventure hs charming characters and hides a darker mystery. Jordan Erica Webber

Flo – Therapy at the Club Out now The British R&B trio return with the follow-up to their Grammy-nominated debut, Access All Areas. Led by the salacious banger Leak It and the retro-soul stomper Remedied, the album also features throwback soul jams on the title track and Don’t Break Her Heart.

Overmono – Pure Devotion Out now Welsh brothers Tom and Ed Russell continue to push the boundaries of electronic music on this follow-up to 2023’s debut, Good Lies. As well as incorporating vintage synthesisers and destabilising vocal techniques, the pair also literally baked a crash cymbal in the oven. Why not?

Ravyn Lenae – Blue Island Out nowAfter releasing a couple of if-you-know-you-know alt-pop albums, Chicago singer-songwriter Lenae scored an unexpected smash last year with Love Me Not. As a result, this third album should garner more attention, and thankfully songs such as the Solange-esque Saturday Night and the loping Handle live up to the hype.

The Anchoress – As We Once Were Out now When she’s not hosting her own podcast, or writing books about epic poetry, Welsh polymath Catherine Anne Davies also makes music. On her first album of new material in five years, her decadent art-rock is augmented by guests including Gwenno and James Dean Bradfield. MC

Writer’s RoutinePodcast Dan Simpson’s long-running series finds nuggets of wisdom in writers’ mercurial schedules. A treasure trove of advice for anyone looking to be creative, Simpson’s bestselling guests explore how to build confidence and set your own pace.

Bayeuxmuseum. comOnline As the Bayeux tapestry prepares to open to the public at London’s British Museum, this high-resolution interactive panorama from Normandy’s Bayeux Museum allows those who can’t get their hands on tickets to experience the next best thing.

Women Not Included: Drugs and Clinical TrialsBBC World Service, 10 August, 8.30pm Dr Ella Hubber’s investigation into the ways that women have been overlooked across decades of research is a deeply troubling yet necessary listen. Alongside expert commentary, she explores how biological differences affect the ways drugs work. Ammar Kalia

Lime bikes hurtling around the city: is this the revenge of a priced-out generation?

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 05:00:38 GMT

From running red lights to dumping bikes, some Lime users get a bad rap. But many who grumble about them don’t appreciate their own privilege

The night belongs to Lime bikes in the capital this summer. Buses and tube carriages are boiling, cars crawl between low traffic neighbourhoods and Thames Water roadworks, and pedestrians plod through the sticky heat. But Lime riders exist in a different, breezier realm: whirring along, chatting in pairs or blissfully alone, weaving through the city’s tree-lined maze, choosing impulsively between destinations, rarely stopping for anything or anyone.

“My favourite part of a night out is Lime biking home,” writes Annie Lord, a dating columnist and author, in Freewheeling: Essays on Cycling. “As I ride up a hill, the bike’s electrics click … And, for a little while, I’m free.”

According to the confidently expansive Californian company that owns Lime, Neutron Holdings Inc, the average age of its London riders is 34. With the capital’s weather becoming warmer and drier, and social media and other online sources making more information about things riders could do instantly available, rented e-bikes seem a perfect tool to unlock the city’s possibilities. Across the globe, they are changing urban life: speeding it up, connecting previously out-of-the-way places, and making many women feel safer at night. Where I live in Hackney, once one of the capital’s more isolated boroughs and now one of the busiest Lime markets, many pubs are enjoying a bike-driven boom on summer nights, with the bright green bikes glowing outside like lurid cocktails before their riders wobble home.

Yet since Limes became available in London and other British cities in 2018, the narrative has focused on their negative impacts. The way their riders often run red lights and cycle on pavements. How bikes are often dumped in pedestrian spaces after use, blocking entrances and vulnerable people’s safe routes. The fact that riders sometimes don’t share space considerately with traditional cyclists, and take over footpaths in parks. The strong sense that some Lime users can barely cycle at all. A 2023 report commissioned by Lime found that “20% of Lime riders in London had never cycled before”. That is not as straightforwardly positive a statistic as the company likes to think.

Other data about Lime usage is hard to come by, as the company considers it commercially sensitive. But information from Transport for London suggests Limes are disproportionately responsible for injuries to pedestrians. It estimates that in 2024 about 12% of the city’s cycling journeys were made on rented e-bikes, of which Lime is by far the biggest provider, yet rented bikes were reportedly responsible for almost a third of cyclist collisions with pedestrians that required police intervention. As anyone who walks much in London knows, Limes have changed the experience of crossing a road.

In truth, the Lime phenomenon is both an imposition and a liberation; an improvement to city life, and a sign of its sometimes alienating intensification; an expression of a certain kind of urban privilege (a half-hour London ride can cost over £10), and evidence of its diminution. It shows how the relationship has changed between mobility and property, especially among the young.

In 1975, Peter Ambrose and Bob Colenutt, two far-sighted British analysts of urban places, wrote in their book The Property Machine: “The city is a zone of conflict between competing claims for land.” In today’s London, as in other cities where space is sought-after and expensive, many Lime riders are young professionals, who in the past would have owned or rented homes close to the best public transport. Nowadays, that’s unaffordable for most of them, as is property ownership of any kind – as shown by the fact that the age of the average London first-time buyer has recently overtaken that of the average Lime rider, at 35.

E-bike rental, whether for commuting or pleasure, is a solution to the scattering of these people to less-connected suburbs. Young Lime riders in a hurry, you could say, represent the revenge of a generation priced out of living near tube stations. Meanwhile, some of those who complain about Lime users are older Londoners who were able to buy properties in more convenient locations. They say Lime bikes are starting to dominate the city, but late-20th-century homebuyers have a much deeper hold on the capital.

Tensions between the two groups can be reduced. This year, Hackney council says it has “worked with Lime … to install a high density of dedicated parking bays for the bikes, and compliance [by riders] is generally good”. To discourage riders from running red lights – a practice Lime’s critics claim is encouraged by its policy of charging by the minute – the council has also agreed with Lime a flat fee for local residents: £1.75 for trips of up to 25 minutes that start in the borough, the same price as a bus fare, and the lowest Lime rate in London. Amid all the acrimony about rental bikes, it’s often forgotten – deliberately so by the much more powerful motoring lobby – that in polluted cities with unequal public health, more cycling is good.

Yet a collaborative, responsible bike rental culture involving Lime, its customers and the overworked local authorities tasked with regulating both is some way off. Partly, this is because of commercial pressures: despite having big investors such as Uber, Lime is heavily in debt and not yet profitable. Meanwhile, as with many tech-enabled enterprises, key aspects of its business model have social costs. “People love the flexibility of being able to start and end their journey anywhere” said one of Lime’s senior executives, Andrew Savage, last year. What he would not – could not – acknowledge was that absolute convenience for his customers can mean inconvenience for everyone else. As usual last night, despite Hackney’s ban on leaving Lime bikes anywhere but official parking bays, someone left one blocking some of my road.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Unless divided, expensive cities such as London build more affordable homes, provide more widely available public transport, and make bicycle ownership less vulnerable to criminals – in other words, make mobility and housing less competitive and hierarchical – the sometimes petty, sometimes dangerous rental bike wars are likely to carry on. But at least we won’t all be stuck in cars.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

‘I couldn’t breathe’: the deadly health burden of wildfire smoke

The Guardian Sat, 08 Aug 2026 05:00:37 GMT

Scientists race to untangle complex links between exposure and mortality as fire weather grows more prevalent

A thousand kilometres from the infernos gorging on northern Ontario’s boreal forests, Erin O’Connor watched the sky above Canada’s biggest city turn an “almost post-apocalyptic” orange as it filled with light-scattering particles of soot and ash. Stepping outside the halls of Toronto General hospital, where air filters were keeping patients safe from the worst of the fumes, she was struck by a smell so strong it felt like standing by a campfire.

“It really hit you in the face as soon as you walked outside,” said O’Connor, who runs University Health Network’s emergency department and saw a rise in patients presenting with allergies and shortness of breath. “As the days progressed, it was like that everywhere. It seemed even inside you could smell that burning.”

Far more than the flames that have engulfed southern Europe and North America in recent weeks, it is the smoke that dominates the astonishing death toll from combusting nature. Thick with toxic gases that inflame the airways and tiny particulates that breach the lungs and ride the bloodstream to hit every organ in the body, fumes from landscape fires kill 1.5 million people each year, a study in the Lancet found in 2024 – more than floods, flames, storms and heat combined.

So damaging are the lung-scarring effects of charred plant matter that people far from the fires may still perish. The plumes spewed by wildfires in Canada in 2023 caused 82,000 early deaths, a study in Nature found last year, with unfavourable winds pushing a third of the mortality burden into the US and another quarter into Europe. About 10% of the UK’s fine particulate pollution (PM2.5) comes from biomass burned abroad, researchers found in March.

Yet while scientists agree the health burden of wildfire smoke is jaw droppingly large, they are only beginning to untangle the complex links between exposure and mortality. The open research questions are growing more pressing as climate breakdown makes fire weather more severe. What if hotter infernos cause pollution to peak at even more extreme levels? What if bad air lasts several days or weeks? What if a severe episode hits before a person has fully recovered from the last bout of smoke?

The lack of answers in the existing research makes it hard to get a handle on how brutal the fallout from this furious fire season will be. Early signs are troubling, with vast tracts of vegetation torched close to big European cities and, after a late but explosive start to the North American fire season, smoke choking major population centres such as Chicago and New York City. In Toronto, which briefly had the worst air quality of any major metropolis in the world last month – a title claimed by Portland in the US on Wednesday – O’Connor said she could not remember the pollution ever having been so bad, with such a sudden onset that took so long to clear up.

“I had never looked outside and had the sky seem orange in the middle of the day,” said O’Connor, who amid treating patients and fielding media requests rushed to pull her son from summer camp. “Certainly, we have had other wildfire smoke, but in more of a transient way.”

Perhaps surprisingly, the death toll from a fire season can depend on the whims of the wind as much as the size of the fire. Wildfires in France spewed record amounts of pollution in the first half of the year and in Spain emissions have so far fallen just shy of the worst it has known. But even though monster infernos were halted alarmingly close to Madrid and Bordeaux, the smoke was mostly blown away from where people live. Daily particulate pollution levels still worsened across southern Europe and peaked at a staggering 342 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic metre (μg/m³) in Bordeaux on 24 July – and 486 μg/m³ in Limoges, 180km (112 miles) away, the following day – but other big cities in southern Europe were spared the extremes that doctors fear.

North America has not been so lucky. As winds blew south and south-east from scarcely populated forests in Ontario and the Northwest Territories, at least 36 million people across the continent were breathing air fouled by “very unhealthy” concentrations of PM2.5 that exceeded 125.5μg/m³ on 16 July, preliminary analysis conducted for the Guardian shows. At least 10 million people were exposed to more than 250μg/m³, according to the estimates, a level of daily pollution that smog-choked New Delhi saw no more than eight times last year.

Scientists say the hit to air quality in some big cities is reminiscent of the megafires in 2023 that came with vast death tolls. “As soon as we have massive population centres exposed, we’re going to see those increases,” said Stephanie Cleland, a wildfire health scientist at Simon Fraser University, who considered only people living within 25km of a measuring station in her calculations for the Guardian and said the figures are therefore conservative. “I would be concerned by the fact that it’s only been three years since this last happened and now we’re having it again.”

In a quiet suburb of Duluth, in north-east Minnesota, the worst of the smoke was seen, smelled and tasted on 16 July. Jae Jeon and Dan McClelland, a married couple who grow flowers for weddings and subscription deliveries, were looking forward to opening the windows after days baking in oppressive heat. Instead, they woke up to a fog that they soon realised was made up of something much worse. By late morning, their local hardware store had sold out of masks and air purifiers. People resorted to attaching furnace filters to box fans instead.

The McClellands were among 12,000 people in west Duluth exposed to an average of 541μg/m³ of fine particulate pollution, the analysis shows, higher than anywhere else in North America. They sent their sole farmworker home early after she complained of a headache but, with two weddings coming up on the weekend and little chance of cancellation, they still had plenty of flowers to pick and arrange. The couple got to work harvesting roses, yarrows, clematises and sweet peas, surrounded by a dystopian haze the likes of which they had never experienced.

“It felt like working in a war zone,” said Jae Jeon. “When I went outside, I couldn’t breathe, so I had to wear a mask, but it was still painful. After just a couple of minutes you started to get a headache.”

Climate breakdown made last month’s fire weather twice as likely in Canada and France, and 20 times more likely in Spain, recent rapid analyses have found, the result of planet-heating emissions that have made it easier for vegetation to dry out. As plants and trees combust, they spew a host of harmful particles that also trigger damaging inflammatory responses as the body seeks to purge foreign objects.

Scientists have relied on general air pollution relations to model the smoke’s chronic health effects, which make up the bulk of the death toll, because they lack long-term studies specific to wildfires. “The reason we don’t have them for wildfire smoke is because we haven’t had to deal with this as kind of a repeated ongoing problem,” said Michael Brauer, a wildfire health scientist at the University of British Columbia and co-author of the study on Canada’s 2023 fires. He first experienced wildfire smoke when he was about 40 years old, he said, while a 10-year-old child where he lives in British Columbia would have breathed it every summer of their life.

But the analogy to regular pollution is imperfect. Compared with other sources of PM2.5, such as factories or cars, wildfire smoke contains a greater share of organic compounds that increase inflammation and a higher concentration of ultra-fine particles that penetrate the deepest recesses of the lungs. PM2.5 from wildfire smoke is up to 10 times more harmful in the short-term, a study in Nature Communications found in 2021, and factoring this into epidemiological models suggests death tolls from short-term exposure to wildfire smoke have been greatly underestimated, a study in the Lancet Planetary Health found last year.

Some researchers suggest high peak exposure during serious smoke episodes better explains why wildfire particulates do more damage than regular ones. “It may be that it’s because the smoke is chemically more toxic, or it may be – what I think is more likely – that it’s basically overwhelming your defences,” said Brauer, who compared it to having one drink a day for a year rather than bingeing 365 in 24 hours. “That’s clearly going to have different impacts.”

When wildfire smoke gets bad, experts recommend wearing masks, closing windows and checking in on vulnerable neighbours, particularly old people with chronic disease who live alone. They also recommend checking air quality monitors in the morning and moving activities indoors when the pollution is too high.

In some cases, actions to keep the air clean may conflict with efforts to stay cool, according to a report from the BC Lung Foundation published last month. “The issue is we have a lot of compound climate exposure events where you have heat and wildfire,” said Cathryn Tonne, an environmental epidemiologist at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health and co-author of the study modelling wildfire-specific PM2.5. “Being home with the windows closed can be very bad – if you don’t have air conditioning – if it’s also hot.”

Can the fires behind the smoke at least be prevented? At the Fifa World Cup final, which barely avoided disruption from bad air, the US president, Donald Trump, asked his Canadian counterpart, Mark Carney, to “stop these fires from coming in and poisoning our air”. The demand was accompanied by threats of sanctions and came as Republican senators blamed Canada’s fires on poor forest management. Scientists countered that the blazes had little to do with land management – most of what has burned is boreal forest in unpopulated areas – and a lot to do with the rise in temperatures caused by burning fossil fuels, which Republicans have expanded.

In Europe, though, changes in land use have alarmed firefighters and wildfire experts about as much as global heating. Rural regions across the Mediterranean have hollowed out, resulting in more overgrown vegetation that dries out and allows fires to spread more easily during the hotter heatwaves that climate breakdown has brought. The combination of the two factors has led Spanish wildfire scientists to warn that we have “entered an era of fires we cannot extinguish”.

It is a problem that other parts of the world, from the western US to Australia, already know well. Adding to the climatic burden in the coming months is the arrival of a strong El Niño, a cyclical warming weather pattern, along with a related natural phenomenon in the Indian Ocean, which is priming countries across south-east Asia to burn.

The McClellands said that – even though they still had their homes and their health – the episode had given them a taste of the suffering that climate breakdown has long caused in other countries. “I know that people all around the world are feeling a kind of helplessness because of climate disasters,” said Dan McClelland. “I feel like this opened my eyes to understand just a sliver of what other people are feeling.”

Five Great Reads: Perils of high-impact exercise, the journo taking on big tech and birthdayzillas

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 22:10:35 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqueline Housden

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Good morning. Maybe you’ve been worrying about the rise of Silicon Valley billionaires and what it means for humanity, or whether your exercise regime is hurting your health, or if those adult birthday invites and plans are just getting way out of hand, or … maybe you have not. Regardless, that is where some of our best reporting went this week. Enjoy.

This story begins at a market in Lagos, Nigeria, where a teenager called Daniel is selling mobile phone accessories out of a wheelbarrow, hoping to escape the dim economic prospects of his country – they call it “japa”, or as one Lagosian tells Alexis Okeowo, “like running for your life”. When Daniel was given the chance to start a new life in the UK, he had no idea what was expected of him in return – and that he would be targeted by an organ-trafficking plot.‘It’s still going on, largely unreported, largely unchecked’: This case is the only successful conviction for organ trafficking under the Modern Slavery Act in the UK. Frank Tietie, a human rights lawyer, says there is a simple reason that such convictions are rare, particularly in Nigeria: “Those who are involved are usually very powerful people, and they’re able to influence our justice system.”

Notable quote: “He had not told me anything about this. I would never have agreed to any of this. My body was not for sale.”

How long will it take to read: 11 minutes

Further reading: ‘For me, there was no other choice’: inside the global illegal organ trade.

Aziz Shavershian was an Australian teenager who became a fitness influencer in the 2000s, a bit of a pioneer – filming his workouts and thoughts, and posting them to YouTube. He was skilled in rage-bait long before anyone had heard of it. But in 2011, “Zyzz” made headlines when he suddenly and unexpectedly died, aged just 22. Now, 15 years later, the truth about his death is finally being revealed.

A ‘camaraderie of training together’: The story has come out via Revealed – Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz, a Stan documentary directed by the film-maker Selina Miles. Aziz and his older brother, Said, were born in Russia to Kurdish parents who then migrated to Australia. In the film, the boys’ friends – many of them first-generation Australians – describe struggling to fit in but finding community in bodybuilding.

Fame, gains and hate: Aziz needed money to maintain his appearance and began to increasingly experiment with substances untested on humans, and without the recommended cycling on and off. As his fame grew, so did the gains. But the hateful comments from strangers also multiplied.

How long will it take to read: Just under three minutes.

Further reading: ‘So destructive’: women are paying for face scans that tell them what cosmetic procedures to get, and From bone smashing to chin extensions: how ‘looksmaxxing’ is reshaping young men’s faces

Extreme exercise seems to be a bit of a theme this week and this story might be enough to make you put off that hardcore session at the gym (did you need convincing?). Anna Moore takes a look at the dangers of people pushing themselves too hard in their workouts and asks what lessons the rest of us can take from them.

Not enough or the wrong kind? Each year, more than a quarter of a million people in the UK have joint replacement surgery and by 2060 demand is expected to have risen by 40%. So what’s going on – is it too much, too little, or the wrong kind of exercise? A consultant orthopaedic hip surgeon, Giles Stafford, has some insight. “There’s clearly a genetic aspect, but also a big mechanical aspect too,” he says. “We all have a certain number of cycles in us before the damage sets in, and someone who is going to the gym, running marathons, taking on high-impact, high-intensity, repetitive exercise programmes might hit their number younger and faster.”

Squatters beware: Several orthopaedic surgeons have expressed reservations about high-intensity, high-impact regimens. “Anything that involves a lot of deep-weighted squats, and repeatedly taking your body to end range under load, can damage your joints,” Stafford says. Another specialist says he has seen patients in their mid 20s and early 30s who have lost a lot of cartilage from under their kneecaps after these (yeeeaargh!).

How long will it take to read: Just under five minutes.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Stuck in an endless doomscroll? Worried about the creeping control technology has over our lives? You are not alone. In a new book, the journalist Gil Durán argues that many of big tech’s billionaire owners have seized economic and political control and are steering the fate of the planet towards their own bizarre, apocalyptic visions. And Durán is fighting back. Everyone’s addicted to the billionaire money: According to the author, who worked in communications for Kamala Harris when she was California’s attorney general, the Democrats are as much as fault as much as the Republicans for failing to tackle this new power. “They have failed tremendously to stand up to billionaire power because the only people as addicted to billionaire money in American politics as the Republicans are the Democrats,” he says.

Notable quote: “In fighting against billionaire power, we find the key to all of our problems. Every moment is an important opportunity to wake people up and to start to fight back.”

How long will it take to read: Just over three minutes.

It’s the weekend, as you might have noticed, and it’s possible you might be going to a birthday party. If your invite started with a WhatsApp group you never signed up for or an expensive-looking invitation in the post, and the actual event seems a bit OTT for a fully-grown adult who isn’t turning a major milestone, then you are not alone. As Meena Alexander finds out.

What IS going on? Where once a slice of cake sufficed to ring in a new age, Meena writes, today it’s not unusual to throw a fully catered party, rope your friends into a series of activities or organise a group holiday abroad. Lauren, a 29-year-old from Edinburgh, has already run through her annual leave allowance. “I’ve been to eight 30ths this year and the most low-key was a dinner in a private room that still set me back £100,” she says.

Lovers, haters and the why-the-hell-not brigade: Some have had their friendships – and bank balances – sorely tested by this phenomenon, which one puts squarely on the “main-character energy” of their generation, and are left feeling like the “poor friend”. But as Krisha, who flew to the Dominican Republic for a week of hiking, safaris, horse riding and massages to mark a new friend’s birthday, asks, why not “spend on a bucket-list experience” in a time when saving for a house deposit feels futile? “I find it interesting that when I tell people I flew across the world for a birthday party they say it’s insane, but when it’s for a wedding they don’t question it.”

How long will it take to read: Five and three-quarter minutes.

The Guardian view on Jason Arday: diversity advocates must stand firm

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 17:00:14 GMT

Serious failings by one academic, and his bosses at the University of Cambridge, should not be allowed to undermine wider progressive goals

Jason Arday’s resignation from the University of Cambridge on Wednesday marked a full stop of sorts, but not an end to the furore surrounding his promotion to a professorship at the age of 37. Academic colleagues have demanded, with justification, that an investigation into his appointment to the faculty of education in 2023, and the subsequent fallout, should include people from outside the university. Allegations of plagiarism and claims made by Mr Arday about his background, career and charity fundraising remain under scrutiny. The memoir for which he said he had received a huge advance, billed as a triumph over adversity including an early autism diagnosis, is scheduled to appear later this month. His publisher, Simon & Schuster, ought to pause while inquiries run their course.

But several things are already clear. By failing to do due diligence on Mr Arday before launching him, with fanfare, as Cambridge’s youngest-ever black professor, and through its inadequate response to later challenges, the university has done a serious disservice to black and neurodivergent scholars more widely. It has also set back the efforts of all the people and groups who have worked in good faith, over many years, to boost the presence of underrepresented groups in influential positions.

Such imbalances, which remain pronounced in many areas of public life, including academia, are the consequence of prejudices and discrimination, as well as unequal access to resources and opportunities. The glee with which some rightwingers have pounced on Mr Arday’s fall from grace is not solely due to relish in his exposure – or the angst among liberals that this provokes. It is because they want to stoke a sense of grievance among white supporters, and to pour scorn on diversity initiatives across the board.

Such efforts to discredit policies aimed at supporting autistic people, and those from ethnic minorities, to achieve their full potential must be strenuously resisted. With hindsight, it seems extraordinary that details of Mr Arday’s remarkable life story were not examined sooner. He was wrong to report a Times Higher Education journalist, Jack Grove, to the police, on the basis of a series of emailed queries. But Mr Arday is an individual. While there are lessons to be learned from his over-hasty ascent, the answer is not to give up on equity as a goal.

The scandal comes at a bad time in more ways than one. Rightwing parties continue to make hostility to migrants part of their core offer to voters, and will seek to capitalise on what will be presented as “Black Lives Matter gone mad”. But consequences within the academy must be taken seriously too. Universities are under massive strain owing to funding shortfalls, which have been worsened by new limits and levies on international students. Some are at risk of going bust, and the reputational blow to the sector inflicted by this scandal can only make the situation worse.

The discipline of sociology, already a target of intellectual conservatives who dislike its radical roots, may also see adverse effects, as its standards are questioned. Needless to say, Cambridge colleges will be relatively insulated from such collateral damage, which is likely to be most severe at less wealthy universities with less privileged intakes. This is a grim irony, and one that should prompt serious self-reflection by an elite institution that should have known better than to be so careless.

The Guardian view on Gianni Infantino: in the interests of the game he professes to love, he should go

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:57:07 GMT

The Fifa president’s attempt to brazen out the storm, after attempting to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity, adds insult to injury

“How did you go bankrupt?” a character is asked in Ernest Hemingway’s novel The Sun Also Rises. “Gradually, then suddenly” comes the reply. Right now, Fifa’s justly besieged president, Gianni Infantino, is experiencing something similar in relation to the loss of his own authority.

Since taking over the running of world football’s governing body in 2016, Mr Infantino has survived regular criticism of a monetising approach which has often come at a sporting cost. But since egregious plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law were leaked to the media, his credibility has been draining away at speed.

After crisis talks this week at Fifa’s lavish new African headquarters in Rabat, Mr Infantino authorised a half-hearted and incomplete apology, acknowledging that the now aborted project “could have been handled differently”. But it is very hard to imagine how a sell-off to private equity that would have imperilled the governance of the world’s most popular sport (and possibly led to Mr Infantino’s personal enrichment) could have been handled well. This was, simply, a betrayal of the game’s interests by the president of an organisation that already sits on billions of pounds worth of reserves.

Mr Infantino should resign. But despite crushing condemnation of his actions from senior Fifa figures, and football greats such as Arsène Wenger and Luís Figo, he appears determined to brazen out the storm. As a result, what happens now looks like becoming increasingly messy. Over the course of 10 years, Fifa’s president has carefully cultivated allies in the global south. Breaking ranks with their regional federation, Mexico and Argentina on Friday joined African nations in expressing support for his continued leadership.

Much will therefore depend on European football’s governing body, Uefa. On Thursday it responded witheringly to Mr Infantino’s attempt to draw a line, and restated a loss of confidence in his presidency. On Friday, Norway became the first federation to call directly for Fifa’s president to stand down. The next step will be to follow through on a threat to boycott Fifa-run competitions, starting with the Under-20 Women’s World Cup due to be held in Poland next month.

That, clearly, would be a very serious move. But it was a serious abuse of power to negotiate a deal mortgaging the World Cup’s future to speculators seeking to extract even more wealth from it. From the dubious award of the 2022 World Cup to Qatar, to Fifa’s suspension of inconvenient red cards, Mr Infantino is used to provoking and ignoring controversies. This one must come with consequences.

With haughty presumption, the statement from Mr Infantino’s Rabat bunker said the organisation “will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process”. The chutzpah is almost impressive. But really, dream on. Unless Fifa’s president resigns, is forced out, or is ousted via an election next March, the global game is in danger of descending into an ugly civil war – all because of one man’s attempt to sell off the family silver in unprecedented fashion. Mr Infantino was much mocked for his “Today I feel gay … today I feel [like] a migrant worker” response to critics prior to the Qatar World Cup. It would be greatly to the benefit of the sport he professes to love if he could show some self-awareness now.
