The Jason Arday affair has much to say about the current state of academia

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:57:02 GMT

Guardian readers reflect on the university system’s approach to Black academics and how it deals with job applications and promotions

Yes, the recent Jason Arday scandal should be a wake-up call to the left, as Jason Okundaye suggests (The takedown of Jason Arday has overjoyed the right, and must be a wake-up call for the left, 6 August), but it should also be a wake-up call to anyone who cares about university systems and protocols around appointment and promotion.

What I have seen at UK universities suggests that Arday was not simply an individual who slipped through the net, but that university systems often fail to detect or challenge exaggerated claims. If anything, those with greater institutional privilege are more likely to get away with exaggerations, embellishments and even falsehoods on their CVs and promotion applications.

I have witnessed and reported on what appeared to be falsehoods in promotion applications with no repercussions; in fact, in both cases the applicants were promoted (and both were white). In one case, an applicant claimed to have given several keynote addresses, while conference websites indicated that he had been only an ordinary conference speaker. In another, an applicant claimed to be a co-author of a book when she was listed as a “data collection contributor”.

Why, after I highlighted inaccurate claims, were these people still promoted? I cannot say. But from speaking with colleagues at other universities, this is far from unusual. Those willing to stretch the truth can rely on overworked colleagues with little time to factcheck and a system depending heavily on applicants’ honesty.

This lack of accountability is grossly unfair on the many academics who report honestly on their accomplishments and do excellent work without resorting to such tactics. Perhaps the pressure to meet increasingly demanding and sometimes unattainable standards is driving this behaviour.

The number of permanent academic jobs has not kept pace with the number of PhD graduates, and competition for academic posts has intensified. Nevertheless, we need more checks and verifiable criteria to help prevent future scandals and to restore confidence in academic integrity. Name and address supplied

The case of Prof Jason Arday is an important insight into the academic world. Public expectation of academia and its most prestigious institutions is that these are purely meritocratic. In my experience this is not the case. One of the questions we should be asking is why an academic would be moved to fabricate a CV? Academic pressures can be intense, as evidenced by the needless suicide of Prof Stefan Grimm in 2014.

Furthermore, low-level racism is common in the university setting, in which there is a “chumocratic” culture that promotes similar or like-minded individuals. Ethnic minorities, or those who question the establishment, may be excluded from reaping the full benefits of their academic endeavours in an environment in which career-defining decisions such as promotion, publication and grant success are subjective.

At present, pending full investigation, it may be unclear if Jason Arday is perpetrator or victim, but the academic environment in which he has operated is unlikely to be completely blameless. Salim KhakooProfessor of hepatology, University of Southampton

Jason Arday’s story has divided opinion among my friends and associates, and Okundaye’s piece articulates why. Whether the accusations of plagiarism or lying hold up, only time will tell. But in the meantime, a man and his family are in an intolerable position.

What troubles me equally is the frame surrounding Arday before any of this surfaced: the youngest Black professor in Cambridge’s history, a story of triumph over adversity. That framing is seductive – it’s the stuff that films are made of – but it sets a trap. It suggests Black excellence is only coherent when it becomes a redemption story. But that isn’t equal opportunity; equality doesn’t require anyone to be a miracle.

I don’t know if Arday lied. I’m not signing petitions declaring the allegations “entirely false”. But I will still buy his book, because I think he has been let down by more than himself. Memuna FornaLondon

Here’s what I think Jason Arday represents: an obsession among liberal Britain with Black people’s “inspiring stories”; a man for whom making things up became a sad habit, and what happens when you become trapped in it; a reminder that, depressingly, the path to flourishing while Black is to be better than perfect, and some people will never believe you’re there by merit; and how a victim of a coordinated campaign can be taken down. All these points are true. It’s a sad story. Colton RichardsLondon

I really appreciated the down-to-earth sanity of Jason Okundaye’s piece on the case of Jason Arday. So much hype, so much spiteful sniping, seldom thoughtful or without an agenda. Underneath it all, I can’t help feeling that Cambridge University did little to cover themselves in glory.

However, I suspect that few have thought about Jason Arday, the person, and what he might be going through. I feel a sense of admiration for him, without being in a position to judge any of the allegations made against him. Some compassion would go a long way. Linda RheadHampton, London

It is a deeply concerning to hear of the resignation of Prof Jason Arday, a huge loss. Your report (5 August) refers to the Guardian’s own investigation, with revelations that this professor may have inflated his running achievements and overstated threats to his personal safety. On the former, instances of much more egregious displays of ego in academia are far from rare, without any apparent damage to the standing or careers of many professors.

On the latter, one has to ask what it takes for an institution to act to protect Black staff and students. Experiences of racism are far from unusual, and the psychological toll they take is well documented. Rather than undermine those who seek help in the face of abuse, the Guardian might wonder: what does it take to make us listen and understand?Dr Isabel ShutesLondon School of Economics and Political Science

Within higher education, Jason Arday is well known for the kindness he promotes; many thousands of the students and staff he has encountered over the years will attest to this. In today’s world – particularly within the context of recent coverage surrounding Arday – the significance of this should not be underestimated.

The accusations against Arday raise many polarising and contentious issues, and debates will no doubt continue for some time. In all of this, I urge commentators and commenters to remember the principles of respect and humanity, not to mention kindness. Name and address supplied

It seems that handkerchiefs, tissues and even the concept of blowing your nose have gone out of fashion. I enjoyed your guide to travel etiquette. It was very sensible and reflective of our modern society. I had to smile at the guidance for offering your seat to elderly people – as a man in my mid-50s who is (happily) fit and healthy, I always have to remind myself that people offering me a seat aren’t commenting on my physical state, they are just being kind to a stranger.

However, you didn’t go into enough detail about one of my biggest bugbears – people who insist on keeping their backpacks on on crowded buses and tubes where standing space is at a premium. As they move or turn they bump into whatever you’re holding, and it reduces the opportunity for others to join the service.

It’s a simple rule: take the backpack off and have it at your feet – always – to avoid encroaching on other people’s personal space and to free up space for others. Or maybe my middle-aged grumpiness is just getting the better of me on this one. Peter AntolikLondon

Recently, after a three day-visit to London, I returned home to Devon and jokingly complained that Londoners constantly made me feel old. Every journey I made on public transport, someone offered me a seat. On two occasions a woman offered me a helping hand as I descended the stairs on a bus. I am a six-foot, healthy 80-year-old and can easily manage to stand for a short journey but, as my wife pointed out, it is much nicer to smile and accept the offers. On another bus, a woman offered to move so that my wife and I could sit together. In conclusion, I felt I should point out that Londoners, in my experience, do not really need much of your advice. I read Luke McLaughlin’s article with a great deal of empathy, yet still with some uneasiness about the taboo of having more than one club (Have you ever switched allegiance as a football fan? You are not alone, 1 August). A world I inhabit.

I too was at the Millwall v Forest game marred by crowd trouble. It was my first! My family are mostly Millwall, who remain my club, but having seen them drop down the divisions and play in the third tier, my head was turned by better technique and Tottenham- and Arsenal-supporting friends. They will never understand my soft spot for both clubs.

Not to mention family in Germany giving me a Freiburg shirt, making them my German team. Then the gift of a Champions League ticket at Celtic Park put another team in the mix, so I’m checking a lot of scores. Now in the Borders, I am agitating to see Gala Fairydean Rovers this season. They will be yet another team for me to keep an eye on.

To this day, when people ask me which team I support, I pause sheepishly and say, “Millwall but…”. I suppose I just love football!Michael OpitzKelso, Roxburghshire

Over the course of his life, a man could well change his wife owing to personal choice or events outside his control. It is quite likely that his political views will sway depending on the ineptitude of governing parties or his own finances. His religious persuasion may be amended or completely turned off. But he must never, ever, change his football allegiance, particularly for the heinous crime of glory-hunting, else he shall always be known as a plastic fan. Neil BageBourne, Lincolnshire

If Luke McLaughlin wants to change teams, good for him. I often wish that I could. However, similar to the last words of Queen Mary I, when I am dead and opened you shall find my blue and white hooped heart. It’s not just that QPR was our local team. It’s not just that going to matches with my father was our time, unbreached by family or his congregation.

Despite its rather rocky record over the last 50 years, I’ve stuck with the club. Chairmen, managers and players come and go. There are promotions and relegations (we don’t do cups). The fans remain. And the longer we stay (and the longer we suffer), we begin to understand how our commitment to the cause is at the root of the club’s identity. We hold its memories, and create new ones. We give it life. And it gives us hope. I understand that Luke feels this is too much for him. I’ll give him a wave at the Millwall game next week. Ariel J Friedlander Modena, Italy

China’s AI ecosystem is not as open as it claims. Nor is any other country’s

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:56:34 GMT

Responding to an article by China’s ambassador to the UK, Prof Paul H Cleverley advocates shared openness standards, while Dr Claire Jenkins says British AI can offer a distinctive path

Ambassador Zheng Zeguang rightly celebrates openly released AI models, and the Chinese labs behind Qwen, DeepSeek and Kimi have led the way – competition that benefits everyone, especially where models can run on modest hardware in the developing world (The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working together, 30 July).

But his claim that openness is a defining feature of China’s AI development deserves scrutiny. Take GeoGPT, the geoscience system from Zhejiang Lab showcased at last month’s World AI Conference as a model of jointly governed open science. It is promoted to countries as open, yet under the model openness framework – endorsed in a recent UN report – it would not qualify as open at all. It releases model weights (built mainly on Alibaba Qwen, whose licences are not Open Source Initiative-compliant), no training data or application source code is released, and its governance committee answers to Zhejiang Lab itself.

Domain rivals show what fuller openness looks like. The European Space Agency’s Earth Virtual Expert (EVE), also built for the Earth sciences, releases its training and evaluation tooling, while the US non-profit Ai2’s OLMo goes further still, publishing everything needed for reproducibility.

The distinction matters. A free hosted service is not an open one: GeoGPT’s users route their data through China’s legal jurisdiction, creating real dependency and sovereignty risks.

None of this is unique to China. The US private-enterprise model raises much the same concerns. That is really the ambassador’s own point extended: no country’s ecosystem is quite as open as its diplomacy suggests. If the UK is to gain from the cooperation he proposes, it should press for shared openness standards like the UN-recommended model openness framework as the basis for any joint work. Honest measurement, not just the language of openness, is where real partnership begins. Prof Paul H Cleverley Robert Gordon University, Aberdeen

Your article rightly argues that Britain cannot afford to be a passive consumer of AI while the US and China shape the technologies that will define the future. Yet the debate should not be reduced to a geopolitical race.

The real question is what kind of AI Britain wishes to build. Our greatest strength is not simply our research universities or life-sciences sector, but the NHS, our public institutions and a long tradition of ethical inquiry. These provide an opportunity to develop AI that is trustworthy, transparent and directed towards the public good rather than solely commercial advantage.

Healthcare illustrates both the promise and the risk. AI can reduce administrative burdens, improve diagnosis and widen access to care. However, public confidence depends on strong governance, meaningful human oversight and assurance that patient data serves citizens rather than corporate or geopolitical interests. Recent work by the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency’s national commission into the regulation of AI in healthcare has highlighted exactly these concerns.

Britain should resist the temptation to imitate either Silicon Valley’s market dominance or China’s state-led model. Instead, it could offer a distinctive path: AI that combines innovation with democratic accountability, scientific excellence and social justice. That would be a form of leadership worthy of Britain’s traditions – and one that others might choose to follow. Dr Claire JenkinsWollaton, Nottinghamshire

The first letter above was amended on 8 August 2026. Because of an editing error, an earlier version said “Open Systems Interconnection-compliant” where “Open Source Initiative-compliant” was meant.

A ‘Keminaissance’ for the Tories is wishful thinking – Badenoch’s Reform-lite summer will only end one way

The Guardian Fri, 07 Aug 2026 16:53:09 GMT

Hiring a convicted antisemite as an adviser; rabble rousing at a time of violent unrest. She is still in a race to the bottom and making too many mistakes

The Keminaissance will be delayed. For nearly a year, Conservative optimists and a clutch of supportive pundits have been forecasting an upturn in the fortunes of Kemi Badenoch, confident that her party will emerge from the crater it fell into in 2024, overtake Reform UK to become once again the main party of the right and, who knows, maybe, with a following wind, even push Labour aside and return to government. Every sign of strength from the Tory leader – a robust conference speech here, a viral clip on social media there – has been hailed as evidence of the coming Keminaissance. On the evidence of the past week or so, we will have to wait a little longer.

It’s quite true that Badenoch’s personal ratings are better than those of her party. True, too, that she ended a long losing streak when the Tories won a Westminster seat at the Aberdeen South byelection in June. But there is a more recent election result that should temper the boosters’ enthusiasm, along with a series of decisions that confirm that, when it comes to both strategy and judgment, Badenoch is badly lacking.

Start with that contest from a week ago. For many, the standout fact of the byelection to replace Andy Burnham as mayor of Greater Manchester was that Reform came a very poor second, taking just 21% of the vote to Labour’s 47%. It was indeed a crushing defeat for Nigel Farage’s party, which a matter of weeks earlier had talked up its chances of winning the mayoralty.

But run your finger further down the vote tally until it finally reaches the Conservative candidate on a mere 7.7%. In all the previous mayoral contests in Greater Manchester, the Tories were in second place. This time they were fifth, behind Restore Britain, a party of the hard right that has become home to all manner of racists and white supremacists.

A Tory result that bad among such a large electorate suggests not merely that Badenoch is making slow progress, but that she is moving her party backwards. When it comes to challenging Labour, other parties are either level with the Conservatives or ahead of them. In that context, it seems an undeserved compliment to call Kemi Badenoch the leader of the opposition.

Her strategic response to this competition on the right has been to move towards her rivals, hoping to blunt the appeal of the nationalist populist parties by matching their offer. The latest step came late on Thursday with, as the Telegraph billed it, a Tory “promise to end council housing for foreigners”. Badenoch’s pledge is to evict almost 230,000 non-EU foreign national households from their homes.

Never mind that many of those turfed out will include people who, while not UK citizens, have been living, working and paying taxes in Britain for years, while others will be refugees fleeing war and persecution. Never mind that, once evicted, those families, including their children, will be rendered homeless, leaving local councils with the choice of either abandoning them to the streets or providing (much costlier) emergency accommodation. Never mind that it’s unclear who exactly would identify and locate these families, unless Badenoch plans to create a British equivalent of ICE, mounting raids, snatching terrified people from their cars and throwing them into detention. Never mind all that; Badenoch doesn’t care.

So much for the policy; now consider the timing. The Tory leader decided the right moment to demand foreigners be kicked out of their homes was as the Norfolk town of Thetford entered its third night of violence and disorder, triggered by a mob surrounding the accommodation of suspected asylum seekers, some in the crowd trying to force their way in, as others threw rocks and chanted: “We want them out.” Into this tinderbox of a situation walked the Conservative party leader, clutching a petrol can.

Just a day or two earlier, she had been defending the selection as a Somerset council candidate of Joshua Bonehill-Paine, a man who has served long jail sentences for, among other things, a sustained campaign of antisemitic harassment and abuse of the Jewish former MP Luciana Berger, a campaign that saw Berger branded an “evil money-grabber”, her face superimposed on the body of a rat and photographs of her doctored into multiple, sexualised images.

Badenoch argued that Bonehill-Paine had renounced his past as a self-described “nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights” and now works to prevent others succumbing to what he calls the disease of antisemitism. In April, he published a lengthy account of how he had come to see Jews as the malign, all-powerful “force operating behind events”, a text that contains some useful insights. (Among them, as my colleague Rafael Behr has pointed out, is an arresting admission by Bonehill-Paine that, though then a full-strength neo-Nazi, he “welcomed Jeremy Corbyn’s election as Labour leader”, which should give pause to those who, at the time, so adamantly dismissed Jewish fears that Corbyn was a draw to those who hate Jews.)

Though candid, the essay is not wholly reassuring. For one thing, it contains no apology to Berger or any of Bonehill-Paine’s other victims. For another, he explains that what changed him was reading the Bible and coming to realise that Jews are “God’s chosen people”. I suspect few Jews will find comfort in that. Instead, they will worry that the would-be politician has traded antisemitism for philosemitism, which means he still singles out “the Jews” rather than seeing Jews as regular people, with the right to be as ordinary and flawed as anyone else.

Still, even if Bonehill-Paine’s disavowal of his past were wholly convincing and he should be regarded as fully rehabilitated, that doesn’t make it obvious that he is acceptable for public office. The bar for that is higher, a point Badenoch herself implicitly conceded when she hinted that Bonehill-Paine would not have cleared the threshold to become an MP. Serving as a councillor was different, she explained, as he would be responsible for nothing more than “parking and bins” – thereby, and at a stroke, insulting the many thousands of Conservatives who devote themselves to public service in their local communities.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Bonehill-Paine eventually withdrew his candidacy, but that did not draw a line under the episode. In her stubbornness, the Tory leader said the former neo-Nazi would now serve the party as an adviser, thereby giving him a role on the very national level she had earlier said was off-limits. Worsening matters still further, the shadow cabinet member Claire Coutinho posted that, while, “Luciana and others are unable to forgive Joshua, I do,” attributing this vicarious generosity of hers to her Catholic faith, and so, doubtless unconsciously, reinforcing that age-old trope of the forgiving Christian and the vengeful Jew.

What a mess to have made in just a few days. If it were only tactical blunders and in-the-moment misjudgments, one might be more, er, forgiving. But the flaw is strategic. Badenoch has chosen to fight a race to the bottom against Reform, but it is a race she can never win. Farage will always be willing to go further. Take that latest proposal on housing. She would give foreign nationals six months to get out of their homes; Reform promises to boot them out in three. The penny has still not dropped that in a contest of Reform v Reform Lite, the real thing will always have the edge.

All the while, as Badenoch chases after Farage supporters, moderate Tory voters grow more disenchanted. There may be room for ex-fascists in Conservative ranks, but the leader will allow no place for Conservatives who support net zero targets and do not want the UK to leave the European convention on human rights. The result is that those “blue wall”, southern Tories who defected to the Lib Dems in 2024 have every reason not to come back.

So, yes, Kemi Badenoch may score a win now and then; she’s bound to land the odd blow on Burnham when normal hostilities resume in September. But a Keminaissance? For the Tories, it looks like the dark ages have a while to run yet.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

Australia are desperate to register back-to-back Test wins for the first time in a year when they take on ⁠Japan. Not since they beat ⁠the British & Irish Lions ⁠and Springboks in ​August last year have the Wallabies managed two wins in a row, but that is the target in Osaka after they beat ⁠Italy in July to end a six-match losing streak. Saturday’s clash also marks the first match in charge for Les Kiss and he will pit his coaching smarts against Eddie Jones, who has twice been in charge of the Wallabies and will be hoping to lead Japan to their first win over Australia. Jonathan Howcroft brings you the action.

And it’s back … in what may seem to some a blink of the eye, football returns in England, barely three weeks since the end of the summer’s World Cup. In Scotland, the season is already up and running and while the Premier League’s elite fine-tune with a host of friendlies – from Manchester United v Paris Saint-Germain in Gothenburg to Chelsea v Milan in Jakarta and all points in between – the core action arrives in the Carabao Cup. Of the 29 matches, the standout comes at the London Stadium where freshly relegated West Ham wake up to the reality of demotion for their first League Cup first-round tie since 2011 when they lost 2-1 to Aldershot on home soil. Portsmouth are the visitors, with Pompey progressing from two of the three prior major cup competition ties between them. Plus there’ll be transfer updates and breaking news. Scott Murray helms our rolling blog.

After Friday’s summit climax at Mont Ventoux, where Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney were expected to make their moves on Marlen Reusser, Saturday’s stage is the longest of this year’s race at 171.9km. Starting in Sisteron, the route heads south along the Route Napoléon for 49km, before switching westward, along the River Var. The riders take on climbs of Col des Robines and Col de Toutes Aures, swoop down towards the Côte d’Azur and then confront two more ascents: Côte de Colomars and Côte de la Ginestière. The finish arrives at Nice’s Promenade des Anglais. Tom Bassam’s rolling liveblog keeps pace with all the stage eight action.

The final stage arrives in the form of a 99.2km circuit around Nice – the very last chance for riders to shake up the overall classification … if it’s not already been sewn up on Saturday. With a severe high-temperature warning over the region, blazing heat in the low 30Cs will be an added challenge for the riders. At last year’s finish in Châtel Les Portes du Soleil, the Olympic champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot finished in style to become the first French rider to win the Tour de France Femmes in 36 years, a huge moment for women’s cycling in the host nation. Join Luke McLaughlin for the grand finale.

Senate Bows to Reality, Leaving Trump’s Voting Bill Undone

The New York Times August 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

The summer exit confirmed what had been apparent for weeks: that Republicans lacked the votes to pass the voting restrictions the president has made a top priority.

By Michael Gold

Reporting from the Capitol, freshly abandoned by senators who have departed for their summer recess.

The Senate bowed to political reality at 4:36 a. m. on Saturday, adjourning and allowing bleary-eyed senators to leave Washington without any concrete steps toward passing the voting restriction bill that President Trump has demanded for months.

Republican lawmakers had insisted they would work tirelessly to enact election changes that Mr. Trump has suggested the party needs in place to win the midterm elections. Instead, they departed with little to show for their efforts, other than a performative pre-dawn procedural vote on a watered-down version of the bill that they knew they could not pass.

Even the staunchest advocates of the election measure eventually conceded what had been clear all along: There was simply not enough Republican support to push through the strict voter identification legislation. With the party’s majority at risk, senators were eager to abandon the futile effort so they could get home to their states to campaign for re-election.

“We are not in a position right now where we have the wherewithal to pass it right now,” Senator Mike Lee, Republican of Utah and one of the most forceful proponents of the legislation, said on Friday night.

Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, had been making that case for months, alluding in increasingly blunt terms to “math” and “reality” that he suggested the president simply did not appreciate as Mr. Trump angrily demanded the Senate find a way to pass the elections bill.

The president’s proposed measure would require Americans to show proof of citizenship to register to vote, impose a nationwide voter identification requirement and severely limit voting by mail. That legislation, which the president has called the SAVE America Act, has neither the majority it would need to pass nor the 60 votes needed to overcome a Democratic filibuster.

Still, Mr. Trump commanded the Senate to cancel its planned five-week recess if it did not pass the measure. Mr. Lee had been one of his loudest allies, threatening to block the Senate from adjourning or force his colleagues to go on the record with a politically unappealing vote in favor of leaving Washington for the summer rather than staying at work at the Capitol.

But in the end, Mr. Lee did neither. Though he forced the Senate to vote to adjourn, he accepted a voice vote that did not require senators to formally register a position.

In a late push to show progress on the elections measure, Republican leaders had rushed to draft a $150 billion budget blueprint to fund the war with Iran and the implementation of new election restrictions, and discussed bringing it to a vote. That plan would pave the way for filibuster-proof legislation known as a reconciliation bill to bypass Democratic opposition.

But it was clear that the measure would have failed overnight, lacking enough support among Republicans to move ahead.

Senator Ron Johnson, Republican of Wisconsin and the chairman of the Budget Committee, said that lawmakers would postpone the effort until they return in September. He and other senators called Mr. Trump to tell him of the plan, which they said he supported.

“We’re in total agreement,” Mr. Johnson said on Friday night. “We were just kind of like, ‘Here’s the reality.’ He would like a better reconciliation bill that will take more time, so he was completely supportive of it.”

But the budget reconciliation process is cumbersome, and Republicans are running out of time to pass their measure before Election Day. The Senate has just three scheduled weeks in Washington before the midterm elections, in which control of Congress is at stake.

Senators who are up for re-election were particularly eager to return home so they can focus on making their cases to voters. Senator Lisa Murkowski pointed to several competitive races, including that of Senator Dan Sullivan, her fellow Alaska Republican, as she made the case for adjourning.

“The most important thing for Senator Sullivan as well as my friend Susan Collins and Jon Husted and Pete Ricketts is for them to be able to go home and be in their states and go to work again,” Ms. Murkowski said, referring to Republican senators in Maine, Ohio and Nebraska who must face voters in November.

Before they left, Republicans held a test vote meant to put Democrats on the defensive on the voter ID piece of the elections bill, seizing upon an idea that polls have shown is broadly popular. They tried to advance a bill sponsored by Mr. Husted, who is facing a difficult re-election race, that would have required voters nationwide to show certain forms of photo identification in federal elections.

Ultimately, the effort failed on a party-line vote, with all Democrats voting against it.

Though some Democrats have said they support federal voter ID requirements, they have argued that Mr. Husted’s measure would too strictly limit what forms of identification were acceptable, potentially blocking eligible voters who lacked the proper documentation from being able to cast ballots.

Catie Edmondson and Carl Hulse contributed reporting.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

The U. S. Is Burning Through Weapons in Iran. Russia and China Are Taking Note.

The New York Times August 08, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The Iran war has depleted U. S. weapons stockpiles, resulting in a significant erosion of firepower. A more drawn-out Iran conflict benefits Moscow and Beijing, some analysts say.

By Anton TroianovskiJonathan SwanEric Schmitt and Julian E. Barnes

Reporting from Washington

President Trump’s war against Iran has depleted U. S. weapons stockpiles to troubling levels, siphoning supplies from Asia and Europe, according to senior officials.

The rapidly shrinking supply of air-defense missiles and other critical weaponry in Europe and Asia not only leaves the U. S. military less equipped, but could also leave Russia and China feeling emboldened should they contemplate a potential conflict with the United States, experts said.

Bombing Iran burned through thousands of multimillion-dollar missiles that contain precision parts from a global web of suppliers and can take years to produce. Defending against Iran’s retaliatory barrages has worn down U. S. stocks of air-defense missiles to an extent that has privately alarmed top officials in the Trump administration and has led to the United States’ delaying deliveries to European and Asian customers.

The Iran campaign has forced the Pentagon to rush ships, aircraft and air-defense units from across Europe and Asia to the Middle East, an effort with cascading consequences for equipment maintenance and troop morale, U. S. officials said. The result is a significant erosion of American firepower in those regions, a shift with long-term implications that are a growing concern in the military and intelligence communities, senior U. S. and Western officials said.

Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, said the United States has “more than enough firepower to carry out any operation the president orders at any time and place.” But experts say the munitions crisis — part of which Mr. Trump inherited from President Joseph R. Biden Jr. — is almost certain to outlast his presidency.

Tom Karako, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, said the depletion of munitions was a “generational annihilation of the means of conventional deterrence.” The impact on how decisions are made in Beijing and Moscow, he said, could resonate for years.

“It’s impossible for that not to have a significant effect on the decision calculus of Russia and China,” said Mr. Karako, who has been tracking U. S. weapons stockpiles. “They may do something quite deliberate and at the time of their choosing, because keep in mind — we’re going to take years to reconstitute.”

In meetings in the lead-up to the Iran war, Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, informed the president of the risks of dipping deeper into drained stockpiles, according to two officials with knowledge of the exchanges. Mr. Trump still decided to go ahead, believing the war would be over quickly. A spokesman for General Caine declined to comment on his private conversations with the president.

After attacking Iran alongside Israel on Feb. 28, Mr. Trump repeatedly promised victory within weeks. More than five months later, he remains unable to bend Iran to his will, or even to find a way to end the war. The munitions shortage is said to have played a role in persuading Mr. Trump to put aside a major bombing campaign late last month. But it also shows how the president’s decision to attack Iran has left the United States and its allies more vulnerable to other threats.

The Trump administration has worked with military contractors to try to accelerate and expand production. But even accounting for those efforts, it could take more than two years for the United States to replenish the more than 1,500 Patriot air-defense interceptor missiles that have been used in the Iran war. The current U. S. inventory of those missiles is fewer than 1,700, according to two people briefed on the stockpile who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military details.

Mr. Trump has been enraged about news stories covering the munitions shortages. He has ordered a massive leak hunt across his government and is demanding criminal prosecutions. He has told advisers in private that any discussion of the munitions crisis signals weakness to the country’s enemies, and he continues in public to downplay the issue, deny it exists or blame his predecessor.

“Our defense companies are making more munitions than ever before, while rapidly expanding their plants and equipment at record levels,” Ms. Leavitt, the White House press secretary, said in a statement. “Anyone entrusted with access to classified military information who leaks it to the media is betraying that trust and breaking federal law, and should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesman, said reports of weapons shortages are false, adding that the United States has “everything required to strike at the time and place of the president’s choosing.”

The most immediate impact of the munitions shortage is being felt in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital. President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said this week that the number of air-defense missiles being provided to his country by Western allies had dropped threefold this year compared with 2025. On Wednesday, Ukraine failed to intercept any of the 28 missiles fired by Russia, which killed at least 17 people. More interceptors, Mr. Zelensky said, “could have saved the lives of those killed today.”

The fundamental problem, analysts say, is that Russia has ramped up its missile production to a greater extent than Ukraine’s Western supporters have been able to manufacture air defenses. The Iran war exacerbated the mismatch.

Representative Jason Crow, a Colorado Democrat who sits on the House Armed Services and Intelligence Committees, said the “antiquated” U. S. defense procurement process “doesn’t allow us to actually keep pace with the rapidly evolving nature of warfare.”

“Frankly, our adversaries don’t have those hindrances,” Mr. Crow said.

The United States and its allies have begun to hoard air-defense missiles amid the global supply crunch. Mr. Trump, asked by a reporter in the Oval Office on Thursday about Mr. Zelensky’s plea for more missiles, shot back: “We want missiles too.”

Mr. Trump regularly insists that Mr. Biden’s support for Ukraine is to blame for any shortfalls in U. S. weapons stocks. He said on social media on Thursday that the United States had “massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types.”

It is true that the United States has a vast arsenal of less advanced munitions, including more than 100,000 guided bombs that are dropped from aircraft, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. The problem with many of those weapons is that they have to be released close to their targets, putting more warplanes at risk of getting shot down.

High-end cruise missiles avoid that risk because they can be launched from hundreds of miles away. But the U. S. military largely exhausted its stocks of certain types of long-range missiles — such as the Army Tactical Missile Systems, or ATACMS, and Precision Strike Missiles — during the Iran war, officials said.

Long-range missiles would be critical in a war against China or Russia, countries with far more advanced air defenses than Iran. Both governments are tracking U. S. stockpiles closely, estimating them through public sources like the congressional budget process and defense contractor announcements, as well as via their spy satellites and other surveillance systems, according to a U. S. official familiar with defense intelligence.

“The situation is shaping up very favorably,” a popular Russian pro-war blogger, Aleksandr Kots, recently wrote. “The less precision-guided weaponry the U. S. has, the less will reach Ukraine.”

Even if Mr. Trump’s successor wants to ramp up aid to Ukraine, Mr. Kots added, “doing so will be impossible with empty arsenals.”

The long-term impact of the depletion may be greatest in Asia, where the United States has long been preparing for the possibility of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan, the self-governing island that Beijing claims as its own. The U. S. military’s Indo-Pacific Command became a major source of munitions for the Iran war, with many of its Tomahawks and other long-range missiles in the region — critical to a fight with China — transferred from its stocks.

Hundreds of advanced air-defense interceptors have been sent to the Middle East from South Korea and elsewhere in Asia, while a carrier strike group and some of the Navy’s highest-end destroyers were deployed from the region to support the Iran campaign. U. S. troops in South Korea would be more vulnerable in a war with North Korea because the Pentagon has redirected tactical surveillance assets to the Middle East and withdrawn air defenses, a U. S. official said.

The depletion has wide-ranging effects. In Asia, some U. S. officials fear that South Korea and Japan will doubt the ability of the United States to protect them with nonnuclear defenses, and will be more inclined to seek their own nuclear weapons to establish more credible deterrence. In Europe, U. S. allies are already looking to increase weapons purchases from other countries, given the production backlog in the United States.

Russia and China have long understood that the U. S. stockpile is limited, officials say, and now understand that inventories will take time to be refilled to levels that would allow for the execution of certain war plans. In that sense, a more drawn-out Iran conflict benefits Moscow and Beijing, some analysts said.

“The longer this war runs and the more we continue to exchange fires with Iran, the worse the munitions problem becomes for the United States, and the larger and more visible this window of vulnerability becomes,” said Todd Harrison, a defense analyst at the American Enterprise Institute.

Dara Massicot, an expert on the Russian military at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said that Moscow had already been reassessing its assumptions about U. S. military stockpiles before the start of the Iran war. The four years of conflict in Ukraine, she said, might have shown Russian military planners that the United States was slower at ramping up weapons production than they had believed.

“That’s the wrong kind of math to go into the Russian system, because then they start changing their perception of their own power vis-à-vis NATO,” said Ms. Massicot, who recently returned from a trip to Ukraine. “It causes them to come to conclusions that we may not want them to.”

Xinyun Wu contributed reporting from Taipei.

Anton Troianovski writes about American foreign policy and national security for The Times from Washington. He was previously a foreign correspondent based in Moscow and Berlin.

Eric Schmitt is a national security correspondent for The Times. He has reported on U. S. military affairs and counterterrorism for more than three decades. Contact him securely on Signal: @ericschmitt.36.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Iran Issues List of Demands, Dampening Hopes of Reopening Strait of Hormuz

The New York Times August 08, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said that the waterway will remain closed until the United States meets certain conditions.

By Yeganeh Torbati and Leily Nikounazar

A top Iranian national security official delivered a sweeping set of demands on Saturday that he said the United States must meet before the Strait of Hormuz can reopen to maritime traffic, throwing the fate of the critical trade waterway into question.

Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, issued a statement carried by state media laying out multiple requirements for reopening the strait. He called for the United States to lift its naval blockade and sanctions on Iran, withdraw the U. S. military from around Iran, pay war reparations and release frozen Iranian assets, as well as end attacks on Iran’s allies in the region and threats against the country.

The Trump administration is unlikely to agree to those demands. A previous cease-fire between Iran and the United States, agreed to in June, had said that sanctions would be fully lifted only in the event of a final deal regarding Iran’s nuclear program. And U. S. officials have said in the past that Iran could only access its frozen funds if it committed to giving up its highly enriched uranium first.

The statement from Mr. Zolghadr came as Iran and Oman have been negotiating an agreement on the future management of the Strait of Hormuz, which sits between the two countries. Iran effectively closed the strait in retaliation for being attacked by the United States and Israel in February.

Mr. Zolghadr’s list of demands upended expectations that a deal with Oman would allow commerce to flow through the strait once more and ease global energy prices. They will likely put pressure on President Trump to consider Iran’s conditions if he wants to lower consumer prices for Americans, which pose a risk for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Even before Mr. Zolghadr’s statement, Iranian officials had hinted on Saturday that the reopening of the strait was not imminent. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, said that reopening the strait was “not contingent on the Iran-Oman negotiations.”

In comments carried by Tasnim, an Iranian news outlet affiliated with the Guards, Mr. Mohebbi said that it would depend “on the United States fully accepting Iran’s conditions.” He did not specify those conditions, other than to say that the United States must not interfere in Iran’s ongoing negotiations with Oman or other countries.

Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, said on Saturday that Iran and Oman were “very close” to an agreement, according to Tasnim.

“However, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on other conditions, including the United States compensating for its violations of the Islamabad Memorandum,” Mr. Araghchi was quoted as saying, referring to the cease-fire agreement that Iran and the United States signed in June.

The June agreement — a “memorandum of understanding” brokered by Pakistani mediators in Islamabad — called for the opening of the Strait of Hormuz and the temporary lifting of oil sanctions on Iran. Yet the deal’s language was vague, and the United States and Iran had differing interpretations of what it meant.

The United States backed a southern route for ships that skirted Oman’s coastline and avoided Iranian waters, and Iran responded by warning and striking ships that took that route. The cease-fire soon collapsed, and the United States reimposed its naval blockade of Iranian ports.

“The Americans were seeking to establish new routes through the Strait of Hormuz, and despite the warnings issued by our country, they sought to undermine Iran’s management of the strait,” Mr. Araghchi said. “Therefore, any violation of the memorandum of understanding or of Iran’s management of the Strait of Hormuz is absolutely unacceptable to the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

Mr. Araghchi said that Iran and Oman were discussing a temporary route through the strait, and that the two countries’ militaries were negotiating the specifics. Officials familiar with the emerging deal have said it could formalize some of Iran’s claims of control over shipping in the waterway.

Raz Zimmt, an Iran expert at the Institute for National Security Studies, an Israeli research institute, said the comments by Mr. Mohebbi and Mr. Araghchi reflected Iran’s view that its negotiations with Oman were intended “at most” to work out how the waterway will be reopened in the future.

Even if Iran and Oman agree to specifics on the strait, “it is clear that Tehran will not agree to implement them without a return to the U. S. commitments under the memorandum, including lifting the naval blockade and resuming the process of sanctions relief,” Mr. Zimmt wrote on social media.

On Saturday, the Emirati foreign ministry said an Iranian attack had targeted a tanker belonging to the state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company as it crossed the Strait of Hormuz. The company said on Friday that at least 15 of its vessels were attacked in the waterway since the conflict began, leading to one death and 20 injuries among crew members.

Just over a dozen ships per day have navigated the strait over the past week, according to Kpler, a maritime data company. Before the war, an average of 130 ships used the route daily.

To avoid detection by the Iranian or American forces imposing blockades on the strait, some ships switched off the transponders that transmit their locations, making an accurate count of crossings difficult to compile.

Yeganeh Torbati is the Iran correspondent for The Times.

New Amazon Data Center Stokes Worry It Would Be the Most Polluting Power Plant in the U. S.

The New York Times August 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The tech giant is investing in the natural-gas-burning power plant as part of a huge data center in Texas, even as it pledges to honor climate commitments.

By Hiroko Tabuchi

Amazon is investing in a large-scale natural-gas-burning power plant as part of a huge data center in Texas, the company confirmed on Friday, a facility that could become the largest single source of climate pollution in the United States.

Amazon and other tech giants are racing to build enough data centers to keep up with surging demand for artificial intelligence services, and to secure the electricity to power them. A company spokeswoman said in a statement that its planned data center, in Pecos County, would be “powered by new on-site generation that won’t raise electricity costs for Texas families.”

The new gas-burning plant, if built to specifications, would be permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide a year, regulatory records show, more planet-warming gases than any other power plant in the country.

Amazon has been struggling to meet its promise that it would effectively eliminate its planet-warming emissions by 2040 as part of the Climate Pledge, a voluntary agreement among companies that Amazon co-founded several years ago. Emissions from the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and natural gas is the main driver of global warming, which is dangerously heating the planet.

Amazon’s emissions have gone up each of the past several years. And the Seattle-based tech giant has acknowledged that rising emissions from A. I. data centers could get in the way of its climate goals.

“The world looks different now than when we co-founded the climate pledge,” said Margaret Callahan, an Amazon spokeswoman. Still, “our commitment hasn’t changed,” she said.

The Texas project seemed to epitomize the difficulty in meeting the goal.

Artificial intelligence data centers require immense amounts of energy to run the trillions of calculations needed to create A. I. systems and services. And the scale and urgency of their energy demands is fast exhausting the electricity-generating capacity of the nation’s power grid.

To avoid years of potential delays in hooking up to electrical utilities, data-center developers are increasingly choosing to build their own dedicated, on-site power plants instead. And gas-burning plants are usually the fastest and easiest to build.

President Trump has supported the construction of power plants like these for data centers and has emphasized “energy dominance” by promoting oil, natural gas and coal over renewable power like solar and wind. Last year, Mr. Trump issued an executive order designed to make it easier to build and operate data centers, and since then federal agencies have introduced policies designed to fast-track their construction.

Amazon said it had recently acquired the Pecos County site, where a developer is building the gas-burning plant. The plant would use 35 natural-gas turbines to generate up to 7.65 gigawatts of power to feed to Amazon’s planned data center, according to permits for the project.

The plant would not initially connect to the wider electricity grid, Amazon’s Ms. Callahan said. The site is in a remote part of West Texas near the state’s major natural-gas-producing regions. Ms. Callahan added that the company was also exploring the use of solar energy and battery storage at the data center, which she said would create thousands of new jobs. The tech company did not disclose how much it had paid.

The power plant “could be a foreshadowing of what’s to come,” said Michael Thomas, founder of Cleanview, a company that tracks data-center energy infrastructure that on Friday reported Amazon’s involvement in the project.

Before this year, Amazon had powered its data centers with electricity from traditional utilities, which usually draw on a combination of fossil fuel generation and clean energy sources, Mr. Thomas said. The A. I. boom is changing that. “We’re going to see an explosion of off-grid gas projects” in Texas and elsewhere, he said.

Environmental groups said the scale of the plant would be damaging both for local air pollution and for the climate. “It’s going to absolutely have a huge impact on the environment, and on public health,” said Kathryn Guerra, a campaign director at Public Citizen, a corporate watchdog group that has opposed data center projects.

While the plant is permitted to release about 33 million tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere each year, facilities don’t usually emit the maximum amounts allowed under their permits. Still, the permits provide the plant with ample room to exceed the emissions of the most polluting plant in the United States, the coal-burning James H. Miller Jr. Power Plant in Quinton, Ala., which emits about 16 million tons of carbon dioxide a year.

Coal burns dirtier than gas per unit of electricity generated. However, Amazon’s planned power plant is far larger in scale. Both gas- and coal-burning power plants also release smog-forming pollutants that can contribute to heart disease, asthma and other health problems.

Hiroko Tabuchi covers pollution and the environment for The Times. She has been a journalist for more than 20 years in Tokyo and New York.

In Confirming Blanche, Senators Endorse a Justice Dept. Under Trump’s Sway

The New York Times August 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

Time and again, Todd Blanche has made it clear that he believes President Trump possesses a nearly limitless right to directly control the actions of the Justice Department.

By Glenn Thrush

Reporting from Washington

The three lame-duck Republican senators who narrowly saved Todd Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general ended up backing him because they believed he was the only person who had earned enough trust, and enjoyed enough access, to rein in President Trump.

One issue with that calculation: Mr. Blanche is a champion of unbridled presidential power.

Time and again during his turbulent nomination process, Mr. Blanche made it unmistakably clear that he believes Mr. Trump possesses a nearly limitless right to directly control the actions of the Justice Department under Article II of the Constitution. It is an argument that formed the foundation of his strategy as the president’s criminal defense lawyer and is the lodestar of his government service.

Mr. Blanche’s confirmation in the pre-dawn hours on Saturday was largely symbolic: as acting attorney general, he could have served indefinitely. But it represented a powerful endorsement by Congress of the philosophy that has guided him under a meddling, demanding boss — that he has a constitutional obligation to execute every lawful White House order, even if it shatters longstanding policy and rule-of-law norms, or contradicts what he thinks is right.

He articulated that view from the moment he took over as acting attorney general in April, telling reporters that Mr. Trump had “the right” and “duty” to order up investigations of people he targets. During his confirmation, both in public and in private conversations, Mr. Blanche sidestepped questions over whether actions Mr. Trump ordered were right, saying only that Mr. Trump had the right to do them.

Barbara McQuade, a University of Michigan Law School professor and former federal prosecutor, said this marked a major break from past administrations. “Just because a president can control the Justice Department does not mean he should,” she said. “Since Watergate, America has prized a Justice Department that is independent from partisan politics.”

While Mr. Trump and allies like Mr. Blanche have repeatedly accused the Biden White House of ordering up prosecutorial hit jobs against Republicans, they have provided little evidence to support the kind of direct interventions that have become commonplace in Mr. Trump’s second term.

In a recent interview, former President Barack Obama said he followed a broad rule of remaining at a distance from the Justice Department to protect its independence, even though he was not legally required to do so.

“The White House shouldn’t be able to direct the attorney general to go around prosecuting whoever the president wants to prosecute,” he said. “The idea is that the attorney general is the people’s lawyer. It’s not the president’s consiglieri.”

Mr. Trump has a different view. Case in point: Late Monday, he browbeat Jeanine Pirro, the U. S. attorney for the District of Columbia, for withdrawing the indictment of a man accused of defacing the Reflecting Pool. While the melodramatic showdown was big news, the fact that the president was issuing marching orders to a federal prosecutor was so typical under this administration it was not noted in most of the coverage.

During his confirmation hearing, Senator Chris Coons, Democrat of Delaware, asked Mr. Blanche whether the department he was running is “independent from the White House?”

Mr. Blanche’s reply: “Article II of the Constitution gives the power of the executive to President Trump.”

When Mr. Coons followed up by asking if he would resign if Mr. Trump directed him do something illegal or unethical, Mr. Blanche said: “That will never happen. But yes, if it were to happen, I’m not going to violate my oath to the Constitution.”

Mr. Blanche shares Mr. Trump’s view that the landmark 2024 Supreme Court ruling that granted Mr. Trump sweeping immunity from prosecution represents a broader endorsement of expanded presidential authority.

“Todd Blanche has lived firsthand the expansion of executive power by the Supreme Court and Trump,” said John P. Fishwick Jr., who served as U. S. attorney for the Western District of Virginia under Mr. Obama. “Look for D. O. J. to aggressively protect this muscular executive power.”

While many Republicans raised questions about Mr. Blanche’s actions and even his independence during his confirmation, few were willing to withhold, or even leverage, their votes to challenge the boss-employee dynamic Mr. Trump has imposed on the department.

“Ultimately, decisions are made by the president,” said Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, who announced in a floor speech Friday that he would deliver the decisive vote for Mr. Blanche’s confirmation.

The adviser Mr. Cassidy consulted before making up his mind was notable. During his speech, he quoted extensively from conversations with William P. Barr, Mr. Trump’s attorney general in his first term who articulated an expansive view of presidential power in a 2018 memo. Mr. Barr quit two years later when pressured by Mr. Trump to help undermine confidence in the 2020 election.

Mr. Barr counseled Mr. Cassidy to support Mr. Blanche in the belief that he could quietly talk the president out of bad ideas, even though Mr. Barr quit rather than comply with Mr. Trump’s demands to investigate an election Mr. Barr found had been fairly conducted.

Mr. Blanche’s experience as Mr. Trump’s private lawyer was not a reason to oppose him, Mr. Barr told Mr. Cassidy — but an asset. It gave Mr. Blanche the capacity to “have tough conversations” and confront Mr. Trump with “difficult truths” that could change his mind, Mr. Barr said to him.

Not every Republican bought into this job description of an attorney general.

Two Republican women, Senator Susan Collins of Maine and Senator Lisa Murkowksi of Alaska, said they would vote no on Mr. Blanche precisely because he had been unwilling to speak truth to Mr. Trump’s power or have enough tough conversations with him.

Ms. Collins, the first Republican to oppose Mr. Blanche, said he had taken several actions “that have further eroded the department’s independence,” including his sign-off of tax protections for the president and his family and the attempted indictments of Democratic lawmakers who criticized Mr. Trump.

Early Friday, Ms. Murkowski, a consistent and plain-spoken Republican critic of Mr. Trump, described her no vote as a moment of major historic consequence — an opportunity to both demonstrate the chamber’s dissatisfaction with Mr. Blanche’s obeisance and reclaim the Senate’s authority to influence the department’s direction.

“The country needs an attorney general who will check the worst impulses of this administration,” Ms. Murkowski said on Friday. “I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case.”

Shortly after, Mr. Cassidy took to the floor to offer Mr. Blanche his support.

The floor fight over Mr. Blanche was preceded by a clash in the Senate Judiciary Committee that followed a similar trajectory.

Two lame-duck senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, briefly withheld their support on the Senate Judiciary Committee over Mr. Blanche’s role in a deal to resolve Mr. Trump’s lawsuit against the I. R. S. The ensuing agreement created a $1.8 billion fund to compensate purported victims of Biden-era abuses at the department and granted Mr. Trump sweeping immunity from tax investigations.

Both made it clear, from the start, that they liked Mr. Blanche and did not consider his reluctance to challenge Mr. Trump to be disqualifying.

They simply wanted him to put in writing his verbal commitment to kill the fund and to include modest limits on the tax provision. Mr. Blanche was amenable, but the White House resisted, and Mr. Trump threatened to temporarily withdraw Mr. Blanche’s nomination until the two lawmakers were out of office.

The president eventually relented, clearing the way for a vote on the floor. But the episode underscored, in the view of critics, the lopsided power dynamic inherent in the partnership between Mr. Trump and Mr. Blanche.

Mr. Cornyn expressed broader concerns about Mr. Blanche’s independence during a confirmation hearing last month, echoing Ms. Murkowksi’s statements.

But he did not withhold his vote to make the larger point as she did and confined his final senatorial stand to a narrower patch of ground — obtaining written assurances over the agreement that emerged from the I. R. S. suit.

After the Senate committee advanced Mr. Blanche’s nomination, Mr. Cornyn conceded that Mr. Trump, resentful of being forced to make even a modest accommodation, might backtrack on the agreement after he retired.

“There’s nothing we could do to rein in the president when he said he likes the fund and wishes it still exists, but the fact of the matter is it’s dead, and that’s all we could do under the circumstances,” he told reporters.

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

Yemen Teeters on Civil War as Regional Stability Hangs in the Balance

The New York Times August 08, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

While the Middle East waits to hear whether a deal can be reached to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the Yemeni government’s conflict with Iran-backed Houthi rebels escalated overnight.

By Ismaeel Naar and Aaron Boxerman

Ismaeel Naar reported from Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Aaron Boxerman from Jerusalem.

The internationally recognized government of Yemen said its forces had retaliated on Saturday against Iran-backed Houthi rebels after days of attacks on the military, the latest in a surge of fighting that threatens to tip the country back into full-scale civil war.

The escalation reflected how the stability of the Middle East now hangs in the balance across multiple fronts. Despite a lull in fighting between the United States and Iran, the region is waiting to learn whether a deal can be finalized to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and stave off another round of conflict. Iranian officials on Saturday issued a set of demands for reopening the waterway, saying the United States must meet these conditions.

The Yemeni government’s counteroffensive follows a rapid escalation that began two days ago, when the Houthis struck military positions in the oil and gas-rich provinces of Marib and Hadramout, killing at least 17 soldiers.

The violence persisted on Friday, with Houthi attacks reported on civilian neighborhoods and a sprawling displaced persons’ camp near the city of Marib, killing two people and wounding 14 others, including children, according to the Yemeni government.

On Saturday, Majed al-Nuzaili, a spokesman for the Yemeni military, said that its forces had “carried out military action against terrorist elements” of the Houthi militia in several areas. He did not provide further details.

The Yemeni government, backed by Saudi Arabia, has been at war with the Houthis since 2014, when the group seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, with Iranian support. A year later, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition in support of the government, but its devastating bombing campaign ultimately failed to oust the Houthis from power.

Since then, Yemen has been effectively divided into two states, with the Houthis in control of large swaths of the north. Observers fear that a fragile truce hatched in 2022 has now all but collapsed. A sustained Houthi push into Yemen’s resource-rich eastern regions would threaten the government’s economic lifeline and risk triggering a fresh humanitarian crisis among millions of vulnerable Yemenis.

The fighting in Yemen has taken on broader significance amid the war that the United States and Israel launched against Iran in late February. The conflict prompted Iran’s allies in the region, like the Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon, to mount their own attacks.

Last month, as tensions escalated in Yemen, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, a major global chokepoint for commercial shipping. Iran has already blockaded the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf, another critical waterway for oil and gas exports, and fired on passing vessels.

Analysts say the latest ground attacks on Yemen will likely further embolden the Houthis against both the Saudi and Yemeni governments on land and at sea.

The Houthis are likely to escalate their attacks in the Red Sea, said Farea al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at Chatham House, a London-based research institution.

“They have proven themselves much stronger there and they can make everyone bleed with relatively low cost and do a lot of harm at the same time,” he said.

Iranian forces blockaded the Strait of Hormuz after the United States attacked in late February alongside Israel. In recent days, Iran and neighboring Oman have been negotiating a framework to allow transit through the waterway to resume.

The Trump administration hoped that a cease-fire in June would restore the strait’s prewar status quo, when ships transited freely. But the truce quickly unraveled as Iran militarily enforced its control over marine traffic, prompting an escalating cycle of American and Iranian attacks.

The U. S. military has retaliated by imposing its own blockade on Iranian ports. As of Friday, U. S. Central Command, which oversees American forces in the Middle East, said it had “redirected 51 commercial vessels,” forcibly disabled two others, and boarded another two as part of that blockade.

Leily Nikounazar contributed reporting.

Ismaeel Naar is an international reporter for The Times, covering the Gulf states. He is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.

Democrats Vow to Unite Behind El-Sayed, but Tensions Remain

The New York Times August 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The party is racing to get behind Dr. Abdul El-Sayed after a poisonous Senate primary in Michigan, but some Democrats still have reservations.

By Tim Balk

Reporting from Detroit

It was just a week ago that one Democratic Senate contender in Michigan said her rival wanted to “blame all” of his “problems on Jewish Americans,” after he called her the “the least capable candidate in America.”

Now Michigan Democrats are rushing to heal the wounds inflicted by the most divisive Senate primary in the state that any of them can seem to remember.

At a unity rally on Friday night in Detroit, the winner of the primary, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, joined the party’s moderate nominee for governor, Jocelyn Benson, and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who lives in Michigan.

Before the event began, the Republican National Committee branded the event the “Michigan Democrat Disunity Rally.”

Mr. Buttigieg acknowledged that the Democratic primary had been “spirited” and that it was “no secret that we all may not have voted the same way.” But, he told the crowd at a packed high school gymnasium, the party would “pull together.”

“Make no mistake,” Mr. Buttigieg said, “the world is watching.”

Democrats have three months to unite the party behind Dr. El-Sayed, who is running against former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, in a race that could determine control of the Senate. The seat is now held by Senator Gary Peters, a retiring Democrat.

The rally was the second unity event held by Michigan Democrats in the two days since Dr. El-Sayed defeated Representative Haley Stevens, a centrist, by a single percentage point.

On Thursday, a breakfast in suburban Detroit was meant to bring Democrats together. Ms. Stevens has had more than one conversation with Dr. El-Sayed since the primary and has endorsed him.

But Dr. El-Sayed’s struggles in heavily Black communities and some working-class areas pointed to potential general-election challenges ahead.

Some Democrats who supported Ms. Stevens are clearly reluctant to rally behind him.

Many Jewish Democrats, in particular, were dismayed by the way Dr. El-Sayed criticized the Israeli government and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, whose main super PAC spent tens of millions of dollars to support Ms. Stevens.

The Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus has not endorsed Dr. El-Sayed. The group’s founder, State Representative Noah Arbit, said on Friday that Dr. El-Sayed had a long way to go to repair trust with the Jewish community, though he said he was eager to meet with him.

Outside the gym, Eric Lerman, 71, a retired doctor who is Jewish, said he enthusiastically supported Dr. El-Sayed, citing the candidate’s support for universal health care. But, he said, many of his friends who are Jewish are gripped by concerns.

“There’s an existential fear factor,” Mr. Lerman said. He hoped, he said, that they might come around to Dr. El-Sayed. “I’ll do my best to get them to.”

Inside the gym, Edgar Faler, 54, who is not Jewish, said he was also uneasy about Dr. El-Sayed’s candidacy. Mr. Faler had supported Ms. Stevens, and did not like the way Dr. El-Sayed sometimes attacked her in personal terms. He did not like the way Dr. El-Sayed spoke about Israel, either.

He said Dr. El-Sayed had “some work to do” to “earn the trust” of Ms. Stevens’s supporters. And though he planned to vote for Dr. El-Sayed, he said, he worried about whether the candidate could win in November.

Mr. Rogers has already moved to exploit the Democratic divisions. In a video on social media on Friday morning, he encouraged Democrats to support him if they were dismayed by Dr. El-Sayed’s victory.

“Just know there is still hope,” Mr. Rogers said. “Michigan deserves a senator who is ready to sit with you, hear from you and represent you.”

He suggested that Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign was filled with “anger” and “divisiveness.” The “fight is far greater than just left versus right,” he added. “The fight is for the very soul of our nation.”

A spokeswoman for Dr. El-Sayed, Roxie Richner, responded in a statement that the Democratic nominee looked forward to earning “every vote” and that Mr. Rogers was “an extreme Republican.”

Republicans were also working on Friday to seize on a years-old video circulating on social media, drawn from a documentary about Dr. El-Sayed’s run for governor in 2018, that shows him saying, “I hate Mackinac so much.” Republicans said he was referring to Mackinac Island, a vacation destination on Michigan’s Upper Peninsula.

Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign said he had been referring not to Mackinac Island but to the Mackinac Policy Conference, an annual gathering of business executives and politicians.

Jim Frank, chair of the Democratic Party in St. Clair County, outside Detroit, acknowledged that many of Ms. Stevens’s supporters felt a lingering bitterness.

“Some of them have some legitimate concerns” about the treatment of Ms. Stevens, said Mr. Frank, whose county supported her.

But he predicted that the party would “get through” its divisions.

“We’ve asked the more progressive members of the Democratic Party to vote blue when it comes time to vote in the election even if their candidate doesn’t get through,” Mr. Frank said. “Well, I think it’s the turn of many Democrats to go ahead and do the same.”
