Socialists Are Winning Because They Listen to People

The New York Times August 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Tressie McMillan Cottom

By Tressie McMillan Cottom

Opinion Columnist

Are we looking at a socialist revival in American politics?

A mash-up of political analysis since Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor of New York City would have you believe that we are living in either the golden age of leftism or that the communists are coming.

That might one day be our electoral reality, but not today. Yes, a lot of left-leaning candidates did well this week, with notable primary victories in Michigan and Kansas. But a lot of moderate Democrats also won their races. Some of the winning candidates had a lot of money to spend. Others were running at an extreme financial disadvantage. But the best of them are running campaigns that acknowledge that to win, Democrats are going to have to organize voters — not just fund-raise off them.

The Democratic Party has a deep structural problem. It is standing in the shadow of a past it yearns for and a future it has not yet built, and, at the moment, the progressive wing appears to be the only side that realizes it.

Establishment Democrats may want to fight about the electability of left-wing candidates, but the party has bigger fish to fry. Labor unions and civil rights organizations are the twin engines of Democratic electoral power. Labor reliably delivered working-class men in the decades after the New Deal, serving as Democrats’ arterial vein in rural areas and the industrial Rust Belt. Civil rights organizations have, of course, reliably and relentlessly delivered the Black vote — and kept Democrats competitive in the South — since Lyndon B. Johnson, a Democrat, signed the Civil Rights Act. Those two groups have long been a stopgap for middling Democratic candidates and muddled Democratic messaging.

What’s most important to understand is that, now, six successive decades of economic, legal, political and cultural challenges have made it difficult, if not impossible, for unions and civil rights groups to do that job.

Black civil rights organizations, in particular, have long worked hard to organize for the Democratic Party. They don’t just march to the polls. They cultivate voters, translate national platforms into local messaging and train candidates and staffers. The party’s electoral workhorses have been the Black women who keep the lights on in churches, drive the vans, canvass the communities, turn out the rallies and reliably deliver on Election Day. Black organizers in the South expected a Democratic cavalry after the Voting Rights Act was gutted by the Supreme Court. Instead, they feel abandoned. They look at conservative groups like Heritage Action and Turning Point USA and wonder what they could do with that kind of support.

The percentage of workers who are in a union is also at a record low. Even if Democrats find a winning, centrist message to bring back working-class voters and energize the South, the churches, schools, union halls and volunteer societies that do the hard work of turning out the vote are under attack. The political strategist Atima Omara says there simply isn’t enough funding for grass-roots organizers “to continue to do the necessary work to meet the moment.”

The candidates shaking up the Democratic Party are trying to fill the gaps these groups no longer can. They are going into neighborhoods that traditional canvassing writes off because people aren’t registered to vote or they’re registered for the other team. They are merging old-school community relationship building with the best of digital data strategies, like microtargeting voters. When they talk about policy, they don’t just focus on blaming Donald Trump for every problem; they talk about issues that their potential constituencies tell them are important. In short, the latest crop of progressive candidates are campaigning like organizers. In doing so, they’re revealing weaknesses in the Democratic machine that have existed since Barack Obama ran for president — the first time.

Starting in the mid-2000s, the Democratic Party adopted a position that retail politics was due for an internet upgrade. Turning up for church hall meetings was well and fine. But haven’t you heard that Americans are bowling alone? Better to email. Phone banking turned into text-a-thons, where volunteers sent millions of text messages to cellphones we had not yet learned to ignore. Canvassing was fine. But the future was turning every voter into an influencer with a customized donation link he or she would text to friends and family. By the time he became President Obama, the onetime organizer was the face of the Democratic Party’s tech-forward 21st-century electoral apparatus.

That apparatus felt like the future in 2008. It would be multiracial and progressive, without trying too hard. And it would empower the little people over big-dollar donors. Which is to say, it would privilege Democrats, not Republicans.

By 2020, the Democratic advantage in digital campaigning was long gone. The G. O. P. caught up, big time, while still growing its grass-roots network. Democrats now had an internet problem — investing in tech innovations and not building their base between elections. As algorithms turned neighbors into unrecognizable partisans with crazy conspiracy theories, Silicon Valley abandoned the Democrats for Trump. Through it all, the frantic fund-raising text messages just kept coming.

The dog has caught its tail. Candidates with big war chests are finding that ad buys don’t guarantee victory. The people who are winning right now are organizing movements, not just raising cash.

You see it in Michigan. Abdul El-Sayed upset the deep-pocketed, establishment choice, Haley Stevens, by building a relational campaign on an economic populist message. El-Sayed won, in part, by characterizing the $62 million in outside money that backed Stevens’s campaign as a sign of the political corruption that has activated the Democratic base. His army of 12,000 volunteers fueled a campaign that took what was once a nuclear position on AIPAC to 110 cities and 500 events. He has work to do with Black voters in the general election, but that doesn’t negate the fact that he overcame some pretty racist attacks and a huge spending deficit to clinch the nomination.

You see it in Francesca Hong’s unabashed socialist campaign for Wisconsin’s governorship. Armed with around 7,000 volunteers who are methodically executing a D. S. A.-backed ground game, Hong is ahead in the polls despite her political weaknesses.

In Tennessee, Justin Pearson, a former organizer who once led a campaign that successfully halted a pipeline, is competing in a district redrawn to favor Republicans. Organizing taught him that you don’t just find a likely voter. You develop a likely voter, through direct communication and a softer touch with fund-raising texts and emails. Organizers call that relational. Or, as one strategist put it to me this week, talking with voters in a way that makes them happy to hear from the campaign.

As the MAGA media empire starts to fracture, Democrats have an opportunity to seize momentum. Like it or not, Democratic grass-roots organizations favor populist politics, which progressive ideology is primed to meet. That, in turn, attracts candidates who are younger and more diverse than the establishment. Not every campaign that exceeded expectations this week is running from the left, but each one is running like candidates on the left. Strategic. Relational. Future-oriented.

It’s always dicey to make election predictions. But if I were trying to read which way the wind is blowing for Democrats in 2026 and 2028, I wouldn’t be looking for a socialist wave. I’d be looking for the candidates who are thinking and running as if they know that bases are made of people, not dollars.

Billy Strings Escaped the Darkness. He’s Playing to Not Go Back.

The New York Times August 08, 2026

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Philip Montgomery for The New York Times

Supported by

By David Marchese

Billy Strings has drawn from something old to do something entirely new. The singer and virtuoso guitarist, who is 33, has broken ground by using the elements of traditional bluegrass to become an arena-filling, chart-topping phenomenon, straddling the worlds of roots music and jam bands. Along the way he has also acquired a Deadhead-like legion of fans who follow his tours from concert to concert.

As improbable as it is that Strings can sell out cavernous venues across the country while playing bluegrass classics — in addition to his own introspective compositions, which he and his drummerless band often spin into long improvisations — it’s even more surprising when you know the path he took to get there. Strings, whose real name is William Apostol, was surrounded by poverty and drug addiction in his family growing up in small-town Michigan. Those demons have continued to haunt him: Strings’s mother died from a drug overdose last year at 64 years old. That loss inspired much of the music on his beautiful new album, “So Much for Goodbyes,” due out Aug. 28. He discussed the genesis of that album, among many other things, in our heart-wrenching conversation, which took place during a rare day off from his summer tour. To see Strings play, check out the video version of this interview.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

It’s pretty wild for someone who got their start playing bluegrass to have achieved what you’ve achieved. Was there a moment when you realized things had gotten really big? I went from playing in my bedroom to playing in coffeehouses, pubs and restaurants, and eventually I was able to put in my two weeks’ at my day job, which was working at a hotel up in Traverse City. At that point I thought, Man, if I never get any bigger than this, I’d be happy, I’m making a living playing music. I remember when I put out my first record, “Turmoil & Tinfoil,” I never thought about how the record would be good for my career. I was just trying to record these songs. Then, when we actually sold some records, I was like, Whoa. It was a big eye-opener.

Can you tell me about the title of the new album, “So Much for Goodbyes”? My mom passed away last June, just over a year ago. I was on my way to a show in Kentucky, and I woke up on the bus. My wife came back, and she told me the news. To me, it was this sad thing, this idea that I didn’t get to say goodbye. But when I told my manager about the title, he’s like: “I like that because it’s not really goodbye. She’s in everything and she’s everywhere.” So I like the idea that it can be taken both ways: So much for goodbyes, like I didn’t get to say goodbye, but also so much for goodbyes because it’s not really goodbye.

I’m sorry for your loss. If you don’t mind me asking, how did your mom pass away? She struggled her whole life with different kinds of substance abuse. She had a lot of unresolved trauma that she never really had proper therapy for, and I think medicating herself was her way of getting through some of that. So she had an illness that eventually she succumbed to. She died of an overdose. It was a shock to me because I had no idea that she was using again, and she seemed to be doing really well. Her addiction has caused a lot of trauma in my own life. She’s kind of like a conundrum because she’s such a beautiful, amazing, artistic person. She always was making art, these little shadow boxes and mixed-media art, and she would always be collecting these trinkets and pieces of junk and would take all this forgotten rusty old crap and glue it together to make something beautiful. Even before I had any of the songs for this record, she was going to make the cover. That was our goal and our dream, and we did it. We got to make her piece of art the cover. It was the piece that she was working on the night she died. It was the last thing she touched.

Are there songs on the album that allow you to feel like you’re saying things to her that you didn’t get a chance to say before she died? The big one on this record is called “Still I Crash.” I wrote that song not too long after she died. That’s the one that’s pretty blatantly me talking to her, just wondering where she went, asking where did she go and why. And explaining that I feel like I have to learn how to walk again, and how difficult it is to be here without her.

It’s hard. My mom died two years ago. She had A. L. S. and she died with medical aid. She decided she didn’t want to suffer, so she had someone come and help her. But I was able to say what I wanted to say to her because we knew when it was going to happen. But then my dad died at the end of April, and like with your mom, it was completely unexpected. I had a hard relationship with him, and when you don’t have the chance to say things that you wanted to say, it’s like an open wound — and you’re not sure when it’s going to close. It’s not better or worse either way, I don’t think. It’s just one of those things we have to learn to live with and try to remember who she was and love and cherish her memory and live up to her wildness. My mom has inspired me to really let loose and let my freak flag fly a little bit more, live more the way she lived rather than trying to be so cautious all the time. I feel like I’ve always tried to stay out of trouble and do the best I can to not get myself hung up. But my mom would just live life to the fullest constantly.

How does playing music help process the feelings that you have, whether it’s about your mom or anything else? It’s always been my coping mechanism, survival strategy and my medicine. Playing bluegrass music, it’s like a portal back to my childhood, back before I knew anything dirty about the earth. And it’s a way for me to go back to a time that was just beautiful and full of light, growing up playing music with my dad. And then songwriting is my cathartic and therapeutic way of dealing with things. I think sublimation is one of my main characteristics. Instead of letting this hard stuff drag me down, I try to make art from it, make lemonade, if you will.

I know you grew up in a chaotic way in Michigan. There was your mom’s substance abuse problems. And earlier you referred to your dad, and he is your dad. But technically speaking it’s your stepfather. Your biological father died when you were really young from an overdose. But how did music fit into your family life? What role did it play for you growing up? My biological father died before I ever knew him. I was 2 years old. And so when I say “my dad,” I’m speaking of Terry Barber. He taught me how to tie my shoes and wipe my ass and how to play guitar. Early on, it was a way for me to bond with him. And the better I got, I would get attention from that, so I just kept trying to get better and better and make him proud. I still do that to this day. I remember when I played with Bob Dylan, I’m calling my mom right before walking onstage and I’m like: “You’re never going to believe this. I’m getting ready to play with Bob Dylan.” But back when I was a kid, before any of the fame, it was just our way of life. If I wasn’t playing old bluegrass tunes with my dad, I was listening to my mom playing Beatles records. I remember being a little kid, maybe 7 years old, and she was playing the White Album backwards for me. Music was always a big deal.

What you just described sounds very buoyant and positive, but then there was the darker side. Was it hard for you to make sense of both the light and the dark in your family? Early on it wasn’t so bad. By the time I was old enough to remember stuff, like 4 years old, my parents were doing pretty good. There were just some Busch Lights and a few joints here and there. It wasn’t anything hard or crazy. So my early childhood was really beautiful and surrounded by music and friends. Then it just started to go downhill. My dad lost his job, and we started struggling more financially. That was at the same time that my parents were falling into addiction. I moved out when I was 13. I was trying to guilt-trip them into seeing what they were doing. There wasn’t any food. My house was no longer a home. So I took off. When I realized that me moving out wasn’t going to change anything, that’s when I was like: “Oh, no. Now I’m actually kind of homeless.” So then I had to just figure it out. But I never disowned my parents or cut ties with them, and it actually became this era of trying things myself. I could show up at their house with several carloads of minors and half gallons of whiskey, and they couldn’t tell me no. My dad would always be like, You’re not having all these minors drink in here. I’m like, OK, well, what are you going to do, call the cops? So I eventually just started partying with them. You know, when you lose people to addiction like that, especially as a young kid, you almost wonder: What is so powerful that basically took them from me? That’s actually what the song “Turmoil & Tinfoil” is about. I was staring right at my mother, but I missed her, she’s not herself anymore. Her soul and her beautiful vibrancy is gone. It’s just this gray shell of a person that is really sick. So you wonder: What is this stuff all about? I was 16 the first time I smoked meth with my mom. And around that time is when I started doing coke and speed and trying crack. And then a couple of years after that, I got to wondering about my biological father. I never knew him, and I always thought, Man, he must have loved heroin more than me. I wondered what was so good that it was better than me. So that’s when I tried heroin, because I just had to see what it was all about. I got a lot of that stuff out of my system early on. I never really got hooked on anything because I was always surrounded by tweakers and junkies. I saw how bad these people’s lives were, and I never wanted to let myself get that far.

When you were younger and partying with your parents, I would bet that there was some part of you inside that felt conflicted or uncomfortable with it. Did you and your parents ever talk about that period in your life? No, it was just what it was. Sometimes we’d get high and I would play guitar with my dad until the sun came up. We’re bonding again and that felt good.

When did you realize that you had a real gift for the guitar? That was early on. I started playing when I was about 4 years old. By the time I was 6 or 7, I could carry a tune, and I was my dad’s rhythm player. He would play all the lead and do all the fancy picking and singing, and I would hold down the rhythm. One of the biggest moments for me was I was sitting in my dad’s bedroom with him, as I would basically do every night, and he was teaching me the song “Beaumont Rag.” We would play the tune and I would mess up the second part every time. And I stopped us right in the middle of the song and said, “Why don’t you just play it and let me listen?” And so that’s what we did. Instead of trying to count, I listened to what he was playing. I listened to the melody. Then I was like, “All right, let me try it again,” and I nailed it. He was awful proud. He called my grandma, made her listen on the phone. That was a big moment for me. That’s when this listening thing started: I was able to listen to the music more intently and I could tell what chord was coming next. I used to think it was magic or something. I had no concept of music theory or anything. But my dad would play a G chord and then he would play a G seventh and my ear would just lead me. I’d be like, Well, the next chord’s probably going to be a C, and then it would be. It’s better to learn bluegrass and folk and hillbilly music that way than to try to learn from some academic point of view. It’s better to learn it on the back porch and to let it get under your skin, because then it’s not some equation, it’s a feeling. It comes from your soul.

Was there a time when you started to think that pursuing music could be a way into a different kind of life than the one you were living? I never considered that. Growing up the way that I did, music as a career seemed like a really far-fetched idea. Although when I was younger, I used to think I was going to be the next Jimi Hendrix. But I never thought of it as a career until I did some open mic nights, just for fun. This was before I was even old enough to be in the bar. I’d go up there and play a few tunes, flat-pick a little number, and I’d get a standing ovation. And I started to realize this bluegrass stuff really gets people out of their seats. It’s like, Wow, these people never heard of Doc Watson before or what?

Your predecessors — Doc Watson, Tony Rice, Clarence White — are some of the greatest musicians who have ever lived. They played this incredibly beautiful music with such skill and heart. And they never attracted tens of thousands of people to arenas. Do you ever wonder why you and not them? Yeah, on one hand, I mean, I don’t know. [Laughs] At a certain point, I stopped wearing a suit and combing my hair back with pomade and trying to pretend I was born in the Appalachian Mountains and my daddy was a coal miner and doing this whole Civil War re-enactment, and I started just being myself. I also allowed in the influences from other kinds of music that I enjoyed, everything from hip-hop to jazz to classic rock and heavy metal, death metal and hardcore. I feel like my whole brain is this musical goulash, and when I stopped trying to just be one thing, I could attract a broad spectrum of people, everyone from metalheads to old bluegrassers to people that are into more improvisational music like the Grateful Dead. I’ve got young teenagers to 80-year-olds in my crowd. And I play a little bit for all of them.

I read an article about you that talked about how before shows, you used to get real anxious and have stomach pain. Is that still an issue? I definitely get nervous before a show. Sometimes moments before I’m walking onstage, I feel like I might pass out. I’ve just got to get into the first song or two, and halfway through the show I’m the complete opposite. I have all this energy. I feel great. I feel super confident, almost cocky even. There is that expectation from the crowd to do something amazing, and also that expectation from myself to always do better than I did the night before, because this is my livelihood and this is my life, and deep in the back of my mind, I’m scared that this is all going to go away, and maybe I’ll have to go back to the way life was when it was really hard. There’s this little devil on my shoulder that tells me I don’t deserve any of this, and thinks that I should be in some little trailer somewhere addicted to drugs, not a penny to my name. So it does feel like I’m playing for my survival a lot. Each time I walk onstage, I’m playing so that I don’t have to go back there.

Has having a kid changed the pressure you put on yourself? Yeah. I used to put too much pressure on myself to the point where I would strangle the life out of the music. It was the most important thing to me. But when my son was born, I had a big change in perspective. Now, if my family’s OK, then I’m free to go play and sing, and I’m singing from a place of joy in my belly. I have this little cosmic listener that I can sing to and sing for no matter what. When I leave my house to go on tour, I’m on a mission to provide for my family. I’m not just out there to stoke my ego.

What was your parents’ relationship with your fans and with the scene around your music? The last few years of my mom’s life, she got really involved with my fans and the whole scene. She loved it. She grew up going to concerts and hanging out, so she would go out there and mingle and take videos of people explaining what my music meant to them and send them to me. She would always tell me, “You have no idea how many people you’ve touched.”

I wonder if that was a tough situation for her, because of the partying. Yeah, I wondered about that, but at a certain point, people are going to do what they’re going to do. One thing I learned from this whole thing is that you can’t change somebody’s life. You’ve just got to love them for who they are and accept whatever happens.

Do you think that’s true? People can’t change? I mean, you can change for sure, but you’ve got to want to be the one to do it. I’m just saying I can’t impose my will on somebody else and expect them to change. I don’t think that’s a possibility. I always wanted my mom and dad to have a good life and for my mom to have a garden. They’re getting older. My mom was 64. In my mind, I just wanted them to start being these boring old people that go up north every once in a while and sit at home and watch “The Andy Griffith Show.” But that’s what was in my mind, not theirs. My mom was living her best life. She was out there having a good time right up until the end, which is still inspiring to me in a way. She didn’t want to grow old. She’d rather run and gun right until the end.

You mentioned this idea of not wanting to go back to the life you had. But if the music had not taken off, what would a good life have been for you? Just working a job that I didn’t absolutely hate, making enough to have some food in the cupboards and a roof over my head, and not being a drug addict. That would be good enough. I’m 10 years sober from alcohol, and I’m definitely drawing a line in the sand. All this generational trauma has to stop with me. I’m going to give my son a life very different from mine.

This interview has been edited and condensed. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

Director of photography (video): Tre Cassetta

David Marchese is a writer and co-host of The Interview, a regular series featuring influential people across culture, politics, business, sports and beyond.

Fact-Checking 3 Competitive Senate Races in Maine, Michigan and Ohio

The New York Times August 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Republican attacks have focused on terrorism and illegal immigration, while Democrats have sought to capitalize on the unpopularity of President Trump’s cuts to Medicaid.

By Linda Qiu

Reporting from Washington

As voters pick the Senate candidates who will face off in the midterm elections in November, with control of the chamber at stake, nominees from both parties have begun sharpening attacks on their opponents.

In three of the most competitive and crucial states — Michigan, Maine and Ohio — Republicans have accused their opponents of justifying terrorism and supporting benefits for unauthorized immigrants. Democrats, for their part, have sought to capitalize on the unpopularity of President Trump’s cuts to health care programs.

Here is a look at some of the claims.

What Was Said

“I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama bin Laden to justice. Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.”— Former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, in a statement on Wednesday

False. Mr. Rogers issued the incendiary statement about his opponent, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the morning after Dr. El-Sayed won the Democratic primary. The New York Times was unable to find an example of Dr. El-Sayed stating that he “believes America deserved” the Sept. 11 attacks, and the Rogers campaign did not respond to questions about whether one existed.

In the statement, Mr. Rogers also echoed a number of other attacks by Republicans that trafficked in anti-Muslim sentiment, calling Dr. El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim elected to the Senate, “a RADICAL ISLAMIST” who would “unleash terror.”

There is no evidence that Dr. El-Sayed has said that “America deserved 9/11.” On the contrary, the Democratic nominee wrote in his 2020 book that the “attack devastated me,” and called it “craven.”

Mr. Rogers might have been referring to comments made and retracted by Hasan Piker, a left-wing political commentator who supports Dr. El-Sayed’s candidacy.

Mr. Piker was reacting in 2019 to a podcast interview featuring Representative Dan Crenshaw of Texas. While discussing what motivated the Sept. 11 attacks, Mr. Crenshaw expressed skepticism of the view that U. S. actions in the Middle East had been to blame, and argued instead that fundamentalist ideology had played a larger role.

Mr. Piker, appearing on Twitch, a livestreaming platform, objected vehemently and said, “This is so insane. America deserved 9/11, dude.”

Those comments immediately incited controversy and led to a one-week suspension on Twitch.

Asked that month if he meant what he had said, Mr. Piker responded, “No, obviously not,” and added that he had been expressing frustration with Mr. Crenshaw’s comments. Mr. Piker argued that his comments had been taken out of context, and that he had been voicing a not-so-uncommon view that foreign policy decisions had destabilized the Middle East, and had a “direct consequence” in leading to Sept. 11.

“I know that I was inappropriate,” he said of his remarks.

In an April interview on Fox News, Dr. El-Sayed addressed Mr. Piker’s remarks, saying, “Of course, I don’t think 9/11 was justified. Because you appear with somebody doesn’t mean you agree with them on everything.”

What Was Said

“Susan Collins helped Trump slash Medicaid to the tune of $990 billion.”— Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate in Maine, in a social media post on July 30

This is misleading. Mr. Jackson was referring to the domestic policy package signed into law by Mr. Trump last summer that included nearly a trillion dollars in cuts to Medicaid. But Ms. Collins, the incumbent Republican senator from Maine and Mr. Jackson’s opponent, was one of three G. O. P. senators to vote against that bill. She did cast an earlier vote to advance debate over the legislation.

As Republicans considered and repeatedly revised the bill between June and early July last year, Ms. Collins said that she supported “reasonable” work requirements to Medicaid. But she expressed concern over the effect of the proposed changes to the program on children, low-income families, seniors and people with disabilities.

In late June 2025, Ms. Collins voted for a procedural step to bring the legislation to the Senate floor, something that had to take place before senators voted on the passage of the bill. The motion passed 51 to 49. Had Ms. Collins voted against taking the procedural step, Vice President JD Vance could have still cast the tiebreaking vote to advance debate. (Later that summer, he broke a tie on a motion to proceed — Ms. Collins had voted against doing so — on a bill to rescind $9 billion in congressionally approved funds for foreign aid and public broadcasting.)

Ms. Collins said at the time that she would offer a number of amendments to alter the bill, and that absent changes, she “would be leaning against the bill.”

Gregory J. Wawro, a political science professor at Columbia University and an expert on congressional procedure, said that “it is not that unusual to vote with the party on a procedural vote but then vote against final passage.”

“Voting against the motion to proceed likely would not have killed H. R. 1, but it certainly would have sent a strong signal of opposition,” he added, referring to Mr. Trump’s signature domestic policy bill.

The Senate then began negotiating and rewriting the bill. Ms. Collins offered an amendment to increase the size of a fund created by the bill to support rural health care providers, but that amendment failed. She ultimately voted against the legislation, citing the Medicaid cuts as the reason for her opposition.

“My vote against this bill stems primarily from the harmful impact it will have on Medicaid, affecting low-income families and rural health care providers like our hospitals and nursing homes,” she said in a statement afterward.

The legislation still passed, with Mr. Vance casting the tiebreaking vote.

Mr. Jackson has at times been more precise and accurate in distinguishing the two votes. In early July, for example, he characterized her vote as “helping advance” the legislation.

Mr. Jackson’s campaign cited praise from a Republican colleague of Ms. Collins’s who called her a “team player” and said that her procedural vote “helped us get on the bill at a time when we needed that help.”

What Was Said

“He supported Social Security payments for illegals, health care for illegals, Covid checks for illegals.”— Senator Jon Husted, Republican of Ohio, in a Fox News interview, referring to his opponent, Sherrod Brown

This is misleading. A spokeswoman for Mr. Husted’s campaign cited three votes cast by Mr. Brown, a former senator and current Democratic nominee, against amendments offered by Republican lawmakers through the years. But Mr. Husted’s claim distorted what those votes would have done.

Social Security

Mr. Husted was referring to Mr. Brown’s vote against a 2007 amendment, sponsored by Senator John Ensign, Republican of Nevada, to an education bill that sought to bar previously unauthorized immigrants who later gained legal status from receiving credit for taxes paid to Social Security using falsified numbers. But under the current law and the law at the time, unauthorized immigrants could not receive Social Security benefits, and Mr. Brown’s vote did not seek to change that.

It is also worth noting that Mr. Brown voted for a similar amendment from Mr. Ensign later that year.

Health Care

Mr. Brown also voted against a 2013 amendment to a budget bill that prohibited unauthorized immigrants and previously unauthorized immigrants from receiving federally subsidized health care. Its sponsor, Senator Jeff Sessions, Republican of Alabama, said at the time that the amendment aimed to pre-empt the effect of immigration reform by barring immigrants who gained legal status from receiving subsidized health care.

But unauthorized immigrants were already largely barred from federally funded health care programs. A counterproposal offered the same day by a Democratic senator, Robert Menendez of New Jersey, reaffirmed existing law and passed by voice vote. The budget bill ultimately passed on a party-line vote.

Covid checks

Mr. Brown voted to pass a pandemic stimulus package in early 2021 that included $1,400 checks for people, but voted against an amendment to bar any “alien who is not lawfully present” from receiving the checks.

That did not mean, though, that Mr. Brown voted to give unauthorized immigrants checks. That is because the legislation barred “any nonresident alien individual” — people who were not U. S. citizens or green card holders — from receiving a payment, and generally required recipients to have a Social Security number. An exception was made for spouses of military members.

Unauthorized immigrants who file taxes instead use an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number. But Republicans argued that the legislation had a loophole for some unauthorized immigrants, like recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, who had Social Security numbers. Regardless, the vast majority of unauthorized immigrants did not have a Social Security number, and the language around eligibility was virtually identical in the previous two rounds of stimulus checks, which both passed in 2020 with considerably more Republican support.

Linda Qiu is a Times reporter who specializes in fact-checking statements made by politicians and public figures. She has been reporting and fact-checking public figures for nearly a decade.

After Supreme Court Win, Trump Officials Under Pressure to Deport Haitians

The New York Times August 08, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

The lack of visible raids aggressively targeting Haitians who lost temporary status has frustrated some of President Trump’s most fervent supporters.

By Madeleine Ngo and Hamed Aleaziz

Madeleine Ngo and Hamed Aleaziz cover the Department of Homeland Security and immigration policy.

The Trump administration is facing pressure on the right to ramp up arrests of about 350,000 Haitians who recently lost their legal status after the Supreme Court cleared the way for termination of a humanitarian program allowing them to live and work in the United States for years.

The Department of Homeland Security has so far focused its enforcement efforts in the Springfield, Ohio, area, where a large group of Haitians with Temporary Protected Status arrived in recent years. At least 50 Haitians have been called into immigration offices and given ankle monitors in recent days, according to advocacy groups.

But logistical challenges to deporting such a large group to an unstable country, and a lack of internal guidance within Immigration and Customs Enforcement, have complicated the effort. Some Republican politicians have also voiced concerns about the impact on certain industries if Haitian workers were deported en masse.

Some ICE officers have expressed confusion to colleagues about whether they can pursue the Haitians and sought guidance on whether they can make arrests quickly, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.

The absence of visible raids aggressively targeting Haitians across the country since the department effectively ended the protections on July 27 has frustrated some of President Trump’s most fervent supporters. Some of them already see Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, as soft on immigration enforcement.

The administration has terminated protections for most T. P. S. holders.

Notes: T. P. S. terminations are as of Aug. 7. Venezuelans were divided into two groups based on arrival date. A small group of Venezuelans who arrived in 2023 will retain their status until Oct. 2. Data for the number of approved individuals with T. P. S. is based on estimates provided by the Department of Homeland Security in the federal register. For people from countries that remain protected, data is as of March 31, 2025. Figures have been rounded.

Allison McCann/The New York Times

“The airplanes and the buses should have been ready,” said Stephen K. Bannon, a MAGA podcaster and former senior aide to Mr. Trump. “One hundred percent of the Haitians should have already left the country. It’s unacceptable they’re not.”

The issue exemplifies the difficult balancing act Mr. Mullin has faced since he was installed to lead the Homeland Security Department. He was tasked with bringing order back to the department after the fatal shootings of two U. S. citizens in Minnesota spurred public backlash against Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown.

But Mr. Mullin’s moves to scale back some tactics have been met with fury by hard-liners who have expressed skepticism about the administration’s commitment to delivering on its pledge of mass deportations. Feeling the pressure, federal officials have rejected the claims and at times backtracked their changes.

A Homeland Security Department spokesperson said in a statement that the department does not discuss ongoing or future operations and encouraged people who have lost protections to self-deport.

Mr. Mullin told NewsNation this week that the department was “going after” Haitians who have lost status and emphasized that the program was intended to be temporary. “We are giving them an opportunity to either leave on their own and we’ll help you, or we’ll arrest you and send you back,” Mr. Mullin said.

A federal judge took the final step on Wednesday allowing the Trump administration to officially terminate the protections for Haitians, which came after the Supreme Court’s June 25 ruling cleared the way for the administration to end T. P. S. programs.

The Trump administration has sought to wind down the humanitarian program, which was created by Congress and signed into law by President George H. W. Bush in 1990.

The administration has moved to end about a dozen T. P. S. programs, which are meant to help foreign nationals who cannot safely return home because of armed conflict or natural disasters in their countries. The protections became all but permanent for nations with continued crises.

The administration’s intention to terminate the programs has upended the lives of more than one million T. P. S. holders, including workers who have filled critical jobs in industries like health care, construction and transportation.

Homeland security officials have considered T. P. S. for Haiti as effectively over since July 27. But ICE’s enforcement actions have been relatively quiet so far.

Guerline Jozef, the executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigrant rights nonprofit, said she had not heard about enforcement actions ramping up outside of Springfield in other regions with large populations of Haitian T. P. S. holders, such as South Florida and New York. In the Boston region, which also has a large Haitian population, other advocacy groups said they had not heard about people receiving ankle monitors in recent days.

It is easy for immigration agents to find and arrest Haitians who have lost their temporary status, given that the government already has their addresses. Deporting them, however, poses a bigger challenge.

The federal government has banned commercial flights to Port-au-Prince because of the risk of violence; gangs control most of the Haitian capital. Nearly every deportation flight under the Trump administration has instead been routed to Cap-Haitien, a port city with a smaller airport that has less capacity to handle more arrivals, said Savi Arvey, whose research team at Human Rights First, a nonprofit, monitors deportation flights.

The security risks involved with sending more deportation flights to Haiti could complicate the administration’s ability to quickly ramp up removals, Ms. Arvey said. The United States has sent one deportation flight a month to Haiti since December 2023. The last removal flight landed in Cap Haitien on July 16 with more than 100 deportees.

It could also take months or years for many cases to go through the immigration court system, further slowing deportations.

Some Haitians could be deported relatively quickly, including those with final orders of removal who have been able to legally stay in the United States with Temporary Protected Status, said Kerry E. Doyle, a partner at Green & Spiegel who was the top ICE lawyer in the Biden administration. But others still have the right to have their cases heard by an immigration judge, a process that could take years.

Only a handful of T. P. S. programs are still valid, including those for El Salvador, Lebanon, Sudan and Ukraine. The administration has not announced plans to end T. P. S. for El Salvador, which expires in September and provides protection to about 170,000 people. But Mr. Trump and his officials tried to do so in his first term.

Federal judges on Friday cleared the way for the Trump administration to end T. P. S. for Myanmar and South Sudan. Terminations are still paused for Somalia and Ethiopia, but those countries are also expected to lose their designations.

The protections for Haitians were first put in place by the Obama administration in 2010 after a devastating earthquake. The program was repeatedly extended after Haiti struggled to fully recover, and its last elected president was assassinated in 2021.

Advocacy groups said that many Haitians who have lost status are now trying to remain in hiding and seek legal advice to figure out if they qualify for immigration benefits like asylum. Many are choosing not to voluntarily return to Haiti, given the escalating violence by gangs who control much of the capital and have attacked, kidnapped and killed civilians.

In an interview, a Haitian woman in Philadelphia in her 20s said she had been on edge since she lost her temporary status and could no longer legally work.

“I’m scared for my life,” said the woman, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of fears she could be targeted by immigration officers.

She said she had mostly stayed inside to avoid encounters with ICE officers, and she feared returning to Haiti, where she had few family members left.

“There is not a safe way for anyone to be deported to Haiti right now,” said Ms. Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance. “That’s not a choice that people can make.”

Madeleine Ngo covers immigration and economic policy for The Times.

Hamed Aleaziz covers the Department of Homeland Security and immigration policy for The Times.

Lindsey Graham Loved to Gab With Reporters. His Sister Won’t.

The New York Times August 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Congressional Memo

Senator Darline Graham, who took her brother’s place after his death and is now seeking to succeed him, has mostly declined to answer questions from reporters at the Capitol.

By Michael Gold

Reporting from the Capitol

After Senator Lindsey Graham died last month, his sister, Darline Graham, essentially inherited his seat in Congress.

With it, she inherited his office on Capitol Hill, his staff in Washington and back home in South Carolina, and his key spots on coveted committees. For a brief time, Ms. Graham was bequeathed her deceased brother’s security detail.

But the new Republican senator from South Carolina did not inherit her brother Lindsey’s gift of gab.

In the weeks since Ms. Graham came to Washington to fill her brother’s seat and then quickly said she would run to succeed him, she has shied away from the media attention that Mr. Graham so often relished. That has left many unanswered questions about the views and positions of a woman who had never held public office.

Where Lindsey was loquacious and often pontificated on the news of the day, Darline has rarely addressed the reporters who ask her questions at the Capitol. She has spoken little in committee hearings, and has taken part in few interviews.

Ms. Graham’s relative silence is particularly striking given her decision to run for Mr. Graham’s seat, one she made just days after being sworn in on July 14. Her decision to run has intensified scrutiny of her statements and has put her in a different light than had she only been a caretaker of the seat.

Because Mr. Graham was running for re-election when he died, Republicans will vote on Tuesday in a special primary election to replace him on the ballot. That has given the public a strikingly short window to evaluate Ms. Graham, a political novice whose views on many major issues are largely unknown.

This week, Ms. Graham remained mum when asked about her support for eliminating the filibuster, a position she took in a debate that marked a notable break with her brother. She looked toward the elevator floor rather than acknowledge a question about the “blue slip,” a longstanding Senate tradition defended by Mr. Graham that gives home-state senators veto power over judicial nominations.

On Wednesday, an aide accompanying Ms. Graham waved off a question about a sanctions bill that was championed by her brother. The aide said that the senator would not grant hallway interviews until she became more familiar with the geography of the sprawling Capitol complex.

Ms. Graham is not the only lawmaker to eschew hallway questions. Most senators, with varying degrees of enthusiasm, routinely answer drive-by inquiries from reporters. But a few resolutely refuse them.

Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas, the No. 3 Republican, has repeatedly advised his G. O. P. colleagues to avoid responding to reporters in hallways, guidance that most of them ignore. Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina routinely refers questions to his office. Before a long absence, Senator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky regularly responded to hallway questions with a silent stare.

Senator Amy Klobuchar, a Minnesota Democrat running for governor of her state, often holds her phone to her ear when heading to votes, a common tactic used by lawmakers to indicate they are unavailable to chat.

But Ms. Graham’s reticence stands out given her late brother’s reputation as a chatterbox who courted the media, and her status as a largely unknown candidate seeking a six-year term.

“Senator Darline Graham is different than Senator Lindsey Graham,” said Taylor Reidy, a spokeswoman. “She’s her own person, and she’s certainly got different life experiences than her brother.”

Since becoming a senator, Ms. Graham has sat for two interviews with Fox News, including a sit-down with the host Sean Hannity in which she announced the launch of her campaign.

On Monday, she took part in a debate with her Republican primary opponents in which she repeatedly highlighted that President Trump had endorsed her. But she offered few policy specifics. She spoke with a South Carolina television station on Tuesday, then released an op-ed on Wednesday echoing points she had made elsewhere.

On Friday, on what was expected to be the final legislative day before her primary, Ms. Graham delivered a speech on the Senate floor about the sanctions bill. But after the bill passed, she declined to comment on it, shaking her head gently when asked by a reporter in the Senate basement.

Ms. Graham’s opponents in the primary, including Representatives Russell Fry and Ralph Norman, have noted that Ms. Graham remains an unknown. They argue that because they have better-defined records, they have stronger qualifications for the job.

“We’re going to elect somebody to be the United States senator for six years,” Mr. Norman said in a separate debate on Tuesday night. “If you were hiring a doctor to operate on you for six years or a pilot to fly your plane for six years, you’d want to know everything about it.”

In a statement on Wednesday, Mr. Fry’s campaign accused Ms. Graham of being insufficiently conservative, and of avoiding hard questions.

Ms. Graham’s spokeswoman, Ms. Reidy, argued that Ms. Graham had “already shown she is more conservative than Lindsey on some issues,” including on abortion and the filibuster.

Still, among the easiest ways for members of Congress to stake out positions on the major issues of the day is for them to share their views with reporters who trail them on Capitol Hill.

Mr. Graham wanted to be a central player in congressional debates, and over his political career, he honed a media-friendly persona. Through his eight years in the House and 23 years in the Senate, Mr. Graham seemed to view his many interviews as a way to elevate his profile and accumulate influence.

Before he died last month, Mr. Graham held key positions on committees that are currently at the center of fervid Senate debates, including the nomination of Todd Blanche as attorney general, a bill to avert a government shutdown at the end of September, and an effort to bypass Democrats and push through funding for the war in Iran and election restrictions.

Mr. Graham was outspoken on those issues when questioned by reporters. Ms. Graham, who has her brother’s spot on those committees, has declined to discuss them with reporters at the Capitol.

Yet in the op-ed published on Wednesday, Ms. Graham blasted the silence of another public figure. She attacked Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, who oversaw the country’s response to Covid, for refusing to answer questions from a congressional committee.

“I think Anthony Fauci should stop staring at the floor and answer the questions,” she wrote.

Hours later, she did the same.

Olivia Diaz contributed reporting.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

She Is Russia’s Richest Woman. Her Business Empire Is Going Up in Flames.

The New York Times August 08, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

As Ukraine repeatedly strikes warehouses of the e-commerce site Wildberries, Tatyana Kim, its billionaire co-founder, faces her biggest test yet.

By Nataliya VasilyevaPaul SonneAlina Lobzina and Oleg Matsnev

She built Russia’s answer to Amazon. She navigated wartime Kremlin politics. And she outmaneuvered her ex-husband — the father of her seven children — in a rancorous business feud that involved a deadly shooting near Red Square.

But Tatyana Kim, the billionaire co-founder of the online marketplace Wildberries and the richest woman in Russia, is now facing a far greater challenge. Ukrainian airstrikes are decimating her company’s facilities and threatening her business empire’s survival.

After months of attacks on Russian oil refineries that caused nationwide gas shortages, Ukraine has expanded its air campaign to Wildberries warehouses across Russia. Kyiv has targeted at least 23 Wildberries facilities so far, hitting them night after night since mid-July, with billions of dollars in merchandise going up in smoke. Nine of the company’s workers have been killed.

The attacks mark a new stage in the conflict, with Kyiv aggressively targeting a single private business for the first time. President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine is attempting to bring the war home for more Russians, hoping that rising discontent and inconvenience in Russian society will increase the pressure on President Vladimir V. Putin to end the war.

Kyiv has argued that Wildberries, which accounts for about 10 percent of all Russian retail sales, is a legitimate target because it provides goods to Russian soldiers.

Ms. Kim, speaking in a video address late last month, condemned what she described as “terrorist attacks.” She said that the goods Wildberries was selling were no different from what was on offer by platforms like Amazon or the Chinese giant Alibaba.

“There is no logic, common sense or rationality in the actions of the terrorists, nor can there be,” Ms. Kim said, referring to the Ukrainians. She said the “enemy” was trying to “apply pressure, destabilize and provoke panic and shock among a large number of people.”

The strikes are hurting Wildberries, and the Russian retail market in general, at a time when the country’s economy is already facing difficulties, though the damage pales in comparison to the destruction Russia has caused in Ukraine.

Consumer spending in Russia for nonfood items on marketplaces like Wildberries has plummeted in recent weeks, amid the airstrikes, according to a research note by SberIndex, a research arm of state-owned Sberbank.

Wildberries has lost up to one-third of its warehouse space and as much as 480 billion rubles’ worth of goods ($5.9 billion) in the Ukrainian attacks, according to Moscow-based Data Insight, an e-commerce consultancy.

Wildberries “has almost run out of its biggest warehouses,” said Sergei Semko, an analyst at Data Insight. “Every single day one warehouse after another is getting methodically destroyed,” he added.

What ultimately happens to Wildberries will depend in part on how long Ukraine’s strikes continue and how effectively and quickly Ms. Kim adapts the company’s logistics. It will also depend on what sort of redress she is able to win from the Russian state.

Born into a Russian family that is ethnically Korean, Ms. Kim is a former English teacher who launched Wildberries in 2004 along with her husband, Vladislav Bakalchuk, as a website that sold clothes from European catalogs.

Over the years, Wildberries grew into a linchpin of the Russian consumer economy, with nearly 95,000 pickup points opening across the country and more than half of the nation’s population making purchases at least once a month. Mr. Putin’s invasion of Ukraine made the platform all the more important, as Western companies retreated from the market.

In 2024, Ms. Kim navigated a merger with a Russian outdoor advertising firm that was reportedly mediated by the Kremlin. The deal was denounced as a corporate raid by her husband. At one point, he showed up at the Wildberries office in Moscow with a retinue of armed Chechens, leading to a shootout that left two people dead and seven wounded. Ms. Kim and Mr. Bakalchuk finalized their divorce the following year.

Faced with a new, even more severe crisis, Ms. Kim, 50, is scrambling to adapt.

In her video address, she said Wildberries was moving to decentralize its distribution and redoing its logistics infrastructure as quickly as possible. In an online post on Thursday, she said the company was holding meetings with regional governments and sellers, adding that “broad support measures at the federal level are also being actively developed.”

The company has made two rounds of voluntary payouts to more than 80,000 small- and medium-sized sellers and rolled out limited insurance that sellers can buy for drone attacks. The Russian government is also working on an aid package for Wildberries’ sellers that will involve tax breaks and grace periods, Aleksei Sazanov, the deputy finance minister, said this week.

But while sellers are finding some relief, Ms. Kim’s staff is now worried about their safety. One 24-year-old Wildberries warehouse worker from St. Petersburg, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of security concerns, said she had felt a terrible inner fear as Ukrainian drones blew up Wildberries facilities in the region.

After the one where she worked and another near her house were hit, she decided to stop working there, even though she had liked the job.

The independent entrepreneurs who sell goods through Wildberries are also feeling anxiety.

Katerina Kordik, 44, had built a business selling boho jewelry from Asia that grew successful enough to support her family of five.

She lost about a third of her inventory, including her most expensive artisan pieces, in the first Ukrainian strike on a Wildberries warehouse, near Moscow, last month. She still had many items stored elsewhere, but as more Wildberries warehouses were blown up by the day, she was unable to retrieve her merchandise.

Then, an attack this week on a Wildberries warehouse in Tula, south of Moscow, took out half of her merchandise. Today, only about 100 of her roughly 2,000 items are available for sale, she said.

For the first time in her life, she has sought the help of a psychiatrist, she said.

“If you live in a country that is at war, it would be strange to expect that it wouldn’t get you at some point,” Ms. Kordik said. She added that she was trying to take it as a lesson, “to learn to cope with situations where nothing depends on you, where you can’t do anything and you just hang out in this uncertainty.”

Ms. Kim is also facing pressure from the competition. Industry watchers are already seeing signs that sellers are fleeing to Ozon, Russia’s second-largest e-commerce platform, which has a more decentralized logistics setup and has not been singled out by Kyiv.

In many places, Wildberries is still functioning normally. The company has such a sophisticated logistics and I. T. infrastructure that it is not going to fold simply because a number of its warehouses have been damaged or destroyed, said a former Wildberries executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of previous contractual obligations.

While Ukraine has accused Wildberries of selling military-related goods, including replacement parts for drones and navigation equipment, Ms. Kim has denounced the strikes as “attacks on peaceful people.”

Wildberries explicitly says in its rules that sales of weapons and armaments are prohibited.

Still, many supporters and family members of Russian soldiers have been known to buy equipment such as body armor and helmets from the site. Drones and other items that can be used on the front are available.

A review by The New York Times found that first-person-view drones were for sale on the site in early August, as were spools of fiber-optic cable, which can be attached to drones to guide them.

One listing — marked as “out of stock” — offered a drone with a dropping system for explosives. In the “questions” section, some users expressed legal concerns. Others inquired about bulk discounts, naming the Russian military unit for which they intended to buy the drones.

One review, using a Russian slang term for Ukrainian soldiers, said: “Drone is good, chops the Ukrops :)))))” The Times was unable to verify whether any of the drones were purchased or shipped.

One potential buyer asked in the questions section whether the drone could be used for the special military operation, the Kremlin’s term for the war. The seller replied, “Hello, yes.”

Paul Sonne is the Moscow bureau chief, leading coverage of Russia, the Caucasus and Central Asia. He is based in Berlin.

What to Know About Wildberries, the Company in Ukraine’s Cross Hairs

The New York Times August 08, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Ukrainian drones have increasingly targeted warehouses belonging to Wildberries, which many Russians rely on as the country’s largest e-commerce business.

By Nataliya Vasilyeva

Ukraine’s campaign targeting Russia’s war-related vulnerabilities has expanded beyond oil facilities and energy infrastructure to a new target: warehouses of the e-commerce giant Wildberries.

Ukrainian drones have hit 23 of its warehouses across Russia in less than three weeks, killing nine Wildberries employees and injuring several dozen others. Several of the company’s warehouses have completely ceased operations.

The company is a household name in Russia: Its purple-and-pink plastic bags are ubiquitous throughout towns and villages.

Wildberries is the most popular marketplace platform in Russia: 79 million people, more than half the country’s population, use it every month.

Its reach in Russia is unmatched, both in the variety of goods sold on the platform and breadth of its operations, touching the most remote corners of the country.

Russians have grown to rely on the company’s fast and easy delivery services. In the sparsely populated countryside, the local Wildberries pickup point is often the only piece of communal infrastructure other than the post office and a corner shop.

That success has made one of its founders, Tatyana Kim, Russia’s richest woman.

Ukrainian officials say they are attacking Wildberries warehouses because Russian soldiers often buy nonlethal equipment from the company.

Weapons or other items that are clearly military equipment are not sold on the Wildberries platform, but soldiers leaving for the war often stock up on essentials from it, just as their families buy pots and pans from the site. Until recently, the company had a search tag for army-related equipment, which has since been removed.

Those products included tactical vests, boots and socks, which are still available on the Wildberries platform, as well as on its biggest rival, Ozon, which has been targeted by Ukraine at least once.

Wildberries, however, is not just about military wear: a $20 pair of red-checkered lounge pants was its biggest seller last year. Other top-selling items, like hair masks, also bear little relevance to military activity.

Punishing strikes on the company’s operations are devised to “shutter the illusion of a peaceful life in a second,” Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s drone forces, said in a statement after the Ukrainian military first destroyed a Wildberries warehouse, outside Moscow in July.

Wildberries is an obvious target for Ukraine as it seeks to damage a linchpin of Russia’s consumer market. Its 95,000 pickup points across the country represent a sense of economic normalcy in Russia, which the Kremlin has been eager to preserve.

Wildberries is an important source of employment.

Each of the company’s pickup points is privately owned and run, and an estimated one million Russian sellers supply the vast variety of goods on the platform. Most are small businesses that cannot afford their own physical stores and would otherwise struggle to find customers.

The company was built from the ground up by Tatyana Kim, a former English teacher, and her husband, Vyacheslav Bakalchuk, an I. T. engineer, in the early 2000s.

Until their highly publicized divorce in 2024, Ms. Kim held 99 percent in the company, with Mr. Bakalchuk owing just 1 percent. A Russian court last year gave Ms. Kim full ownership of the company as part of their divorce proceedings.

The couple split up just as Ms. Kim agreed to a controversial merger with Russ Outdoor, an advertising company valued at a small fraction of Wildberries’s worth. Ms. Kim now holds 65 percent of Wildberries; a 35 percent stake was transferred to Russ Outdoor, which many critics have called a front for a Kremlin-connected billionaire tycoon, Suleyman Kerimov.

Before the merger, Wildberries had an estimated valuation of about $10 billion.

Speculation about who else may be linked to Wildberries resurfaced earlier this year when the company’s earnings report showed that Ms. Kim’s own firm had not received any dividends last year, and that the entire 51 billion rubles ($640 million) in dividends went to Russ Outdoor.

The drone strikes disproportionately affected small businesses that use Wildberries as a marketplace platform. Wildberries receives, stores, processes and ships their goods. An estimated 100,000 businesses are believed to have lost their stocks in the attacks.

Just a few days before the first Ukrainian strike on its warehouses, Wildberries amended its standard service agreement with its sellers, relinquishing any liability related to losses incurred in terrorist attacks or natural disasters.

Wildberries has since pledged to support its partners with one-off payments, prioritizing the smallest businesses. Ms. Kim recently said the company had already deposited 40 million rubles (some $500,000) in the accounts of 88,000 sellers.

A Russian deputy prime minister, Aleksandr Novak, met in late July with top officials and several Wildberries sellers, promising to draft a comprehensive package of financial aid.

Hackers Stalked Me by Hijacking a Smartwatch for Kids

Wired August 06, 2026

On a rainy New York morning earlier this week, a WIRED reporter strapped to his wrist a lavender and pink plastic child’s smartwatch and headed to work. As he approached his nearby subway station to commute to WIRED’s office, he texted Vangelis Stykas, the Greek security researcher who had shipped him the watch via Amazon, to let him know that he was going into the station and might lose cell signal.

“I know,” Stykas wrote back.

In fact, Stykas had been monitoring the reporter’s location via the watch since the moment he left his apartment. The watch’s GPS feature, intended to let a parent track their child, was malfunctioning, but the wearable device was still picking up and transmitting to a faraway server identifiers from every nearby Wi-Fi network, which allowed Stykas to nonetheless pinpoint the reporter’s exact location as he walked down a particular Brooklyn block.

A WIRED reporter wearing the GPS-enabled smartwatch while holding an umbrella and walking to the subway earlier this week.

When the reporter arrived at WIRED’s Manhattan headquarters half an hour later, Stykas hijacked a feature in the watch that allowed him to silently take a photo from its camera, capturing the moment when the reporter stepped into an elevator. After a few minutes, he took another snap of the reporter at his desk, then used a different feature to pick up audio from the watch’s microphone, transmitting it to another researcher, Felipe Solferini, who listened as the reporter’s coworker described his weekend visit to an art exhibition. At no point did the watch show any sign that it was listening, taking photos, or otherwise being hacked.

As WIRED reporter Andy Greenberg entered the elevator at WIRED's New York office, the hackers used the smartwatch to surreptitiously take a photo…

…and then again as he sat at his desk.

The watch’s insecurity and the spying it enabled might be expected given the gadget’s pedigree: It’s sold by an obscure company called CJC, costs less than $30, and was made by an equally obscure manufacturer, YiQingTeng Electronics, in Shenzhen, China. More troubling, perhaps, is that the online platform it’s built on—and the one that allowed Stykas and Solferini to so thoroughly hack it—is used by dozens of other brands of smartwatch, many of which have likely been left vulnerable to the same forms of digital stalking.

At the Black Hat cybersecurity conference today, Stykas and Solferini plan to present their findings from analyzing the supply chain and security of more than 70 GPS-enabled watches and car accessories. They found that more than 30 of those geolocation devices use the technology and backend servers of YiQingTeng, also identified by the brand name Wonlex, the name of a partner firm Shenzhen 3G Electronics, or their associated app, SETracker. Another 30-plus brands of tracking devices for cars and kids are all run on another Shenzhen-based platform known as NewGPS2012.

Combined with another major GPS platform known as SinoTrack that sells car trackers and smartwatches, the two researchers found that tens of millions of GPS tracker gadgets came from just three supply chains. All three, the researchers found in their analysis, had significant security flaws—in some cases as simple as a lack of authentication that allowed anyone to access any device—leaving children’s watches vulnerable to tracking by a hacker, location disabling and spoofing, interception and spoofing of text and audio messages sent to them, replacement of emergency contacts with ones a hacker chose, silent audio eavesdropping, as well as photo and video capture for camera-enabled devices. (Once the GPS started working on the smartwatch WIRED tested, the hackers showed that feature, too, could be hijacked to follow the wearer’s every move.)

For some GPS-enabled car accessories, the researchers found they could similarly track the devices’ locations or spoof messages to them that could potentially unlock or disable cars, though the researchers didn’t go so far as to test this out on actual vehicles. They also say they found server-side vulnerabilities that exposed consumer information, would have allowed them to execute their own code on the servers, or even in one case appeared to show that someone else had already gained unauthorized access to the system’s backend.

“Millions of kids are being exposed and vulnerable to exploitation. It's just catastrophic. It's really low-hanging fruit for a lot of bad actors,” Stykas says. “Your criminal mind is the only limitation in exploiting those devices.”

The researchers say they’ve been warning the companies behind all three Shenzhen-based GPS platforms about their vulnerabilities for months. When WIRED reached a representative of SETracker, the person initially claimed in an email that “the issues you mentioned have been resolved long before,” adding that “we attach great importance to the security of Setracker and keep strengthening its security continuously.” When WIRED pointed out that researchers had been able to hack a smartwatch running on SETracker just this week, the person repeated their claim that the issues had been fixed, then asked for evidence of the exploitation, which WIRED provided.

Only today, hours before the researchers’ talk at Black Hat, did the researchers find that their hacking techniques against SETracker’s platform have stopped working—though they’re still not sure if the flaws they found are fully fixed. After this article published, SETracker wrote in a statement that it had blocked certain ports on its servers used by a “legacy” version of its clients' systems, forcing “a small subset of clients” on that older system to upgrade to protect “a small number of devices” that were affected. “The vulnerability has now been thoroughly remediated,” the SETracker staffer wrote. “Thank you for your oversight and attention.”

Sinotrack and the NewGPS2012 platform didn’t respond to WIRED’s requests for comment, and the researchers say their hacking techniques against those systems still appear to work.

For more than a decade, cybersecurity experts and privacy advocates have warned that cheap, GPS-enabled children’s smartwatches and aftermarket vehicle accessories are riddled with security vulnerabilities that leave kids and drivers susceptible to hacking and tracking. But the sheer number of different brands and models of those devices has often made identifying the truly insecure gadgets feel nearly impossible for consumers.

More than any specific vulnerability, Solferini and Stykas say, they wanted to highlight that much of that daunting diversity among GPS devices—along with consumers’ sense of choice among them—is essentially an illusion.

“A parent in Sweden buying a ‘SafeKid’ watch and a parent in Spain buying a ‘SaveFamily’ watch are both sending their child's location data to the same vulnerable myaqsh. com backend on Alibaba Cloud in mainland China, without knowing it,” they write in a whitepaper shared with WIRED ahead of their Black Hat presentation, referring to the online services of YiQingTeng. “The white-label model means a vulnerability in one backend aﬀects dozens of consumer brands at the same time, and consumers have no way to tell which backend their product uses.”

The smartwatch WIRED tested was made by Shenzhen-based YiQingTeng Electronics and runs on the SETracker platform used by dozens of brands and millions of devices.

Solferini and Stykas aren’t revealing the full details of the vulnerabilities they discovered in the three major platforms, in part because not all of them have been fixed despite sharing their findings with the companies for months. In the case of YiQingTeng, the manufacturer of the watch WIRED tested, however, they say an authentication security flaw would have allowed anyone to send commands to any SETracker-based device. That would let hackers exploit and take over devices at random or to target specific watches if they can determine an identifier for them, such as the parent’s email address the device is registered to. (To hack the smartwatch worn by a WIRED reporter, for instance, the reporter gave Stykas his email address but no other information about the device. Stykas says he could have easily targeted devices in other ways, such as hacking numerous watches and searching through them to find the nearest vulnerable devices or one associated with a target’s identifying information.)

In the case of SinoTrack, the researchers say they found that an account intended for demonstration purposes could be used to send commands to any of the platform’s millions of devices. They also found a SQL injection vulnerability—a flaw that essentially allows anyone to send commands disguised as data that are then executed by the SinoTrack server—that gave them access to tens of thousands of devices’ locations, passwords, and vehicle records.

Finally, for NewGPS2012 devices, the researchers say they found similar SQL injection vulnerabilities and were able to run their own code on the company’s servers. They also say they found evidence of a previous compromise of the company’s systems, suggesting other unauthorized users or hackers may have had access to it for an unknown period of time.

Given the sheer number of different brands and resellers of those Shenzhen-manufactured gadgets, the researchers didn’t confirm the vulnerability of all of the individually branded devices they found to use YiQingTeng’s SETracker platform or the NewGPS2012 platform. WIRED couldn’t independently confirm each device’s vulnerability either. But the table below lists brands whose products were based at least in part on those platforms, as well as the company’s response when WIRED reached out for comment on the researchers’ findings.

Stykas and Solferini’s Black Hat talk is far from the first warning about the dangers of cheap GPS devices—even from these researchers themselves. Stykas and another researcher, Michael Gruhn, revealed a broad collection of vulnerabilities in GPS-enabled devices in 2018, which they called Trackmageddon. GPS-enabled automotive devices plugged into the OBDII port on cars’ dashboards have proven again and again to be vulnerable to hacking and tracking.

Children’s GPS-enabled watches have also been shown to be especially prone to critical privacy and security vulnerabilities: Pen Test Partners and the Norwegian government issued warnings about certain hackable children’s watches in 2017 and 2018, and another study by the Münster University of Applied Sciences in 2020 tested six children’s smartwatches and found serious vulnerabilities in five. “It was crazy," Sebastian Schinzel, one of the Münster researchers, told WIRED at the time. "Everything was basically broken."

Yet somehow, Stykas says, people keep putting cheap, GPS-enabled devices on their loved ones. And the companies that make them, too, have often completely ignored his warnings about the hackable bugs in their devices. As he tested his surveillance techniques against the newly purchased smartwatch on a WIRED reporter’s wrist a few days ago, they worked as well as ever, and some of the devices’ flaws remain unpatched even now.

“I really hoped we could tell a nice story that there were vulnerabilities and they fixed them. But in many cases, they didn’t,” Stykas says. “It's a position I really didn't want to be in.”
