The Best Smart Glasses That Aren’t Just a Gimmick

Wired August 07, 2026

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The idea of smart glasses has been around for decades, but the technology is finally catching up. The best smart glasses let you listen to music, answer texts hands-free, or teach you about the world, even as you're looking at it. And they're getting more popular: Meta and Ray-Ban sold more than 7 million pairs of smart glasses in 2025. Google, Samsung, and Apple are releasing their own versions soon. Even better than helpful smart glasses becoming more available is that these specs can also make you look fabulous.

Before you pick your pair, you should know that smart glasses are hugely varied, even more so than many other product categories that we test. Some are glorified headphones for everyday wear; others have very specific use cases, like for sports, gaming, or working. They also come in a wide variety of designs, with varying specs and price points.

The WIRED team has tested just about every pair of smart glasses on the market. In addition to our recommendations, I also explain what you need to know about this category and give a quick history lesson about the space. Think you might need something else instead? Don't forget to check out the rest of our buying guides, including the Best Meta Glasses and the Best Virtual Reality Headsets.

Updated August 2026: I updated product information and added a FAQ section. Specs, prices, and links were also updated.

What Am I Testing Next?

I am currently testing the Lucyd Reebok Optical frames.

Ray-Ban

Amazon

Best Buy

Meta

Ray-Ban

Arguably, the success of the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses is what spurred the current AI glasses boom. These are the updated version of the OG Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarers that were the category's first certified hit. As the sales numbers reinforce, these are the best and most popular smart glasses available.

Why WIRED recommends: The second-generation Ray-Ban Meta glasses let you choose different frames, including the Wayfarer ones, and lenses (including prescription lenses), and they look the most like regular glasses. They don’t have any virtual screen—instead, you get a 12-MP camera, open-ear speakers, and five microphones. There’s 32 GB of storage, and they run for around eight hours when fully charged, with a case that can add another 48 hours. They have an IPX4 water resistance rating, so they'll be OK in light rain. The photo quality can’t match the latest phones, and videos are limited to one minute in length, but the quality is much better than what the originals offered, enabling you to record in up to 3K at 30 frames per second. You also get a host of AI features, including live language translation and the ability to ask about what you're seeing. But using these features requires you to connect to a smartphone, plus Meta AI also needs an internet connection.

The trade-offs: If you go to any outdoor or sporting event, you will undoubtedly see people wearing these to record snippets for TikTok or Instagram. The glasses have given rise to a new term, “pervert glasses”. More than 70 organizations have formed a coalition to demand that Meta kill face recognition, an upcoming feature dubbed “Name Tag” in Meta's house. If you’re OK with all this, you're not alone—millions of people are as well! I like these glasses, but only with a lot of precautions, like disabling the Vibes videos and keeping my photos and videos off the Meta AI cloud. Smart glasses with cameras can also provide audio descriptions and answer questions about what you are seeing, which may be useful for folks with vision loss. The glasses also have an integrated Be My Eyes service that doesn't rely on AI. —Adrienne So

Viture

Amazon

Best Buy

Viture

Viture Beast's 2026 model has a screen that's bigger, brighter, and with a wider field of view than our previous winner for best virtual screen, the Xreal One Pro. I spent a week using the Beast for work, watching movies with my 2024 MacBook Pro and my iPhone 16, and fighting with my family to take turns playing Tears of the Kingdom in 3D using my Nintendo Switch 2. I'm excited to take the Beast traveling with me this year and eliminate the need for a portable monitor.

Why WIRED recommends: It's easy to dial in a comfy fit, thanks to a wide variety of nose pads. You can buy prescription lenses, and my kids and I could switch lenses quickly enough to take turns using the glasses. The glasses now feature an onboard chip letting you control features like screen-width customization and three DoF (degrees of freedom), which makes your setting fixed around you as you turn and rotate. The chip eliminates the need to use cumbersome third-party apps (like SpaceWalker) to take advantage of the glasses' capabilities.

I tested the glasses with MacOS Spaces. 3 DoF and Smart Follow are effective, though there is a noticeable lag with Smart Follow—I didn't mind it, but it may bother some people. The screen was plenty bright enough that I could watch Somewhere on my patio in the sun, but you can also adjust the light transmittance. In order to use the glasses, you have to plug them into a device, but the upside of that is that they work well with many companion systems.

The trade-offs: Before using the glasses for the first time, you have to calibrate the evenness of the virtual screen by setting them down on a flat surface for 10 seconds, and they just cannot lie flat with the plug coming out of the right arm. So, even after calibration, the view is just a little crooked. These glasses will also drain the battery on any device incredibly quickly. Watching Casino Royale with my phone drained the battery about 70 percent in 1.5 hours. Keep a charger handy. —Adrienne So

Xreal

Amazon

Xreal

The Xreal One Pro is the major competitor to the Viture Beast right now. Virture's model wins for a brighter, crisper, and bigger screen, though the One Pro does still offer an excellent-quality virtual display of up to 171 inches at 1080p resolution, up to 120-Hz refresh rate, and a 57-degree field of view.

Why WIRED recommends: Where the One Pro really shines is its sound quality. The built-in Bose stereo speakers deliver richer sound than Viture’s Harman speakers. These smart glasses work great as a virtual theater. Xreal’s X1 built-in chip allows for 3 DoF, so you can pin the screen without an accessory or app. The electrochromic film can dim the lenses to dial up the contrast.

These aren’t the lightest smart glasses, but Xreal’s switch to a flat prism design makes them sleeker and allows them to sit comfortably closer to your eyes. Three sizes of nose pads enable you to get a comfy fit. There are also several accessories you can snag to enhance the experience. That includes the Xreal Eye ($99) camera, which sits below the bridge of the nose and supports 12-megapixel photos and video recording (1080p at 60 fps). There’s also the Beam Pro ($199) Android computer for content streaming, remote play, and cloud gaming, and it has dual 50-megapixel cameras to create 3D videos. It’s also worth noting that Xreal's upcoming Project Aura will be the company's first Android XR glasses, promising a 70-degree field of view, but details are slim.

The trade-offs: The One Pro display can get brighter than its predecessor at 700 nits of perceived brightness, but it doesn’t hit the highs of some other smart glasses, like the Viture. They lack diopter dials, but you can tweak settings like screen size and distance, IPD (interpupillary distance), calibration, and button mapping on the glasses. Lastly, while Xreal’s free Nebula app unlocks more features, the system is kind of underbaked. —Simon Hill

Oakley

Amazon

Meta

Oakley

These are former editor Adrienne So’s favorite smart sunglasses for running. The Oakley Meta Vanguard is inspired by the iconic Oakley Sphaera sports sunglasses, which cost almost $300. For about $200 more, you can get this smart pair that's essentially sunglasses with workout headphones, a five-mic array, and a 12-megapixel action camera built in.

Why WIRED recommends: The headphones are 6 decibels louder than any other pair of Meta glasses, and the IP67 rating means these glasses can be worn in all types of weather (or even on ski slopes) without fear of water damage. The lenses are also interchangeable and are easy to swap when you need something different for your activity or season. You can also set up automations like Meta AI alerting you when you're out of your heart rate zone or select Garmin watches triggering auto-capture for photos and videos. (For example, you can set your Garmin to capture a 30-second clip for every mile on your 10-mile run.)

The trade-offs: The camera quality doesn't compare to a GoPro camera or other popular action cameras. It has a 12-MP sensor, 32 gigabytes of storage, and a 122-degree ultrawide field of view, but competing action cameras typically offer larger sensors, at least two times more storage, wider fields of view, and longer recording times.

Even Realities

Even Realities

If you're not comfortable with everything Meta's doing, then your best bet is the Even Realities G2, the upgraded version of the Even Realities G1.

Why WIRED recommends: With these glasses, there's no need to fear privacy-invading cameras or microphones. Instead, the glasses have a huge, bright display, and are what reviewer Chris Haslam calls “the sharpest-looking smart glasses available.” You can choose between two styles of frames, the oval G2 A and the rectangular G2 B, both of which are available in gray, brown, or muted green. The G2 also supports prescription lenses from −12.00 to +12.00 diopters. You can control the glasses via the new R1 smart ring, which also helps keep interactions with the glasses subtle, or by toggling the responsive touch panel on the temple.

The G2 glasses are aimed at business professionals, offering an Even HAO 2.0 (Holistic Adaptive Optics) display, which you can use to read crisp green digital text in a small rectangle within the lenses. There's Even AI, a helpful onboard assistant that feeds responses to your questions as digital text; a Teleprompt feature, which is useful if you give frequent presentations; and translation support for 33 languages, as compared to Meta's six.

The trade-offs: The newest feature is Conversate, an AI conversational assistant that aims to help you become a more interesting conversationalist. The feature suggests topics or facts as you speak, records transcripts of your conversations, and provides AI-generated summaries. Haslam found this mildly helpful but very distracting, as it's hard to both talk to your friend and read text-prompts onscreen. The ethical implications are also disturbing, since there's no indication that the conversation is being recorded (the Meta glasses have a bright LED that lights up when you're being recorded). At least you can read the staggeringly bright 1,200-nit display in almost any lighting conditions. —Adrienne So

RayNeo Air 3s Pro for $299: TCL-owned RayNeo offers many models, and I've tested several. The latest Air 3s Pro glasses boast a 201-inch virtual screen (1080p, 120 Hz, 1200 nits), but the 46-degree field of view lets it down a little. Both color vibrancy and brightness are improved over previous releases like the Air 2s and the older TCL RayNeo Air 2 XR Glasses. You can just about see the whole screen clearly (even after adjusting, I had to slide them down my nose a little to avoid blurring at the bottom). You will also need the lens shade to use them in brighter environments. While they are cheaper than our other virtual-screen picks, I found them inferior in design, fit, and comfort. Rayneo has added some more on-device options, including spatial sound, but it didn't work well for me, though the standard sound is fine. RayNeo’s software, required for 3 DoF, is still buggy and unpolished. This is a good virtual screen for the money, and perfectly suitable for watching movies and light gaming, but if you want more from your smart glasses, I'd pick a different pair. —Simon Hill

Viture Luma Pro for $499: Every time a company comes out with a new pair of smart glasses, the old one instantly looks dated. The same is true here with the older Viture Luma Pro and the newer Viture Beast. The Beat's display is better, and it has the onboard chip, so you don't have to deal with the hassle of the SpaceWalker app. If you're using the glasses for gaming, you're probably going to spend whatever you save buying the older Luma Pro's on accessories anyway. That said, if you exhausted your budget, the Luma Pro is a cheaper way to get a small, portable screen for traveling. —Adrienne So

Engo3 for $400: These sports sunglasses are for high-performance aerobic athletes going at such high speeds that looking down at your wrist might place you in peril. The glasses are a miracle of engineering, weighing only 38.5 grams (half that of the Oakley Meta Vanguard). I tested the version with the photochromic lenses, which have an ambient light sensor to dial the transmittance up or down. You can connect the glasses with a compatible Garmin or Apple Watch and customize the HUD (heads-up display) to show real-time data on a color display as you're working out. It's accurate, and the text is crisp. Unfortunately, the HUD is located right near the bridge of my nose, which means I'm cross-eyed when I check it. Also, it's debatable which is more distracting during a long run: having to look down at my smartwatch or having a giant HUD mirrored display in the middle of my face, falling down my nose when I sweat. —Adrienne So

Chamelo Music Shield for $229: These are the simplest smart glasses on this list. If you're too cool for auto-transition photochromic lenses, you can just slide your finger along the right arm of these electrochromatic sunglasses to dim them anywhere from 17 to 64 percent light transmittance. They also play music. These are comfortable and work well, but the sound is nowhere near as clear or loud as other options. They're also not polarized and are pricey considering their limited functionality. —Adrienne So

Rokid Max 2 Glasses for $429: The Spider-Man–esque lenses give these comfortable smart glasses a bit of character, though they won’t be to everyone’s taste. They project a 215-inch screen (1080p, 120 Hz, 600 nits, 50-degree FoV) and have diopter dials for focus adjustments, but I struggled to eliminate blurring around the edges, and instead of using stylish electrochromic dimming, there’s a clip-on plastic blackout shield. I also tried the Rokid Station 2, which adds an Android TV interface to access entertainment apps, but also a trackpad and an air mouse for easier control. —Simon Hill

Lucyd Reebok Octane for $199: Designed in partnership with Reebok for cyclists and runners, these lightweight Bluetooth sunglasses feature silver polarized lenses, quality speakers, and an eight-hour battery life. I enjoyed listening to music and podcasts on them while hiking. I also like that you can hear the world around you, but the sound leakage isn’t too bad, so you won’t bother the people you pass. They also have physical controls that are much easier to use than touch controls, even when your hands are wet or sweaty (the glasses are water-resistant, too). You can take calls, get directions, and ask your preferred AI assistant questions. Lucyd has been making Bluetooth sunglasses for several years now and offers a wide range of different styles. We also tried the Lucyd 2.0 Bluetooth Sunglasses a couple of years ago, rating them a 7 out of 10. —Simon Hill

Here's the eyewear that fell short.

Asus AirVision M1 for $699: I was excited to see Asus launch smart glasses, but the lack of fanfare was a red flag. My first impressions of the lightweight design were promising, and the M1 offers up to a 100-inch virtual display and impressive 1100 nits brightness. Designed to plug into your phone, laptop, PC, or handheld gaming device via USB-C, the M1 also features built-in speakers and a microphone. Sadly, the refresh rate maxes out at 72 Hz and is limited to 60 Hz unless you employ the Airvision software, which also enables you to select different modes (working, gaming, infinity), tweak screen position, and set interpupillary distance (IPD). I found the in-focus sweet spot was small, and most of my virtual screen was blurry, no matter how I tweaked the settings. This made the glasses uncomfortable to use, especially for work. There’s also a basic plastic shield to block light, rather than electrochromic dimming, and the speaker quality is decidedly average, leaving me puzzled about why the price is so high. —Simon Hill

Halliday Glasses: While these could almost pass for chunky regular glasses thanks to a clever ring controller and a tiny unobtrusive display, I can confidently say they are not the future of smart glasses. After spending several uncomfortable hours trying to adjust the display to be readable, all I got was a headache. The ring seemed like a smart idea, but it’s big, plastic, and laggy. The eavesdropping AI is slow, and squinting up to try and see the screens of unhelpful text it churns out is painful. The sound quality and battery life are likewise disappointing. —Simon Hill

Solos AirGo Vision for $299: With a built-in AI assistant powered by ChatGPT, the Solos AirGo Vision adds a camera on top of the Bluetooth-connected speakers in the rest of its range. Grant it unfettered access to your location and photo library, and it can describe what you are seeing. The most obvious use cases are translation and navigation, though I’m not convinced about the accuracy of its suggestions. The design is interesting, with chunky temples housing the smarts and interchangeable frames. There’s no virtual screen or HUD, but you can get prescription lenses, and they look relatively normal. Sadly, the photo and audio quality are horrible, and the touch controls are frustratingly finicky. The app is also power-hungry and demands too many permissions. The Ray-Ban Meta glasses do the same things better. —Simon Hill

What Are Smart Glasses? A Brief History

While prototype facial computers date back as far as the late ’60s, it was Google Glass that popularized the idea of smart glasses. First released as a developer kit, Google Glass is more than a decade old. They gave rise to a serious privacy debate but were also beloved by early adopting “Glassholes.” After failing to take off as a consumer product, Google Glass pivoted into factories and warehouses, highlighting the potential of augmented reality in the workplace.

The first wave of augmented reality glasses were unappealing and largely unsuccessful. They were chunky and heavy, were light on features, and made wearers look like cyborg extras from a sci-fi B-movie. The first pair I tried from Vuzix made me question the entire category. There was a lot of hype about augmented reality, but most of these chunky glasses offered relatively low-resolution displays superimposed over your field of view. For smart glasses to truly blend the real world in front of you with the virtual world, they would need cameras, processing power, and some very smart software.

Many players, big and small, have tried and failed to make an impact in this space. The early excitement generated by companies like Magic Leap evaporated amid clunky hardware at high prices. The trouble with some of the most ambitious examples thus far, like Microsoft HoloLens 2 or Apple’s Vision Pro, is that they are relatively big and heavy and, more importantly, horribly expensive. The most successful smart glasses so far are more focused, less ambitious, and cheaper, though they also fall well short of the original vision.

There’s currently a palpable sense that smart glasses are right on the brink of breaking through into the mainstream. Google’s Android XR opens up the space for developers to make the killer apps needed to drive adoption, and it has begun showing off new AI-powered smart glasses and a mixed-reality headset developed with Samsung. Xreal is also working on some new Android XR glasses dubbed Project Aura that are expected to arrive later in 2026. Many other smart glasses are in development, like Meta’s Artemis glasses, new Snap Spectacles, and Emteq’s inward-looking smart glasses. —Simon Hill

Are Smart Glasses Worth It?

Smart glasses aren't for everyone, but they can be a worthwhile investment if you value portability and convenience. They’re especially useful if you want texts, notifications, or directions displayed in your line of sight instead of reaching for your phone. And if hands-free features like photo and video capture, open-ear audio, and live translation are important to you, smart glasses are worth it.

What Are the Different Types of Smart Glasses?

Smart glasses exist on a continuum of simple to complicated. Like a wearable face computer, they can have a wide variety of price points and specs to accommodate the different types of onboard tech.

What Does HUD, DoF, and FoV Mean?

Are Smart Glasses a Privacy Risk?

Smart glasses raise legitimate privacy concerns. While recording a video in public is socially acceptable, many people are understandably uncomfortable with how discreetly smart glasses can capture photos and videos. Some models even incorporate AI features that can recognize objects and faces, validating concerns about surveillance and consent. If you decide to wear smart glasses, be mindful of local recording and privacy laws.

It's also important to consider your own privacy. Many smart glasses and their companion apps request access to messages, photos, and other sensitive information that you may rather keep private. Before granting permissions, review the privacy policies and consider whether each request is necessary for the features you plan to use.

The ‘Manosphere’ Isn’t a Movement. It’s a Multibillion-Dollar Grievance Industry

Wired August 07, 2026

For many years now, a dark question has haunted parents, teachers, the internet, and media institutions: What’s wrong with young men?

Why, people ask, are boys so politically extreme, spouting misogynist rhetoric, and increasingly drawn into risky crypto schemes and online gambling? How did they become so lonely, with their depression symptoms often overlooked? The male youth vote broke for Trump in the 2024 election following a GOP campaign built on naked appeals to meathead machismo. Yet there are signs that his second term in office has done little to stem the anger of Gen Z men, whose support for the president is now plummeting.

The most common explanation of these interrelated phenomena is that younger men have banded together online under the umbrella of something known as the “manosphere,” usually conceived as an organic right-wing rebellion driving the culture wars. A new study, however, suggests that this is entirely backward: The digital ecosystem that produces red-pilled men is less of a movement than it is a pyramid scheme.

In “The Grift Economy: How Young Men Are Being Sold Fake Belonging and Fake Wealth Online,” researchers from the digital safety organization Reset Tech and the nonprofit Equimundo map how men are “algorithmically routed into paid communities, unregulated supplements, crypto schemes, and high-ticket ‘coaching’ programs,” which together make up a “multibillion-dollar industry.”

“‘Masculinity’ has become a commercial category that is constructed, curated, and financially incentivized online,” write the authors of the 153-page report.

First, men encounter aspirational self-help content when looking up advice on dating, fitness, or finance. Bad actors then exploit their areas of vulnerability by offering a misleading, grievance-based narrative to explain their frustrations. The paper cites, for example, a verified “business” account on X that used real economic data to falsely claim that the high rate of youth unemployment is only affecting men.

“By framing credential competition and labor market dynamics as a coordinated attack on men,” the researchers write, “this operation converts genuine economic anxiety—which is real and documented—into resentment with named targets: women, immigrants, foreign workers.”

Once men feel they are in community with one another based on a shared sense of victimhood and betrayal, and hostility toward a mutual enemy, the same predatory characters can then sell them the dubious solution, whether that’s a class, access to an exclusive club, or gray-market pills. In breaking down the sources of the misogynist influencer Andrew Tate’s income, the researchers estimate that he makes $184 million in annual gross revenue just from his subscription-based “Real World” education platform, which costs $99 per month. Reset Tech and Equimundo call these kinds of membership and course systems “fraud at scale,” noting their manipulative character: “Recycled content, affiliate pyramids, deliberate cancellation barriers, and deceptive testimonials characterize the industry’s flagship products.” (Tate’s attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Tate and his brother, Tristan Tate, are fighting extradition to the UK on charges of rape and sex trafficking after being arrested in Florida last month; their attorney has said they are innocent.)

Meanwhile, the report pegs the range of hourly streaming revenue for top-tier streamers such as Adin Ross (who also has an equity stake in Kick, the site that hosts his live content) at around $30,000 to $50,000. Figures like Joe Rogan command speaking fees upwards of $200,000. And top creators in the space, the study estimates, can earn anywhere from $1 million to $10 million in annual revenue across income streams including “platform payouts, sponsorships, courses, memberships, and speaking fees.” (Neither Rogan’s manager nor Ross’ entertainment company immediately returned a request for comment.)

Gary Barker, founder and CEO of Equimundo, which advocates for gender equality and positive masculinity, says we can better understand the so-called manosphere by looking at how those at the top are cultivating and then monetizing resentment and anger among young men. “They're being duped,” he says of these consumers. “They deserve to be getting straight information on products that actually do what they say they do, and not [be] swindled out of their money.”

The platforms, of course, take a cut of the profits and reward masculinity influencers for pushing extreme views while generating controversy and conflict. Reset Tech performed a cross-platform analysis of “looksmaxxing” content, heavily amplified this year by the Kick streamer Braden Peters, better known as Clavicular, to capture the scale of trends that drive men to pay exorbitant sums for the supposed means to improve their status. “Across 216 influencers tracked on TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook, the combined reach of looksmaxxing-related operations exceeded 14.6 billion views during the analysis period,” they concluded. “The reach is not organic—it is a product of recommendation architecture.”

The report draws a parallel between this harmful material and the kind of pro-eating-disorder content that targets women. It notes that while platforms were eventually pressured to take action against the latter—though not always with success—they have not pursued the same kind of enforcement against users reinforcing men’s negative body image to promote unhealthy behaviors. (Meta, TikTok, X, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on their guidelines around potentially harmful manosphere content.) In an email statement, YouTube spokesperson Boot Bullwinkle told WIRED the platform's guidelines “strictly prohibit content that promotes, glorifies, or encourages self-harm and eating disorders, as well as content that encourages dangerous behaviors that can lead to physical injury. We also have stricter policies on what can monetize on YouTube. When we identify content that violates these guidelines, we take swift action.” The platform terminated Tate's channels in 2022. A Kick spokesperson told WIRED via email that moderation in livestreaming is “reactive" to prohibited activity, and can include warnings, bans, and demonetization. The platform's guidelines prohibit content that “promotes, encourages, or instructs acts that pose a serious risk to personal safety, including self-harm or suicide.”

Clavicular’s rise to fame also provides evidence of how outrage fuels clicks that ultimately line the pockets of masculinity gurus. In January 2026, he and other influencers including Andrew and Tristan Tate, Nick Fuentes, and Sneako livestreamed themselves listening to Kanye West’s antisemitic song “Heil Hitler” in a sprinter van in Miami. Clips spread far beyond the original Kick audience via aggregator accounts on mainstream platforms, drawing widespread condemnation.

While the better-known Tates saw little change in their audience following the incident, Clavicular, who was then far less prominent, saw an explosion in engagement. Two weeks later, he was averaging close to 3 million views on his X posts, compared to about 500,000 two weeks before the stream. The larger viewership meant more potential students for his looksmaxxing “academy,” which costs $49 at the lowest tier and up to $3,000 for private coaching.

Barker says that while younger kids can be kept out of this pipeline by their parents, advocacy groups, and legislatively imposed protections, men entering adulthood don’t have the same support. “If we're looking at the 18- to 29-year-olds, which is where we see the biggest traffic to these spaces, nobody's got their back,” he says. This demographic “falls through the cracks” because society expects that they “should be able to handle this by themselves” as skeptical media consumers, he adds.

However, in post-2024 focus groups, Reset Tech found that young men could demonstrate a “striking lack of self-awareness” when it came to their sources of news and perspectives on current events, considering podcasts like The Joe Rogan Experience essentially unbiased. They also “believed women were trapped in echo chambers looking at makeup and lifestyle content while they themselves received information from neutral, verified sources,” the researchers write.

“We've got to reach them to basically be more critical with what they look at,” Barker says. “They do want to call out when stuff is bullshit,” he adds, it’s just that the digital ecosystem and its algorithms have, by their very nature, “narrowed” men’s opportunities to experience views that meaningfully challenge their own.

In the absence of action from the platforms, Barker says, it will be up to the users to recognize that the people selling them peptides, dating hacks, and get-rich-quick schemes are taking advantage of them—and leave the associated online communities or even mobilize others to do the same by calling out the harms they cause. Maybe a young male commentator who devotes themselves to exposing the toxic lies and scams of the grievance economy would become an influencer in their own right.

“I think it's not gonna be a tomorrow thing, that we get a group of young men who are like, ‘Yeah, I'm gonna be the warrior for calling out injustice online,’” Barker says. “But I think it's kind of where some of the action has got to come from.”

8/7/26, 1:19 PM EDT: WIRED updated this story to include statements from YouTube and Kick.

The Hottest New AI Chatbot Is Just a Guy Answering Your Questions

Wired August 07, 2026

What if, instead of typing the next silly question you have into Claude or ChatGPT, you asked a random guy instead?

That’s the idea behind ChatTJB. It’s the creation of 32-year-old Tucker Bryant, a public speaker, artist, and former project manager at Google. A San Francisco billboard describes ChatTJB as “the leading chat interface powered by AI.” In this case, though, AI stands for “average individual.”

Bryant didn’t train an LLM to respond based on how he writes. He literally sits down and answers the prompts himself. If you request an image of a skunk wearing sunglasses, he’ll scribble one up. If you ask how to fry an egg, he’ll respond with a suggestion. Maybe. (WIRED asked ChatTJB how to become a morning person, and at the time of writing, we haven’t received a response. The website notes that “thousands of people are writing in right now.”)

Bryant tells WIRED he launched ChatTJB back in April, but it didn’t take off until July 27, when his $6,000 billboard went up in San Francisco. News coverage soon followed. As of August 6, he says, ChatTJB has received over 30,000 queries. At its peak, he says, he was receiving about 5,000 prompts per hour.

Bryant says that he “first and foremost” considers ChatTJB to be an art project, not just a funny bit or a social experiment.

“It was sort of an opportunity for me to provide a little bit of commentary on a strange moment that I feel like we're in,” Bryant says. He doesn’t consider himself anti-AI—in fact, he vibe-coded the ChatTJB website using Lovable—but he’s clear-eyed about the risks of the technology.

He’s concerned about the risk of “cognitive surrender,” which refers to accepting AI outputs with increasingly little critical thinking or scrutiny. He says the concept made him reflect on his own back-and-forths with LLMs, like the time he asked if he should wear short or long sleeves on a 65-degree day in San Francisco.

“And then I'm like, dude, I've been living in this city for whatever, like seven years,” Bryant says. “Like, I know how to handle the weather. And yet, it felt like an easier thing for me to defer to a LLM for advice on that.”

“It felt like something that I wanted to speak on,” he adds, “because I was like, what am I doing here?”

Over the past couple of days, he has drawn a frog eating spaghetti, San Francisco mayor David Lurie as Godzilla, and two black cats eating grass on a table, among other things. The written requests, Bryant says, have been diverse.

“People were asking things like, ‘Oh, it's my birthday in two weeks, and I don't really want to have a party—what do you think I should do?’” Bryant says. Other people ask what they should have for dinner or how they can use the ingredients in their fridge.

“A lot of people initially were interacting with this thing as a joke or as a funny thing,” Bryant says. “And then I think when they realized that they could chat and get actual conversation, some of what people would share would be more personal, sincere, genuine, et cetera.”

Bryant is quick to note that he’s not a good artist, and his advice is no better than any other person’s. (On YouTube, he described it as “the worst LLM of all time.”) But he thinks people understand that.

“The way I'm interpreting it is that the value for them is just getting a human to bounce those questions off of, as opposed to getting super expert advice,” Bryant says. “It's very tender to see.”

At first, Bryant tells WIRED, he expected the project to last only a couple of days. But after seeing people’s enthusiasm, he says, he plans to keep it going. He has enlisted the help of 10 volunteers, but they’re a select crowd. Bryant says that over 3,000 people applied.

For ChatTJB superfans, there’s an option to financially support the project: ChatTJB Pro. Bryant is clear on the website that “this is a worthless tier,” and users get nothing but the knowledge that they’re supporting his art. So far, he says, about four people have paid the $5 per month fee—so he hasn’t exactly made up the cost of the billboard, which will remain up until late August. But Bryant says he didn’t create ChatTJB to make money.

“I really just want people to have an opportunity to take a second look at both their own relationship to technology as well as the world's relationship to technology,” Bryant says. He adds that in a time when people are bombarded with companies claiming to sell world-changing technology, alongside frightening coverage of a looming AI bubble, he wants to bring some levity.

“I hope that that just makes a weird time sit a little bit lighter,” Bryant says, “because I think sometimes that's the best that we can do.”

Plastic-Free Drip Coffee Is a Holy Grail. These Machines Deliver It

Wired August 07, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The era of plastic-free drip coffee has finally arrived. It couldn't come soon enough.

Drip coffee is my first true love when it comes to caffeine. But sadly, my first love is hopelessly addicted to plastic. From the very first Mr. Coffee machines in the 1970s, nearly every drip coffee maker on the market, including many of my favorite drip coffee makers, has included plastic at some point in the brewing process.

But plastic, as we're now learning, can leach tiny particles called microplastics into coffee or water, which you then happily drink in your morning cup. The science isn't all in on health risks, but it doesn't seem great.

Luckily, in the past year, a couple new machines have arrived with the promise to remove plastic from the equation: the Ratio Eight Series 2 ($799) and the Simply Good Coffee Plastic-Free Coffee Brewer ($480). Each promises to deliver delicious, high-end coffee without the plastic.

Each costs significantly more than machines made with injection-molded plastic parts that are easier to manufacture. And each has a couple quirks and trade-offs. But the Ratio Eight in particular makes drip coffee that rivals the best pour-over, and the best drip coffee I've ever tasted—and never brings hot water into contact with plastic.

But for those who want to avoid plastic completely, including on the cold water tank, there's really only one drip coffee maker I've tested that fits the bill: the Simply Good Coffee plastic-free brewer, which comes in at a much lower price.

If flavor is a primary consideration, I'd still recommend upgrading to the Ratio Eight. It's also the coffee maker that's become my daily driver when testing new coffee roasters and my favorite coffee subscriptions. But I understand that its price brings it out of reach for some. Here's the rundown.

Simply Good Coffee

SimplyGoodCoffee

Simply Good Coffee is a fairly new name in the coffee world, founded in 2022 by former Bonavita CEO Laura Sommers. Until last year, it was also a reasonably obscure brand, devoted mostly to making more affordable takes on premium, precision coffee makers like the Bonavita and Moccamaster, whose design Simply Good Coffee somewhat resembles.

The plastic-free machine rocketed Simply Good into sudden prominence—and indeed, it's sold out its production runs more than once since its release last year, riding a wave of interest in plastic-free drip coffee makers. The design is similar to Simply Good's previous model, but with plastic parts removed from the equation.

The frame is made of 304 “food grade” stainless steel. The reservoir, carafe, and boiler tube are borosilicate glass. Certain connections, including the drip stop, are made with medical-grade, sand-based silicone fittings that are not thought to produce nanoparticles easily. It is, quite simply, the least plasticky drip coffee machine I am aware of. There's no plastic contact, hot or cold, and very minimal silicone contact.

Operation is dead simple. There are, in fact, just two switches. One turns on the brewer and the warming plate; the other controls the pour-over style “bloom” function, adding a small phase to wet the grounds before brewing a full batch. The machine will turn itself off after 40 minutes, or you can do so manually.

So how's the coffee? It's good. It's generally light-bodied, brewing in six minutes even on full 40-ounce batches. It's tested, but not certified, to maintain precise brewing temperatures throughout the entire brewing process. The results are better than most basic drip coffee makers, but don't quite keep pace with the best-of-the-best coffee makers: the Moccamasters, the Fellows, the Ratios. There's a coffee warmer, which I don't prefer, but many do.

Some parts aren't machined as precisely as I'd hope, leading to a little jiggle or awkward fits. And customer service is also a lesser-known quantity with Simply Good. Calls to the customer service center during business hours reached only AI operators. But I did receive a call back a couple days later from someone I believe to be human. And the replacement warranty is an excellent five years.

In the end, if you're buying this, you're buying it because, for now, it is the drip coffee maker that is the most dedicated to ensuring that your coffee maker isn't adding microplastics to your cup. If you filter your water for microplastics, the Simply Good Coffee will likely not add any microplastics after the fact. That's a lot of peace of mind.

Plastic Content

The Simply Good Coffee machine is, quite simply, the most plastic-free drip coffee machine I've tested.

The frame is made of “food grade” 304 stainless steel. The reservoir, carafe, and boiler tube are borosilicate glass. Some of its connections and fittings are made with silicone—specifically medical-grade, sand-based silicone. A couple handles, and the reservoir lid, are also made with silicone.

For what it's worth, silicone is sometimes called a plastic by the plastics industry, and it's certainly a polymer. But its properties are different, and modest heat is not thought to cause leaching of nanoparticles unless the silicone has also been subjected to significant mechanical wear.

In any case, no hot or cold water contact with plastics, and quite minimal contact with silicone. The result is that the Simply Good is the least plasticky drip coffee machine I am aware of. I still docked a point for the existence of silicone.

Plastic Content: 9/10

Coffee Flavor

The Simply Good Coffee brewer, like the Moccamaster it resembles, has been tested for compliance with “Golden Cup” parameters laid out by the Specialty Coffee Association, designed to describe best coffee brewing practices.

These include, but aren't limited to, the ability to keep coffee within tight time and temperature parameters while brewing—specifically, between 92 and 96 degrees Celsius. Each batch also remains within optimum times, brewing even a full batch in about six minutes. Simply Good received independent lab testing showing its capability to stay within tight brewing parameters. But it did not go through the far more rigorous and expensive SCA certification process.

This effort places Simply Good squarely in the “premium” category, and the coffee is going to taste better than most standard drip machines whose temperature can range wildly over the course of the brewing process. However, while the coffee tastes good, it doesn't taste as good as the Ratio—nor any of my other top drip coffee maker picks.

I noted some trouble with wetting coffee grounds evenly, especially on full 40-ounce batches, which can lead to under-extraction in some places and over-extraction in others. Which is to say: less precision of flavor, and a certain flatness. I didn't detect off notes, but I've also never had a cup with the Simply Good that I've been extremely excited about. And I've brewed dozens of batches.

Note that the warming plate gets quite warm, and it stays on during the brewing process, which means the coffee gets overheated during the early phases of brewing, leading to a small bit of diner-coffee oxidation in every batch—even if you take the carafe off after the batch completes.

Most coffee drinkers won't notice these quibbles much. But aficionados will. And among high-end coffee makers topping $400, Simply Good quite simply does not taste as good.

Flavor: 7/10

Ease of Use and Cleaning

Like the Moccamaster it resembles, the Simply Good machine has almost no buttons. Its operation is mostly as simple as turning it off and on, and choosing whether you'd like a “bloom” function that mimics pour-over.

But also like the Moccamaster, there are a lot of little parts: a reservoir lid, a shower attachment, a detachable brew chamber, a top for the chamber, a carafe with a detachable lid. Not all of these fit perfectly, or comfortably. The showerhead attachment has a little wobble to it.

The lid to the carafe can grind a bit, metal on glass, if you put it on even slightly crookedly—an uncomfortable form of friction that makes me worry about longevity. More parts also means more parts to clean. And while they can be put in the dishwasher, I doubt you'll do so daily.

The drip stop is both helpful and a potential hazard, depending on who you are. If you don't use the drip stop, there'll be a bit of dripping after the main brew. But if you do, there's a risk you won't notice it's still activated when you go to brew a batch. This'll cause an overflow if you let it. Entirely user error. And yet I've done it more than once.

Still, simple is simple. And it's dead simple to use, and hard to screw up. And stainless steel and borosilicate glass both clean quite easily.

Ease: 7/10

Ratio

Ratio

The Ratio Eight Series 2 ($799) is a beautiful machine. Its brew basket and carafe are as hourglass-shaped as a 1960s movie bombshell. The machine is sleek-lined, walnut-trimmed. The stainless steel brew basket and even the lid to the reservoir arrive with pleasing heft.

The coffee that arrives from it is also lovely. Ever since Portland-based Ratio released the original Ratio Eight in 2013, the company has been on the forefront of artful, aromatic drip coffee—drip coffee that can compete with pour-over as a vehicle for beautiful flavor. Ratio previously certified all of its machines according to Specialty Coffee Association standards, and all are capable of maintaining excellent temperature precision.

But in some ways, Ratio has moved beyond the SCA, after testing extractions on batch after batch. Ratio brews a little longer and extracts a bit more fully—as long as nine minutes for a full 40-ounce batch, with a leisurely bloom cycle. The showerhead leads to admirably even wetting of coffee grounds and even extraction. The results are full body, round flavor, and a surprising wallop even from quite delicate beans.

Controls are as simple as whispering your hand across the device’s single button. Press longer, and the machine will optimize itself for half batch, its button glowing faintly and satisfyingly.

This excellent coffee flavor is also evident in the Ratio's other devices, whether the 40-ounce Ratio Six or the small-batch Ratio Four (8/10, WIRED Recommends). Each of these is available for a much lower price than the Eight.

Aesthetics aside, the Eight's true reason for being is that it minimizes plastic contact. Neither hot water, nor hot coffee, ever comes into contact with plastic. The internal tubing is borosilicate glass. The pipe connectors are sand-based silicone. The reservoir chute and brewing basket are stainless steel.

This does not mean it's plastic-free. Its cold-water reservoir is a BPA-free Tritan copolymer. Much of the machine's frame is also made of polymer, a decision made for durability over and above painted stainless steel.

Some will not forgive that the reservoir is plastic, even as they might acknowledge it's nice not to have to worry about fragility. Contact time is minimal—and where coffee is concerned, leaching occurs almost entirely when hot water is in contact.

I privilege the beauty of the coffee and of the device. But for some, the plastic chassis and reservoir amount to too much polymer compromise. And while the device's operation is simple, note that the brew basket does steam up the top of the device, meaning you might want to wipe it with a dry cloth. Because there's no drip stop, the brew basket also comes with a little drip tray to place it on.

But as with all beauty, I accept the idiosyncrasies that come with it. In these weary times of plastic in my liver and gonads, this has become the drip coffee maker I use most often.

Plastic Content

The Ratio Eight does not bring hot liquid in contact with plastic, which is why I've included it as a plastic-free brewer. But plastic exists, notably in the BPA-free Tritan polymer of its cold-water reservoir.

A study published last year showed pretty clearly that hot-water contact with plastics is the main source of microplastic leaching in coffee. But long-term contact with cold water and light can still lead to some leaching, as evidenced by the microplastics content in bottled water. I'm not concerned about the 10 minutes or so at a time that cold water is in the reservoir, but some might be.

Much of the frame of the Ratio Eight Series 2 is also plastic, a decision made in part for durability: Steam and moisture are actually pretty hard on painted stainless steel. There’s a bit of BPA-free plastic used in the heating element that doesn’t come into contact with water. But though it's not relevant to coffee brewing, the Eight's plastic exterior doesn't fully pass the vibes check on a plastic-avoidant brewer.

Otherwise, the internal tubing is borosilicate glass, the brewing basket is hefty stainless steel, and the carafes are either stainless steel or borosilicate glass. While pipe fittings are silicone, The Eight arguably has less silicone contact than Simply Good's plastic-free brewer on the hot side of brewing, and less chance for mechanical wear at those sites.

Plastic-Free Content: 8/10

Coffee Flavor

Flavor is where Ratio excels across all of its brewers. Despite single-button operation, and limited customization compared to a sophisticated drip brewer like the Fellow Aiden, Ratio pulls downright shocking amounts of flavor from light and medium-roast coffee beans.

The key, in consultation with Ratio's designers and owners, is an obsessive-compulsive yen for extraction testing, and constant iteration and experimentation. The temperature curves are carefully modulated, and a bit individual: Brew times are longer by a couple minutes with the Ratio than with other devices. The bloom cycle is quite leisurely.

The result is fullness. It is coffee that speaks its flavors loudly, and clearly, with a roundness I don't find often from other drip brewers. I do find that I might grind my coffee slightly more coarsely with Ratio than with some other comparable brewers, to avoid over-extraction.

But among showerhead brewers, the evenness of extraction in the Ratio Eight 2 is exemplary, leading to some of the best and most balanced cups I've had this year.

Flavor: 10/10

Ease of Use and Cleaning

The Ratio Eight's operation is, quite simply, as simple as any drip coffee machine I've ever used. Press its only button quickly, and you'll be optimized for a full batch. Hold down the button for three seconds and you'll be optimized for a half-batch.

That's it. That's the instructions. The machine handles the rest. One button leads to beauty.

Still, there are a couple extra fiddly parts. Unlike a lot of machines, the brew basket is removable and must be stacked atop the carafe. Because there's no drip stop, you'll have to rest this in a cradle that comes with the machine, lest it dribble coffee onto your counter.

You also have to manage steam and condensation a bit. Namely, steam comes out while brewing, and causes condensation on the top of the frame. After brewing, you'll also want to pull the lid off the water reservoir for 10 minutes or so to avoid condensation lingering in the tank.

These are very small complaints on a machine whose operation is otherwise so simple.

But note that Ratio's parts are not meant for dishwashers. Reservoir cleaning involves running a cycle with a descaler like Halefresh Cleaning the accessories, such as the carafe and the brew basket, happens by hand with soap and water, and ideally also nwith specialized Urnex coffee cleaner that helps remove coffee oils.

Ease: 7/10

It is expensive and difficult—given the needs for tight valves and internal tubing—to make drip coffee machines and home espresso machines that are entirely plastic-free. But there are a few of WIRED's favorite, more affordable, and lower-tech options for those wishing to avoid plastic, if you're willing to put in a little effort.

Kalita

Amazon

Kalita

WIRED consumer tech editor Michael Calore swears by the majesty of the flat-bottomed Kalita Wave 185 stainless steel coffee dripper for his morning pour-over. Just as I prefer a flat-bottomed brewing chamber for drip coffee courtesy of the Ratio Eight, the flat-bottomed Kalita Wave likewise leads to better-controlled and more even saturation of your coffee grounds. While a lot of pour-over drippers are plasticky, this one is not. And it still only costs $34. Just note that if you're getting into pour-over, you'll need a good gooseneck kettle like the rightfully ubiquitous Fellow Stagg EKG ($200).

Secura

Amazon

A lot of modern French presses use plastic plungers or nylon mesh netting that's likely to sustain wear and leach out microplastics over time. Even worse, many modern French presses are entirely made out of plastic. Pish. Just get a stainless steel one. Maybe you won't get to stare longingly at your coffee while you wait, but it'll do the job. There are fancier stainless steel presses from Yeti ($110) and design-conscious brands like Aarke ($130). But this one from Secura is $40 and works great.

AeroPress

Williams Sonoma

The AeroPress is an ingenious device, using pressure applied by hand to extract a smooth, rich, flavorful, aromatic cup of coffee through a paper filter at its bottom. The process, and the flavor, is somewhere between French press, filter drip, and espresso. But the AeroPress was a famously plasticky device for most of its lifespan. Lately, AeroPress is changing this. First, there was the Premium AeroPress (7/10, WIRED Recommends), which subbed in a fragile but beautiful glass tube for the usual plastic.

This year, AeroPress added a stainless steel coffee maker to the fold. It's not see-through, which means you'll need to measure your water and coffee by volume or weight rather than eyeball it. But that's what I do anyway. I appreciate that the brewing setup is 100 percent stainless steel. The plunger does contain a silicone liner, which will only have brief coffee contact for about 15 seconds.

This is not an easy question to answer, because scientific research is still in the early stages. The study of microplastics in the human body is new, and long-term studies still aren't in.

First things first: Coffee is likely not the biggest source of microplastics in your life. According to a study last year, hot coffee contains orders of magnitude fewer microplastics than water that's been bottled in cheap plastic. It also contains fewer than tea, because of nylon teabags. Depending where you live, you may have more to fear from your tapwater—and should first look into a good stainless steel water filter.

The general consensus, however, is that we should not welcome any additional tiny plastic particles in our digestive tracts and bloodstream, unless we need to.

Plastic is not very chemically reactive. But microplastics can transport other bad things into the body, such as bacteria. They can also just kinda … irritate your body. When they enter your bloodstream, they can reach vital organs and set off inflammatory responses and oxidative reactions.

Depending on the organ, this can do all sorts of stuff: imbalance hormones, mess with reproductive function, or even cause nervous system damage. Cancer, of course, is also a risk that's heightened by inflammation. Some reports show microplastics might weaken the immune system. Others that they may weaken the bones.

And so while coffee is not the worst risk where microplastics are concerned, caution is also not the worst approach.

B&H Photo is one of our favorite places to shop for camera gear. If you’re ever in New York, head to the store to check out the giant overhead conveyor belt system that brings your purchase from the upper floors to the registers downstairs (yes, seriously, here’s a video). Fortunately B&H Photo’s website is here for the rest of us with some good deals on photo gear we love.

B&H Photo has plenty of great deals, including Nikon's brand-new Z6III full-frame mirrorless camera for $2,196.95 ($300 off). The Z6III (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is a huge update for the Z6 line, and a great all-around camera for Nikon fans. There are also great deals like the Nikon Zf (8/10, WIRED Recommends) full frame mirrorless camera for $200 off, or the Nikon Z8 for $600 off.

Not in the market for the latest Nikon cameras? There are plenty of other deals, like our favorite action camera, the GoPro Hero 13 for $70 off (7/10, WIRED Recommends), and Sony’s a7R V full frame mirrorless camera for $400 off.

Google Workspace Promo Codes for August 2026

Wired August 07, 2026

Google Workspace is the modern business world’s de facto productivity suite, and it’s only gotten better over the years. There’s the centralization of Google Docs, Drive, and Gmail, of course, but Google has bolstered its productivity suite with an AI infusion via Gemini, as well as simplified its offerings to work for massive corporations all the way down to individual users. If you want to get the best price, you need a Google Workspace promo code.

Thankfully, you’ve landed in the right spot. Google is offering Workspace discounts until the end of 2026, allowing you to save up to 14 percent on a plan for your first three months. You just need to use one of the coupon codes linked above. Google Workspace works for both individual users and businesses, but if you’re just looking for more Drive space and a few extra features, take a look at Google One.

There are some notable differences between each Workspace plan – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three plans come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.

Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.

Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.

Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.

Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of if you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.

Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.

At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access – basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.

Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.

Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i. e. update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.

You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.

Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.

Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and it can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized to Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.

Google Workspace Flows is a new tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow up message. No apps or links are needed.

Then in 2014, Uber leveled up with Uber Eats. Much like Uber was the convenient, modern answer to taxis, Uber Eats was the equivalent to the world of food delivery.

If you’re someone who uses the rideshare app often or orders take out multiple nights a week, an Uber One membership will pay for itself within a few weeks. One of my go-to gifts recently is an Uber Eats gift card. I find it’s especially thoughtful and useful as a gift of convenience, whether that’s after a death, loss, birth, or big life change. One of China’s Most Powerful AI Models Has Also Escaped Containment

Wired August 07, 2026

The AI industry is having a rogue agent summer. The latest model to escape onto the open internet during security testing is Kimi K3, a powerful open-weight offering from the Chinese company Moonshot AI.

Frontier Security, a US startup, says that Kimi K3 went outside of its sandbox while testing its defensive cybersecurity skills. As with incidents previously reported by OpenAI and Anthropic, the escape was partly enabled by a misconfiguration in the sandbox designed to contain it. Frontier claims, though, that the incident shows Kimi has fewer cyber safeguards than most other powerful AI models, something that allowed it to go off and use the internet without express permission.

“We found a leak in the sandbox,” says Yaron Singer, CEO of Frontier Security. “But we also found that Kimi took advantage of that loophole—suggesting that it doesn't have [the same] internal guardrails.”

Unlike other recent incidents of AI agents going off-script, Kimi K3 did not hack anything after accessing the internet—because the answers to the problems it was seeking were easily attainable on GitHub.

Moonshot did not respond to a request for comment by time of publication.

The incident is the latest in a string of agent mishaps that suggest increasingly cyber-capable AI models are becoming more challenging to control.

Last month, OpenAI disclosed that an unreleased model had broken out onto the internet and then hacked Hugging Face, a company that hosts AI models and data, in order to find answers to problems it was tasked with solving. OpenAI subsequently shared that its AI agents had in fact hacked into four additional services as part of the spree.

Shortly after OpenAI reported its incident, Anthropic revealed that several of its models had also gained access to the internet and attacked outside systems. Last week, the UK government’s AI Security Institute (AISI) also disclosed that in its own testing, versions of OpenAI and Anthropic models that had security safeguards disabled perpetrated multiple hacks across the internet, including a particularly ambitious attempt by Anthropic’s Mythos 5 to plant malicious code in an open-source project on GitHub.

While these AI hacking episodes all vary in both cause and degree, the Kimi K3 is similar to several of them in that a misconfigured sandbox allowed access to a number of websites rather than keeping it contained to a simulated environment. The model was expressly tasked with solving problems that should not have involved going off to find the answers online, and appears to have gone outside of those instructions. The model had to figure out for itself that it had access to certain websites by probing the network settings of the sandbox.

While human error appears to have played a major role in each of the breakouts, the consequences have been compounded by the fact that advanced AI models are designed to use reason and take complex actions in order to solve problems.

Another key difference between previous incidents and the one discovered by Frontier Security is that it involves a model that is already widely available, with the same safeguards an average user would encounter.

“Kimi K3 is very good at following a goal by any means necessary and also doesn't have the guardrails to prevent it from cheating or escaping the sandbox,” says Paul Kassianik, a researcher at Frontier Security.

Kassianik and Singer both say that Kimi and other open-weight models are also excellent tools for cybersecurity defense. (Hugging Face ultimately used an unnamed AI model from China to defend itself against the OpenAI agent hack.) Their company has developed benchmarks that measure a model’s capacity to find vulnerabilities in software and networks, which show that Kimi excels at these tasks.

Frontier Security says the sandbox it used was the default included in AISI's Inspect framework for testing AI systems.

“These claims are inaccurate and irresponsible. Inspect is open-source software, made freely available to support AI safety testing globally. Users are responsible for configuring the tool to suit their needs, and we have published detailed guidance on how to do so," an AISI spokesperson told WIRED. "The company has offered no evidence or wider detail offered to support the claims made. The issues they highlight result from how they chose to configure the tool."

In response, Frontier told WIRED that it provided details of the incident privately to AISI, and that it used the tool's default configuration, and did not modify it. AISI did not respond to WIRED's follow-up questions.

Some cybersecurity experts say the issue discovered by Frontier Security reinforces how important it is to configure the environments that frontier AI models are placed in carefully.

“It's not surprising at all,” says Matt Fredrikson, CEO of Gray Swan, another cybersecurity startup, and associate professor at Carnegie Mellon University. “As a general phenomenon, if you give one of these models an objective, and if you're not very explicit, like walls you're putting around it, it'll find a way to get the answer.”

Fredrikson says this means that people using AI models as agents, including in tools like OpenClaw, which use AI to automate a wide range of useful chores, could find their systems misbehaving if they aren’t careful. “It is a cautionary tale,” he says.

Update 08/07/26 6:20pm ET: This story has been updated to include comments from AISI and Frontier Security.
